7zNyEJETvE.authors: Sinjae Kang, Dong Kyu Shin, Jaehong Kim, Kamin Lee, Hyoeun Kim, Kaixin Wang, Li Zhao, Seonghyeon Ye, Kimin Lee
7zNyEJETvE.abstract: Robot policy evaluation often relies on a binary success signal for task completion. In real-world deployment, however, desired execution behaviors are also defined by quality attributes such as execution speed and motion smoothness, which need to be dynamically controlled according to task requirements. To address this, we introduce Quality-Controllable Policy (QCP), a robot policy that enables inference-time control over both individual quality attributes and their combinations. To extend the controllable quality range beyond initial demonstrations, we introduce an iterative hindsight relabeling loop: QCP collects online rollouts under target quality labels, adds successful trajectories to the dataset, relabels the accumulated trajectories in hindsight according to their measured quality, and fine-tunes the policy. Experiments on robomimic and RoboEval demonstrate that QCP consistently improves both task execution quality and success rates across iterations, producing successful rollouts that exceed the quality of the initial demonstrations. Finally, we validate QCP on real-world manipulation tasks, showing that controlling speed increases throughput in conveyor operations and controlling transport stability improves success when carrying wine glasses, showing that quality-controllable policies yield practical gains in physical deployment.
workshops: Continually Self-Improving Robots Workshop (CSIR-2026)

QOk1IWyCYw.title: MimicAgent: Quadruped Skills via Prompt-to-Trajectory Generation
QOk1IWyCYw.authors: Lucky Kant Nayak, Narayanan Palghat Parameswaran, Neehar Peri, Deva Ramanan
QOk1IWyCYw.abstract: We present MimicAgent, a prompt-to-trajectory generation framework for learning dynamic quadruped skills. Although reward shaping is extensively used when training quadruped policies, navigating the resulting reward landscape is notoriously difficult, requiring hours of ``graduate student descent''. Eureka attempts to automate reward design with LLMs, but we find that it struggles to generalize across diverse skills and morphologies. Our key observation is that it is far easier for a human -- and by association, an LLM -- to generate reference motions than to shape reward functions. Our hypothesis is motivated by the success of example-guided RL for humanoids, which exploits large-scale motion capture datasets as references for training locomotion policies. Unlike humanoids, quadrupeds lack such reference motion data. Towards this end, we propose MimicAgent, an agentic harness that, given a skill prompt, generates quadruped reference trajectories with coding agents. These coarse reference trajectories are then used to train example-guided RL policies that are deployable in simulation and in the real-world. Notably, we find that when prompting Claude Fable 5.1 within our agentic harness, 87\% of prompts yield semantically aligned reference trajectories.
workshops: Continually Self-Improving Robots Workshop (CSIR-2026)

w0tP2CmTiI.title: Multisensory Continual Learning: Adapting Pretrained Visuomotor Policies to Force
w0tP2CmTiI.authors: Jaden Clark, Changhao Wang, Yihuai Gao, Seongheon Hong, Hojung Choi, Mark Cutkosky, Yifan Hou, Shuran Song
w0tP2CmTiI.abstract: Robot manipulation often depends on sensory data beyond vision, especially in contact-rich tasks where force, tactile, or audio feedback reveals interaction states not directly visible from images. Yet such modalities are hardware- and task-specific, and large multisensory datasets remain scarce, making it impractical to pretrain policies with every sensor they may encounter. We study multi-sensory continual learning: adapting a pretrained robot policy to new tasks with newly introduced modalities while preserving performance under the original sensor suite. We propose MultiSensory World Model (MuSe), which integrates limited multisensory data into pretrained vision-only policies using  multi-stage fusion, multisensory future prediction, and experience replay on pretraining data. We instantiate MuSe by adding force-torque sensing to a pretrained vision-only policy and evaluate it on real-world manipulation tasks. Experiments show that MuSe not only performs well on contact-rich finetuning tasks but also has performance gains on pretraining tasks - suggesting that a modest multisensory dataset can enhance general model capability beyond the finetuning distribution. https://multisensorylearning.github.io/multisensory-world-model/
workshops: Continually Self-Improving Robots Workshop (CSIR-2026)

AFcBurihjY.title: Never Stop Learning: From Simulation to Hardware with Maximum a Posteriori Policy Optimization
AFcBurihjY.authors: Serena Liu, Mathieu Decker, Patrick Spieler, Harley Wiltzer, Andrej Orsula, Pedro Roque, Abbas Abdolmaleki, Amir Rahmani, Joel W. Burdick, Jean-Pierre de la Croix, Elena Sorina Lupu
AFcBurihjY.abstract:
A common practice in robot learning is to learn policies in simulation and deploy them on hardware without further learning.
However, the world in which robots operate is dynamic and too complex to anticipate every possible change in a simulator.
We empirically demonstrate how an off-policy actor-critic method such as Maximum a Posteriori Policy Optimization (MPO) enables a robot to learn in simulation and then not stop learning, but continue on hardware, allowing the policy to adapt to changes encountered in the real world. 
We evaluate vanilla MPO, MPO with categorical (C51) critic, and propose Q-DMPO, which uses a quantile-regression critic and removes the need to specify return bounds.
On Open Ant hardware and in simulation-to-simulation transfer on Open Ant, Swimmer-v5, HighTorque Mini Pi, and an electric crane, the MPO variants continues to learn despite altered environment dynamics, whereas Soft Actor-Critic degrades or collapses as the dynamics shift grows. We trace this ability to a specific component: the Gaussian prior in MPO's policy update, whose Fisher-weighted regularization matches the penalty of Elastic Weight Consolidation. These results suggest that the choice of algorithm, critic, and regularization can replace transfer-time heuristics in permitting real-world learning without performance collapse.
workshops: Continually Self-Improving Robots Workshop (CSIR-2026)

t66Jsm3yFC.title: One Phase Is Enough: Sim-to-Real Transfer with Direct Visual Reinforcement Learning
t66Jsm3yFC.authors: John Marangola, Antonia Bronars, Younghyo Park, Stephen Andrews, Kushal Kedia, Pulkit Agrawal
t66Jsm3yFC.abstract:
Sim-to-real reinforcement learning (RL) has enabled impressive robotic behaviors, yet deploying policies directly from vision remains challenging. A common approach first trains a teacher policy with RL using privileged state observations, then distills its behavior into a vision-based student via imitation. However, the resulting student can substantially underperform its teacher. Directly training visual policies with RL offers a promising alternative, but learning task-relevant visual representations from scratch can be sample-inefficient, making one-phase visual RL intractable.

We propose DRIFT, a simple recipe for efficient one-phase visual RL using image observations available at test time. Our key insight is to use frozen, pretrained foundation vision encoders, allowing RL to focus on learning control from existing visual representations. Freezing the encoder avoids costly back-propagation through the vision backbone, while its pretrained representations enable real-world transfer from fast, rasterized simulation renders. Under matched architectures, observations, and compute budgets, DRIFT outperforms two-phase distillation and achieves a 58.8% relative improvement in average real-world success rate across three manipulation tasks. Controlled simulation evaluations demonstrate that DRIFT's relative advantage grows from roughly 9% in-distribution to over 61% under out-of-distribution shifts, suggesting that stronger generalization contributes to superior real-world transfer.
workshops: Continually Self-Improving Robots Workshop (CSIR-2026)

JHdJL42sle.title: One World, Many Hypotheses: Self-Play with Plural Curiosity
JHdJL42sle.authors: Caiyi Zhang, Yuejiang Liu, Yilun Du
JHdJL42sle.abstract:
Self-play enables robots to improve through their own experience, but its efficiency depends on identifying informative trajectories. 
A common approach uses disagreement among models as an intrinsic curiosity signal. Yet models with similar inductive biases may fail in similar ways, suppressing curiosity precisely where it is most needed.
To address this, we introduce Plural Curiosity, a mechanism that guides self-play through disagreement by design. The key idea is to construct hypotheses with deliberately different inductive biases, enabling them to offer competing explanations when evidence is scarce. These hypotheses can become more consistent as experience accumulates.
We instantiate Plural Curiosity in two ways: (i) perceptual diversity, using image-based and point-cloud-based encoders, and (ii) decision diversity, varying temporal dependencies through bidirectional and causal attention in action decoders.
We evaluate the proposed method in world action models, using self-play to improve the inverse dynamics models that translate predicted visual futures into actions. Experiments on ManiSkill show that Plural Curiosity achieves about 45% higher correlation with ground-truth error than previous methods and improves sample efficiency, with about 10% higher self-play success rates than random selection under the same data budget.
workshops: Continually Self-Improving Robots Workshop (CSIR-2026)

19LRDddFhj.title: Playful Agentic Robot Learning
19LRDddFhj.authors: Junyi Zhang, Jiaxin Ge, Hanjun Yoo, Letian Fu, Zihan Yang, Yaowei Liu, Raj Saravanan, Shaofeng Yin, Justin Yu, Dantong Niu, Zirui Wang, Roei Herzig, Ken Goldberg, Yutong Bai, David M. Chan, Ion Stoica, Angjoo Kanazawa, Jiahui Lei, Haiwen Feng, Trevor Darrell
19LRDddFhj.abstract:
Current agentic robot systems can write executable Code-as-Policy
programs, observe feedback, and revise behavior across multiple attempts, but
they remain largely task-driven: reusable skills are acquired only after explicit instructions. We study Playful Agentic Robot Learning, where an embodied coding
agent uses self-directed play as a continual skill-learning stage before downstream
tasks arrive. We introduce RATS, Robotics Agent Teams designed for play-time
skill acquisition. During play, RATS proposes novel yet learnable exploratory
tasks, plans and executes robot-code policies, verifies intermediate progress, diagnoses failures, retries with dense, step-level feedback, and distills successful
executions into a persistent code skill library. At test time, the agent reuses
relevant skills from this frozen library to help solve new tasks. Experiments in
LIBERO-PRO and MolmoSpaces show that play-learned skills improve held-out
downstream tasks over no play and random-play baselines, with a 20.6 and 17.0
percentage-point gains over CaP-Agent0 on LIBERO-PRO and MolmoSpaces, respectively. Moreover, the learned skills can be plugged into other inference-time
Code-as-Policy agents by simply retrieving them into the context, improving RoboSuite and real-world transfer by 8.9 and 8.8 points, respectively, without finetuning the underlying model.
workshops: Continually Self-Improving Robots Workshop (CSIR-2026)

lHfkUGnhMt.title: RECALL: Recovery Experience Collection for Active Lifelong Learning in Vision-Language-Action Models
lHfkUGnhMt.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are typically trained offline on large demonstration datasets and updated post-deployment through additional fine-tuning. Deployed VLAs should instead identify where supervision is useful and adapt without forgetting. We present RECALL, a controlled empirical study of active lifelong adaptation in pretrained VLAs, investigating two coupled questions: where to collect new supervision and how to incorporate it into a pretrained policy. We evaluate a VLA's ability to retain prior behaviors while adapting to new data, comparing start-state demonstrations against policy-induced recovery states, uncertainty-guided versus non-uncertainty-based state selection, sparse versus dense recovery collection, and continual adaptation strategies including reduced learning rates, elastic weight consolidation, and replay. Key findings include: recovery-state supervision is often more useful than repeated start-state demonstrations, though this advantage does not require uncertainty-based selection; more recovery data is not always better; targeted recovery data alone can cause severe forgetting; and preserving prior behavior requires maintaining appropriate behavioral coverage. We further demonstrate uncertainty-triggered recovery collection as a pre-execution intervention on a physical robot. Together, these findings establish an empirical foundation for active lifelong learning in VLAs and offer practical guidance for building robot policies that improve continuously from deployment experience.
workshops: Continually Self-Improving Robots Workshop (CSIR-2026)

TxrH4y1Zh0.title: Robo-Cortex: Continual Strategy Induction for Self-Evolving Embodied Navigation
TxrH4y1Zh0.authors: Nga Teng Chan, Yi Zhang, Yechi Liu, Renwen Cui, Fanhu Zeng, Zeyuan Ding, Xiancong Ren, Zhang Zhang, Jian Liu, Qifeng Chen, Yong Dai, Xiaozhu Ju
TxrH4y1Zh0.abstract: Embodied agents increasingly retain their past through memory and reflection, yet retaining experience is not the same as learning from it. Most systems retrieve prior trajectories to inform the current decision while the reusable principles that map evidence to action stay fixed. We call this limitation strategic stasis: the agent accumulates experience, but its decision strategy never changes. We introduce Robo-Cortex, a self-evolving framework for embodied agents that maintains a persistent, versioned navigation strategy and revises it based on the outcomes of its own interactions. After each evolution round, Robo-Cortex diagnoses successful and failed episodes, induces candidate heuristics, and, rather than writing them straight into its knowledge base, selectively consolidates them into strategic guides. A confidence- and support-aware gate selects which guides enter the persistent strategy. The resulting strategy is subsequently redeployed through a closed-loop Imagine-then-Verify planner, while a multi-scale experience memory supplies the evidence required for diagnosis and evolution. On image-goal navigation, active recognition, and active embodied question answering, strategies Robo-Cortex induces for itself transfer to unseen environments and outperform strategies written by human experts by +9.72% SR, improving SPL by +15.30% over an unguided pipeline; under continued evolution the agent reaches 55.56% SR on IGNav against 38.57% for the strongest prior method. Real-world robot deployments show the navigation strategies support failure recovery in physical environments.
workshops: Continually Self-Improving Robots Workshop (CSIR-2026)

RM7kcceIJA.title: RoboLongR: Causally-Consistent Rewards Teach Robots to Progressively Master Long-Horizon Manipulation
RM7kcceIJA.authors: Zixuan Chen, Lin Cao, Fenggang Zhang, Haotong Zhang, Yangtao Chen, Jieqi Shi, Jing Huo, Yang Gao
RM7kcceIJA.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation requires actions whose validity depends on earlier interactions, yet visual progress can conceal missing task prerequisites. We propose RoboLongR, an offline-to-online framework that learns history-dependent rewards to guide policy adaptation to new tasks. Its central objective is causal consistency: aligning rewarded progress with prerequisites supported by execution history. Stage-shuffle supervision encourages execution-order sensitivity, recurrent memory preserves evidence of earlier interactions, and two-round training refines trajectory segments using predicted progress. The resulting rewards guide stage-conditioned policy refinement from behavior cloning to online reinforcement learning. Sparse terminal feedback connects policy experience to reward learning by triggering correction for repeated high-scoring failures. Pretrained on demonstrations from 88 RLBench tasks and Open-X data, RoboLongR achieves 31.8% average success on 18 long-horizon tasks excluded from reward pretraining, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 9.2 percentage points. Across four real-robot tasks, it achieves 57.5% success, a 32.5-percentage-point improvement over the comparison method. Reward-level controls probe sensitivity to synthetic order perturbations, while ablations examine the contributions of individual components to policy improvement. Project website: https://chenzixuan99.github.io/RoboLongR-public/.
workshops: Continually Self-Improving Robots Workshop (CSIR-2026)

aPS3938Wc2.title: Self-Correcting Imaginative Planning for VLM Embodied Agents
aPS3938Wc2.authors: Kai-Po Chang, Chang-Hsun Wu, Yen-Siang Wu, Yu-Han Huang, Kai-Chen Yang, Yu-Chiang Frank Wang
aPS3938Wc2.abstract: Recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated their remarkable capability to serve as embodied agents in interactive environments. However, these agents often make plans (i.e., action sequences) that appear linguistically plausible but fail upon execution, without considering the visual consequences of each action. While prior works have explored enhancing VLM agents through language supervision or self-correction with text-based verification, enabling them to self-correct invalid plans against visual consequences before execution remains an open challenge. To tackle this, we propose Self-Correcting Imaginative Planning (SCIP), a training framework that enables VLM agents to self-correct their plans against imagined visual consequences before execution. SCIP integrates an imagination-guided policy learning scheme that grounds the VLM agent's planning in visual consequences, and a verification-driven imagination learning scheme that calibrates the imagination process to faithfully reflect the actual environment dynamics. Extensive experiments show that SCIP outperforms existing embodied VLM agents across multiple embodied planning tasks.
workshops: Continually Self-Improving Robots Workshop (CSIR-2026)

SSzIQ2yg7E.title: Steering Multirobot Behavior via Closed-Loop Affine Activation Editing
SSzIQ2yg7E.authors: Satyajeet Das, Darren Chiu, Shashank Hegde, Gaurav S. Sukhatme
SSzIQ2yg7E.abstract: Real-world robots need to adapt their behavior beyond the envelope of their pre-trained policy. Policy finetuning or retraining are options, but they risk catastrophic forgetting, degrading the pretrained policy's base performance. To combat this, we introduce CLAE: Closed-Loop Affine Activation Editing, an inference-time framework for steering the behavior of a frozen policy by editing intermediate activations while keeping the base policy weights and downstream action head untouched. CLAE approaches behavior steering as a closed-loop problem whose outputs edit policy activations that adapt online to the robot state, environment, target behavior, and multi-robot context. It trains a sparse autoencoder over frozen-policy activations, selects behavior-relevant latent features via post-hoc probing, and learns a lightweight RL-based steering policy that applies state-dependent affine edits to selected latents during inference. We validate CLAE on a frozen multi-quadrotor navigation policy trained to perform a single task: navigating robots to a set of goal locations while avoiding obstacles. Through extensive simulations and physical tests, we show that while navigating to their goal positions, CLAE can 1. steer individual robot behavior by controlling each robot's velocity profile; 2. coordinate multirobot behavior by preserving a desired formation, and 3. produce entirely new behavior wherein robots are required to reduce their exposure to surveillance cameras in the environment.
workshops: Continually Self-Improving Robots Workshop (CSIR-2026)

V8hQBmyydD.title: TacHarness: Agentic Infrastructure for Continually Improving Visuotactile Robot Policies
V8hQBmyydD.authors: Jingxiang Guo, Gujie Shao, Yuxin Hu, Bingsheng Xie, Jiaxin Shi, Chen Gao, Yuhang Zheng, Haoyu Zhao, Weihao Yuan, Fei Wang, Shuicheng YAN
V8hQBmyydD.abstract: Visuotactile robot learning involves environment construction, multimodal data production, policy training, and evaluation. TacHarness integrates agents into these stages to coordinate tool execution and manage dependencies between datasets and trained models. Agents interpret requirements, select tools and configurations, inspect execution evidence, and coordinate bounded retries or repairs. Collection integrates agentic environment generation with DataEngine. Environment-generation agents interpret text or visual requirements, select assets and layouts, invoke compilation and simulation, and diagnose and repair failures. After robot-task binding, DataEngine agents select trajectories, configure embodiment retargeting, and synthesize synchronized visual, tactile, state, and action observations through simulation. Quality checks connect accepted episodes to versioned datasets. For training, agents select policy backends, initialization, and optimization budgets, bind accepted datasets to compatible configurations, and invoke training executors. They inspect progress and failure evidence and coordinate recovery through backend checkpoint mechanisms. Training checks cover optimization steps, finite losses, and checkpoint availability; the resulting checkpoints record data sources and sensor–action conventions for downstream serving and evaluation. Evaluation decouples policy inference from benchmark execution and returns task outcomes, timing, and failure evidence for subsequent decisions. Shared formats link scenes, datasets, models, and evaluation reports, while deterministic tools enforce task-specific acceptance criteria. We present the system architecture and adapters alongside recorded agent execution and multimodal replay across six environments. Execution records connect data inspection and repair to policy training, checkpoint verification, and online benchmark evaluation, showing how agents coordinate tools and use results throughout the learning workflow.
keywords: Agentic Robotics; Visuotactile Robot Learning; Autonomous Data Collection; Continual Learning; Robot Learning Infrastructure
workshops: Continually Self-Improving Robots Workshop (CSIR-2026)

rcLTiMdxUa.title: Test-Time Gradient Guidance of Flow Policies in Reinforcement Learning
rcLTiMdxUa.authors: Zhiyuan Zhou, Andy Peng, Charles Xu, Qiyang Li, Jost Tobias Springenberg, Kevin Frans, Sergey Levine
rcLTiMdxUa.abstract: Expressive continuous control policies, such as diffusion and flow models, form the backbone of recent advances in scaling imitation learning for simulated and real robot control. While they are known to scale stably in the supervised imitation learning setting, incorporating them into reinforcement learning (RL) pipelines for policy improvement has proven more difficult. It often requires specialized training objectives or back-propagating through denoising processes, which cause well known issues with stability and affects scalability. In this paper we study the question of whether simple policy improvement schemes at test time alone, leaving stable supervised policy training intact, can be a competitive alternative which side-steps these issues. To this end, we propose QGF (Q-Guided Flow), a new RL algorithm that performs policy optimization entirely during test time. QGF works by pre-training both a reference flow policy (via a standard behavioral cloning objective) and a value function critic and, during test-time, using the value gradient to guide the reference policy to generate higher-value actions without any additional policy learning. Empirically, QGF outperforms prior test-time RL methods while being much cheaper to run, and is competitive with state-of-the-art training-time algorithms on single-task and goal-conditioned offline RL benchmarks with high-dimensional action spaces. Moreover, it exhibits favorable scaling with model size by avoiding the instability of actor-critic training, offering a practical and effective alternative RL algorithm with expressive policies.
workshops: Continually Self-Improving Robots Workshop (CSIR-2026)

gbpBmOKEBt.title: The Evaluation Tax on Self-Improving Robots: Exact Operating Characteristics of Evaluation-Gated Improvement Loops
gbpBmOKEBt.abstract: A self-improving robot proposes a policy update, evaluates it with a handful of real-world trials, keeps it or discards it, and repeats; every trial spent on evaluation is one not spent on learning. We give an exact account of this evaluation gate. Modelling each update as a shift in success rate drawn from a proposal distribution and each gate as a rule on n trials per policy, we compute by binomial enumeration the probability of accepting a regression, the expected progress per trial, and the exact distribution of the loop's success rate after a fixed trial budget, for 8 accept rules and 7 proposal distributions. When fewer than half of proposals help, the intuitive "keep it if not worse" gate makes the loop lose performance for every n below a closed-form threshold; with 20% good proposals and n=5, a loop starting at 50% success ends at 0.02 after 2000 trials. The progress-maximising n depends on proposal quality, from 3 to unbounded, and a paired sequential race is 1.68x more trial-efficient than the best fixed-n gate. Selecting the best of ten candidates on ten trials each inflates the measured gain 18x. The evaluation budget per iteration is a design variable of the loop, and we give the numbers needed to set it.
workshops: Continually Self-Improving Robots Workshop (CSIR-2026)

LbJs3jw9BW.title: The Experience Machine: A Conceptual Computation Model for Experience-Driven Intelligence
LbJs3jw9BW.abstract:
Humans learn from experience, while most current embodied agents do not. Modern robots are largely trained from offline demonstrations and exhibit only limited adaptation after deployment, often within specific domains. We argue that intelligence should continuously adapt to experience. We introduce the Experience Machine (EM), a conceptual model for this setting as a computational paradigm for experience-driven intelligence. EM draws inspiration from the computational abstraction of the Turing Machine and views experience as a paper-tape written with state, intent, action, and consequence critique in temporal order. The machine continuously reads the tape and performs processing and prediction, unifying policy inference, world modeling, and outcome evaluation, while updating its own internal belief. 
The key idea is that the context written on the tape can come from diverse sources: internal imagination, real-world interaction, and human supervision. We demonstrate that this provides a natural path toward embodied reasoning, self-exploration, reinforcement learning from environment, and human-machine interaction. Rather than treating these capabilities as isolated research problems, EM places all of them within a single computational framework. It also naturally supports adaptive test-time computation, allocating more computation to complex or uncertain situations while using less for simple ones. Rather than proposing specific empirical results, this paper aims to introduce a unified computational framework that connects a growing set of directions and capabilities toward next-generation intelligence. We envision EM as a new paradigm for experience-driven intelligence and hope it inspires concrete instantiations in the future.
workshops: Continually Self-Improving Robots Workshop (CSIR-2026)

81O8s78vu9.title: The Open Ant: A Robot Platform for Reinforcement Learning Research
81O8s78vu9.authors: Elena Sorina Lupu, Patrick Spieler, Khurram Javed, Kris De Asis, John D Martin, Martha Steenstrup, Joseph Modayil
81O8s78vu9.abstract:
Reinforcement learning (RL) research has demonstrated success in both physical and simulated domains; however, the predominant methodology remains rooted in simulations. The predominance of simulations makes translating research to physical reality uncertain for both algorithms and researchers.
We propose a physical platform that is designed to simplify the transition. 
In this paper, we present the Open Ant: a physical variant of the commonly used Gymnasium Ant environment, along with a simulation. 
We demonstrate that competent walking policies can be learned from scratch in approximately one hour directly from the physical robot's experience for two substantially different RL algorithms: SARSA($\lambda$) and Soft Actor-Critic (SAC). 
Separately, we show policies that were learned in simulation transfer to reality. 
We also examine how well the platform supports a nimble experimental ecosystem. Specifically, we observe the speed with which new users from diverse backgrounds achieve their first success with the platform, and how easily the platform can be repaired and updated when hardware issues arise.
Both the hardware design and software are available as open-source GitHub for ease of customization.
In summary, we advocate for the use of the Open Ant for RL researchers who frequently use simulated environments, so they can more easily include robot experiments in their evaluations.
workshops: Continually Self-Improving Robots Workshop (CSIR-2026)

xOgueo5zGr.title: Uncertainty-Gated Exploration Noise Suppresses Task Collapse in Online RL Fine-Tuning of a Flow-Matching Vision-Language-Action Policy
xOgueo5zGr.authors: Mehmet Turan Yardımcı, Yunus Emre Cogurcu
xOgueo5zGr.abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning of pretrained flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) policies promises robots that keep learning after deployment, but continued updates frequently destroy competence on individual tasks while the aggregate still looks healthy. We study this failure mode, which we call task collapse, under a matched small-compute budget on LIBERO-10 with a 450M-parameter SmolVLA policy trained by PPO in the stochastic (SDE) sampling regime. Three exploration-noise policies differ in a single live variable: a fixed noise scale, a learned noise network in the style of ReinFlow, and an uncertainty-gated controller that redistributes exploration across task streams from task-agnostic novelty and competence signals, without task labels or episode boundaries. Under the pooled definition, fixed noise collapses tasks in two of three seeds and learned noise in every seed measured to iteration 200, while the controller collapses none in any of its three seeds. Measured parameter displacement confirms that the controller's action expert continues to change, while its mean applied noise is close to the fixed scale in the available logs. The matched comparison supports the controller's effect on task preservation; the separate contributions of its adaptation across states and over time are not disentangled. A lower fixed scale slows the decline but does not stop it. No arm improves on the behavior-cloning baseline in this budget. Two properties of that regime are measured beside this result rather than offered as its cause: following the reference recipe, training runs in bfloat16 with no fp32 master copy, under which 96.02% of the action expert's elements stay bit-identical across three consecutive iterations, and an fp32 master copy at the reference learning rate collapses both arms in a single-seed observation. We release measurement tools for per-task collapse under four definitions, run-to-run rescoring noise and instrument tares.
workshops: Continually Self-Improving Robots Workshop (CSIR-2026)

ajd27grKXj.title: Value Sim-to-Real: Simulation Values for Efficient Real-World RL
ajd27grKXj.authors: Weijun Dong, Yilin Wang, Jiawei Fu, Yuchen Zhou, Henrik I Christensen, Zhao-Heng Yin, Hao Su
ajd27grKXj.abstract: Real-world reinforcement learning (RL) is a promising approach for advancing robotic manipulation, but how to obtain informative and robust reward signals remains a central challenge. Recent works have explored reward models trained on real robotic data to enable efficient real-world RL. However, this formulation can be expensive and infeasible due to the high-dimensional state space and its dependence on real-world expert data. In this paper, we address this limitation with Value Sim-to-Real (VSR), a novel framework that leverages simulation-trained value functions to define informative, high-quality reward functions for efficient real-world RL. We evaluate our method with both sim-to-sim and sim-to-real experiments on several vision-based contact-rich tasks. We show that VSR learns a smooth value function that strongly correlates with task progress and improves the performance and sample efficiency of downstream RL with its induced reward function.
workshops: Continually Self-Improving Robots Workshop (CSIR-2026)

RiCX6mW1vX.title: VeriFine: Scaling Verification for Self-Improvement in Embodied Reasoning
RiCX6mW1vX.authors: Zewei Zhou, Rachel Luo, Yulong Cao, Chaowei Xiao, Chensheng Peng, Boyi Li, Thomas Tian, Zheng Lian, Yan Wang, Jiaqi Ma, Boris Ivanovic, Marco Pavone, Wenhao Ding
RiCX6mW1vX.abstract: Self-improving policies continually expose new failure patterns, changing what their judges must be able to verify. However, current fixed judges constrain both optimization feedback and the discovery of useful training examples, limiting further self-improvement. This challenge is even more acute in embodied reasoning, where reliable evaluation must account for spatial grounding, causal reasoning, and safety-aware decision-making. We introduce VeriFine, an agent harness framework that scales verification through the co-evolution of the policy, training curriculum, and judge. The Policy Improvement Loop uses a rubric judge to diagnose recurring failures, construct an adaptive curriculum, and optimize the policy. When progress plateaus and verification becomes a bottleneck, the Judge Improvement Loop selectively queries human guidance on informative failure cases and refines the judge through coactive calibration, in which humans and agents resolve disagreements and converge toward the objective rubric of physical reasoning. The revised judge then guides the next stage of data selection and policy optimization. Experiments on driving and robot navigation tasks demonstrate continuous self-improvement in both policy and judge capability across reinforcement and supervised fine-tuning. These results show how scaling verification supports continuous self-improvement as policy failure patterns evolve.
workshops: Continually Self-Improving Robots Workshop (CSIR-2026)

2VMRk0ojD2.title: VETO: Reward-Supervised World Models as Action Verifiers for Sample-Efficient RL
2VMRk0ojD2.authors: Skand Peri, Matthew M Hong, Chaoxiang Zhang, Ross Worobel, Suraj Shivakumar, Dieter Fox, Jesse Zhang, Abhishek Gupta
2VMRk0ojD2.abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained manipulation policies with reinforcement learning (RL) is a promising route to real-world adaptation, but its sample efficiency remains the limiting factor on real robots. A key source of wasted interactions comes from *credit-assignment lag*, i.e., RL policies repeatedly reattempting failure modes they have already observed because observed outcomes must be propagated through a slowly converging temporal-difference (TD) critic, and then through the policy, before behavior changes.  Model-based RL methods are often used to improve sample efficiency since they rely on supervised learning, but they can introduce model-error bias into policy gradients. Our key insight is that action ranking need not rely on TD learning: a latent world model trained with *supervised reward prediction* can provide useful rankings with fewer transitions than TD-trained $Q$-functions. We introduce **V**erifying **E**xploratory **T**rajectories **O**nline, which uses a continually learning, lightweight world model as an online action verifier. The policy proposes candidate action chunks, and the verifier scores them by rolling out latent dynamics and predicting rewards to veto poor action candidates. Because policy and critic targets use real transitions rather than imagined rollouts, world-model errors do not enter the Bellman backup, allowing for asymptotic optimality. Across 7 tasks in 2 simulation suites and on real-world YAM and Franka platforms, $\texttt{VETO}$ adapts in fewer environment interactions than off-policy and model-based baselines and improves pre-trained policies in the real world.
workshops: Continually Self-Improving Robots Workshop (CSIR-2026)

V7OW0Ar0yl.title: VICTR: Value-Informed In-Context Learning for Vision-Language-Action Models
V7OW0Ar0yl.authors: Luca Macesanu, Tianluo Zhang, Aditya Anant Patil, Archit Sharma, Kevin Angers, Christopher Clark, Chen Feng, Juexiao Zhang
V7OW0Ar0yl.abstract:
Recent advances in robot foundation models have highlighted the potential of in-context learning (ICL) for adapting robot behavior from demonstrations without further fine-tuning. 
Previous work has used retrieval-based post-training to equip pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models with the capability for ICL by teaching them to condition action predictions on retrieved visually-relevant demonstration chunks. However, the effectiveness of retrieval hinges on selecting context relevant to the current execution stage, which visual similarity alone may not capture.
We introduce VICTR, a framework enabling in-context learning in VLAs via progress-informed context retrieval built around an In-Context Value Function Estimator (IC-VFE). IC-VFE conditions on a reference demonstration video, a language instruction and the current observation to estimate task-relative \emph{progress}.
By conditioning progress estimation on a reference demonstration, IC-VFE can align the current state with a demonstrated execution even for tasks unseen during training.
VICTR uses the estimated progress to select demonstration chunks at corresponding stages of execution and supplies them to a $\pi_{0.5}$ policy post-trained for in-context action generation.
On unseen out-of-domain real-world manipulation tasks, VICTR raises the success rate from 2.7\% for a fine-tuned $\pi_{0.5}$ baseline to 25.0\% and more than doubles the task progress rate, from 26.8\% to 58.2\%.
workshops: Continually Self-Improving Robots Workshop (CSIR-2026)

lSCER7Mc61.title: Visual Verification Enables Inference-time Steering and Autonomous Policy Improvement
lSCER7Mc61.abstract: Robots deployed in the real world should learn from their experience and improve over time. This requires a mechanism of practicing and learning from feedback. In this paper, we propose VERITAS, a generator–verifier framework for generalist robot policies for inference-time policy steering and self-improvement. We use a pre-trained generalist robot policy as a “generator” and pair it with a gradient-free “visual verifier” that evaluates actions at inference time. This framework enables inference-time steering that improves policy performance without additional training. We demonstrate that inference-time verification consistently outperforms vanilla generalists without training on additional demonstration data. Additionally, we demonstrate that the verified rollouts provide effective supervision for offline policy improvement: policies fine-tuned on verified self-generated trajectories achieve consistent performance gains. Notably, we find that post-training with verified rollouts achieves comparable efficiency to expert demonstrations, while requiring no human interventions. Our results highlight inference-time verification as a practical and scalable mechanism for improving robotic policies during deployment.
workshops: Continually Self-Improving Robots Workshop (CSIR-2026)

eKIoWYRtrD.title: WEAVER, Better, Faster, Longer: An Effective World Model for Robotic Manipulation
eKIoWYRtrD.authors: Arnav Kumar Jain, Yilin Wu, Jesse Farebrother, Gokul Swamy, Andrea Bajcsy
eKIoWYRtrD.abstract: The potential impacts of world models (WMs, i.e., learned simulators) on robotics are far-reaching—policy evaluation, policy improvement, and test-time planning—all with limited real-world interaction. To unlock these downstream capabilities, a WM needs to jointly satisfy three desiderata: (i) fidelity (i.e., producing simulated trajectories that correlate with reality), (ii) consistency (i.e., producing simulated trajectories that are coherent over long horizons), and (iii) efficiency (i.e., producing simulated trajectories quickly). We propose WEAVER (World Estimation Across Views for Embodied Reasoning): a WM architecture that simultaneously achieves all three desiderata, providing state-of the-art results on robotic manipulation tasks. WEAVER is a multi-view WM trained to predict future latents and reward values via a flow-matching loss. We distill the key design decisions across model architecture, memory, and prediction objectives required to unlock the kinds of long-horizon dynamic manipulation tasks that have confounded prior world modeling approaches. We apply WEAVER in robotic hardware, demonstrating its effectiveness at policy evaluation (ρ = 0.870 correlation with real-world success rate), policy improvement (real-world success rate improvement of 38% on top of the π0.5 robot foundation model), and test-time planning (real-world success rate improvement of 14% with a 5 − 10× speedup over prior WMs). WEAVER also demonstrates better performance than prior WMs when evaluated on out-of-distribution scenarios. Website:https://weaver-world-model.github.io.
workshops: Continually Self-Improving Robots Workshop (CSIR-2026)

GALvgShgor.title: A Scene-Grounded Data Engine for Mobile Manipulation
GALvgShgor.abstract: Mobile-manipulation policies are usually trained on demonstrations teleoperated in the room where the robot will be deployed, because a policy that navigates and manipulates learns the room along with the task. We present a data engine that removes the teleoperation while keeping the room: one handheld walkthrough of the deployment scene is reconstructed into a 3D Gaussian Splatting appearance model and a contact mesh, rollouts are generated and verified in Isaac Sim, and observations are rendered by compositing the simulated robot against the captured scene. We evaluate on the physical robot rather than in simulation, on a dual-arm mobile manipulator across four tasks with 30 trials per condition. At matched demonstration counts, generated and teleoperated data train equally capable policies; because generated data costs only compute, scaling it to 300 demonstrations per task raises success to 60.0% against 43.3% for the best teleoperation baseline ($p=0.013$), after 13 person-minutes of effort per scene. Controlled comparisons identify what makes the simulation predictive: the same engine run in a different scene collapses to 5% success, a reconstruction built for manipulation alone or navigation alone recovers less than half, and rendering against a textured mesh instead of the captured appearance halves success. We release the engine, the scene captures, and 10,000 generated demonstrations across five real scenes.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

DxSjwUQTbO.title: AlphaNIST: Emergent Assembly Skills from Binary Task Rewards
DxSjwUQTbO.abstract:
The NIST Assembly Task Board #1 remains a challenging benchmark for learning-based robotic manipulation. Demonstrations, task decomposition, and dense progress rewards have advanced research by guiding robots on how to assemble. But how much of that strategy must be specified? The progression from AlphaGo to AlphaGo Zero showed that reinforcement learning at scale can discover superhuman strategies without prescribing how to win. AlphaNIST asks whether a sparse binary task reward, together with the task diversity it permits, can similarly let a robot discover how to assemble.

In simulation, we train a single policy from scratch across all 20 assembly tasks on the NIST Assembly Task Board #1. It reaches 98.2% overall training success without demonstrations, progress shaping, scripted primitives, or per-task tuning. The framework also trains policies to complete ten assembly pairs in a single episode without a prescribed order, rewarding success only when all ten pairs are simultaneously complete.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

Ou6gexinc9.title: An Empirical Study on What Matters for Viewpoint-Generalizable Policies in Visual Imitation Learning
Ou6gexinc9.abstract: Visual imitation learning is a promising approach to training robot manipulation policies capable of completing a wide variety of tasks. However, policies today remain brittle to viewpoint perturbations, making deployment in diverse environments a challenge. We present a controlled empirical study of which design choices allow visuomotor policies to generalize across viewpoints. We find that viewpoint generalization improves when dense visual tokens are retained and the action head participates in geometric reasoning. On a suite of simulated tasks that span a wide range of camera poses, we show that these design choices yield a policy that remains performant across viewpoints. As a practical consequence, a policy trained with these design choices also transfers zero-shot from simulation to the real world under random camera configurations.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

GE27RKiwrk.title: Beyond Task Success: Diagnostic Safety Evaluation of Robot Policies
GE27RKiwrk.abstract: Scalable simulation evaluation is useful only when its metrics distinguish the behaviors needed for deployment. We present a diagnostic safety study of OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, and $\pi_{0.5}$ using 22,200 retained LIBERO rollouts, unsafe/safe instruction pairs, initial stop requests, and visual instruction controls. Stop requests still produce object displacement in 28.7–91.0% of episodes, while pooled unsafe/safe outcome-proxy differences are below 0.13 percentage points. Neutral, blank, and blurred signs reproduce most of OpenVLA's task-success loss under an injected command. Across 23 safety-guard configurations, template accuracy does not predict robustness to rewording or contextual risk: the best GuardianBench pair accuracy is 43.6%. A hidden-state probe reaches AUROC 0.810 on new verbs but has 28.7% false positives. Matched controls, common-input comparisons, and record audits expose distinct failures that binary task success conceals. These simulation and classification findings motivate richer benchmark reporting; they do not establish real-robot safety or sim-to-real transfer.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

C9Ugz7LftC.title: Blind Precise Assembly: Proprioceptive Sim-to-Real Peg-in-Hole for Diverse Parts
C9Ugz7LftC.abstract:
Every robot already carries high-resolution contact sensors: its own joints.
Legged robots and humanoids exploit them to walk, run, and track whole-body
motions without vision, but there the contacts are large and forceful. Is joint sensing also enough for precise, contact-rich assembly, where the robot must
find a millimeter-scale opening, mesh gear teeth, or catch a thread through light
contact? We study this question by training blind assembly policies that observe
only a short history of joint positions, velocities, and their own actions, without
visual, force, torque, or tactile sensing. The poses of both the fixture and the part
are unknown to the policy, and the grasp is randomized substantially. The policy must
therefore assemble the parts through contact, sensed exclusively through its own
proprioception. Trained with reinforcement learning entirely in simulation over
randomized parts, grasps, and contacts, such policies learn peg insertion, gear
meshing, and nut threading. The peg insertion policy transfers zero-shot to the real
world and inserts pegs of different shapes and sizes in 73% of trials.
Controlled comparisons with matched visual policies in simulation show that blind policies generalize far better to unseen part shapes and sizes, though they can be slower.
Training such policies needs thousands of different assemblies, each
simulated with its clearance intact, so we also release an
open-source generator that builds them procedurally from exact convex pieces
for MuJoCo; it is more accurate and faster than convex decomposition or
MuJoCo's signed-distance collision.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

U7x8v6c0Bh.title: CableTac: Scalable Visuo-Tactile Learning for Cable Routing
U7x8v6c0Bh.abstract: Cable routing requires reasoning about both global cable geometry and local contact interactions, yet collecting large-scale visuo-tactile robot data is expensive. We present CableTac, a simulation and learning framework for scalable visuo-tactile cable manipulation. CableTac combines GPU-accelerated cable dynamics, general-purpose tactile simulation, and a full-scale replica of the ManipulationNet cable-routing benchmark. A demonstration-reuse engine expands 10 human demonstrations into more than 1,000 simulated trajectories, which we use to pretrain diffusion policies before reinforcement-learning post-training. Across three routing tasks, we find that policy performance improves with increasing amounts of generated data, while the value of tactile feedback is task dependent: tactile sensing provides little benefit for unconstrained round-peg routing, but improves success by 4.7 and 8.0 percentage points for Y- and U-clip insertion, where local contact is critical. RL post-training further improves success to 88.7% and 92.0% on Y- and U-clip routing. These results establish CableTac as a scalable testbed for studying when and how tactile feedback benefits linear-deformable-object manipulation.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

urBMgWMjjh.title: Colosseum V2: Benchmarking Generalization for Vision-Language-Action Models
urBMgWMjjh.abstract: Vision–Language–Action (VLA) models demonstrate promising generalization in robotic manipulation, driven by advances in large-scale vision and language pre-training. This progress can be misleading. Despite the zero-shot perception and language capabilities of VLAs, their overall task performance often degrades under distribution shifts, revealing gaps in how these systems translate high-level understanding into robust behavior. To systematically study this gap, we introduce ColosseumV2, a large-scale simulation benchmark for evaluating VLA generalization in robot learning across diverse conditions. The benchmark comprises 28 tasks spanning 13 task categories and two robot morphologies, covering a wide range of manipulation primitives and long-horizon behaviors. Built on the ManiSkill simulator, ColosseumV2 enables fast, GPU-parallelized evaluation and supports both in-domain and out-of-domain testing at scale. We evaluate state-of-the-art methods, including Action Chunking Transformers (ACT) and $\pi_{0.5}$, and reveal limitations in both base performance and generalization. We demonstrate strong correlations between simulation and real-world metrics that support the ecological validity of the benchmark. By standardizing tasks, metrics, and evaluation protocols within a unified benchmark, ColosseumV2 enables reproducible and fair comparisons, reduced evaluation overhead, and accelerated progress toward general-purpose robot policies.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

cstwyT14lz.title: Eden: One Task Definition from Simulation to Real Robots
cstwyT14lz.abstract: Robot policies are increasingly trained in simulation, yet deploying one on a physical robot usually means rewriting its observation and action processing against the robot's SDK, a second implementation that can silently diverge from training. We present Eden, a robot-learning framework built on Genesis in which a task is one typed, serializable configuration whose terms declare their own parameters and access robots and objects only through entities they reference by name. Replacing the simulated robot entity with one that reads the physical robot runs the training task's observation, action, and command code on hardware; the same configuration also drives teleoperated data collection and selects the solver and contact model. Five whole-body tracking policies deployed this way succeed in 47/50 Unitree G1 trials with no observation or action code rewritten, and a vision-language-action policy fine-tuned on 100 demonstrations collected in Eden succeeds in 27/30 real pick-and-place trials. We evaluate the design with a coding-agent benchmark that holds the agent, task description, documentation, and success checker fixed and varies only the framework. Agents reach a working policy in Eden, IsaacLab, and mjlab in a similar fraction of five independent rollouts. On tasks that must be built from components, they reach it in less wall-clock time in Eden, although coding models have likely seen less Eden code; on tasks adapted from shipped code, Eden gives no clear advantage, and it does not reduce token use in general.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

aLuF2Kdb7L.title: Embodiment-Classifier Guidance: Transferring Frozen VLAs Across Robot Dynamics without Demonstrations
aLuF2Kdb7L.abstract: Flow-based policies such as $\pi_0$ are trained on a fixed set of embodiments, and transferring them to new ones is an open problem. To adapt a frozen $\pi_0$ to a new embodiment without additional demonstrations or parameter updates, we train a lightweight embodiment classifier to distinguish successful action chunks on the source body from those on the target body, using a few calibration tasks. On transfer tasks that $\pi_0$ saw on its source body but the classifier was never trained on, we nudge each denoising step of $\pi_0$ with the classifier's gradient, which estimates the direction from the distribution of successful actions on the source body toward that on the target body. On the LIBERO simulation benchmark with four modified controllers, embodiment-classifier guidance raises $\pi_0$'s average success on the target bodies from 72% to 80% across 12 settings, with a 31% relative reduction in failures (11 of 12 gain; 5 significant after Holm correction). In simulation, guidance is data-efficient, needing few target-body rollouts per task, which makes it promising for sim-to-real transfer, where rollouts are costly. On weak or locked wrists, guidance is mixed and can hurt when the classifier lacks data or favors infeasible motions. Collecting more target-body data with guided $\pi_0$ can fill such gaps: on one weak-wrist arm, guided $\pi_0$ solved a task on which unguided $\pi_0$ had zero successes in the original data, and retraining the classifier on these successes raised success from 52.5% to 70.7%.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

Y3aiT0YAhn.title: Evaluating Test-Time Scaling in Robot Policies and World Models
Y3aiT0YAhn.abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World Models (WMs) make sample-based test-time scaling natural for robot decision-making: sample candidate actions, imagine their consequences, execute the most promising one.
We introduce a test-time evaluation benchmark that reveals what current foundation decision-making models do well and poorly, when additional samples improve action selection, and how well WM-imagined futures help, spanning VLAs, integrated World-Action Models (WAMs), VLAs augmented with action-conditioned WMs, and GPT-6 Astra with a waypoint scaffold.
The evaluation covers three dimensions: \emph{sampling potential} (oracle headroom from sampled actions), \emph{selection effectiveness} (selector gains over random selection on the same pool), and \emph{uncertainty informativeness} (whether dispersion in sampled actions predicts failure).
Additional samples expose substantial oracle headroom, nearly 50 percentage points for Astra on LIBERO, but tested selectors fail to achieve it consistently; we identify where current models fall short and what this implies for WM research.
(Anonymous project page: \url{https://robot-tts.github.io/})
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

Xcta1vUXKa.title: Getting Out and Getting Back: World and Behavior Grounding in Real2Sim2Real Co-Training
Xcta1vUXKa.abstract: Simulation can expand scarce real demonstrations, but how world fidelity and similarity to human behavior affect co-training remains unclear. We independently vary world grounding, which aligns simulation with the real system, and behavior grounding, which aligns simulated trajectories with human motion. On dynamic dexterous pick-and-sort, fully grounded co-training raises the success rate from 52% to 86% using 100 real demonstrations and 1500 simulated trajectories. Rollout observations suggest that policies follow real-derived behavior in demonstrated states and simulation-derived behavior elsewhere. We investigate these transitions through latent-space analysis and examine how both grounding axes affect task performance. We further show that both grounding axes remain consequential when co-training foundation models.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

kHdCCwDovE.title: HyperDrone: Simulation-to-Reality Transfer at Millions of Frames per Second
kHdCCwDovE.abstract: We present HyperDrone, an extremely fast quadrotor simulator focused on high-performance batch rendering that is more than 20x faster than existing state-of-the-art batch quadrotor simulators. HyperDrone combines highly optimized multirotor dynamics with HyperLux, a new ray-tracing engine that takes full advantage of modern ray-tracing hardware, capable of running both components entirely on the GPU. HyperLux renders RGB, depth, semantic/instance segmentation, surface normals and optical flow observations at configurable levels of fidelity, including reflections, motion blur, anti-aliasing, and Physically Based Rendering (PBR). Even in the highest-fidelity settings, HyperLux achieves millions of Frames Per Second (FPS) on consumer-grade GPUs. We demonstrate the merits of HyperDrone by training a vision-based yaw-control policy purely in simulation and transferring it to a real small-scale quadrotor (Crazyflie) with a camera, running completely onboard.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

qi9nUxw0vH.title: Improving Generalist Policies with Simulation Post-Training
qi9nUxw0vH.abstract: We present an ongoing study of how simulation can be used for post-training generalist robot policies. We consider the setting where a pretrained generalist policy already exhibits non-zero success on a target task and investigate a recipe to improve the policy without additional human demonstrations or enforcing task structure beyond sparse rewards. Our work focuses on unpacking the expert learning process, which most sim-to-real works treat as a black box, to simplify state-based expert learning and improve downstream student-teacher distillation. We leverage the following insights to set up a recipe for policy improvement with simulation: generalist policy rollouts can reduce the burden of exploration in expert learning and privileged critics from expert learning can improve the distillation step beyond standard supervised finetuning. We additionally discuss opportunities to push performance, expand recovery behavior, and improve policies without needing distillation.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

CrsTwWeBUH.title: ManiLadder: Benchmarking Robot Manipulation Through a Categorized and Multi-Difficulty Level Task Ladder
CrsTwWeBUH.abstract:
Recent advances in robotic manipulation have enabled increasingly
complex and dexterous behaviors, yet existing benchmarks still focus on sim-
ple pick-and-place tasks and lack a systematic framework for measuring progress
along the axis of task difﬁculty. We present ManiLadder, a large-scale and orga-
nized simulation benchmark containing 112 tasks stratiﬁed into 4 difﬁculty lev-
levels, with 8 categories in each level, spanning rigid-body and deformable-object
manipulation, single-arm and dual-arm settings, and gripper and dexterous-hand
end-effectors. To calibrate difﬁculty, we ﬁx the data amount for every task and
use a uniﬁed ﬂow-matching imitation learning policy under the same training and
evaluation protocols, using its success rate as an empirical difﬁculty signal. All
tasks are iteratively reﬁned until they fall into target difﬁculty ranges, which are
then veriﬁed across random seeds and policies. We further analyze task prop-
erties, compare policies, study data scaling, and conduct real-world experiments
showing that the tasks preserve their difﬁculty ordering beyond simulation.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

YjNJtvKpD4.title: MASSMARL: Measuring Population Scaling in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
YjNJtvKpD4.abstract:
Many widely used multi-agent reinforcement learning benchmarks evaluate small teams of up to a few dozen agents. GPU acceleration often increases throughput by batching these small worlds rather than increasing the population within each world. We present MASSMARL, a GPU-native JAX engine and grid-world benchmark with twenty tasks in five families, including four inspired by swarm robotics. MASSMARL simulates a single world of 16.1 million agents at 7.4 × 10^7 agent-steps/s on one A100-80GB. This simulation measurement excludes policy inference and learning. We evaluate ten shared-parameter baseline implementations across tested population sizes with 20 training iterations and four-step rollouts. Seven complete the test at 1,013,888 learners on an A100-80GB.
A QMIX variant first fails at 663,552 learners, and compact attention and retention baselines at 41,472, with first failures at the same tested populations across three tasks. These are tested feasibility bounds, not exact population limits or evidence of convergence. The results distinguish simulation capacity from training feasibility and provide a computational diagnostic for population scaling in swarm-inspired learning; physical fidelity and transfer to robots remain untested.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

r0P7V6z0kD.title: MimicShape: From One Real Object to Many via Real-to-Sim-to-Real Trajectory Replay for Manipulation Policy Learning
r0P7V6z0kD.abstract: Generalizing imitation-learned manipulation policies to unseen objects requires demonstrations across many object instances, making real-world data collection costly. Demonstration augmentation can reduce this collection burden, but demonstrated motions are tied to the source object’s geometry, making object diversity difficult to expand while reusing recorded trajectories. We present MimicShape, a real-to-sim-to-real system that expands object diversity in demonstration data by keeping real-world trajectories unchanged and generating compatible objects in simulation. A synchronized digital twin extracts contact and clearance constraints from the recorded trajectories, and an agentic system generates diverse, textured objects that satisfy these constraints. Simulation replay verifies that the original actions succeed on each candidate, yielding new visual observations paired with unchanged real-world actions. Across eight tasks on rigid, articulated, and deformable objects, four real and four simulated, MimicShape improves success rates on unseen objects over the strongest applicable baseline on every task by 15.5 percentage points on average. On real-world mug hanging, augmenting 50 demonstrations on one mug raises success on unseen mugs from 19% to 51%, against 63% for 250 demonstrations collected on five real mugs.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

LDuEhoeyLc.title: MoMa-NMP: Scene-Scale Neural Motion Planning for Mobile Manipulators
LDuEhoeyLc.abstract: Mobile manipulators operating in homes and other complex environments must coordinate their base and arm over long horizons, navigating around obstacles, through narrow passages, and between constrained workspaces. Neural motion planners can provide fast closed-loop planning from partial observations, but scaling them to room-sized environments is difficult because generating high-quality training trajectories is itself a challenging motion-planning problem. To address this, we introduce MoMa-DemoSmith, a demonstration-generation pipeline that separates the problem into global path discovery for large complex scenes and local motion refinement for collision avoidance. This key separation enables the generation of millions of challenging whole-body trajectories across our procedurally generated scenes. These demonstrations are used to train MoMa-NMP in two stages: behavior cloning (BC) followed by privileged on-policy distillation. The resulting policy plans from depth-camera and LiDAR observations, achieving 87.0\% success without environment collisions in simulation and 77.5\% across 80 trials in unseen physical scenes. See video results at https://adamhkan.com/moma-nmp/.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

Up1WVICrlD.title: NeRD2Real: Adapting Neural Robot Dynamics for Humanoid Control from Real-World Data
Up1WVICrlD.abstract: Accurate simulation is essential for transferring humanoid control policies to hardware, yet calibrating dynamics models from limited, noisy onboard data is challenging. We present NeRD2Real, a framework for learning Neural Robot Dynamics (NeRD) through extensive pretraining with analytical simulation data and adapting with limited real-world data. Simulation pretraining learns a dynamics-conditioned transition model and a trajectory-level missing-state estimator. Adaptation recovers unobserved states, identifies a real-world dynamics-latent, and fine-tunes the model on a mix of reconstructed real and simulation data. On Unitree G1, an adapted NeRD supports whole-body policy learning and enables sim-to-sim and sim-to-real transfer. A walking policy trained in the adapted NeRD without dynamics randomization transfers zero-shot to the real robot.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

U1RYGhLTYR.title: Neural Fidelity Calibration for Informative Sim-to-Real Adaptation
U1RYGhLTYR.abstract:
Deep reinforcement learning (RL) can transfer agile robot skills from simulation to the real world, but closing the sim-to-real gap by domain randomization requires expert physics knowledge, and simulator calibration from real data typically targets a few hand-picked parameters. Even then, simulators miss real-world effects, and environments reconstructed from onboard perception inherit sensing errors that limit policy improvement.
We propose Neural Fidelity Calibration (NFC), which uses conditional flow matching to calibrate simulator physical parameters and residual fidelity domains online during deployment. Residual fidelity captures sim-to-real dynamics discrepancies and perception-induced environment uncertainty. NFC operates in a latent space so that realistic environments can be sampled from the inferred posterior for real-to-sim policy fine-tuning. The framework is informative: the pretrained policy is fine-tuned only when an anomaly is detected, sequential NFC seeds its proposal from the simulation-pretrained estimator, and a hallucination policy modulates posterior uncertainty following optimism in the face of uncertainty.
NFC attains the most accurate posteriors among established simulation-based inference methods on five robots with up to 39 physical parameters and a 128x128 residual terrain. On a wheeled robot with a broken wheel axle deployed on snow, mud, and wet grass, NFC raises success on rough terrain from 26% to 70% and reduces orientation jerk by 88%. Code and videos will be released upon publication.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

tvGTA10xJG.title: One Phase is Enough: Sim-to-Real Transfer with Direct Visual Reinforcement Learning
tvGTA10xJG.abstract: Sim-to-real reinforcement learning (RL) has enabled impressive robotic behaviors, yet deploying policies directly from vision remains challenging. A common approach first trains a teacher policy with RL using privileged state observations, then distills its behavior into a vision-based student via imitation. However, the resulting student can substantially underperform its teacher. Direct visual RL offers a promising alternative, but learning task-relevant visual representations from scratch can be sample-inefficient and computationally expensive making one-phase visual RL intractable. We propose DRIFT, a simple recipe for efficient one-phase visual RL using frozen pre-trained foundation vision encoders, allowing RL to focus on learning control from existing visual representations. Freezing the encoder avoids costly back-propagation through the vision backbone, while its pretrained representations enable real-world transfer from fast, rasterized simulation renders. Under matched architectures, observations, and compute budgets, DRIFT outperforms two-phase distillation and achieves a 58.8\% relative improvement in average real-world success rate across three manipulation tasks. Controlled simulation evaluations demonstrate that DRIFT’s relative advantage grows from roughly 9\% in-distribution to over 61\% under out-of-distribution shifts, suggesting that stronger generalization contributes to superior real-world transfer.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

m2Y1UmhnRu.title: Reflex: Visually Grounded Reactive Humanoid Control
m2Y1UmhnRu.abstract: Humans effortlessly react to the world; they catch a falling cup, step aside from a passing cart, or receive a box tossed during truck unloading. These everyday actions require anticipating a moving object and responding with the whole body within about a second, often by making contact with the arms and torso. Such visually reactive, contact-rich whole-body control remains challenging for humanoids, which must (1) coordinate whole-body contact, (2) react to object dynamics in real time, and (3) ground perception in egocentric vision. We study catching thrown boxes as a representative task that demands all three. We present Reflex, a three-stage framework that learns these capabilities stage by stage while connecting them through a compact representation of object dynamics: a state policy first learns whole-body catching with reinforcement learning, the policy then learns to infer box dynamics from delayed and incomplete observations, and an egocentric RGB-D encoder finally learns to recover this representation while the controller stays fixed. In simulation, Reflex catches 85.7% of throws from egocentric RGB-D, compared with 87.9% with privileged box observations. On a real Unitree G1, it catches human-thrown boxes with 65% and 40% success at 2.5 and 5 m, reaching 76% and 59% of human catchers’ success.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

5dGydIVmrk.title: RoboCommons: Open, Evolving Evaluation for Generalist Robot Policies
5dGydIVmrk.abstract: Generalist robotic manipulation policies are rapidly expanding in capability, but their evaluation remains largely tied to fixed benchmarks designed and defined at benchmark design time. We introduce RoboCommons, a language-driven multi-framework harness for open-ended evaluation that lets users specify what they want to test while handling framework-specific task implementation. RoboCommons generates executable, verified tasks across existing manipulation frameworks and accumulates them into a reusable evaluation repository. Using more than 300 generated tasks, we show that evaluation diversity continues to grow as the repository expands. Its automated verifier produces tasks that are 98.5% correct under human adjudication while retaining 93.6% of valid tasks. Across three frameworks, RoboCommons is rated significantly more usable and less cognitively demanding compared to GenSim and Cursor in a 26-participant user study. Finally, across 15 policy-framework combinations and 42,576 episodes, targeted task families reveal distinct capability gaps that are obscured by aggregate success rates. These results show that robotic evaluation can be made easier to author, reliable to execute, and extensible as policy capabilities evolve. Project page: https://robocommons2026.github.io
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

xxVgTVAjnv.title: RoboRender: Robot-Oriented Video Generation for Visual Sim-to-Real Transfer
xxVgTVAjnv.abstract: Simulation enables large-scale, low-cost robot data generation, but policies trained in simulation often fail to transfer to the real world due to the sim-to-real visual discrepancies. Existing approaches often rely on intermediate representations, which can discard rich semantic information or require additional perception modules at deployment. We address this visual sim-to-real gap with RoboRender, a framework that converts simulated trajectories into photorealistic RGB videos for policy learning. RoboRender trains a robot-oriented video generation model conditioned on simulated depth videos, language instructions, and robot RGB mask videos, preserving simulator geometry, robot motion, and action labels while synthesizing realistic textures, backgrounds, and distractors. The generated RGB videos are paired with simulator-provided states and actions to train policies for zero-shot real-world deployment. On robot video test sets, our video model outperforms depth-conditioned video generation baselines in generation quality. In real-world experiments across pick-and-place, articulated-object manipulation, and mobile manipulation tasks, policies trained on RoboRender-generated data achieve a 71% average success rate, outperforming raw simulation renderings and conventional visual domain randomization by approximately 7.1×and 3.6×, respectively. We further show that policy performance improves with more generated videos per simulation trajectory, increasing opening-task success by 65 percentage points. These results demonstrate that generative video rendering mitigates the visual sim-to-real gap for zero-shot policy transfer.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

Z4fyPsIQZU.title: Rollout Aggregation Stabilizes On-Policy Reinforcement Learning
Z4fyPsIQZU.abstract: Large-scale parallel PPO can struggle on complex, long-horizon tasks with high-dimensional action spaces. Prior work has emphasized exploration bottlenecks and diminishing returns from increasing environment parallelism. We instead present evidence that learning instability offers a compelling alternative explanation for PPO's poor performance. To improve stability, we introduce rollout aggregation, a minimal modification that retains the previous rollout and trains on it alongside newly collected samples. We show that overlapping rollout batches regularize the policy's optimization trajectory by preserving pressure to retain recently learned behavior while incorporating new experience. Across several challenging manipulation tasks, rollout aggregation prevents the collapse observed with standard PPO and outperforms strong baselines, including SAPG and CPO, with several-fold improvements in sample efficiency. Our findings motivate studying recent-data reuse as a mechanism for stabilizing policy learning and achieving strong, sample-efficient performance at scale.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

F9mbPCXVi8.title: ScheduleGen: Demonstration Generation via Skill Scheduling for Multi-Arm Imitation Learning
F9mbPCXVi8.abstract: Multi-arm robot platforms, including bimanual and humanoid robots, have the capability to complete tasks with lower cycle times than single-arm systems, but they are more difficult to safely control due to the presence of multi-arm constraints. The paradigm of training generalist robot policies from massive datasets is a promising approach to address general-purpose multi-arm manipulation, but the acquisition of large multi-arm manipulation datasets remains a bottleneck. Automated demonstration generation can alleviate this burden by synthesizing new demonstrations from a handful of source demonstrations, but existing algorithms ignore multi-arm constraints and as a result often induce unsafe and unsuccessful behaviors. We address this limitation by introducing ScheduleGen, an integrated planning & scheduling algorithm for multi-arm demonstration generation. We evaluate ScheduleGen on 28 simulation task variants, including seven externally authored RoboDojo tasks and settings inaccessible to prior systems; it achieves 79.6% mean data-generation success and trains policies with 65.5% mean success. ScheduleGen policies outperform those trained on a state-of-the-art data generation baseline, and achieve 50-80% success across eight real-world tasks through zero-shot sim-to-real and real-to-sim-to-real transfer. Videos and more at: https://schedulegen.github.io/
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

EfNYDXLSUP.title: SidewalkBench: Benchmarking Visual Navigation on Urban Sidewalks
EfNYDXLSUP.abstract: Urban sidewalk navigation presents significant challenges due to complex structural layouts, dynamic pedestrian behaviors, and long distances. While recent visual navigation models offer a promising solution, the lack of a unified benchmark hinders quantitative and reproducible evaluation. To bridge this gap, we propose SidewalkBench, a comprehensive benchmark designed for visual navigation on urban sidewalks. Built upon NVIDIA Isaac Sim, SidewalkBench brings GPU-accelerated simulation of diverse, high-fidelity sidewalk environments, including both procedurally generated and real-world scanned scenes. We further populate the scenes with rich, reactive event-based pedestrian behaviors and flexible, efficient animation, enabling standardized model evaluation under realistic real-world settings. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of 9 visual navigation models on 330 unit-test scenarios, 800 pedestrian-reactive scenarios, and 105 long-horizon scenarios.
