Our findings highlight that pedestrian interaction and long-horizon robustness remain critical bottlenecks for existing models, and scaling up sidewalk training with synthetic data emerges as a promising solution.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

gB9zlGOMek.title: Sim-to-Real Transfer for Muscle-Actuated Robots via Generalized Actuator Networks
gB9zlGOMek.abstract: Tendon drives paired with soft muscle actuation enable faster and safer robots while potentially accelerating skill acquisition. Still, these systems are rarely used in practice due to inherent nonlinearities, friction, and hysteresis, which complicate modeling and control. So far, these challenges have hindered policy transfer from simulation to real systems. To bridge this gap, we propose a sim-to-real pipeline that learns a neural network model of this complex actuation and leverages established rigid body simulation for the arm dynamics and interactions with the environment. Our method, called Generalized Actuator Network (GenAN), enables actuation model identification across a wide range of robots by learning directly from joint position trajectories rather than requiring torque sensors. Using GenAN on PAMY2, a tendon-driven robot powered by pneumatic artificial muscles, we successfully deploy dynamic but precise goal-reaching, ball-in-a-cup, and table tennis policies, trained entirely in simulation. To the best of our knowledge, this result constitutes the first successful sim-to-real transfer for a four-degrees-of-freedom muscle-actuated robot arm.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

eJRu9hYSJO.title: SimFoundry: Modular and Automated Scene Generation for Policy Learning and Evaluation
eJRu9hYSJO.abstract:
Training and evaluating robot policies in the real world is costly and difficult to scale.
We introduce SimFoundry, a modular and automated system for zero-shot real-to-sim scene construction from a video.
SimFoundry generates sim-ready digital twins and supports object, scene, and task editing, enabling the automated generation of diverse digital cousins: affordance-preserving variations of reconstructed real-world scenes.
Policies trained on SimFoundry data transfer zero-shot to challenging real tasks involving multi-step manipulation, articulated object interaction, and bimanual interaction, and its digital cousins facilitate generalization to new real-world conditions.
Across 7 manipulation tasks and 5 policy architectures, SimFoundry simulation evaluations correlate well with real-world performance and strongly predict real-world policy rankings, with mean Pearson correlation 0.909 and mean maximum ranking violation 0.027. 
When evaluating sim-trained policies zero-shot in the real world, policies trained with object, scene, and task cousins in simulation show average task success rate improvements of 20\%, 21\%, and 40\%, respectively. Additional details at https://simfoundry.github.io/.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

0O2Q2idELA.title: SkillWeaver: Agentic Exploration over Neural Interaction Skills for Scalable Robot Data Generation
0O2Q2idELA.abstract: Large-scale demonstrations have driven rapid progress in robot learning, yet collecting robot data through teleoperation is expensive and difficult to scale to diverse environments and long-horizon tasks. GPU-accelerated simulation can generate experience at scale, but existing data-generation pipelines still rely on open-loop controllers, scripted skill sequences, or task-specific programs to produce behavior. We introduce SkillWeaver, an agentic framework that autonomously generates robot experience by exploring over Neural Interaction Skills (NIS): reusable, parameterized, closed-loop policies that expose learned physical interaction capabilities to a reasoning agent. A VLM agent invokes and parameterizes NIS in simulation, observes their outcomes, and organizes exploration as verifier-guided tree search with reflection and memory, discovering successful long-horizon behaviors without predetermined execution pipelines. SkillWeaver autonomously generates 39.1K verified demonstrations across 14.1K scenes, which we distill into visuomotor policies. Training on this experience substantially improves generalization on simulation benchmarks, enables zero- and few-shot sim-to-sim transfer, and more than doubles average real-world success on a Franka robot without any real-world teleoperation.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

vmsPJdwqwl.title: Steel: Simulation for Generalist Robot Learning
vmsPJdwqwl.abstract: GPU-accelerated simulation at scale has enabled reinforcement learning to produce locomotion and whole-body control policies that transfer to physical robots: thousands of identical environments simulated in parallel under a simple on-policy recipe such as proximal policy optimization (PPO). Manipulation presents a different scaling problem: robots must learn across a large space of tasks and embodiments, interacting with different objects, layouts and mechanisms, so simulation must scale not only the number of environments but their diversity. We present Steel, a GPU rigid-body contact solver for the open-source Newton physics engine whose arrays are laid out per environment: each environment's constraint rows and response vectors occupy a range of fixed capacity, its mass-matrix factor a range sized to its degree-of-freedom group, and the factorization kernels run over groups of articulations of the same degree-of-freedom count, so robots, objects, contact sets and degrees of freedom may differ across the environments simulated in parallel and no robot's factorization is padded to the largest one present; contact rows use a fixed per-environment budget. Steel reaches 4.6× PhysX's throughput (geometric mean over 20 Isaac Lab tasks, faster on all 20) and 1.8× MuJoCo Warp's (geometric mean over the same 20); with 5 to 20 scene types simulated in parallel, each solver at its own peak environment count, its throughput ratio to PhysX rises from 7.5 at 5 types to 12.6 at 20, with no result reported for MuJoCo Warp, whose evaluated backend shares model structure across worlds.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

DVSfvV3mAs.title: SUN: Agentic Robot Policy Learning with Persistent Task Programs
DVSfvV3mAs.abstract: Model-based control can directly execute specified objectives, while learning can amortize such behaviors into reactive policies, making their combination a natural solution to multi-stage manipulation. We introduce Semantically UNified (SUN) Programs, typed executables that compile grounded relations into aligned optimal control objectives, satisfaction predicates, and learning rewards. Our harness, Kuafu, equips a foundation model as a task-level agent to orchestrate scene preparation, verification, residual RL, and data production. The agent uses program feedback to repair candidate programs and training diagnostics to calibrate relative reward weights, retaining accepted task semantics across tool calls. Across nine multi-stage manipulation tasks, Kuafu achieves 82.03\% average success rate, significantly outperforming all learned baselines. The downstream visual-policy transfer zero-shot to physical Franka and Kinova robots, demonstrating sim-to-real generalization.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

7RmW8P1qnE.title: Support-Constrained RL Enables Real-World Policy Improvement without Additional Real-World Experience
7RmW8P1qnE.abstract: Robots trained on real world data tend to be imprecise, slow, and brittle to perturbations. Improving these policies with reinforcement learning (RL) is an appealing alternative, but this process often requires expensive training in the real world. Performing policy improvement in simulation instead provides a far cheaper alternative, but unconstrained RL in simulation can exploit contact and dynamics mismatches, resulting in unsafe behaviors that do not transfer to hardware. Common forms of regularization can furthermore limit improvement by overconstraining to an imperfect behavior prior.  In this work, we propose Support-Constrained Off-Domain REinforcement (\texttt{SCORE}), a real-to-sim-to-real framework that constrains RL in simulation to stay near the \textit{support} of a generative policy pretrained on real data. We instantiate this constraint through \textit{flow steering}, restricting \texttt{SCORE} to explore through modes of the base policy, which ensures transferable behaviors while maximizing policy improvement. Improving a policy with \texttt{SCORE} requires minimal effort: it learns from sparse rewards, avoids distillation, and leaves the base policy untouched. Across eight real-world dexterous multi-fingered robotic manipulation tasks, \texttt{SCORE} improves average success rate from $38.6\%$ to $89.3\%$, compared to $59.8\%$ for the best baseline, and completes tasks $36.7\%$ faster than the base policy. Ultimately, through extensive experiments and ablations, we show that simulation can substantially improve real-world manipulation policies when policy optimization is appropriately constrained, introducing a new paradigm for real-to-sim-to-real policy improvement. Videos are available at https://score-anon.github.io.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

jmZMj6QkeI.title: What Can Three Seeds and Fifty Rollouts Resolve? A Preregistered Audit of Operator and Seed Variance on robomimic Multi-Human Benchmarks
jmZMj6QkeI.abstract: Results on the robomimic Multi-Human benchmarks are conventionally reported as a mean over three training seeds, each evaluated with 50 rollouts. We preregistered the hypothesis that the variance caused by which operators' demonstrations are in the training set exceeds the variance caused by training seed. We tested it with 138 BC-RNN runs on Lift, Can and Square: ten seeds at fixed data, six leave-one-operator-out partitions, and six size-matched random partitions as a control, all evaluated at the final checkpoint on fixed initial states. The preregistered tests were not met on any task, and with six operators the procedure detects a true ratio of two only 18% of the time. With 50 rollouts, seeds cannot be told apart by success rate on any task, and two three-seed means on Square must differ by 12.7 points to be distinguished. Re-evaluating the 46 Square checkpoints with 500 rollouts, the 50-rollout success rates correlate only r = 0.56 with the 500-rollout ones, an apparent proficiency-tier pattern vanishes, and the operator contrast is not established.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

JG9LX2V3XN.title: When Robots Outweigh Objects: How Inertia Mismatch Shapes Robot Policy Learning
JG9LX2V3XN.abstract: Conventional robot arms can be extremely heavy compared with the everyday objects they manipulate, creating a significant inertia mismatch at contact. Even a small accidental bump from a heavy arm can knock a light object out of place. Modern learning methods have nevertheless demonstrated a wide range of successful manipulation behaviors on these platforms, suggesting that even extreme inertia mismatch can be overcome with sufficient data. However, it remains unclear whether high inertia imposes a hidden cost on learning, potentially worsening scaling with data and lowering the performance ceiling of modern robot learning methods. This question is hard to answer on hardware, where a robot's mass cannot be varied in isolation, so we use GPU-accelerated simulation as a controlled instrument: pushing experiments that vary robot and object masses while matching the free-space controller response. A reinforcement-learned policy succeeds across a broad range of masses, while behavior cloning learns more reliable policies when a lighter robot manipulates a heavier object. This finding can also guide how we use an existing robot: an arm's task-space mass varies with its posture. Choosing workspace placements and demonstration trajectories that favor lower contact inertia improves closed-loop imitation on contact-rich manipulation tasks in simulation, and the same workspace intervention also improves imitation on a real robot.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

p6yUjibJia.title: ZAP: Zero-shot Acceleration of Robot Policies Through Impedance-Augmented Residuals
p6yUjibJia.abstract: Robot policies trained by imitation inherit the slow pace of their demonstrations, and existing methods for accelerating them require per-task training. We present ZAP, a framework for $\textit{zero-shot}$ policy acceleration with impedance-augmented residuals: learned corrections that offset the policy's pose targets and modulate the gains of the underlying controller. We train per-task residuals in simulation under a shared reinforcement learning objective and distill them into a single task-agnostic residual that transfers to new tasks and base policies. Across 20 held-out tasks in simulation, ZAP achieves the highest throughput among state-of-the-art acceleration baselines, without any in-domain demonstrations or interactions; on a real-world task, ZAP achieves throughput comparable to these baselines while maintaining the highest success rate, demonstrating zero-shot, sim-to-real transfer to an unseen scene and base policy.
workshops: From GPU-Accelerated Simulation to Scalable and Generalizable Real Robot Policy Learning

g52Xqypuwy.title: $\tau_0$-VLA: a Hierarchical Robot Foundation Model with World-Model-Guided Test-Time Computation
g52Xqypuwy.authors: Xiaowei Cai, Yunuo Cai, Bingao Chen, Jingxiao Chen, Zhi Chen, Siyuan Feng, Tengyu Hou, Jingshun Huang, JiangHan, Runkun Ju, Dong Li, Mingxiang Li, Shaowei.Li, Xinchen Li, Yifan Li, Yi Liu, Zhongyuan Liu, Jianlan Luo, Junwen Miao, Ruiqi Ni, Buqing Nie, Mingjie Pan, Xinlin Ren, JianHeng Song, Jiaxu Wang, Peiqi Wang, Wangsen, Xiaoyan Wang, DafengWei, Dongming Wu, Pengwei Xie, Pu Yang, Hangjian Ye, Xiangyu Yue, Jinyu Zhang, Zhang Qinglin, ZhaoXueyong, Pengfei Zhou, Yue Zhou
g52Xqypuwy.abstract: Long-horizon robot manipulation requires a robot to both execute individual skills reliably and sequence them coherently over extended tasks. Most hierarchical vision-language-action (VLA) models make each such decision with a single forward pass, leaving no mechanism to allocate additional computation to difficult or consequential choices. We introduce $\tau_0$-VLA, a hierarchical robot foundation model that formulates high-level subtask generation as a compute-scalable inference problem through world-model-guided test-time computation. At each inference step, the high-level policy uses execution memory to generate a subtask and, when needed, searches over alternatives before committing to its output. A low-level policy then executes the generated subtask across multiple robot embodiments. The policy is trained on 40,115 hours of heterogeneous real-world data with multimodal co-training. Across in-domain and distribution-shifted settings, allocating additional test-time computation substantially improves next-subtask prediction accuracy, and these gains translate into higher closed-loop success on long-horizon robot manipulation tasks.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

Wc7zx1QgwO.title: $k$-WM: Predicting $k$ Steps at Once for Long-Horizon Planning with World Models
Wc7zx1QgwO.authors: Xiaole Alex Jiang, Yinuo Wang, Lerrel Pinto, Yann LeCun, Gaoyue Zhou
Wc7zx1QgwO.abstract: Latent world models are learned abstractions of environment dynamics that can be planned over at test time, enabling goal-conditioned optimization and generalization across tasks with a single model. In practice, however, planning success remains limited to short horizons, and gradient-based planners driven by autoregressive rollouts still underperform sampling-based methods. We hypothesize that two properties of next-step prediction contribute to these limitations: autoregressive rollouts compound prediction errors, and planning gradients must traverse a chain of nested model calls. We introduce $k$-WM, a minimal extension to transformer-based JEPA world models: a multi-horizon training objective and input layout that let the predictor map an action sequence to the future latent states in a single forward pass. Across three classes of JEPA world models and four environments, $k$-WM improves gradient-based planning by 37\% and sampling-based planning by 15\% over the existing next-step world models it extends, and reduces long-horizon inference cost. Our analysis shows that the gains coincide with substantial changes in the learned representation, suggesting that the prediction horizon shapes the abstraction a world model learns for planning. Additional results and planning rollouts are available at https://anon-k-wm.github.io.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

6yJrUIPvj2.title: Agent Priors-guided Policy Learning
6yJrUIPvj2.authors: Puming Jiang, Tianrun Hu, Haozhe Du, Yibo Li, Zhiwei Xue, Xinhu Li, Harold Soh
6yJrUIPvj2.abstract: Robots that learn from a few demonstrations often require two forms of generalization. Compositional generalization recombines skills to solve new tasks, and skill generalization lets the learned policy behind each skill work in new situations. The two depend on each other, yet information is lost between composition and the skills it calls. Where a skill works is determined by the structure its policy is trained with, while composition sees the skill only through a separate description, such as a name, an instruction, or a symbolic operator, that omits this structure. Our key idea is to use each policy's structural prior as part of the interface between composition and the skill. A structural prior states what a behavior depends on, for example that a grasp depends only on the gripper's pose relative to the object. Built into training, it shapes where the policy generalizes; stated in language, it tells composition where the policy applies. We instantiate this idea in Agent Priors-guided Policy Learning (APPL). A construction agent segments complete demonstrations into reusable skills, proposes several structural priors for each skill, and trains and verifies one policy per prior. A runtime agent then selects among these prior-specific policies and composes them toward new task goals using their interfaces. Across MetaWorld and long-horizon ManiSkill tasks, APPL improves out-of-distribution skill generalization and enables previously unseen skill compositions; ablating the interface information substantially reduces performance. These results support the use of training-time structural assumptions as a bridge between skill learning and skill composition.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

gxEC7M0oZj.title: Agentic Hypothesis-Driven Active Learning of Natural-Language Robot Skill Models
gxEC7M0oZj.authors: Benned Hedegaard, Naman Shah, Sumeet Batra, Rohun Tripathi, Alvaro Herrasti, Dieter Fox
gxEC7M0oZj.abstract: To operate safely and effectively, a robot must understand, and therefore model, the bounds of its capabilities. Prior work has traditionally sought to learn such models using symbolic abstractions, imposing strong biases on the space of expressible and learnable models. The recent advent of agentic systems has opened the possibility of using frontier models for robot decision-making. In place of symbolic models, an agentic system (i.e., agent) interfaces with its skills as modular tools, documented by text descriptions of their arguments and behavior. We study how agents can use experimentation to adapt these interfaces, and whether such experimentation can allow them to autonomously learn skill models that improve downstream planning capabilities. Our evaluations use simulated block-stacking tasks whose motor skills have hidden preconditions and stochastic effects, comparing a naive agent free to experiment as it chooses against a structured agent whose harness requires explicit hypotheses and planned trials, each experimenting either open-ended or guided by example tasks. We find that skill descriptions learned through experimentation improve downstream planning performance, and can even outperform expert-designed descriptions; that our structured harness provides complementary benefits to those obtained through example task guidance; and that the structured agent's experiments are more controlled and replicated, beyond what its harness explicitly requires.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

d0QoEpVBxX.title: AIDA:  A Neuro-symbolic Framework for Planning and Residual Learning of Multi-task Robot Policies
d0QoEpVBxX.authors: Ziyi Yang, Jiayuan Mao, Stefanie Tellex, George Konidaris, Karl Berntorp
d0QoEpVBxX.abstract:
Pretrained robotic foundation models can be adapted to a new environment by finetuning on human demonstrations, enabling a single network to perform multiple skills. However, after this initial adaptation, two challenges remain: composing the resulting skills to solve long-horizon tasks, and further improving their reliability without collecting additional demonstrations. Abstraction learning supports skill composition, but the learned abstractions rarely contribute to improving the underlying skills. Reinforcement learning offers a way to improve skill execution, but existing approaches rely on task-specific reward design and do not directly support skill composition.
To address this gap, we propose Abstraction Invention for Decision-making and Adaptation (AIDA), which learns a symbolic transition model to support task planning and uses it to train residual policies that improve the base policy. We present preliminary results on the CALVIN benchmark showing that learned abstractions allow multiple skills of the same base policy to be both composed and improved.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

zIR8mVMqdd.title: Are Vision-Language-Action Models ready for Task and Motion Planning?
zIR8mVMqdd.abstract:
Current task and motion planners (TAMP) are limited by the human engineering required to design motor skills. Could learned generalist policies such as vision-language-action (VLA) models supply the motor skills that TAMP systems such as TiPToP lack? We discuss what is necessary to use VLAs as skills inside TAMP and show that current VLAs fall short. We believe that to effectively utilise learned generalist policies inside of task and motion planning, the policy must meet four conditions: it must only manipulate objects specified by invoked operators, it must cause no unintended side effects, it must know when to terminate, and its competence must be predictable from a symbolic state. We build a hybrid system, based on TiPToP [1], which learns operators for VLAs from training data, and uses a vision language model (VLM) to check each step executed successfully, and triggers a replan if not. On five RoboLab tasks, no method completes any task, yet the hybrid system scores highest on four of the five. We also found that aligning actions produced by the motion planner to the VLA’s training
distribution increases the VLA’s downstream competence.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

2usjb66X4r.title: Beyond Point Transitions: Learning Skill Effect Sets for Compositional Planning
2usjb66X4r.abstract: Robots complete long-horizon tasks by chaining together a sequence of pre-trained skills. Existing approaches use coarse high-level abstractions for planning with skills, often producing plans that are not feasible for execution. This infeasibility is only discovered after many unsuccessful attempts to refine skill parameters for execution.  We present Skill Effect Sets (SES), an approach to learn the range of states that a skill can reach under its continuous parameterizations. SES is learned from skill executions with a contrastive objective. We also present SES-Guided Interleaved Skill Chaining (SES-ISC), a planning algorithm that leverages SES by refining skills over sets of reachable states rather than individual skill parameters. SES-ISC focuses exploration on previously unreached state regions, allowing it to quickly prune infeasible plans from imperfect high-level abstractions.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

HtIg8Z5LnU.title: BIFROST: Bridging Invariant Feature Representation for Observation-space Sim2Real Transfer
HtIg8Z5LnU.abstract:
Sim2real transfer for robot policy learning suffers due to mismatch between simulation and reality. Existing methods typically address each gap in isolation through separate adaptation modules, which are composed or layered when both gaps coexist. Yet the basis for attempting sim2real in the first place is that there is shared structure between a task in simulation and reality, where equivalent actions from equivalent configurations produce equivalent long term outcomes regardless of domain specific differences in rendering or physics. In this paper, we study whether we can identify and exploit this shared structure from raw observations to train a policy that enables zero shot transfer.
% 
We introduce BIFROST, which learns a shared history encoder on paired cross-domain data via cross-domain bisimulation objective: observation-action sequences leading to equivalent long-term behavior are mapped to nearby latent states, regardless of domain. 
Policies trained on these latent states in simulation transfer zero-shot to reality. We provide empirical evidence on sim2sim visual navigation and sim2real contact rich manipulation task and visual servoing task that BIFROST achieves effective transfer where domain adaptation and co-training baselines fail under both visual and dynamics domain gaps.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

eznUHGM2SP.title: CaPE: Code as Path Editor for Grounding Language Communication in Multi-Agent Coordination
eznUHGM2SP.authors: Haojun Shi, Suyu Ye, Katherine M. Guerrerio, Jianzhi Shen, Yifan Yin, Daniel Khashabi, Chien-Ming Huang, Tianmin Shu
eznUHGM2SP.abstract: Successful coordination among decentralized agents requires each agent to quickly adapt its plan to the behavior of other agents. One common way to achieve such adaptation is to ground other agents’ language communication in plan adjustment. Despite recent advances in language-conditioned policy learning, it remains difficult for existing methods to achieve robust, safe, and fast language grounding in multi-agent coordination. In particular, there are two unique challenges for path-level coordination: (1) selecting among multiple plausible coordination path plans and (2) continuously refining a selected path locally. To address these challenges, we propose CaPE (Code as Path Editor), a novel method for grounding language communication in multi-agent coordination. CaPE first generates topologically distinct candidate paths for the target agent and predicts other agents’ paths using a homotopy-aware joint planner. It then leverages a vision-language model (VLM) to write a path-editing program based on language communication from a partner, selecting a path and adjusting it as intended by the partner. To ensure feasibility and safety, a verifier checks each edit line by line and rejects any that violate physical constraints. We evaluate CaPE in simulated multi-robot coordination, human-robot teaming in cluttered household apartments, and real-world joint carrying with human partners using a mobile manipulator. CaPE substantially outperforms strong baselines, including frontier VLMs, across all settings. Driven by a small fine-tuned VLM, CaPE also runs efficiently, supporting on-the-fly adaptation.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

QMhuFDn7GI.title: CausalDreamer: Learning Predictive World Models with Latent Disentanglement
QMhuFDn7GI.authors: Prince Jha, Nils Lukas, Kun Zhang, Salem Lahlou
QMhuFDn7GI.abstract: World models for control must capture which aspects of the environment respond to the agent's actions and which are relevant to reward. Generative world models such as Dreamer 4 consist of a video tokenizer, which encodes each frame into a latent, and a dynamics model, which is pretrained to predict future latents from past latents and actions. Yet the tokenizer is trained with a reconstruction objective, without action or reward supervision, so its latent provides no explicit mechanism to separate controllable, uncontrollable, reward-relevant, and reward-irrelevant information. We propose \textit{CausalDreamer}, which keeps the tokenizer frozen and re-encodes its latent into a factored representation of four groups along two axes: controllability, where only the two controllable groups receive the action, and reward relevance, learned by predicting the reward from the two reward-relevant groups. The pretrained dynamics model is then fine-tuned to predict the factored representation. We evaluate \textit{CausalDreamer} and the pretrained world model it starts from with model-predictive planning on 20 MMBench2 tasks: 10 clean tasks seen during training and 10 unseen tasks, of which 6 are manipulated variants of clean tasks with a changed background, object, or maze layout, and 4 are new environments. We normalize returns so that a policy taking uniformly random actions scores 0 and an expert scores 1. \textit{CausalDreamer} achieves a 14\% higher normalized score than the pretrained world model on the clean tasks (0.199 vs.\ 0.175) and a 25\% higher score on the manipulated variants (0.307 vs.\ 0.246), while neither model scores meaningfully above the random policy in the new environments. Additionally, our analysis shows that the factored representation separates reward-irrelevant changes, such as a changed background, from its reward-relevant groups.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

BDE6ZgxpKm.title: CLEAR: Capability-Aware Latent Ordering for Adaptive Interaction with Movable Objects
BDE6ZgxpKm.authors: Joonhyung Lee, Sangbeom Park, Jeongsoo Lim, Jaesang Sun, Kyeong-Jae Lee
BDE6ZgxpKm.abstract:
Planning physical interactions in cluttered environments requires reasoning about robot capabilities.
For example, a legged robot may climb stairs, while a wheeled robot may need an alternative route.
However, the ability to move objects does not ensure task completion, as the interaction order and resulting object configurations can block subsequent actions.
To address this challenge, we propose a capability-aware planner that jointly determines which objects to interact with, in which order, and how to move them.
Our planner, Capability-Aware Latent Ordering for Adaptive Interaction with Movable Objects (CLEAR), learns to select objects and propose alternative interaction orders from scene observations and robot structure.
For each proposed sequence, it generates object references, conditioning each prediction on those planned for preceding interactions.
The planner checks whether candidate plans are feasible in the proposed interaction order, selects the valid candidate with the fewest object interactions, and replans from updated observations during execution.
Our approach is evaluated in three simulation environments: 2D grids, ordered manipulation, and maze navigation.
The maze experiments assess the effect of robot-structure conditioning and the ability to replan when environmental perturbations block access to required objects.
Code, videos, and results are available at
\url{https://joonhyung-lee.github.io/clear/}.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

QxJUFGvpNs.title: Collision-Conditioned Reasoning and Planning for Autonomous Manipulation from Partial View Point Clouds
QxJUFGvpNs.abstract: Placing an object in a cluttered scene requires choosing a grasp, a placement pose and a collision-free trajectory that work together. Prior work shows that jointly reasoning about pick and place is essential for place success, but relies on hand-defined placement costs and slow optimization. Learned collision models can screen candidate placements from partial-view point clouds, but existing pick and place systems that use them commit to a grasp before searching for a placement. We present a collision network that predicts, from partial-view point clouds of the object and environment, whether the object collides with the environment at a candidate placement pose. We combine this network with a learned grasp generator and a GPU-vectorized motion planner to form a collision-conditioned pick and place planning framework that plans for many grasp and placement pairs in parallel. In hardware experiments, our approach is roughly 3.5$\times$ faster than a joint pick and place optimization baseline.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

liZo8BXIJ5.title: cuArms: GPU-Accelerated Conflict-Based Planning for Multi-Arm Manipulation
liZo8BXIJ5.authors: Philip Huang, Fabio Ramos, Jiaoyang Li, Caelan Reed Garrett, Lars Johannsmeier
liZo8BXIJ5.abstract:
Multi-arm manipulation has the potential to dramatically improve the throughput, efficiency, and dexterity of many manipulation tasks. Recent work coordinates multiple robot arms in a shared workcell by allocating and scheduling tasks for greater parallelism, jointly planning multi-arm motions, or directly learning multi-arm policies. So far, these approaches are either too slow, rely on domain-specific assumptions, or scale poorly with the number of robots and task horizon. Thus, we introduce cuArms, a conflict-based planner co-designed with GPU parallelism that efficiently decomposes the search space using reusable multi-modal roadmaps for individual robots and resolves conflicts and deadlocks through a lazy search. To jointly optimize task assignment, schedules, motions, and manipulation
skills, we integrate a high-level scheduler that proposes candidate skeletons for cuArms to ground into coordinated manipulation
plans. This scheduler can also be a coding agent: given the cuArms API, an off-the-shelf coding agent writes and optimizes the samplers, schedule skeletons, and costs for each new problem, while cuArms generates highly coordinated multi-arm motions. Experimental results show that our method establishes a new state of the art, with real-time initial solutions and anytime improvements in both motion quality and scheduling, without days of domain-specific training required by learning approaches. With Claude Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra as the
scheduler, the system outperforms our hand-designed schedulers, with 31% and 52% lower makespans, respectively. Videos of
both simulated and real-world industrial tasks are available on https://cuarms.github.io/.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

6sFbcwHnEn.title: DemoStream: Batched Task-and-Motion-Plan Optimization for Automated Learning from Demonstration
6sFbcwHnEn.authors: Caelan Reed Garrett, Neel Jawale, Fabio Ramos
6sFbcwHnEn.abstract: Learning from demonstration is an effective strategy for endowing robots with manipulation capabilities but requires training on datasets comprised of massive amounts of demonstrations. Existing demonstration collection approaches either require constant human involvement, for example, via teleoperation or are specialized for a single task. Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) systems are able to autonomously solve and therefore generate demonstrations for general-purpose tasks; however, learning from their demonstrations has proven difficult due to multi-modality in their solutions. In this work, we build on recent work leveraging GPU acceleration for TAMP and propose DemoStream, a TAMP system that optimizes demonstration quality in order to improve behavior cloning success rates. First, we introduce batched TAMP sampling operations along with a new TAMP algorithm that correspondingly performs batched constraint satisfaction in order to explore many solutions in parallel. We conduct simulation experiments ablating different action spaces, cost functions, and batch sizes to analyze the effect of these choices on downstream policy success rates. Finally, we show that we can leverage the safety guarantees of TAMP to directly collect real-world demonstrations at an average rate of 66 demos per hour. See our website for policy rollout videos: https://demostream.github.io.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

AcBIRCFRq8.title: Disentangled Representations Enables Zero-Shot Visual Generalization in Robot Manipulation
AcBIRCFRq8.authors: Sumeet Batra, Jeremy Morgan, Gaurav S. Sukhatme
AcBIRCFRq8.abstract: Training vision-based manipulation policies that are robust across diverse visual environments remains an important and unresolved challenge in robot learning. Current approaches often sidestep the problem by relying on invariant representations such as point clouds and depth, or by brute-forcing generalization through visual domain randomization and/or large, visually diverse datasets. However, historically and across disciplines, simple, parsimonious solutions have stood the test of time. In this work, we investigate whether emergent compositional representations, specifically disentangled representations, from a self-supervised learning auxiliary objective on high-dimensional RGB data can yield the same, if not better, visual generalization on robot manipulation tasks as brute-force scaling from pretraining. We provide empirical results that disentangled representations improve zero-shot visual generalization capabilities on modern robot learning benchmarks under adversarial visual perturbations in simulation and on real hardware. We believe this work marks a significant step towards manipulation policies that are adaptable out of the box, and a path towards compositional generalization that does not rely on large-scale pretraining.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

Lt6tewJ0RI.title: DynaCoDiff: Density-Space Diffusion for Multi-Robot Planning in Dynamic Environments
Lt6tewJ0RI.authors: Chunxuan Jiao, Han Gao, Dusk Ding, Yunze Hu, Jiayu Yuan, Zhejia Wen, Luolina, Chang Liu
Lt6tewJ0RI.abstract: Online planning for large robot teams must coordinate collective motion under moving obstacles and uncertain observations. DynaCoDiff represents group motion as Gaussian mixture model (GMM) trajectories. Differentiable collision costs guide a learned motion prior using group spatial spread and obstacle-prediction uncertainty. Gaussian transport generates individual references for distributed model predictive control, while planning continues during execution. In mixed dynamic–static environments with 500 robots, DynaCoDiff achieves 86% task success, compared with 0% for a reactive reinforcement-learning policy. Gaussian safety margins outperform isotropic-inflation and mean-only alternatives across four observation-noise settings. These results support density abstractions for connecting learned motion priors, obstacle beliefs, and individual execution.
keywords: Multi-robot motion planning; diffusion models; density abstraction; dynamic obstacle avoidance; uncertainty-aware planning
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

u3JzQTSt1e.title: EMBODIEDSWE: Coding Agents for Long Horizon Dexterous Robotics
u3JzQTSt1e.authors: Haoxiang You, Zeyu Shen, Yilang Liu, Zhicheng Zheng, Lihan Zha, Kashu Yamazaki, Mingtong Zhang, Suning Huang, Jiankai Sun, Qianzhong Chen, Luxi He, Kaiyuan Liu, Haoran Chang, Katerina Fragkiadaki, Dhruv Shah, Mac Schwager, Peter Henderson, Ian Abraham, Canwen Xu
u3JzQTSt1e.abstract:
We study coding agents for long-horizon, dexterous robotics and ask whether their solutions can provide scalable supervision for learning general robot policies. To test this, we develop EMBODIEDSWE-BENCH, a simulation benchmark for coding agents spanning contact-rich manipulation, deformable objects, and long-horizon tasks requiring up to half an hour of continuous interaction. We
find that frontier coding agents can solve complex long-horizon tasks and transfer prior solutions across both tasks and embodiments. We also design supporting tools that help agents more effectively solve these tasks. However, the resulting solutions require substantial iterative interaction and are typically specialized to individual task instances. We therefore introduce EMBODIEDSWE-GEN,which expands a single solution from coding agent into large diverse trajectories for training a VLA. VLA performance improves with more generated demonstrations, and agent-aided diversification improves generalization to held-out task variations. We also show that a VLA finetuned solely on coding-agent-generated simulation demonstrations completes a long-horizon task on real robot. Together, our framework uses coding agents to solve complex robotics tasks and turn verified solutions into scalable supervision for robot policies
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

jxmiIoO6At.title: EMPIRIC: Experiment-Driven Learning of Residual World Models for Robot Planning
jxmiIoO6At.authors: Yichao Liang, Amber Li, Dat Nguyen, Emily Bunnapradist, Michelangelo Naim, Sreela Kodali, Matteo Merler, Bowen Li, Kiran Gopinathan, Yiyun Liu, Nikhil Pimpalkhare, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, Adrian Weller, Zenna Tavares, Tom Silver, Kevin Ellis
jxmiIoO6At.abstract:
A robot should be able to learn through experiments how unfamiliar objects behave and interact, then plan with that knowledge.
It need not start from scratch: physics engines supply knowledge of motion and contact, but can omit entire mechanisms, such as glue curing, water heating, or wind.
We present EMPIRIC, an agent that learns a residual world model: a physics engine extended with code for the missing mechanisms.
The learned programs can introduce new forces, constraints, and hidden state, 
and Bayesian inference estimates their parameters and states from noisy observations.
The resulting model lets the agent predict the outcomes of actions, choose informative experiments, and revise its hypotheses when predictions fail.
Across five simulated domains, EMPIRIC learns interpretable, reusable models, and solves more tasks with fewer environment interactions than all three baselines. On a physical robot, it learns wind forces and domino masses to solve a manipulation task.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

Kcx90cUpXn.title: Evaluating and Improving Task-Relevant Prediction in Robotic World Models
Kcx90cUpXn.authors: Haibo Zhao, Jesse Zhang, Dieter Fox
Kcx90cUpXn.abstract:
Using action-conditioned world models as simulators requires preserv-
ing task-relevant physical states and outcomes beyond visual plausibility. We eval-
uate agentic, latent, and video-generative models on paired successful and failed
manipulation trajectories spanning pick-and-place, contact-driven reorientation,
and long-horizon composition. Object and end-effector pose errors complement
outcome prediction over full trajectories and local interaction segments on seen
and held-out starts. Reliability depends on task and configuration: an agent-built
simulator predicts pick-and-place well but struggles with reorientation and com-
position, while the evaluated Wan 2.2 configuration better preserves these out-
comes. Latent-model readouts can be accurate on observed images yet degrade
to near-chance outcome prediction during rollout. An additional study finds im-
provements from multiview and multimodal learning.
keywords: world models; planning with world models
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

ELddZJx2NU.title: Evaluating Long-Horizon Robot Planning under Uncertainty
ELddZJx2NU.authors: Harsh Muriki, Gayathri Aravindan, Yuchen Zheng, Sonia Chernova
ELddZJx2NU.abstract: Household robots must successfully navigate imperfect circumstances, both in their internal models and the external world. We introduce a benchmark of seven long-horizon household tasks in Habitat that vary initial robot memory and environment configurations. We evaluate adaptations of ReAct, VLM-TAMP, and Tru-POMDP within a shared execution framework across 90 tasks--environment--memory combinations, totaling 1,350 episodes. Our evaluation measures task success, partial completion, and action efficiency, along with rule-based analysis of execution traces. ReAct achieves the highest overall task success (45.3\%) and completion (71.7\%), while having accurate initial memory does not consistently yield the highest performance for every planner. We identify recurring placement errors, precondition errors, and redundant actions through trace analysis. These findings highlight differences in how the evaluated planners use initial knowledge and respond to uncertainty.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

661Q6HJnfB.title: Evaluating Representational Reliability Across World Models
661Q6HJnfB.authors: Shobhit Gupta, Maanya Cola Bharath, Chirag Shah
661Q6HJnfB.abstract: The term "world model" now spans latent predictive encoders, masked reconstruction models, recurrent dynamics models, and video predictors, increasingly proposed as general engines for prediction, planning, and physical reasoning. We treat world model evaluation as a problem of matching claims to evidence: what information is recoverable from frozen, pooled representations, and how does it relate to their benchmark-label geometry? We analyze V-JEPA 2, VideoMAE v2, and DreamerV3 on IntPhys2, combining latent geometry metrics, supervised probes, and saliency-based background suppression. Condition and camera-type labels are recoverable under the evaluated protocol, while global condition clustering remains weak despite positive unsupervised clustering. Background suppression increases 5-NN condition accuracy with small observed changes in condition silhouettes, while nearest neighbor margins change in different directions. Together, these diagnostics characterize label recoverability, local neighborhoods, and global condition geometry as distinct properties of the evaluated readouts. The findings are specific to the pooled representation pipelines; they do not establish a causal explanation of world model unreliability or demonstrate planning utility.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

Ess8wZF1rg.title: FEIJOA: Task-Driven Grounding and Execution for Mobile Manipulation
Ess8wZF1rg.authors: Aditya Agarwal, William Shen, Sahit Chintalapudi, Lucy Cai, Nishanth Kumar, Aidan Curtis, Travis Manderson, Tomás Lozano-Pérez, Leslie Pack Kaelbling
Ess8wZF1rg.abstract: A mobile manipulator asked to ``put the toys away in the toy box'' must decide which objects are toys and which container the user means, then find base poses, grasps, and placements it can execute. Because a scene representation is built before the instruction is known, it may lack the attributes, affordances, or concepts needed to resolve the task. We present FEIJOA, a language-model agent that grounds the instruction at test time. It queries a grounding tool over a posed RGB-D scan, inspects the returned candidates, and refines its queries until they resolve the instruction. An embodiment-aware harness checks each skill's preconditions, samples base poses from which the target is reachable, and verifies the skill's effect from observations before and after execution. On 103 open-ended grounding queries, FEIJOA resolves 94.2% exactly, compared with 68.0% for the best prebuilt representation. Over 50 real-world trials on Spot, it completes 35 tasks; 17 of these successes follow recovery from a failed tool call or verification check. Of the 15 failed trails, 13 were caused by the robot's physical skills, and only 2 by grounding or the agent's reasoning.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

YOmlZrbwsb.title: FRAME: Towards Neuro-Symbolic World Models for Task and Motion Planning
YOmlZrbwsb.abstract:
Latent world models are an increasingly popular way to learn the dynamics and control of manipulation tasks. However, especially for longer-horizon tasks like TAMP problems, symbolic task-level representations are useful abstractions to increase their tractability. FRAME represents ongoing work towards combining these two concepts into a single predictive model, using a bi-level scene graph as the underlying state representation. As a first step towards such a model, given demonstrations of existing tasks, we learn to predict the next high-level symbolic action, and deploy FRAME together with a motion planner as a heuristic to guide high-level search. 

Applied to 2D manipulation tasks based on the KinDER benchmark, our approach solves more instances than the planner that provided its demonstrations, and its next-action predictions adapt to several held-out task families from as few as 20 demonstrations, indicating high generalization potential of training on various task families over a unified symbolic vocabulary. We plan to extend FRAME  to predict high-level and low-level action dynamics, working towards a single model for both the task and motion levels.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

TPgII7ldC6.title: From Graphical Manuals to Robot Execution: Task and Skill-Level Behavior Trees for Assembly
TPgII7ldC6.authors: Praveen Kumar Menaka Sekar, Charles A Meehan, ION MATEI, HON YUNG WONG, John Baras
TPgII7ldC6.abstract:
Robots that assemble products from instructions written for humans face
two errors that often remain unnoticed until a later assembly step fails: the visionlanguage
model (VLM) that reads the instructions can misread a step, and the
robot can execute a step imperfectly. We study where such a robot should inspect
its work and when it should query a human operator. Experienced workers ask a
supervisor when a drawing does not show which part goes where, check connectors
before the next part covers them, and look closely before a tight insertion. We
encode these behaviors in a hierarchical behavior tree (BT). Before execution, an
off-the-shelf VLM answers one yes/no question per part and manual step, and a
decoder combines the answers into an assembly plan with an error probability
for each step. A task-level planner, a dynamic program, then synthesizes the
task-level BT, which places inspections and operator queries at minimum expected
cost under a bound on the expected number of undetected failures. Each assembly
action of this BT expands into a skill-level subtree whose skills execute only inside
success regions measured in simulation. On 21 products with an 8B VLM, the
decoder recovers 42% of the annotated assembly operations, against 21% for a
single plan query, and its mean error probability matches the fraction of operations
that it decodes incorrectly. Querying the operator about uncertain steps reduces
the expected number of undetected failures over the 21 products from 20.5 to 4.0.
At the same risk, the synthesized BT costs 14–21% less than inspecting only the
finished product or every operation, and up to 0.7% less than simple query rules
that use the same error probabilities. In simulation, a Franka Panda completes
an IKEA chair frame in 35 of 39 runs, with no undetected failure. Project page:
https://praveen1098.github.io/IKEA-Assembly-Planning/.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

NpgQtQTORa.title: Guava: Distilling Frontier VLMs into a Compact Agent through a Robotic Manipulation Harness
NpgQtQTORa.authors: Haowen Liu, Xirui Li, Shaoxiong Yao, Peng Shi, Tianyi Zhou, Jia-Bin Huang, Furong Huang, Jiayuan Mao
NpgQtQTORa.abstract: Frontier vision–language models (VLMs) can perform robotic manipulation by interpreting visual observations, invoking robot tools, and adapting to execution feedback, but repeated model calls incur high costs and latency. In this paper, we study the problem of distilling these capabilities into compact VLMs. The key challenges are designing an interaction interface that enables efficient and generalizable distillation, and a data collection protocol that captures diverse scenarios. We present $\texttt{Guava}$, a framework built around a manipulation harness and a simulation-based data generation pipeline. We first study how harness design affects both frontier and compact models, and use the resulting interface for teacher data generation and student deployment. Through this harness, a frontier VLM generates physically executed and validated interaction trajectories in simulation, which we augment with perturbation branches that expose the teacher to execution deviations and recovery trajectories. Using $\texttt{GPT-5.4}$ as the teacher, we collect 2,268 interaction trajectories and fine-tune $\texttt{Qwen3.5-4B}$ to obtain $\texttt{Guava-4B}$. $\texttt{Guava-4B}$ substantially outperforms its base model and approaches $\texttt{GPT-5.4}$ performance across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, while generalizing to unseen objects, instructions, and task compositions. Perturbation trajectories particularly improve unseen-task generalization. With substantially lower inference latency and token usage compared to a frontier model, $\texttt{Guava-4B}$ enables efficient local deployment.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

x6WSoDx3im.title: H-JEPA: End-to-End Learning of Hierarchical World Models for Visual Planning
x6WSoDx3im.authors: Wancong Zhang, Basile Terver, Michael Rabbat, Yann LeCun, Randall Balestriero
x6WSoDx3im.abstract: Long-horizon planning with latent world models requires reasoning across timescales and levels of abstraction. Existing task-agnostic JEPA world models predict and plan in a single latent space, often at a single timescale. We introduce H-JEPA, an end-to-end recipe for training a hierarchy of action-conditioned JEPAs in which each level predicts farther ahead in its own learned latent space. Planning proceeds top-down: the top level optimizes progress toward the goal, and each level's predictions become subgoals for the planner below it. When factors in the data evolve at separated timescales, higher levels discard fast, unpredictable detail and retain slower task-relevant state. Across four simulated navigation and manipulation environments, hierarchical planning improves over a flat JEPA; on Visual AntMaze, a three-level hierarchy raises success from 18% to 73% using less planner compute. Ablations attribute these gains to both temporal decomposition and higher-level goal representations. With inverse-dynamics supervision, the approach extends to diverse real-robot videos from DROID, where hierarchy improves offline planning fidelity at lower planner compute.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

Z5aG3kttiF.title: How Long, Not How Close: Blending a Learned Temporal Embedding into Latent World Model Planning
Z5aG3kttiF.authors: Lama Moukheiber, Haotian Xue, Yongxin Chen
Z5aG3kttiF.abstract: Latent world models plan by choosing actions whose predicted end state is closest to the goal. This works one plan from the goal but fails several plans away, because latent distance measures how closely a state resembles the goal, not how long it takes to reach it: two positions can look alike yet be separated by a wall or a long sequence of contacts. We hypothesise that the planning cost, not only the model’s predictions, contributes to this failure. We therefore propose TEMPO, which blends a learned temporal embedding into the planner’s existing latent cost, so that plans are ranked by how long they take to reach the goal as well as by how visually close they are. It leaves the world model untouched, learns from the recorded trajectories already used to train it, and adds negligible cost to the planner’s search. The embedding is a small map of the frozen latent and requires no rewards, policies or success labels. We evaluate TEMPO on eleven simulated environments (e.g., maze navigation, tabletop pushing, robotic arm control and three-dimensional manipulation) with the LeWM and PLDM planners. With a 0.13M-parameter map that adds at most 0.3% to a plan’s arithmetic, TEMPO improves both planners at every goal distance, including the one-plan setting of their evaluations, raises LeWM from 36% to 99% on TwoRoom three plans from the goal, and remains competitive on a broad range of 2D and 3D navigation, reaching and manipulation tasks.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

dOmYraWbU7.title: Incorporating Natural Language Preferences in Deep Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning
dOmYraWbU7.authors: Zachary Alan Daniels, Aswin Raghavan, James Zachary Hare, Daniel N. Cassenti
dOmYraWbU7.abstract: Deep Hierarchical Reinforcement learning (DHRL) enables end-to-end learning of policies that use temporally extended skills. This paper addresses DHRL with natural language preference feedback. Preferences allow flexible annotation of higher levels of the hierarchy without restricting the possible policies. We propose an end-to-end learning method that incorporates preferences into language-augmented termination functions in the Options framework. Our method does not assume that a complete set of skills is provided. Rather, the method learns an additional ``bridge policy'', that helps complete the task and satisfies the preferences by connecting the terminating states of one skill to the appropriate starting states of another skill. We discuss applications where preference feedback arises naturally. We validate the method in sparse reward problems: BabyAI tasks and a micromanagement task in StarCraft-2. Our method demonstrates lower sample complexity and stronger task performance, when compared to prior DHRL methods and reward-shaping baselines. Further, our method shows transfer learning to out-of-distribution tasks. We examine scalability with number of preferences and skills and find that handling many preferences with low skill coverage is challenging.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

tM70M4QE78.title: Knowing Where to Look: Interactive Object Search via Spatial-Semantic Fusion
tM70M4QE78.authors: Aditya Agarwal, Lucy Cai, Kelly Lu, Travis Manderson, Nicholas Roy, Tomás Lozano-Pérez, Leslie Pack Kaelbling
tM70M4QE78.abstract: When searching for an object, humans naturally combine semantic intuition – reasoning about where the object is likely to be stored – with geometric awareness of what parts of the space are visible, occluded, or unexplored. Effective robot object search requires the same joint reasoning, yet existing methods rely on only one: geometric methods maintain principled spatial beliefs but lack deep semantic understanding, while language-model based methods leverage commonsense knowledge but maintain no explicit belief over space. We argue that jointly reasoning over semantic and geometric evidence in an explicit 3D belief enables human-like interactive object search that outperforms either modality alone. To test this claim, we build a system that accumulates per-object VLM plausibility scores and geometric occupancy evidence via Bayesian log-odds filtering into a unified 3D voxel belief field. High-belief regions in the combined belief field drive action selection at each step: taking a closer look from a different viewpoint, navigating toward an unexplored region of the workspace, or physically interacting with a closed cabinet. We deploy this system end-to-end on a bimanual mobile humanoid and find that it outperforms geometry-only search and LLM-based planning methods. Project website https://skymanaditya1.github.io/objsearch-website/
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

jRpRFHdh8d.title: Koopman World Model: Structured Dynamics for Efficient Planning
jRpRFHdh8d.authors: Qianhong Zhao, Yunfu Deng, Peng Wang
jRpRFHdh8d.abstract:
Latent model predictive control plans through a learned world model, and with an unconstrained neural transition the planner relies on sampling, which requires many rollouts of the model at every control step.
This paper introduces the Koopman World Model (KWM), a latent world model for continuous control in which the encoder output is a vector of learned observables and the latent dynamics are an enhanced linear approximation of the Koopman evolution of these observables.
KWM is trained within the online learning framework of TD-MPC2, and planning is performed on the frozen model at evaluation.
The bilinear form makes the one-step prediction and its Jacobians available in closed form, and a hybrid planner uses them to refine policy-generated action sequences by local quadratic updates instead of scoring a population of sampled rollouts.
keywords: Koopman Operator; World Model; Representation Learning
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

zC6xSGkG5l.title: Latent Skill Acquisition and Composition for Contact-Rich Manipulation
zC6xSGkG5l.authors: Wenlong Huang, Jiayuan Mao, Tomás Lozano-Pérez, Leslie Pack Kaelbling, Li Fei-Fei
zC6xSGkG5l.abstract: Human-level generalization in manipulation requires composing known behaviors to reach novel goals in scenarios never seen in training. The challenge sharpens in contact-rich settings, where behaviors must be recomposed at the granularity of contact rather than of a semantic subtask. Without relying on per-task demonstrations, a promising approach is to leverage test-time compute to perform physical reasoning that searches for novel solutions and improves them incrementally during deployment. To effectively perform search in the large space of motions, we propose SkillReasoner, which learns temporal abstractions of actions (i.e., skills) from unstructured offline interactions, and then reasons over and recomposes them at test time. Crucial to the formulation is a latent skill space learned with varying temporal horizons, so that composition can happen at varying granularity, as required by different stages of the task, while minimizing the number of decisions. To realize a novel goal at test time, the robot searches over latent skill sequences in its imagination, decodes a chosen skill into low-level actions, and replans in closed loop, up to 30 Hz. We demonstrate on a series of contact-rich real-world and simulated tasks that the robot chains behaviors to achieve novel goals that require far longer behaviors than those seen in training, and adapts zero-shot to unseen perturbations, changing dynamics, and constraints, all trained purely from unstructured play data without task-specific demonstrations.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

NIKVkZBCSZ.title: Learn2Search: A Contextual Transformer Model of a Planner's Search Procedure
NIKVkZBCSZ.authors: Ashwin Misra, Stephen F Smith, Zachary B. Rubinstein
NIKVkZBCSZ.abstract: Scalability to problems with large numbers of tasks remains a significant challenge for heuristic search approaches to planning, particularly in multi-agent domains where tasks must be assigned to specific agents in addition to being sequenced and situated in time. This is often addressed by restricting the amount of search performed, at the expense of an increasingly sub-optimal solution. We instead explore shifting computation offline: using a baseline planner's domain model to learn a model of its search procedure, substituted at runtime as a surrogate search that gains efficiency without sacrificing performance. We solve randomly generated problems with the baseline procedure and autoregressively train a contextual transformer-based decision model on these solutions to predict how the plan should be extended with a new task. Applied to a timeline-based HTN planner generating multi-robot pick-and-place plans, the learned model predicts the planner's decision 85\% of the time, with almost an order of magnitude speedup; evaluating its top $k$ choices before deciding brings accuracy to nearly 100\% while still substantially reducing search time.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

6t1RDvnoja.title: Learning Coarser Markov State Abstractions
6t1RDvnoja.authors: Fatih Dogangun, Cameron Allen, George Konidaris, Alper Ahmetoglu
6t1RDvnoja.abstract: State abstractions in reinforcement learning create compact representations, and increase sample-efficiency, by keeping information in observations that is relevant for decision-making while discarding other regularities. Recently introduced Markov state abstractions (MSAs) define reward-free sufficient conditions under which the learned representation is Markov. However, current implementations of the MSA objectives satisfy a stronger (kinematic inseparability) condition, which results in over-refined abstractions that preserve all transition regularities in the observation. We show for the first time how to align the training objective with the original theoretical MSA conditions and thus build coarser abstractions. This objective drives the representation to satisfy sufficient Markov conditions, but does not, by itself, guarantee minimality. We therefore provide an additional heuristic to push the representation towards minimality. Our experiments in pixel-based domains show that the learned abstractions recover the underlying complexity of the problem, which improves downstream performance.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

eOc1MqyEV8.title: Learning Dexterous Action Representations from Human Videos
eOc1MqyEV8.authors: Hongyi Zhou, Maximilian Arnold, Mohamed Omran, Pietro Mazzaglia, Rudolf Lioutikov, Daniel Dijkman
eOc1MqyEV8.abstract:
We introduce DexVAE, a latent action representation pretrained on human motion that transfers dexterous motion priors from egocentric human videos to robot policies. 
Although dexterous robot hands promise human-like manipulation, learning to control them requires large and costly robot datasets. Human videos provide dexterous experience at scale, but differences in morphology and action spaces prevent their direct use for robot control. DexVAE bridges this gap by compressing temporally extended hand trajectories, expressed in a shared canonical representation, into compact latent action tokens. We transfer knowledge through a staged pipeline consisting of human-motion pretraining followed by human–robot co-training. We adapt a pretrained VLA model to generate actions in this latent space using flow matching. 
We evaluate our approach on six real-world manipulation tasks using a Unitree H1-2 humanoid with dexterous hands. With only 25 robot demonstrations per task, our method improves average task progression from $38.5\%$ to $49.1\%$, with the largest gain on high-dexterity tasks—from $35.7\%$ to $58.6\%$. Overall, DexVAE matches the raw-action baseline using $1/2$ the robot data and, on high-dexterity tasks, outperforms it using only $1/4$ the data.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

Y3Mn29j1aC.title: Learning Generative Motion Manifolds for World Models
Y3Mn29j1aC.authors: Renhao Zhang, Bruno Castro da Silva
Y3Mn29j1aC.abstract: We introduce Parameterized Latent Motions for Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (PaLMR), a framework that learns generative motion manifolds as reusable action interfaces for world models. From task-independent motion experience, PaLMR learns behavior-aligned latent coordinates and a parameterized flow model for executing and interpolating motions. The learned interface remains fixed during model-based RL, providing shared coordinates for predicting motion outcomes and composing motion sequences. We establish conditions for predictive generalization and show how denser motion coverage tightens planning-error bounds, supported by controlled experiments demonstrating more accurate prediction and effective use of interpolated motions. Across navigation and robotic manipulation benchmarks, PaLMR outperforms primitive-action and generative-policy RL baselines in overall task performance and online sample efficiency.
keywords: Model-Based Reinforcement Learning; Skill Discovery; Flow Matching Policy
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

LuxsPk6Zvg.title: Learning to Drive on Mars: Visual Multimodal Traversability Estimation for Off-World Navigation
LuxsPk6Zvg.authors: Darren Chiu, Cole Wilson, Andrei Tumbar, Gaurav S. Sukhatme, Steven Myint
LuxsPk6Zvg.abstract: Autonomous navigation on Mars requires vehicles to distinguish between traversable terrains across diverse and visually challenging environments. However, progress in learning-based navigation for off-world environments has been limited by the lack of large-scale datasets. Since landing in Jezero Crater, the Mars 2020 Perseverance rover has traversed terrain ranging from sandy dunes, rocky patches, and flat bedrocks. As a result, this paper presents a dataset spanning 500 sols and 45km of trajectories driven by both human operators and the onboard planner, ENav. Our dataset contains grayscale stereo image pairs, poses, accelerometer readings, rocker-bogie angles, and estimates of tilt and wheel slip. Building on this dataset, we introduce an uncertainty-aware traversability-estimation framework that learns terrain representations from multimodal driving experience. We compare our proposed method against existing approaches on the Mars 2020 dataset and show that our method achieves an AUROC of 0.874 and an F1 score of 0.758, outperforming the strongest baseline by 0.058 and 0.156, respectively, while also achieving the highest average precision and recall. Finally, we show that the visual representations can be integrated into path planners, such as ENav, on a physical rover test bed.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

HoSt0Ayish.title: LeWAM: A JEPA World Action Model with Diffusion-Steering-Based MPC
HoSt0Ayish.authors: Shashank Hegde, Alexander Popov, Elie Aljalbout, Nikolai Smolyanskiy
HoSt0Ayish.abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict actions and future observations, typically from a reconstruction-based representation that carries noisy, redundant information which can complicate downstream predictions. We introduce LeWAM, a bidirectional transformer for forward, backward, inverse dynamics and policy prediction, on a decoder-free JEPA latent trained end-to-end through all four modes. We see the following benefits. 1) Alignment: linear probing better reads robot and object state over a regular Le World Model (a forward-only JEPA world model), while successfully ignoring distractors, which a regular WAM considerably reconstructs. 2) Acting: Closed-loop evaluations of LeWAM match or exceeds a regular policy (without a world model) on the same encoder and at matched size. 3) Planning: While sampling raw actions in planning with WAMs allows MPC to exploit dynamic model inaccuracies, we show that planning in the noise space of these WAMs improves their closed-loop performance.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

ZjQmIjxoOQ.title: Matryoshka World Models: Test-Time Scaling Beyond Search
ZjQmIjxoOQ.authors: Jianing Qian, Ethan Yu, Siddharth Ancha, Nicholas Roy, Dinesh Jayaraman
ZjQmIjxoOQ.abstract: Planning with learned world models requires trading off predictive fidelity against computational cost. Existing approaches typically vary search effort while keeping the latent representation fixed, or train separate models for different representation sizes. We introduce Matryoshka World Models (MWM), a framework for training world models to operate at multiple nested predictive fidelities. Unlike independently trained fixed-dimensional models, MWM learns a shared hierarchy of predictive representations that can be truncated or expanded at test time without retraining. This variable-fidelity world model enables a new form of planning-time flexibility: predictive fidelity can change across episode-level replanning steps, CEM optimization iterations, and rollout depth. The planner can therefore allocate high-fidelity computation selectively while using cheaper representations where fine-grained prediction is unnecessary. We evaluate variable-fidelity planning against standard fixed-fidelity planning baselines across navigation and manipulation tasks. MWM matches the success rate of the full-fidelity baseline at up to 108.8$\times$ less compute and exceeds the best baseline by up to 59% at the same compute budget. By making predictive fidelity a resource that can be dynamically allocated across different stages of planning, MWM establishes a new axis of test-time scaling for world models.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

6eF9XQkWQT.title: Memory from Mistakes: Self-Improving Robot Memory through Policy Feedback
6eF9XQkWQT.authors: Sooyoung Ryu, Yinpei Dai, Yuejiang Liu
6eF9XQkWQT.abstract: For long-horizon manipulation, high-level policies are often trained to remember relevant information through textual summaries or visual keyframes. Existing approaches formulate this as supervised learning from fixed memory annotations provided by human experts or LLMs. However, these annotations may be suboptimal: they may omit critical information, specify memory that the policy cannot reliably reproduce, or retain irrelevant content. We introduce MeMi, an offline self-improvement LLM framework for robot memory annotation. At its core are three principles of effective memory: (1) sufficiency, retaining the information needed for future decision-making; (2) predictability, ensuring that the policy can reliably reproduce the annotated memory; and (3) necessity, removing information that does not contribute to downstream decisions. MeMi jointly optimizes a reusable memory annotation rule and the instruction prompt of a high-level LLM policy using textual feedback from evaluating the policy against these principles. Across 16 RoboMME tasks, LLM policies using the optimized instructions improve mean rollout success by 19.9% points with textual memory and 20.9% points with visual keyframes over policies using the initial instructions. Moreover, separate vision-language model (VLM) policies trained on the optimized memory annotations outperform those trained on the initial annotations, demonstrating that the benefits of annotation optimization transfer to a different policy class.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

uXSeu0eVk9.title: MoMa-NMP: Scene-Scale Neural Motion Planning for Mobile Manipulators
uXSeu0eVk9.authors: Adam Kan, Jason Jingzhou Liu, Jim Jiahui Yang, Kenneth Shaw, Deepak Pathak
uXSeu0eVk9.abstract: Mobile manipulators operating in homes and other complex environments must coordinate their base and arm over long horizons, navigating around obstacles, through narrow passages, and between constrained workspaces. Neural motion planners can provide fast closed-loop planning from partial observations, but scaling them to room-sized environments is difficult because generating high-quality training trajectories is itself a challenging motion-planning problem. To address this, we introduce MoMa-DemoSmith, a demonstration-generation pipeline that separates the problem into global path discovery for large complex scenes and local motion refinement for collision avoidance. This key separation enables the generation of millions of challenging whole-body trajectories across our procedurally generated scenes. These demonstrations are used to train MoMa-NMP in two stages: behavior cloning (BC) followed by privileged on-policy distillation. The resulting policy plans from depth-camera and LiDAR observations, achieving 87.0\% success without environment collisions in simulation and 77.5\% across 80 trials in unseen physical scenes. See video results at https://adamhkan.com/moma-nmp/.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

EaFj5ACTKC.title: Normalizing Flows are Capable World Models
EaFj5ACTKC.authors: Zijia Li, Yong-Hyun Park, Jiatao Gu
EaFj5ACTKC.abstract:
We study goal-conditioned planning with world models that preserve
observation information. Normalizing-Flow World Model (NFWM) combines an
invertible encoder with a probabilistic latent predictor. We train both components
jointly by maximizing the exact observation likelihood. An auxiliary inverse-
dynamics objective encourages action-sensitive coordinates. We evaluate candidate
actions directly in latent space using a fixed Euclidean goal-distance cost. NFWM
achieves competitive or improved performance relative to deterministic JEPA-
based baselines on deterministic control, stochastic navigation, and LIBERO action
selection. Ablations show improved planning with inverse-dynamics supervision,
while representation probes provide complementary evidence of more accessible
and locally regular action-related variation. A ranking analysis on LIBERO reveals
a remaining gap between goal distance and task success. These results demonstrate
that information-preserving world models can learn representations useful for
planning.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

AWZAN0VA0q.title: Particle Belief Representations for Reinforcement Learning under Partial Observability
AWZAN0VA0q.authors: Himanshu Gupta, Brendan Crowe, Chris Heckman, Bradley Hayes, Zachary Sunberg
AWZAN0VA0q.abstract:
Particle filters flexibly represent complex, multimodal beliefs but expose them as weighted, unordered sets incompatible with conventional fixed-dimensional policies. We study particle-belief encodings as inputs to reinforcement-learning policies while holding belief estimation and policy optimization fixed. We compare statistical summaries, cumulant-generating-function (CGF) features, and permutation-invariant
set encoders. Trainable encoders are learned end-to-end or pretrained through belief reconstruction or task-specific prediction. Across eight tasks, pooling-based set encoders and gradient CGF features are reliable end-to-end, while the Set Transformer achieves the highest performance with appropriate pretraining. Task-specific pretraining helps when its target captures decision-relevant belief structure, whereas reconstruction and latent alignment provide more selective benefits. These findings provide practical guidance for selecting and training encoders for particle-filter beliefs in continuous-space partially observable Markov decision processes.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)
