jFPFss9lsg.title: Physical Agency: Better Robot Performance Through Better Interfaces
jFPFss9lsg.authors: Liane Galanti, Dhruv Shah, Tri Dao
jFPFss9lsg.abstract: Frontier models increasingly act as robot-use agents, calling a robot's motor skills as tools much as they interact with a browser or code editor. But exposing skills as tools leaves open how the model should use them: what it emits, what feedback it receives, and when it decides again. We study the interface through controlled comparisons with the robot, cameras, scenes, and motor-policy weights held fixed, and separately measure the benefit of adding a complementary frozen skill. We introduce Pigey (Physical Agency), an agent that (1) issues language-level actions one at a time over a persistent task state, (2) uses verified execution, checking post-action images and robot state and recovering when it detects failure, and (3) draws on an open set of skills exposed as tools it selects for each subgoal. No additional policy training or demonstrations are required. On 30 real-robot tasks designed to probe decisions over existing motor skills, the same frozen π0.5 policy succeeds in 16.7% of trials when called directly and 84.0% through Pigey. Adding a frozen motion planner as a second skill raises success to 97.3%. Removing verification and recovery lowers success by 28 percentage points, the largest ablation drop. Gains also hold in simulation and across Claude, Gemini, and Qwen reasoners. Most of what the policy was missing was an interface, not a skill.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

krdSzlzUam.title: Predicting What Matters: interaction-Centric 4D World-Action Models
krdSzlzUam.authors: Luoxin Ye, Baichuan Huang, Kai Gao, Dylan Randle, Jeroen Vanbaar, Alan Yuille, Manikantan Nambi, Jose Barreiros
krdSzlzUam.abstract: Robotic manipulation requires anticipating the evolution of task-relevant entities and translating these predictions into actions. We introduce a compact world-action model that grounds control in functional semantic entities and their 3D motion, without dense RGB reconstruction. A capable System-2 model reasons about task-relevant entities and subtask structure, guiding the construction of dense semantic masks, 3D point tracks, and subtask goals. This structured supervision trains a compact System-1 model to jointly predict goal semantics, interaction-centric scene evolution, and robot actions. By concentrating future prediction on entities and motion that matter for interaction, the model supports reactive control with approximately 0.3B trainable parameters (1.3B total). It achieves a 98.6% success rate on LIBERO and averages 86.0% across seven LIBERO-Plus categories. On real-world dexterous tool use and sequential object removal, it achieves an average success rate of 87.5%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 27.5 percentage points. Controlled ablations examine the choice of future supervision targets and the importance of a capable System-2 model. These results support task-centric semantic and geometric prediction as an effective basis for compact world-action modeling.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

z5p66Kha58.title: Rational Inverse Reasoning: Few-Shot Imitation by Inferring Programmatic Intent through Planning
z5p66Kha58.authors: Ben Zandonati, Tomás Lozano-Pérez, Leslie Pack Kaelbling
z5p66Kha58.abstract: Humans learn a manipulation task from one or two demonstrations, and perform it in a new room, with new objects, under new constraints. This requires identifying which object roles, subgoal orderings, and constraints should persist when the scene changes, as opposed to cloning object motions. We present Rational Inverse Reasoning (RIR), which infers this task structure as an explanation program: a compact, executable description of intent that maps an object-centric scene to a task-and-motion planning (TAMP) specification of goals, subgoals and constraints. This allows the robot to generate new actions for new objects and layouts, while preserving the demonstrator's intent. A vision-language model proposes candidate programs, a planner-derived score evaluates whether each candidate makes the demonstrated behavior rational, relative to alternative strategies. These scores guide iterative program refinement. We evaluate RIR on 30 simulated, and four real-world tabletop tasks (using a Franka FR3), and 35 two-dimensional reasoning tasks. In all cases, RIR recovers transferable task structure from only 1-3 demonstrations. Generalizing to new layouts and object sets, it outperforms VLM, planning and few-shot learning baselines that lack explicit rationality and planning-grounded inference. See our interactive supplementary material and videos: https://rir-project-f3a281.pages.dev
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

6ydZ7SJP4W.title: Remembering What You Don’t Know: Planning with Persistent Identity Beliefs under Perceptual Aliasing
6ydZ7SJP4W.authors: Brendon T. Murphy, Keonyoung Koh, Woobean Seo, Hoseong Kwak, CHUNG HUN HA, Du Hyun Ro
6ydZ7SJP4W.abstract: Robots that share tools with people must preserve object identity across occlusions and unobserved human manipulation, even when multiple instances are visually aliased. We present a persistent identity belief that maintains competing joint entity--observation hypotheses instead of collapsing to a single assignment, augments them with relocation uncertainty after human interaction, and exposes probabilistic identity marginals to a belief-aware planner. The planner chooses between acting on the current belief and inspecting a candidate when the expected cost of disambiguation is lower than the risk of a wrong handover. We evaluate the critical human-intervention event from a closed-loop Allen-key handover task over 99 replayed real episodes. Joint hypotheses and relocation modeling substantially reduce confidently wrong beliefs, while belief-aware planning reduces wrong handovers relative to maximum a posteriori (MAP) action and avoids the fixed overhead of always inspecting. Project page: https://keonyoungkoh.github.io/PIB/
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

ZTGTv7B0Rp.title: Retriever: Composing the Perception-Reasoning-Action Loop for Long-Horizon Manipulation
ZTGTv7B0Rp.authors: Linfeng Zhao, Haojie Huang, Jiayuan Mao, Weiyu Liu, Lawson L.S. Wong, Mykel Kochenderfer
ZTGTv7B0Rp.abstract: Building long-horizon robot agents requires composing closed-loop pipelines for perception, belief update, planning, and control whose components run at different clocks and with variable latency. Today, these systems are often assembled with ad-hoc concurrency and pub/sub conventions that make timing and input-consumption semantics implicit, yielding schedule-dependent behavior that is hard to reproduce, debug, and reuse. Current solutions typically solve parts of this problem at either the algorithmic or the systems layer, but not both. In this work, we propose Retriever, which spans the entire stack: an asynchronous decision model, a programming model, a runtime, and an example closed-loop agent pipeline. Retriever represents an agent as a graph of stateful causal stream functions executed on explicit run clocks. We formalize this view via an asynchronous environment-agent loop over continuous-time streams and show that finite-memory causal policies can be represented by compositions of these operators. Retriever compiles these graphs to multiple backends and provides a deterministic replay contract when consumed inputs, clock/commit traces, and stochastic outputs are logged. We evaluate Retriever through a real-robot case study.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

VWvW5GdIEs.title: RoboRSI: Stable, efficient, and reusable robot self-evolution in complex real-world environments.
VWvW5GdIEs.authors: Zimo Wen, Yijin Chen, Yuxuan Cao, Wendi Chen, Yanwen Zou, Wenye Yu, Fuhang Kuang, Han Xue, Jun Lv, Chuan Wen, Cewu Lu
VWvW5GdIEs.abstract: A generalist robot should not only perform diverse tasks but also improve through experience, turning what it learns during execution into capabilities that later tasks can reuse. Robot agents that act through code can already repair programs from execution feedback, yet it remains a central challenge to organize this experience around the task structure that gives it meaning, so that each repair is attributed to the responsible capability, supported by execution evidence, and validated before it is reused. We introduce RoboRSI, a robot self-improvement system built on Top-Down Skill Refinement (TSR). TSR decomposes tasks into compound, atomic, and base skills with scoped responsibilities and explicit input--output contracts, attributes each execution outcome to the responsible branch, and confines revision to that branch. Building upon this structure, a Manager, Planner, Engineer, and Reviewer coordinate planning, execution, diagnosis, and the validated release of new skills, while people steer the process through objectives and corrections; stable skill sequences are further consolidated into reusable compound skills. On a mobile manipulator, RoboRSI develops multi-object household cleanup over 104 rounds. In simulation, it achieves the highest success rate on LIBERO, LIBERO-PRO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin, exceeding the strongest baseline by 2.7 to 11.0 percentage points.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

Pk5ogqJbfj.title: SHAPE: Scaling Collaborative Planning in LLM-Powered Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Systems
Pk5ogqJbfj.authors: Hanqing Yang, ZixuanWeng, JunJia Guo, Jingdi Chen, Carlee Joe-Wong
Pk5ogqJbfj.abstract: Planning in heterogeneous robot teams requires agents to coordinate work allocation based on task requirements and their capability compositions. Adding robots to heterogeneous teams can enable concurrent work and combine complementary capabilities, but coordination overhead may limit performance gains. Understanding this trade-off requires distinguishing opportunities within a task from how effectively a planning method uses them. We systematically study how collaboration scales across task configurations, collaboration patterns, and team compositions. We characterize tasks with two measures: parallel participation, which captures opportunities for additional robots to work concurrently; and heterogeneous participation, which captures the need for contributions from different robot types. These measures guide the construction of eight embodied tasks across four configurations and two scenarios. We propose SHAPE (SHared Asynchronous Planning with Evolving tasks), which supports adaptive, asynchronous multi-robot planning through a shared, evolving, agent-built task graph and selective notifications. The graph provides a shared task-level representation that agents update as they plan and execute. We evaluate teams of 3, 9, and 15 robots, comparing SHAPE with Individual, Centralized, and Chain in task performance and coordination overhead. Results highlight a trade-off: shared task understanding and timely agreement support effective collaboration, but synchronization costs can limit scaling. SHAPE achieves higher average completion with lower overhead across scales. A shared-channel ablation examines the role of structured task state, and a case study assesses the effect of grouping robots by type.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

WioPsk5AUH.title: SIR: Structured Image Representations for Explainable Robot Learning
WioPsk5AUH.authors: Paul Mattes, Jan Schwab, Jens Oliver Bosch, Nils Blank, Maximilian Xiling Li, Rudolf Lioutikov
WioPsk5AUH.abstract:
Existing robot policies based on learned visual embed-
dings lack explicit structure and are sensitive to visual dis-
tractions. Thus, the representations that drive their be-
haviour are often opaque, making their decision-making
process difficult to interpret. To address this, we intro-
duce Structured Image Representations (SIR), a method
that leverages Scene Graphs (SGs) as an intermediate rep-
resentation for robot policy learning. Our approach first
constructs a fully connected graph, using image-derived
features as initial node representations. Then, a module
learns to sparsify this graph end-to-end, creating a task-
relevant sub-graph that is passed to the action generation
model. This process makes our model intrinsically explain-
able. Evaluations on RoboCasa show that our sparse graph
policies outperform image-based baselines on average with
19.5% vs 14.81% success rate. Most importantly, we show
that the learned sparse graphs are a powerful tool for model
analysis. By analysing when the model’s sub-graph devi-
ates from human expectation, such as by including distrac-
tor nodes or omitting key objects, we successfully uncover
dataset biases, including spurious correlations and posi-
tional biases.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

2XvNWy8Mnf.title: Structure over Latent Maps: A Neuro-Symbolic World Model for Interactive Object Navigation
2XvNWy8Mnf.authors: Owen Bluman, Maxfield Ma, Thao Nguyen
2XvNWy8Mnf.abstract: Interactive object navigation agents can leverage natural language feedback from users to find personalized goal objects in unseen environments. Existing frameworks such as ORION pair a large language model (LLM) controller with a voxel-level vision-language map, but this mapping carries no explicit notion of rooms or global scene structure. When search stalls, the system falls back to prompting the user with questions. We present a system that layers a symbolic scene graph, built automatically from the robot's own scans and self-supervised object labels, on top of this voxel-level map, enriching the controller's existing retrieval with room membership and nearby-object context. This reduces the agent's dependence on the user: across five independent trials on 10 HM3D scenes, our approach lowers average interaction rounds per goal from 1.93 to 1.72 while raising success weighted by interaction turns from 42.5\% to 53.5\% under mixed feedback and from 39.2\% to 49.8\% under confirmation-only feedback. The scene graph also improves task performance, raising navigation success rate from 63.1\% to 71.1\% under mixed feedback, and from 58.8\% to 67.5\% under confirmation-only feedback, compared to the baseline ORION model. We further compare the automatically constructed graphs against reference graphs built from ground-truth semantic annotations to assess how graph quality affects this improvement.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

nLArgtsCYy.title: Synthesizing Uncertain World Models as Probabilistic Programs for Planning
nLArgtsCYy.authors: Zachary S Siegel, Xianda Sun, Nitay Alon, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, Tomás Lozano-Pérez, Leslie Pack Kaelbling
nLArgtsCYy.abstract: How should intelligent agents plan to achieve their goals when they are uncertain about how the world works? We argue that world models should represent this uncertainty so that agents can plan actions that help them learn about the world. Because world models cannot generally anticipate every mechanism of the world, agents must also be able to revise their hypotheses when experience contradicts their model. We propose Planning over Uncertain World Models (PLUM), a system that meets these desiderata by representing its world model as a probabilistic program that it updates through inference, plans over, and revises. PLUM uses a language model to synthesize its programs online without prior demonstrations, revises them within an episode, and uses a belief-space planner to choose actions. Across simple games and a simulated robot task, we show that planning over uncertainty and revising programs each improve reward over ablations without them. PLUM also outperforms the same language model prompted to select actions directly. These results suggest that agents should construct approximate probabilistic models suited to their tasks, plan over the uncertainty those models represent, and revise their hypotheses through interaction.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

znnQvLbsl7.title: TAMPAgent: Agentic Belief-Space Planning for Mobile Manipulation
znnQvLbsl7.authors: Utkarsh Aashu Mishra, Alperen Degirmenci, Yongxin Chen, Danfei Xu, Tucker Hermans, Caelan Reed Garrett
znnQvLbsl7.abstract: Open-world robotic mobile manipulation requires acting in physical environments with only partial information. While recent Large Vision-Language Model (LVLM) agents show strong open-world reasoning capabilities, existing architectures that rely on direct tool calling struggle with geometric uncertainty and thus are limited to fully-observable tabletop environments. In contrast, Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) systems can solve long-horizon tasks under partial observability but incur high computational costs and require closed worlds. We propose \textbf{TAMPAgent}, an agentic planning framework that unifies the reasoning of LVLMs with the structured constraint satisfaction of TAMP systems. We endow an LVLM agent with a belief-space planning model operating over an extensible API of perception, planning, and control tools. The agent formulates a partial task plan composed of parameterized observation and execution actions, which is subsequently completed using classical search algorithms. After extracting the plan's geometric constraints, the agent leverages its tool API to bind valid parameter values, satisfying feasibility requirements and producing an executable motion plan. Upon execution, the agent continuously updates its belief history and repeats this closed-loop process by interleaving observation and manipulation actions. Evaluated across complex household mobile manipulation tasks on Rainbow Y1 and Unitree G1 platforms, TAMPAgent significantly outperforms direct tool-calling agentic baseline, demonstrating that integrating TAMP constraint satisfaction into agentic planning loops is essential for unstructured, partially observable environments. More information: \url{tampagent.github.io}.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

jh4hcshrPS.title: TaskScape: Planner-Guided Difficulty Spectra for Robot Policy Evaluation
jh4hcshrPS.authors: Yan Zhuang, Jiawei Ren, Xuhui Kang, Sung-Wook Lee, Yen-Ling Kuo
jh4hcshrPS.abstract: A central challenge in constructing such evaluations is how to define and measure task difficulty. Existing benchmarks often introduce variations in lighting, obstacle configurations, or robot initial positions. While these variations provide useful robustness tests, their effects on task difficulty is hard to quantify. For example, randomly placed obstacles may block critical paths and require substantial replanning, or may serve as a background object without having impacts on task execution. We observe that planners provide a principled way to estimate task difficulty: given a task abstraction, planning metrics such as solution length and search effort offer measurable difficulty proxies that can guide the generation of progressively challenging tasks. Building on this insight, we introduce TaskScape, an open-source framework for planner-guided evolution of embodied tasks and environments. TaskScape adopts a generator–validator architecture, where a generator proposes task–environment variations and a planner-based validator assesses their feasibility and difficulty. By iteratively accepting variations that satisfy feasibility constraints and increase the targeted difficulty measure, TaskScape constructs progressively challenging evaluation sequences. Its decoupled architecture supports different generators and planners, enabling difficulty evolution across diverse task abstractions and evaluation objectives.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

QQFq2HGyGl.title: Toward Planning Representations That Separate Task Structure from Visual Content
QQFq2HGyGl.authors: Aarav Srivastava, Vishwas Sathish, Rajesh P. N. Rao
QQFq2HGyGl.abstract:
Effective planning requires representations that preserve task-relevant geometry and object identity while ignoring visual variation that does not alter the task.
Existing evaluations of visual generalization often change several factors simultaneously, making the source of a failure difficult to identify.
We introduce a controlled evaluation of object-goal navigation (ObjectNav), the task of reaching an instance of a named object category, in procedurally generated ProcTHOR houses. Training and evaluation houses share floor plans, object locations, goals, and start states, while visual factors are changed individually or in combination.
Across model-free reinforcement learning (RL), model-based RL, and agents using frozen pretrained visual representations, our results show that appearance changes impair navigation, but their effects differ sharply by factor.
Surface-material changes account for most of the average change in success, whereas clutter and lighting have little effect.
The magnitude of a global image-statistics shift does not reliably predict performance: changing only the goal object's appearance can substantially impair an end-to-end agent despite a small image-level change.
We found that a model-based agent that plans over frozen features from the pretrained DINOv2 image encoder achieves the highest success (0.83) under the full shift, but remains sensitive to surface appearance.
Our experiments reveal an important requirement for planning representations: they must separate invariant spatial task structure from appearance.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

eLTh89JM1i.title: Unifying Deep Predicate Invention with Pre-trained Foundation Models
eLTh89JM1i.authors: Qianwei Wang, Bowen Li, Zhanpeng Luo, Yifan Xu, Vineet Kamat, Carol Menassa, Alexander G. Gray, Tom Silver, Sebastian Scherer, Katia P. Sycara, Yaqi Xie
eLTh89JM1i.abstract: Long-horizon robot planning requires abstractions that are both grounded in observations and useful for choosing actions. Foundation models provide semantic priors for proposing symbolic predicates, but their proposals can be inconsistent with a robot's environment. Learning predicates from demonstrations grounds them in data, yet searching for their symbolic effects is expensive. We present UniPred, which combines these approaches through an iterative loop: a language model proposes predicate effects, neural classifiers learn from the resulting transition constraints, and validation feedback guides subsequent proposals. A derived-aware selection procedure then evaluates predicates for planning while recomputing quantified conditions from basic atoms. Across five simulated and two real-robot domains, the resulting abstractions support generalization to new object configurations and longer tasks. UniPred reduces total learning time by approximately $3$–$4\times$ relative to IVNTR in three shared simulated domains. On held-out real-image planning tasks, it achieves $92\%$ and $98\%$ success in table cleaning and cluttered retrieval. These results support combining foundation-model priors with data-grounded evaluation to learn task-relevant symbolic world models.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

Z5ZdkoxJyq.title: UniWALM: Unified World Action Language Model for Embodied Robot Control
Z5ZdkoxJyq.authors: Rahul Sajnani, Diego Romeres, Mingyuan Zhang, Kai Gao, Carl Qi, Baichuan Huang, Srinath Sridhar, Dylan Randle, Lillian J. Ratliff, Jose Barreiros, Manikantan Nambi, Jeroen Vanbaar
Z5ZdkoxJyq.abstract: We introduce UniWALM, a unified world-action-language model in which the policy itself produces three learned, in-loop abstractions inside a single mixture-of-transformers backbone: (i) generated language that emits, at every control step, a subtask (what to do next) and a textual memory (what has been done so far), re-consumed as the prompt on the next step; (ii) a task-completion channel that signals subtask boundaries and gates when the textual memory is updated; (iii) a visual-memory anchor frame that preserves past visual context after occlusion. All three are co-denoised with video and action by per-modality diffusion heads in one forward pass, with no external VLM, planner, or retrieval buffer. Together they give the policy a learned plan, memory, and decision boundary, replacing the hand-specified keyframes, retrieval buffers, and within-step chain-of-thought that prior memory-augmented policies rely on. We study: (i) does this generated-language abstraction improve manipulation? and (ii) does it drive memory-dependent tasks such as counting button presses, trial-and-error ordering, and recovering hidden objects? On MolmoSpaces, UniWALM leads the three compositional Pick&Place variants, improving over FastWAM by +13.4% on average. On RMBench's memory-dependent M(n) subset (Press Button, Blocks Ranking Try, Cover Blocks, Battery Try) UniWALM reaches 34.5% without any pretrained language or reasoning model, +21.2 points over same-backbone FastWAM (13.3%), and above Mem-0's keyframe-equipped setup (28.5%) using a single anchor frame instead of per-task privileged keyframes. On a real-world Find-the-Item task, textual memory lifts success from 11.1% (FastWAM, no language) to 61.1%, while VLA and WAM baselines stay at or below chance.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

RcljTi36NQ.title: Watch, Infer, Coordinate: Inferring Robot Partner Constraints for Zero-Shot Coordination
RcljTi36NQ.authors: Suyu Ye, Zheyuan Zhang, Vaishnav Tadiparthi, Hossein Nourkhiz Mahjoub, Ehsan Moradi Pari, Tianmin Shu, Homanga Bharadhwaj, Nakul Agarwal
RcljTi36NQ.abstract: Robots operating in the physical world will increasingly need to coordinate with other robots, particularly in manipulation tasks where an object may be too large or heavy for a single robot to carry alone. Physical limitations caused by hardware degradation or actuator faults can restrict the actions a robot can reliably execute, yet these limitations may be unknown to its partner. We study whether a helper can infer a robot partner's physical constraints from observing it coordinate with another robot, then use the inferred capability to coordinate with the same partner on a new task. This is difficult because a demonstration shows what the constrained robot did, but not what it could have done. In physically coupled tasks, the other robot may also compensate for its limitations, making those limitations difficult to identify from the constrained robot's behavior alone. Our key insight is that these constraints shape the joint behavior of the team, making the actions of both robots informative about the constrained partner’s capability. We introduce Watch, Infer, Coordinate, a benchmark spanning three physically coupled manipulation settings, together with an inference approach that scores candidate constraints using observed joint behavior. Across all three settings, our method substantially improves constraint inference and zero-shot coordination, approaching an oracle with access to the true constraints.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

jxMdDMGtHJ.title: What If? Counterfactual Simulation for Sample-Efficient Visual Reward Learning
jxMdDMGtHJ.abstract: Pretrained visual robot reward models capture generic notions of task success, not necessarily a person's specific preferences for how their task should be done. The robot can learn these preferences from user demonstrations, but with only a few demonstrations, a reward model may latch onto spurious correlations without learning what the person actually wants. To better express their preferences, a person could directly specify a preference axis—or an aspect of the task that they care about—in language. But a language-conditioned reward model may still reward the wrong behavior when training demonstrations don't fully cover the entire preference axis. Our key idea is to use the person's instruction to cover this axis by imagining what they don't want. We introduce COVER, which uses a video world model to generate counterfactual trajectories: alternatives that are not preferred along the preference axis but keep the rest of the behavior and scene the same. Comparing the original demonstration against its counterfactual isolates the quality that should make the reward different, without asking the person to demonstrate both versions. We train the reward to score each demonstration higher than its corresponding counterfactual, alongside learning from the demonstrations directly. Across four simulated and two real-robot tasks, COVER learns rewards that capture user preferences better than language-conditioned baselines under the same demonstration budgets, matching the strongest baseline's accuracy with up to 10× fewer demonstrations. On a real robot, selecting training demonstrations with these rewards yields policies that follow both stated preferences of each task more closely than training on unfiltered demonstrations.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

cW6YVaGb73.title: Where Should a Skill End? Discovering Skills from How the Robot's Action Moves Objects
cW6YVaGb73.abstract: Bottom-up skill discovery segments demonstrations into reusable skills for planning, but where a segment should end and how many skills a task has remain open questions. Existing methods place segment boundaries at changes in pretrained visual embeddings or robot motion, with the number of skills fixed a priori or chosen by likelihood-based model selection. We argue that, in manipulation, a skill is a recurring effect of the robot's action on objects, and a segment boundary marks a change in that effect. The number of skills should follow out-of-sample prediction: two candidate skills merge when one effect model predicts held-out demonstrations within a region of practical equivalence of two. Discovery should be evaluated jointly by held-out prediction, cross-demonstration consistency and agreement with annotated boundaries, since a timing prior alone already agrees well with annotation. We instantiate this position with a label-free method that fits switched linear models of object motion given the gripper's motion and aligns each task's demonstrations to a shared transcript. On real-robot demonstrations with a parallel gripper and a five-finger hand, its boundaries reach an F1 of 0.85 at a 1 s tolerance on the gripper tasks without observing gripper events, and it recovers about the annotated number of segments, whereas likelihood-based criteria double it. Whether an object follows the gripper explains most of this agreement, while merging determines which effects warrant separate skills. Effect models learned on other tasks also segment held-out tasks without refitting.
workshops: 4th CoRL Workshop on Learning Effective Abstractions for Planning (LEAP)

aRnYWh9YDW.title: $k$-WM: Predicting $k$ Steps at Once for Long-Horizon Planning with World Models
aRnYWh9YDW.authors: Xiaole Alex Jiang, Yinuo Wang, Lerrel Pinto, Yann LeCun, Gaoyue Zhou
aRnYWh9YDW.abstract: Latent world models enable goal-conditioned optimization at test time, but in practice planning success remains limited to short horizons, and gradient-based planners driven by autoregressive rollouts still underperform sampling-based methods. We attribute this to two properties of next-step prediction: autoregressive rollouts compound errors, and planning gradients must traverse a chain of nested model calls. We introduce $k$-WM, a minimal extension to transformer-based JEPA world models whose multi-horizon training objective and input layout let the predictor map an action sequence to the future latent states in a single forward pass. Across three classes of JEPA world models and four environments, $k$-WM improves gradient-based planning by 37\% and sampling-based planning by 15\% over the next-step world models it extends, and reduces long-horizon inference cost. The gains cannot be explained by parallel rollout alone: they persist under autoregressive inference and coincide with substantial changes in the learned representation. Videos are available at https://anon-k-wm.github.io.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

w5njU39M9b.title: ActiveAlign: Aligning Egocentric Manipulation via Active Perception
w5njU39M9b.authors: Ri-Zhao Qiu, Bowen Wen, Yifeng Jiang, Chen Tessler, Eric Heiden, Xue Bin Peng, Xiaolong Wang, Stan Birchfield, Erwin Coumans
w5njU39M9b.abstract: Real-to-Sim-to-Real (Real2Sim2Real) enables structured world representations for planning, interpretability, and safe execution. Most existing approaches rely on passive perception, which creates gaps in real2sim2real transfer. In contrast, humans perceive actively through actions. Inspired by this observation, we propose ActiveAlign, a framework that leverages active perception to align the Real2Sim2Real gap from active robot interactions. ActiveAlign introduces two complementary modules: (i) ActiveAlign-Waving, which performs hand-eye calibration by exploiting active hand motions and differentiable rendering, and (ii) ActiveAlign-Touching, which refines object alignment through tactile feedback to achieve millimeter-level precision. Together, these capabilities enable simulation representations accurate to millimeter scale or calibrating unknown cameras on open-sourced datasets. We demonstrate that ActiveAlign-Waving can be used to curate simulation environment of open-sourced uncalibrated robot manipulation datasets, and demonstrate on a real Unitree G1 robot that ActiveAlign enables fine manipulation of millimeter-scale objects such as pressing buttons and moving sliders.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

TuauQxZrHE.title: ACTS: Learning Visuo-TactileWorld Models from Human Physical Interaction
TuauQxZrHE.authors: Yuxiang Ma, Weihan Xu, Pengfei YE, Anna Mei, Yuxin Ray Song, Tingle Li, Haonan Chen, Edward H Adelson
TuauQxZrHE.abstract:
Action-conditioned world models for contact-rich manipulation must learn how
contact forms and breaks as the applied force changes, yet they are mostly trained
on robot teleoperation, which is slow and gives the operator little force
feedback. We train ACTS, a visuo-tactile world model,
only on human interaction. Operators move handheld GelSight sensors over three
objects while we record scene and wrist video, tactile images, 6-DoF sensor
poses, and tactile-estimated normal force; the resulting dataset, React, spans
4.9 hours. Each action is defined at the sensor as its relative motion plus a
displacement proportional to the change in normal force, so a human hand and a
robot arm carrying the sensor share one action space. On held-out human data,
ACTS improves scene-view PSNR by 0.7--2.0\,dB over two visuo-tactile world
models trained on the same data. Applied to robot teleoperation without
fine-tuning, its predicted tactile imprints appear and disappear with the
recorded contact, while its wrist-view predictions blur or add structure that
is not in the scene. Videos: https://acts-anon.github.io/.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

fJfSDfwY4U.title: Branching Fidelity: Do World Models Branch Where Physics Does?
fJfSDfwY4U.abstract:
World models for manipulation are usually judged by average prediction error or by the task success of policies trained or planned with them, yet
picking from a stack, pushing a tall object or inserting a peg can succeed or fail on
a few millimetres of error in the start or the action. We call a state whose futures,
sampled over the robot’s own small errors, split into separate outcomes a fork,
and propose the fork probe to evaluate a world model’s branching ﬁdelity: does it
branch where physics branches? With a physics engine as the upper reference, the
probe catches 88% of forks with 9% false alarms. In an example evaluation, two
world models with similar average error, 3–4× lower than predicting that nothing
moves, differ sharply: a stochastic one catches 18% of forks, a deterministic one
60%, and 72% with uncertain starts. The probe’s split test also curates training
data: oversampling the rare branches it ﬁnds lifts the deterministic model from
72 to 82% of forks. Finally, in rigid-body tasks where one branch is irreversible,
a fork marks the edge of the safe set, so the probe doubles as a label-free safety
signal, much as people judge a stack precarious by imagining it fall.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

cDazPj3tcm.title: CableTac: Scalable Visuo-Tactile Learning for Cable Routing
cDazPj3tcm.authors: Zhuo Chen, Jie Xu, Elie Aljalbout, Yixuan Wang, Alperen Degirmenci, Fabio Ramos, Yashraj Narang, Iretiayo Akinola
cDazPj3tcm.abstract: Cable routing requires reasoning about both global cable geometry and local contact interactions, yet collecting large-scale visuo-tactile robot data is expensive. We present CableTac, a simulation and learning framework for scalable visuo-tactile cable manipulation. CableTac combines GPU-accelerated cable dynamics, general-purpose tactile simulation, and a full-scale replica of the ManipulationNet cable-routing benchmark. A demonstration-reuse engine expands 10 human demonstrations into more than 1,000 simulated trajectories, which we use to pretrain diffusion policies before reinforcement-learning post-training. Across three routing tasks, we find that policy performance improves with increasing amounts of generated data, while the value of tactile feedback is task dependent: tactile sensing provides little benefit for unconstrained round-peg routing, but improves success by 4.7 and 8.0 percentage points for Y- and U-clip insertion, where local contact is critical. RL post-training further improves success to 88.7% and 92.0% on Y- and U-clip routing. These results establish CableTac as a scalable testbed for studying when and how tactile feedback benefits linear-deformable-object manipulation.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

SShpr1qMfl.title: CLAW: Continuous Latent Action World Models via Adversarial Regularization
SShpr1qMfl.authors: Tewodros W. Ayalew, Samuel Wheeler, Matthew Jeung, Xiao Zhang, Andre de la Cruz Arce, Kaylene Caswell Stocking, Michael Maire, Matthew Walter
SShpr1qMfl.abstract: We introduce CLAW, an end-to-end framework for learning continuous latent actions and a predictive world model from action-free video. CLAW uses reciprocal supervision to jointly learn the latent action model and world model, with adversarial regularization preventing the latent from taking the shortcut of encoding the future frame rather than the action. The learned latent actions support imitation learning, model-based planning, cross-context action transfer, and real-robot pretraining. Across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, CLAW achieves strong overall performance.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

VqqILc2b1e.title: Constraint prioritization for world model planning
VqqILc2b1e.authors: Francisco Roldan Sanchez, Pau de las Heras Molins, David Fridovich-Keil, Georgios Bakirtzis
VqqILc2b1e.abstract: Learned world models enable model-based planning by predicting the consequences of candidate trajectories, but planning becomes challenging when task objectives and constraints conflict. In such settings, planners must determine which requirements to preserve and which to relax, while penalty-based formulations can produce solutions that violate intended priorities depending on the choice of weights. We introduce TierCEM, a variant of the cross-entropy method that incorporates strict constraint priorities directly into elite selection, without requiring per-constraint importance weights, by sequentially filtering candidate trajectories according to their constraint priorities. We evaluate TierCEM for planning with a learned world model in contact-rich pushing, showing that changing constraint priorities changes which requirements are violated under conflict.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

QVvS7Z2bQh.title: ContactWorld: What Representations Matter for Vision-Tactile Latent World Models in Contact-Rich Manipulation
QVvS7Z2bQh.authors: Zhiyuan Zhang, Pokuang Zhou, Kaidi Zhang, Adeesh Desai, Temitope Ibrahim Amosa, Davood Soleymanzadeh, Jiuzhou Lei, Yuhao Zhou, Minghui Zheng, Yu She
QVvS7Z2bQh.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation poses a fundamental challenge for world models: visual and tactile observations capture different aspects of physical interaction, and their utility depends critically on how this information is represented. We introduce ContactWorld, a controlled benchmark and empirical study of vision-tactile representations across 12 contact-rich manipulation tasks. Using a fixed world-model architecture, training procedure, and planning framework, we examine representation effects through three complementary properties: spatial fidelity, motion coherence, and predictive stability. Point clouds preserve task-relevant geometry and track physical motion more reliably than image observations, helping explain their higher average planning success of 32.1%, compared with 20.7% and 22.0% for wrist- and front-view RGB, respectively. Tactile observations generally reduce long-horizon prediction-error accumulation, but these gains do not translate uniformly into task success. Structured tactile force fields provide the most consistent downstream improvements, with PointCloud+TacFF achieving the highest overall simulated success rate of 36.1%. We further validate these trends through 900 physical trials spanning six tasks, two robot platforms, and three tactile sensing systems. Together, ContactWorld identifies sensory representation as a central design factor in vision-tactile world models and provides empirical guidance for predictive planning in contact-rich manipulation.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

E8268t87nn.title: Data-Free Continual Learning for World Action Model with Rectified Generative Replay
E8268t87nn.authors: Kaipeng Fang, Hangxu Liu, Chaojian Shi, Yunsong Zhou, Jingkuan Song, Lianli Gao
E8268t87nn.abstract: World action models (WAMs) built on pretrained video generation models adapt quickly to new robotic tasks, but they forget previously learned tasks under sequential fine-tuning. Experience replay (ER) mitigates forgetting by rehearsing data of previous tasks, yet this data is often unavailable in robotics, where a policy is deployed as weights only and its training data is not shared along with it. In this work, we ask whether a WAM can achieve data-free continual learning by regenerating its own past. We observe that a WAM can indeed autoregressively regenerate complete rollouts of previously learned tasks and replay them to mitigate forgetting, yet such raw rollouts still lag far behind real data for two reasons: the WAM is unable to recognize task completion and keeps generating purposeless motion after the task is done, and under open-loop generation the generated actions gradually drift away from the generated observations. To address both issues, we present rectified generative replay (R$^2$-WAM), which truncates generated rollouts at task completion with an agentic evaluator and filters out rollouts whose actions are physically inconsistent with the observations. On the four LIBERO suites and five real-world tasks, R$^2$-WAM reduces forgetting by over 90% relative to sequential fine-tuning and nearly matches ER without accessing any data from previous tasks. Our analysis further reveals that forgetting in WAMs concentrates in inverse dynamics modeling: a forgotten WAM still produces visually plausible observations of previous tasks while its generated actions fail.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

Bsr5qDMoJy.title: Decomposing Residual Dynamics to Identify Nonlinear Mechanisms
Bsr5qDMoJy.authors: Sriya Karambor Chakravarty, A. Wicks, Simon Stepputtis
Bsr5qDMoJy.abstract: Physics-informed system identification must balance built-in structure against learning. Hybrid models do this by pairing an analytical prior with a learned correction,  but it is rarely clear what the learned correction captures. To address this problem, we introduce PARSE (Physics-Anchored Residual Slot Encoding), which subtracts a single-mode linear prior from frequency responses measured at several drive levels and decomposes the complex residual with slots that compete for frequency lines. Features read from the slots around each mode are used to detect a nonlinearity, characterize its mechanism and localize the mode that carries it. On simulated systems with one to four degrees of freedom and cubic stiffening, dead-band clearance or Jenkins friction, PARSE reaches a balanced accuracy of 0.74, against 0.31 for a direct FRF classifier that has no model of the structure.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

9fpJFJqOV3.title: DefFlow: Goal-Conditioned Deformable Object Manipulation using 3D Point Flows
9fpJFJqOV3.authors: Gaurav Singh, Sergio Orozco, Ryan Duong, Mete Tuluhan Akbulut, George Konidaris, Srinath Sridhar
9fpJFJqOV3.abstract: Manipulating deformable objects toward desired 3D configurations is a fundamental capability for robots operating in unstructured physical environments. However, as the range of possible initial and target configurations grows, goal-conditioned deformable manipulation requires a robot to infer increasingly diverse manipulation behaviors in addition to precise continuous actions. We introduce DefFlow, a framework for goal-conditioned manipulation of deformable objects toward a broad range of 3D configurations. DefFlow learns a “3D World Action Modelling objective” from demonstrations by jointly predicting the goal-conditioned 3D point flow of the robot and deformable scene. We show that this formulation effectively captures both the manipulation decisions, such as when and where to grasp, release, or re-grasp, and the precise continuous motions required for goal reaching. Across rope, granular-media, and cloth manipulation settings with diverse initial and target configurations, DefFlow substantially outperforms goal-conditioned action-prediction and robot-flow-only baselines on success rates and goal-distance metrics.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

guDXS2ATqZ.title: Dexterity from Supervised Play
guDXS2ATqZ.authors: Botao He, Yiming Dou, Yiannis Aloimonos, Jitendra Malik, Akash Sharma, Ruoshi Liu
guDXS2ATqZ.abstract: How can robots autonomously collect the contact-rich experience needed to learn dexterous manipulation? We present DSP: Dexterity from supervised play, a framework in which a robot learns a play policy from minutes of human play through behavior cloning, then deploys it autonomously to collect hours of interaction data to train a world model. During inference, the same play policy then guides model-predictive control (MPC) by proposing candidate action sequences for evaluation under the learned world model. To accelerate inference, we also introduce a method for distilling a closed-loop, goal-conditioned policy through self-play within the learned world model. We evaluate this framework on underactuated pushing and any-to-any in-hand pose reorientation with a multifingered hand, in simulation and real world. In simulated reorientation, our method reaches 91.4% SR@0.6 rad, compared with 53.9% for hindsight behavior cloning; a task-specific PPO operating point reaches 86.7% after about 490× more counted interaction frames. In the reported hardware evaluation, MPC remains within 4.1 percentage points of simulation at all three thresholds. These results demonstrate that supervised play can autonomously collect interaction data, guide model-based planning, and enable policy learning without task-specific demonstrations.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

5dVWzPpmVP.title: DiagGen: Agentic Generation of Deformable Assets with Sim-based Diagnostics for Robotic Simulation
5dVWzPpmVP.authors: Guanxiong Chen, Yiduo Qu, Qianjun Xia, Pengyu Jing, Yixian Cheng, Bole Ma, Pengzhi Yang, Bingyang Zhou, Ziming Li, Shashwat Suri, Gongbo Sun, Chao Liu, Peter Yichen Chen, Ziqiu Zeng, Fan Shi
5dVWzPpmVP.abstract: While simulation-ready deformable assets are essential for in-silico robotic manipulation tasks, existing generation frameworks typically assess physical plausibility after generation, leaving an object's simulated response unused as feedback for repairing upstream errors. We present DiagGen, an agentic framework that turns a single in-the-wild image into a simulation-ready deformable asset through a generate--simulate--diagnose--refine loop. DiagGen constructs part-aware geometry and material parameters, then uses a VLM (vision-language model)-based agent to select semantically informative regions, probe them in a physics simulator, observe material responses, and route evidence-backed repair cues to the responsible generation stage. Experiments on 40 assets show that diagnostics provides useful repair cues and can moderately improve the quality of generated deformable assets. Finally, we show that unlike assets generated from visual foundation models which may not be simulatable, DiagGen-generated deformables can be directly dropped into a high-fidelity physical simulator for the planning and simulation of contact-rich pick-and-place tasks. The project's website is https://diaggen.github.io/.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

8y3HdoXk8H.title: Do Better Videos Mean Better Robot Control? Offline Checkpoint Selection for Video-Action Models
8y3HdoXk8H.authors: Jessie Li, Isar Meijer, Carl Brander, Liam Achenbach, Marc Pollefeys, Oier Mees
8y3HdoXk8H.abstract:
Recent video-action models build robot policies on pretrained genera-
tive video backbones fine-tuned on robot videos, using their internal representa-
tions as predictive features for action decoding. Yet visually plausible predictions
provide limited evidence about which representations will support effective con-
trol. We investigate whether interaction-relevant information accessible in video
activations helps explain downstream policy quality. We introduce Contact Gain,
an offline metric that uses simulator contact labels to measure how much video
activations improve future-contact prediction beyond an observed-input probe, en-
abling checkpoint selection before training a separate action decoder for every
candidate. Across fine-tuning checkpoint sweeps of two video-model families in
two simulators, MolmoSpaces and RoboCasa, Contact Gain tracks downstream
policy success and identifies a checkpoint with the highest observed success in
each sweep, while training loss and Fréchet Video Distance are less reliable for
checkpoint selection. Perturbing contact-associated activations also produces sub-
stantially larger changes in predicted actions than matched random perturbations,
connecting the information accessible in video representations to action predic-
tion.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

d9auTZxYvS.title: DoomShift: How Much Adaptation Do World Models Need Under Domain Shift?
d9auTZxYvS.authors: Rohan Nagabhirava, Keerthana Chirumamilla, Changliu Liu
d9auTZxYvS.abstract: World models have become capable simulators, but they are evaluated almost exclusively on held-out rollouts from the domain they were trained on. A small domain shift, such as a new map of the same game, lighting, textures or enemies, can make their outputs drift even when the underlying physics and game engine are unchanged. With DoomShift, a controlled version of this shift in Doom, we measure what breaks and how much adaptation is needed to repair it. We train three diffusion backbones, initialized from pretrained diffusion image models, on four Doom maps and evaluate them on 13 unseen maps. All three preserve their response to controls but fail to reproduce the new scene: scene PSNR drops by 2.8–3.3 dB and LPIPS rises by 0.126–0.145 across the three backbones. This consistent gap shows that action-conditioned behavior transfers more reliably than scene appearance, independent of architecture or model scale. Yet the lost appearance is relatively cheap to recover: rank-16 adapters trained on only eight episodes with 2% of the original training updates recover 72–76% of the LPIPS rise and about half of the lost PSNR. Together, these results suggest that adapting a world model to a new environment may require restoring the scene's appearance rather than relearning the underlying game.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

JrkcpyQWy6.title: DROID-3D: Lifting Large-Scale Teleoperation Data into Robot-Grounded Metric 3D
JrkcpyQWy6.authors: Jai Bardhan, Josef Sivic, Vladimir Petrik
JrkcpyQWy6.abstract: Learned world models for manipulation are trained almost entirely on RGB video, yet the quantities that matter for control, such as metric distances and where the arm is relative to an object, are inherently 3D. Large real-world teleoperation datasets record geometry only as a byproduct of collection, at a quality too low for supervision. We present DROID-3D, a robot-grounded metric 3D version of DROID covering $71{,}100$ episodes from $28$ robots in $13$ labs, with dense metric depth for all three stereo cameras and extrinsics in the robot's base frame. It combines learned stereo depth with one joint factor graph per robot, which renders the URDF into each view as a kinematic anchor and pools all of the robot's episodes to identify its hand-eye transform and joint-encoder offsets alongside per-scene extrinsics. Compared with a PointWorld-like per-scene calibration baseline, DROID-3D lowers the median external-camera reprojection error from $5.84$ to $0.25\,\mathrm{px}$ and the robot depth error from $111$ to $14\,\mathrm{mm}$, and on a replicated rig it recovers extrinsics to within $4.9\,\mathrm{mm} / 0.39^\circ$ of ChArUco ground truth. Used as an additional prediction target, DROID-3D depth improves the RGB predictions of a video world model by $+1.48\,\mathrm{dB}$ PSNR.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

kgiBog3R4w.title: EgoPhys: Physics-Informed Digital Twins for Deformable Objects from Egocentric Video
kgiBog3R4w.authors: Hyunjin Kim, Ri-Zhao Qiu, Rocktim Jyoti Das, Guangqi Jiang, Dinesh Manocha, Xiaolong Wang
kgiBog3R4w.abstract: Predicting how deformable objects respond to manipulation from unconstrained visual observations remains challenging. We present EgoPhys, a framework for constructing predictive deformable physical twins from a single egocentric RGB interaction. EgoPhys combines persistent correspondences with monocular 3D observations to identify a sequence-specific spring--mass model, with adaptations for manipulation coupling, support contact, and thin-object dynamics under moving-camera observations. Since short interactions weakly constrain local properties, EgoPhys learns a compact state-conditioned residual that predicts bounded stiffness corrections and remains frozen at test time. EgoPhys improves held-out future prediction over an adapted deformable-twin baseline, while its structured residual further improves independently identified twins, including unseen instances. The resulting predictive models also support deformable-object planning, with representative open-loop robot executions.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

Xzw0q6xbUx.title: FACT: Failure-Aware Causal Training for World‑Action Models
Xzw0q6xbUx.authors: Quanquan Peng, Yutong Liang, Rui Yan, Nicklas Hansen, Xiaolong Wang
Xzw0q6xbUx.abstract: Recent world-action models (WAMs) show that co-training policies with future prediction can provide physical priors for action generation. Building on the future-prediction ability of video models, many WAMs generate future videos and recover actions with inverse-dynamics models, or use these predicted videos as goal conditions for action generation. In both cases, the world model is trained mostly on successful demonstrations and has little reason to predict the consequences of bad actions. We introduce FACT, a causal World-Action Model that predicts future video and task progress conditioned on the candidate action. This action-conditioned interface allows failure rollouts to supervise action consequences, turning bad actions into valid future targets rather than being discarded. Failure-aware training makes the progress predictor aware of both successful and failed action outcomes, which can optionally be used to score sampled action candidates at inference. Extensive experiments on simulation and real-world bimanual manipulation tasks show that FACT improves policy success when failure data are incorporated into training, and reduces success-biased future hallucination under bad actions.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

4LCGyDUVpt.title: Few-Shot Residual Adaptation of Pretrained Latent World Models
4LCGyDUVpt.authors: Jakub Suliga, Pankhuri Vanjani, Nisarga Nilavadi, Wolfram Burgard, Rudolf Lioutikov
4LCGyDUVpt.abstract: Pretrained latent world models support visual planning, but their predictions can fail when physical dynamics change at deployment. We adapt such models from a few interactions without modifying their weights or identifying the changed physical parameters. We introduce a few-shot residual adaptation approach that learns self-supervised corrections from latent prediction errors that act both inside the frozen predictor and on its output. We evaluate the approach in simulation and on a real robot under center-of-mass and friction shifts. These dynamic changes reduce the success of the frozen model to near zero. After three interaction episodes on a real robot, our dual-site approach recovers 90\% success under the center-of-mass shift and 100\% under modified friction, and it outperforms single-site adaptation. Our diagnostics suggest that much of the correction reduces a general prediction mismatch, while control also depends on shift-specific information captured during adaptation.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

0gR9IYOCfs.title: FORM: Identifying Material Laws from Robot Interaction for Deformable Object Manipulation
0gR9IYOCfs.authors: Stepan Tretiakov, Ruihan Zhao, Cheng-Hsi Hsiao, Xingjian Li, Adam Thorpe, Hassan Iqbal, Sandeep P. Chinchali, Ufuk Topcu, Krishna Kumar
0gR9IYOCfs.abstract: Hybrid world models that combine neural networks with physics simulation can help robots manipulate deformable objects, but they require the object's material law, which is usually unknown. We present FORM, which identifies deformable material laws through physical interaction. FORM uses weak-form momentum balance to reduce identification to a linear least-squares problem over analytic or learned basis functions. The recovered model transfers directly to an MPM simulator for prediction and planning under new actions and geometries. In simulation, FORM is competitive with baselines at a fraction of their cost. On a real Franka Panda, models identified from a separate probing interaction enable open-loop shaping of unseen deformable specimens and target-volume pouring.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

UmNvW45IvN.title: GeomVLA: Unifying Scene, Motion, and Action in 3D
UmNvW45IvN.authors: Ziyin Xiong, Nikolaos Gkanatsios, Moritz Reuss, Katerina Fragkiadaki
UmNvW45IvN.abstract: Robot policies increasingly predict how a scene will evolve, but such predictions are usually made in pixel space while actions are executed in metric 3D, and it is unclear how a controller should consume predictions that are inevitably imperfect. We study these questions with GeomVLA, a vision-language-action (VLA) model that couples a language-conditioned 3D scene-motion model, trained on 3D point tracks extracted from demonstration videos, with a 3D action denoiser in a shared metric frame. Rather than executing predicted trajectories, the policy reads intermediate motion features from a single velocity-field evaluation. GeomVLA achieves state-of-the-art performance on CALVIN, competitive results on LIBERO and RoboTwin2.0, and strong real-world performance without robot-action pretraining. Ablations show that predictions help most when expressed in the same metric geometry as perception and action, and that early latent motion features are more useful to the policy than fully denoised trajectory predictions.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

PU8VtCeGAA.title: Getting Out and Getting Back: World and Behavior Grounding in Real2Sim2Real Co-Training
PU8VtCeGAA.authors: Samuel Liu, Youngsun Kim, Martin Matak, Gilwoo Lee
PU8VtCeGAA.abstract: Simulation can expand scarce real demonstrations, but how world fidelity and similarity to human behavior affect co-training remains unclear. We independently vary world grounding, which aligns simulation with the real system, and behavior grounding, which aligns simulated trajectories with human motion. On dynamic dexterous pick-and-sort, fully grounded co-training raises the success rate from 52% to 86% using 100 real demonstrations and 1500 simulated trajectories. Rollout observations suggest that policies follow real-derived behavior in demonstrated states and simulation-derived behavior elsewhere. We investigate these transitions through latent-space analysis and examine how both grounding axes affect task performance. We further show that both grounding axes remain consequential when co-training foundation models.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

biEo1T1I2K.title: GPWM: Generative Particle World Models for 3D Prediction and Planning
biEo1T1I2K.authors: Robert Ren, Matthew Bronars, He Zhu, Yikai Tang, Jianing Zhang, Sergey Zakharov, Pavel Tokmakov, Katerina Fragkiadaki
biEo1T1I2K.abstract: We introduce GPWM a generative world model that learns 3D physical dynamics directly from particle trajectories. Its shared representation and architecture covers rigid, deformable, cloth, and granular materials, in both passive physics and robotic interaction. GPWM is an object-aware multi-resolution transformer that combines flow matching with diffusion forcing to enable streaming generation far beyond the training horizon. We train and evaluate GPWM on ParticleWorlds, a 25.5-million-frame corpus spanning diverse geometries, physical properties, interactions, and robot embodiments. When trained within individual domains, GPWM reduces prediction error by 29-53% relative to the strongest applicable prior learned-dynamics models. Going beyond the domain-specific setting of prior methods, a single Unified GPWM jointly models heterogeneous physical regimes within one set of weights. GPWM further generalizes to unseen geometries, physical properties, object counts, and rollout horizons. Beyond prediction, GPWM enables contact-rich planning. An object-space goal reward is backpropagated through the learned interaction dynamics to the latent noise, steering actuator motion and the contacts it establishes. Executed open-loop in simulation, the resulting plans outperform unguided generation and planning with prior learned dynamics models on pushing, picking, and granular manipulation.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

VFvsy2qVnP.title: GRAIL: Generating Humanoid Loco-Manipulation from 3D Assets and Video Priors
VFvsy2qVnP.authors: Tianyi Xie, Haotian Zhang, Jinhyung Park, Zi Wang, Bowen Wen, Jiefeng Li, Xueting Li, Qingwei Ben, Haoyang Weng, Yufei Ye, David Minor, Tingwu Wang, Chenfanfu Jiang, Sanja Fidler, Jan Kautz, Linxi Fan, Yuke Zhu, Zhengyi Luo, Umar Iqbal, Ye Yuan
VFvsy2qVnP.abstract: Scaling humanoid loco-manipulation requires robot-compatible demonstrations across diverse objects, whole-body motions, and scene geometries, but teleoperation and motion capture are difficult to scale because each collection depends on physical setups, instrumented actors, and robot operation. We present GRAIL, a digital generation pipeline that remains fully virtual until deployment: it composes 3D assets, simulator-ready scenes, and video foundation model (VFM) priors to synthesize interactions without physical scene rebuilds or robot teleoperation. GRAIL starts from fully specified 3D configurations with known object geometry, camera parameters, metric scale, environment depth, and a robot-proportioned character. This privileged setup conditions interaction-aware reconstruction of metric 4D human-object interaction (HOI) trajectories with reduced depth ambiguity and morphology mismatch. We retarget the recovered motions to a humanoid and train complementary task-general trackers: an object-aware latent adaptor for manipulation and a scene-aware tracker for terrain traversal. GRAIL produces over 20,000 sequences spanning pick-up, whole-body manipulation, sitting, and terrain traversal. Egocentric visual policies trained on this generated task data achieve 84% real-world object pick-up success and 90% stair-climbing success on a Unitree G1.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

n4eAEcfgFE.title: Grip, Trace, Write: Force-Aware Imitation and Reinforcement Learning for High-DoF Robotic Handwriting
n4eAEcfgFE.authors: Rongqian Chen, Yiding Chen, Jijie Zhou, Tom Z. Jiahao
n4eAEcfgFE.abstract: Most robotic handwriting rigidly mounts the pen and reduces writing to trajectory tracking. A freely held pen instead couples grasp stability, tip motion, and contact force. We present Grip, Trace, Write, a force-aware simulation environment and learning framework for high-DoF handwriting. A two-branch actor separates pen retention from arm-wrist writing while preserving their closed-loop coupling. Training learns a grasp controller, initializes writing from inverse-kinematics demonstrations by behavior cloning, and improves writing through reinforcement learning with rewards on ink, force, time, and retention. Across diverse tasks, the policy improves completion, precision, force regulation, and efficiency over behavior cloning and inverse kinematics, and generalizes without fine-tuning to unseen English and Chinese content. These results establish force-aware handwriting as a testbed for dexterous tool use.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

ay8BLSIaIS.title: Hallucination in World Models is Predictable and Preventable
ay8BLSIaIS.abstract: Modern generative world models render increasingly realistic action-controllable futures, yet they frequently hallucinate: rollouts remain visually fluent while drifting from the ground-truth dynamics. We hypothesize that hallucination concentrates in low-coverage regions of the state-action space, where lightweight data-centric signals can both detect it and guide mitigation. To test this, we introduce MMBench2, a 427-hour, 210-task dataset for visual world modeling with ground-truth actions, rewards, and live simulators, and train a 350M-parameter world model on it. We identify three distinct hallucination modes: perceptual, action-marginalized, and scene-diverging -- each anchored to a different stage of the pipeline, and develop three signals that accurately predict where the model will fail. To close coverage gaps at training time, we develop a coverage-aware sampling technique; to close them online, our hallucination predictors serve as curiosity rewards for targeted data collection, yielding a data-efficient finetuning recipe that adapts the pretrained world model to entirely unseen environments with as few as 50 real environment trajectories. Overall, our findings reveal that hallucination in world models is inherently a data coverage issue, and that the same signals used to detect it can also be used for mitigation.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

hmGPhNTkQu.title: How Long, Not How Close: Blending a Learned Temporal Embedding into Latent World Model Planning
hmGPhNTkQu.authors: Lama Moukheiber, Haotian Xue, Yongxin Chen
hmGPhNTkQu.abstract: Latent world models plan by choosing actions whose predicted end state is closest to the goal. This works one plan from the goal but fails several plans away, because latent distance measures how closely a state resembles the goal, not how long it takes to reach it: two positions can look alike yet be separated by a wall or a long sequence of contacts. We hypothesise that the planning cost, not only the model’s predictions, contributes to this failure. We propose TEMPO, which leaves the world model untouched and blends a learned temporal embedding into the planner’s latent cost, so that plans are ranked by how long they take to reach the goal, not only by how visually close they are. The embedding is a small map of the frozen latent, learned without rewards or labels. On eleven simulated environments, from maze navigation to contact-rich pushing and 3D manipulation, a 0.13M-parameter map adding at most 0.3% to a plan’s arithmetic improves the LeWM and PLDM planners at every goal distance, raising LeWM from 36% to 99% on TwoRoom three plans out and PLDM from 76% to 90% on Push-T one plan out, and keeps helping when physical parameters change.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

qBAoakQhlG.title: Hydra-0: Action Flow for Generalist World Modeling and Control
qBAoakQhlG.authors: Hongyu Li, Bowen Wen, Xinghao Zhu, Yixuan Wang, Yilun Du, Yunzhu Li, George Konidaris, Stan Birchfield, Soha Pouya, Chenran Li, Yan Chang
qBAoakQhlG.abstract: A world model useful for manipulation must do more than generate plausible video: its inputs should correspond to executable actions, and its predictions should preserve outcomes relevant to control. We present Hydra-0, which represents robot actions as sparse image-plane motion trajectories called action flow. During deployment, action flow bridges physics simulation and the learned world model: a controller-and-physics rollout projects each command into kinematically feasible image-plane motion that conditions learned scene-consequence prediction. During training, the same representation is recovered from heterogeneous interaction videos without native robot actions. Across five held-out datasets, our best model reduces robot- and object-motion error by 90.4% and 60.2% relative to an action-conditioned baseline, while predicted and reference policy success rates correlate at r=0.96 on RoboLab. The same interface can be inverted in a proof of concept that maps desired object flow from a human demonstration to executable robot actions, suggesting that visual action abstractions can connect simulation, learned dynamics, evaluation, and control.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

UWhLunukQn.title: JACK: Joint Axis Correction from Kinesthetic Feedback
UWhLunukQn.authors: Arthur Jakobsson, Eugene Lee, Bardienus Pieter Duisterhof, Huang Huang, Jeff Tan, Romina Mir, Jonathan Francis, Jean Oh, Jeffrey Ichnowski
UWhLunukQn.abstract: A robot that opens a cabinet or repositions a desk lamp needs each joint’s type, axis direction and pivot point. We pose estimating these through interaction as system identification and train the estimator entirely in physics simulation, which samples joint physics, object placement and the error of the starting estimate per world and records the motion of every part exactly. The robot proposes the object’s joints from its first point cloud, pushes or pulls parts, tracks points on their surfaces, and fits screw motions to the tracked points. A learned belief weighs these fits against the proposal and holds each joint as a mixture of candidate axes, each with a calibrated angular and positional spread that narrows over successive actions. Because every training label comes from the simulator, the simulator’s physics and the quantities it exposes determine what the belief learns. We discuss considerations for anyone training such a model: training actions that leak the true joint, when action planning pays off, the range of starting errors, failed actions as evidence, and the simulator physics that make tracked motion meaningful. We close with open problems in moving the tracking pipeline to real cameras and a physical robot.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

dmCrseuxNh.title: JEPA-x: Cross-Predictive Physics Grounding for Forecastable Latent Dynamics
dmCrseuxNh.authors: Kehan Wen, Ziming Li, Yiduo Qu, Siyuan Luo, Fan Shi
dmCrseuxNh.abstract: Latent world models plan by predicting the outcomes of candidate actions in a learned representation space. In self-predictive models, however, the encoder and predictor are optimized jointly and can co-adapt to latent transitions that are easy to predict in the training distribution but weakly constrained by the physical evolution of the scene. We introduce the cross-predictive JEPA (JEPA-x), which grounds latent dynamics in privileged physical trajectories. JEPA-x treats visual observations and physical states as corresponding views of the same action-conditioned trajectory, advances both through a shared predictor, and matches each prediction to the future representations of both modalities. This encourages the action-conditioned predictor to learn a common transition rule across the two views. Privileged physical state is used only during training, leaving a visual-only model at deployment. Empirical results show that JEPA-x reduces the rollout drift of a newly fitted predictor from 0.361 to 0.104 and increases mean control success from 53.6% to 78.2% on a multi-task suite spanning six evaluation subfamilies. We additionally show that direct full-state regression improves position decodability without improving forecastability or control, indicating that the benefit comes from shaping latent dynamics rather than merely encoding physical variables.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

lQn92Sva7n.title: Latent Skill Acquisition and Composition for Contact-Rich Manipulation
lQn92Sva7n.authors: Wenlong Huang, Jiayuan Mao, Tomás Lozano-Pérez, Leslie Pack Kaelbling, Li Fei-Fei
lQn92Sva7n.abstract: Human-level generalization in manipulation requires composing known behaviors to reach novel goals in scenarios never seen in training. The challenge sharpens in contact-rich settings, where behaviors must be recomposed at the granularity of contact rather than of a semantic subtask. Without relying on per-task demonstrations, a promising approach is to leverage test-time compute to perform physical reasoning that searches for novel solutions and improves them incrementally during deployment. To effectively perform search in the large space of motions, we propose SkillReasoner, which learns temporal abstractions of actions (i.e., skills) from unstructured offline interactions, and then reasons over and recomposes them at test time. Crucial to the formulation is a latent skill space learned with varying temporal horizons, so that composition can happen at varying granularity, as required by different stages of the task, while minimizing the number of decisions. To realize a novel goal at test time, the robot searches over latent skill sequences in its imagination, decodes a chosen skill into low-level actions, and replans in closed loop, up to 30 Hz. We demonstrate on a series of contact-rich real-world and simulated tasks that the robot chains behaviors to achieve novel goals that require far longer behaviors than those seen in training, and adapts zero-shot to unseen perturbations, changing dynamics, and constraints, all trained purely from unstructured play data without task-specific demonstrations.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

82UCImH1eY.title: Latent World Models Enhance Imitation Learning with Foresight
82UCImH1eY.authors: Hengkai Pan, Gaoyue Zhou, Yann LeCun, Lerrel Pinto, Deepak Pathak
82UCImH1eY.abstract: Imitation policies acquire useful manipulation behaviors but can struggle in long-horizon and unfamiliar scenarios. ForesightIL augments behavior cloning with planning on demand through a latent world model and a self-supervised goal value. A shared visual representation allows repeated policy queries on imagined states, focusing multi-step search on plausible behaviors. VIP with temporal straightening ranks candidate outcomes, while a learned prediction-error signal determines when to invoke planning. Experiments across four simulated and four real-world manipulation tasks show improvements over the underlying imitation policy, including on long-horizon bimanual tasks. Uncertainty gating retains much of the benefit of planning at every decision while reducing planning frequency.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

cf1iBgypTi.title: Learned Differentiable Physics for Planning with and Designing Deformable-Manipulation Tools
cf1iBgypTi.abstract: Model-based planning requires dynamics models that are accurate across a wide range of scene configurations. Our technique uses a graph neural network (GNN) trained on RGB-D observations from a real robot using nine tools spanning three distinct interaction modes. We introduce a feature parameterization for the GNN which provides rotation and particle density invariance by construction, and show that this is crucial for enabling generalization to new tools and new manipulation trajectories. Trained on all nine tools, our model outperforms a state-of-the-art machine learning baseline, in both the “in-distribution” and “out-of-distribution” setting. Our model is also more accurate than a differentiable material point method fit to the same data, at an order of magnitude lower cost per planner query. Given a target dough shape, our model can design a tool to achieve this shape (conditioned on a manipulation trajectory), or come up with a manipulation trajectory for up to 4 grippers to match the target shape.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

FUsD7vN1nb.title: Learning Contact Residuals for In-Hand Manipulation Transfer
FUsD7vN1nb.authors: Zhuoyang Chen, Jianshu Hu, Yutong Ban
FUsD7vN1nb.abstract: Dexterous in-hand manipulation relies on contact-rich dynamics that are difficult to simulate accurately.
