Existing work such as system identification of simulator parameters and dynamics randomization is constrained by the expressiveness of the simulator, while hand-focused learned dynamics can leave object contact effects implicit. We introduce an object-centric residual that learns contact-conditioned momentum corrections from target trajectories and applies them as impulses in a nominal simulator for policy fine-tuning. Preliminary sim-to-sim tests from MuJoCo/MJWarp to Genesis show improved transfer over fine-tuning without the residual on multiple objects, two tasks, and two hands.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

VqcbxEBuKH.title: Learning Force-Safe Diffusion Policies with a Differentiable Physics World Model
VqcbxEBuKH.authors: Ryan Teoh, Sean Liu, Jason Jangho Choi
VqcbxEBuKH.abstract:
NOTE: full content is hidden based on the author's request.

Abstract: Diffusion policies learn strong manipulation behaviors from demonstrations, but demonstrations show a policy what to do, not what physically happens when it acts. In cooperative manipulation this gap matters: a policy can transport an object successfully while generating excessive internal forces that arise from the closed-loop interaction between multiple arms, the object, and the controller. We use a differentiable rigid-body model as an action-conditioned physics world model: from states the policy itself visits, it predicts the physical consequences of each candidate action chunk, including the internal force rates its own actions produce, which demonstrations never show. Penalizing predicted force-rate violations provides an on-policy fine-tuning signal that requires no force labels and no deployment-time safety filter. On a two-robot fragile-object transport task, this physical feedback raises force-safe episodes from 42.5% to 94.0% while preserving placement success (90.0% → 91.0%). The same world model supports decentralized policies without inter-robot communication: distillation into local-observation policies loses force safety (55.8%), and predicting the joint outcome of both robots’ independently sampled chunks restores it (93.7%).
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

CbbmDRbb0a.title: Learning Tactile-Aware Hierarchical Whole-Body Control Policies for Quadrupedal Loco-Manipulation
CbbmDRbb0a.authors: Pokuang Zhou, Le Mao, Xiyue Chen, Zhiyuan Zhang, Joseph Campbell, Yu She
CbbmDRbb0a.abstract: Touch provides direct information about contact state, force, slip, and interaction transitions, yet most mobile manipulation policies treat tactile signals only as passive observations rather than explicit control targets. We propose a hierarchical framework consisting of high-level and low-level policies, both conditioned on visual and tactile information. The high-level policy is responsible for planning and generating commands, while the low-level policy executes these commands through whole-body control. The high-level diffusion policy is trained from human demonstrations collected with a handheld visuotactile gripper, whereas the low-level policy is first trained through large-scale reinforcement learning in simulation and then post-trained with reward functions to jointly execute end-effector motion and tactile commands, enabling zero-shot transfer to the real robot. Our system demonstrates the capability to perform challenging long-horizon, complex, and contact-rich loco-manipulation tasks on a Unitree Go2 equipped with a D1 arm and a tactile gripper, including marker reorientation and insertion, valve tightening, delicate object manipulation, wrench-based bolt tightening, and cabinet-door opening. We further evaluate the generalization of the low-level policy across substantially different manipulator configurations, demonstrating the effectiveness and generalizability of our low-level architecture. Despite the nearly twofold difference in manipulator mass, the joint torques remain within approximately $-15$ to $27$ N$\cdot$m during real-world deployment. We also compare our method against an advanced world action model approach. Across real-world trials, the full framework improves the average task success rate by 43.7\% over the average performance of all other baselines, demonstrating that tactile information can serve as a planned and controlled action-level representation for robust contact-rich loco-manipulation.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

ZL0jgrWi25.title: LeWAM: A JEPA World Action Model with Diffusion-Steering-Based MPC
ZL0jgrWi25.authors: Shashank Hegde, Alexander Popov, Elie Aljalbout, Nikolai Smolyanskiy
ZL0jgrWi25.abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict actions and future observations, typically from a reconstruction-based representation that carries noisy, redundant information which can complicate downstream predictions. We introduce LeWAM, a bidirectional transformer for forward, backward, inverse dynamics and policy prediction, on a decoder-free JEPA latent trained end-to-end through all four modes. We see the following benefits. 1) Alignment: linear probing better reads robot and object state over a regular Le World Model (a forward-only JEPA world model), while successfully ignoring distractors, which a regular WAM considerably reconstructs. 2) Acting: Closed-loop evaluations of LeWAM match or exceeds a regular policy (without a world model) on the same encoder and at matched size. 3) Planning: While sampling raw actions in planning with WAMs allows MPC to exploit dynamic model inaccuracies, we show that planning in the noise space of these WAMs improves their closed-loop performance.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

5Yxc4gE3nt.title: MixWorld: Sim-And-Real Co-Training for Robot World Models
5Yxc4gE3nt.authors: Lei Huang, Abhay Deshpande, Samuel M Bateman, Edison Zhu, Muhammad Zubair Irshad, Sergey Zakharov, Zhengbo Zou, Dhruv Shah
5Yxc4gE3nt.abstract: Action-conditioned world models (ACWMs) require diverse interaction data to accurately predict robot actions, yet real-world datasets underrepresent off-nominal behaviors. We investigate whether large-scale simulation can complement real-world data for training robot world models. We introduce MixWorld, an ACWM jointly trained on 95k real and 550k simulated trajectories, where simulation expands coverage of off-nominal interaction dynamics and camera viewpoints while real data grounds predictions in the deployment domain. Our results suggest that sim-and-real co-training improves multiview consistency, object permanence, and robot-arm controllability in real-world video predictions, particularly during object-contact interactions and under randomized exocentric camera views. These improvements also translate to downstream applications. Compared to the base world model, MixWorld increases Spearman correlation in policy evaluation from 0.196 to 0.475 and improves the performance of a base policy via $\textit{Best-of-N}$ inference-time search by 16.7-30.0 percentage points.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

c3FEZjbVuq.title: MS-MEM: Multi-Skill Manipulation-Enhanced Mapping via Uncertainty-Aware Belief-Space World Models
c3FEZjbVuq.authors: Nils Dengler, Yitian Shi, Jesper Mücke, Sicong Pan, Rania Rayyes, Maren Bennewitz
c3FEZjbVuq.abstract:
Accurate scene understanding in confined, cluttered spaces such as shelves is essential for service robots, yet it remains challenging due to severe occlusions, restricted accessibility, and the need to avoid excessive scene changes. In this paper, we propose Multi-Skill Manipulation-Enhanced Mapping (MS-MEM), an evidential framework for uncertainty-aware mapping that integrates active viewpoint selection, object pushing, and grasping. At its core, MS-MEM plans by rolling out learned world models that operate directly in belief space, predicting how the metric-semantic belief and its epistemic uncertainty evolve under each candidate action instead of predicting raw observations. Since these world models are trained entirely in physics simulation and share a single evidential belief, candidate perception and manipulation actions are evaluated within a unified action selection pipeline using a common information gain criterion.
Grasping additionally relies on a novel full-evidential grasp estimator that models both grasp affordance and orientation uncertainty, while a collateral disturbance constraint (CDC) discourages excessive changes to confident regions of the scene belief. Experimental results show that, compared with single-skill and unconstrained baselines, MS-MEM achieves higher mapping accuracy while reducing scene disturbance by 55% in simulation and 28% in the real world.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

g8EDN2DJzk.title: NeRD2Real: Adapting Neural Robot Dynamics for Humanoid Control from Real-World Data
g8EDN2DJzk.authors: Chang Yu, Iretiayo Akinola, Eric Heiden, Eliot Xing, Chenfanfu Jiang, Miles Macklin, Yashraj Narang, Jie Xu
g8EDN2DJzk.abstract: Accurate simulation is essential for transferring humanoid control policies to hardware, yet calibrating dynamics models from limited, noisy onboard data is challenging. We present NeRD2Real, a framework for learning Neural Robot Dynamics (NeRD) through extensive pretraining with analytical simulation data and adapting with limited real-world data. Simulation pretraining learns a dynamics-conditioned transition model and a trajectory-level missing-state estimator. Adaptation recovers unobserved states, identifies a real-world dynamics-latent, and fine-tunes the model on a mix of reconstructed real and simulation data. On Unitree G1, an adapted NeRD supports whole-body policy learning and enables sim-to-sim and sim-to-real transfer. A walking policy trained in the adapted NeRD without dynamics randomization transfers zero-shot to the real robot.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

r0vW2eFo05.title: OrbiSim: World Models as Differentiable Physics Engines for Embodied Intelligence
r0vW2eFo05.authors: Jiajian Li, Jingyuan Huang, Junru Gong, Qi Wang, Xiaokang Yang, Yunbo Wang
r0vW2eFo05.abstract: We present OrbiSim, a robotic simulation paradigm that redefines world models as fully differentiable physics engines for embodied intelligence. Unlike world models focused on unconstrained imagination in latent or visual domains, OrbiSim establishes a physically grounded pathway connecting structured scene assets, neural dynamics, visual observations, and downstream policy learning. End-to-end differentiability throughout the simulation loop supports differentiable contact modeling, gradient-based policy optimization under sparse rewards, and physical-parameter inference. Experiments show improved predictive fidelity and control performance over the evaluated world-model baselines, while consistent responses to asset configurations and physical parameters make OrbiSim a differentiable tool for robot simulation and policy training.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

ebmsvnGn5K.title: PhysiCalWorld: In-Context Physics Calibration for World Models
ebmsvnGn5K.authors: Yunhao Luo, Wentao He, Yinpei Dai, Hyelin Nam, Hongze Fu, Joyce Chai, Nima Fazeli, Jeong Joon Park
ebmsvnGn5K.abstract: Existing world models typically perceive a scene through current visual frame or a narrow history window. However, these observations may not reveal the physics properties that govern transition dynamics, such as an object’s mass distribution, joint damping, or surface friction. Without calibrating these physics factors for world models, predictions tend to regress toward an empirical prior and induce severe drift in novel test scenes. To this end, we propose PhysiCalWorld, which calibrates action-conditioned world models to the instance-specific dynamics via in-context prompting, without fine-tuning or analytical physics modeling. Our method encodes an exploratory interaction clip collected within the test scene into a compact physics descriptor token, which grounds subsequent predictions in the scene’s actual physical behavior. PhysiCalWorld is trained end-to-end with the latent prediction loss alone, without physics labels. At inference time, the descriptor token is extracted once and can be reused across rollouts with negligible compute overhead. We evaluate PhysiCalWorld across four environments covering diverse physics variations and show that it substantially improves rollout prediction accuracy and visual planning success rate. The learned descriptors also form a physically structured latent space and generalize beyond the physics ranges seen during training.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

dmEcKsHkXs.title: Recursive Successor Models
dmEcKsHkXs.authors: Nitish Dashora, Richard Li, Dan Haramati, John Marangola, Chuning Zhu, Sunshine Jiang, Abhishek Gupta, Pulkit Agrawal, Zhang-Wei Hong
dmEcKsHkXs.abstract: Planning with world models enables improvement beyond the dataset, but compounding prediction errors hinder long-horizon planning. To prevent one-step compounding error, we instead model longer-term future state distributions, known as successor measures. We introduce Recursive Successor Models, which combine (1) a stable supervised training objective that avoids bootstrapping with (2) a recursive sampling procedure for planning that composes short-horizon distributions into long-horizon distributions. We demonstrate the capabilities of RSM in simulated benchmarks and real-world robot experiments by showcasing improvements in policy performance, planning latency, and training convergence speed across long-horizon and visual tasks.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

W0UyFSPVMU.title: RoboSimStudio: An Interactive Toolkit for Rapid Real2Sim of Robot Manipulation Tasks
W0UyFSPVMU.authors: Kaiyuan Chen, Shuangyu Xie, Uksang Yoo, Xinyue Zhu, Alvin Zhu, Daehwa Kim, Eric Heiden, Erwin Coumans, Miles Macklin, Spencer Huang, Ken Goldberg
W0UyFSPVMU.abstract: It has been difficult to accurately model the physics of the interaction between a robot and the objects it manipulates, including contact mechanics, coupled contact dynamics, deformation, stiffness, and friction. We present RoboSimStudio (RSS), an interactive toolkit that makes choices of solver, contact model, and physical parameters explicit and editable, allowing both humans and coding agents to quickly create and iteratively refine simulations based on observed physical behavior. We implement RSS with the open Newton physics simulation system and describe experiments with human-guided Real2Sim using (1) visual feedback and (2) force feedback, and (3) agentic Real2Sim2Real. RSS will be open-sourced; code, videos, and additional information are available on the project website: https://robosimstudio.github.io.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

JzHjX5ihIV.title: Rolling-WAM: World Action Models with Rolling Imagination
JzHjX5ihIV.authors: Yinghua Zhou, Junjie Ye, Yiqi Zhao, Hao Dong, Celina Shiyu Wang, Ruohai Ge, Tingyi Yang, Basile Van Hoorick, Gaurav S. Sukhatme, Vitor Campagnolo Guizilini, Yue Wang
JzHjX5ihIV.abstract:
World Action Models (WAMs) couple action generation with future visual prediction, but iterative joint denoising incurs substantial latency in closed-loop control.
We present \methodname, which distributes video--action denoising across successive replanning cycles.
A sliding window maintains aligned video--action chunks at progressively higher noise levels toward the future, completing the imminent chunk while retaining partially denoised future predictions.
Reusing partially denoised predictions reduces the steps needed to prepare the next executable chunk, while new observations guide continued refinement.
Experiments demonstrate competitive performance on LIBERO and the highest success rates on RoboTwin 2.0 and real-world humanoid manipulation, alongside a $4.5\times$ steady-state replanning speedup over standard joint WAMs.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

yjSj65R40C.title: SceneRig: An Agentic System for Simulation-Ready 3D Scene Reconstruction from Single Images
yjSj65R40C.authors: Rundong Luo, Yunong Liu, Di Cao, Matthew Tancik, Shyamal Buch, Colton Stearns, Wenqi Xian
yjSj65R40C.abstract: Simulation supports robot policy evaluation, but constructing realistic scenes at scale remains difficult. Reconstructing simulation-ready scenes from single images requires accurate object recovery, placement, and physical grounding. Post-hoc settling can yield stable scenes that no longer match the observed workspace. We present SceneRig, an agentic system that reconstructs editable 3D scenes using visual, geometric, and physical tools. Agents recover objects and supports, construct the surrounding scene, and refine placement through simulated edit-and-validate loops. Across diverse tabletop images, SceneRig improves instance recovery, object-centric appearance, and 3D placement while maintaining physical stability. In calibrated RGB-D robotics experiments, its scenes predict real-robot policy outcomes more accurately than the baseline and more reliably replay recorded manipulations without trajectory adaptation. See our [project page](https://scenerig.github.io/).
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

wfmWFjHEhJ.title: SD-MJX: Shape-Differentiable Rigid Contact Simulation for Real-to-Sim
wfmWFjHEhJ.authors: Fuquan Wang, Zofie Christian, Yifan Zhu
wfmWFjHEhJ.abstract: Real-to-sim requires object geometry and physical parameters that reproduce observed behavior. However, image-based reconstructions can contain geometric interpenetrations that destabilize simulation. We present SD-MJX, which integrates SDF-based differentiable contact manifold generation into MJX, enabling efficient computation of geometry gradients through multi-step simulation. A local FP64 gradient check over a 100-step collision rollout yields a relative $L_2$ discrepancy of $2.46 \times 10^{-4}$ against central finite differences. We evaluate geometry refinement on two static scenes reconstructed from real images. Over 5-second physical rollouts, the complete refinement pipeline reduces maximum object displacement from 19.778 to 0.783 mm and from 25.941 to 1.472 mm, respectively.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

oeIWkYO2DW.title: SimFoundry: Modular and Automated Scene Generation for Policy Learning and Evaluation
oeIWkYO2DW.authors: Nadun Ranawaka, Josiah Wong, Wei-Lin Pai, Wei-Teng Chu, Tianyuan Dai, Masoud Moghani, Hang Yin, Yunfan Jiang, Wesley Durbano, Brandon Bryce Huynh, Yu Fang, Danfei Xu, Ruohan Zhang, Li Fei-Fei, Linxi Fan, Bowen Wen, Ajay Mandlekar, Yuke Zhu
oeIWkYO2DW.abstract:
Training and evaluating robot policies in the real world is costly and difficult to scale.
We introduce SimFoundry, a modular and automated system for zero-shot real-to-sim scene construction from a video.
SimFoundry generates sim-ready digital twins and supports object, scene, and task editing, enabling the automated generation of diverse digital cousins: affordance-preserving variations of reconstructed real-world scenes.
Policies trained on SimFoundry data transfer zero-shot to challenging real tasks involving multi-step manipulation, articulated object interaction, and bimanual interaction, and its digital cousins facilitate generalization to new real-world conditions.
Across 7 manipulation tasks and 5 policy architectures, SimFoundry simulation evaluations correlate well with real-world performance and strongly predict real-world policy rankings, with mean Pearson correlation 0.909 and mean maximum ranking violation 0.027. 
When evaluating sim-trained policies zero-shot in the real world, policies trained with object, scene, and task cousins in simulation show average task success rate improvements of 20\%, 21\%, and 40\%, respectively. Additional details at https://simfoundry.github.io/.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

PMQrKL7EbR.title: SIMPACT: Simulation-Enabled Action Planning using Vision-Language Models
PMQrKL7EbR.authors: Haowen Liu, Shaoxiong Yao, Haonan Chen, Jiawei Gao, Jiayuan Mao, Jia-Bin Huang, Yilun Du
PMQrKL7EbR.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) exhibit remarkable common-sense and semantic reasoning capabilities. However, they lack a grounded understanding of physical dynamics. This limitation arises from training VLMs on static internet-scale visual-language data that contain no causal interactions or action-conditioned changes. Consequently, it remains challenging to leverage VLMs for fine-grained robotic manipulation tasks that require physical understanding, reasoning, and corresponding action planning. To overcome this, we present $\textbf{SIMPACT}$, a test-time, $\textbf{SIM}$ulation-enabled $\textbf{ACT}$ion $\textbf{P}$lanning framework that equips VLMs with physical reasoning through simulation-in-the-loop world modeling, without requiring any additional training. From a single RGB-D observation, SIMPACT efficiently constructs physics simulations, enabling the VLM to propose informed actions, observe simulated rollouts, and iteratively refine its reasoning. By integrating language reasoning with physics prediction, our simulation-enabled VLM can understand contact dynamics and action outcomes in a physically grounded way. Our method demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on seven challenging, real-world rigid-body and deformable manipulation tasks that require fine-grained physical reasoning, outperforming existing general-purpose robotic manipulation models. Our results demonstrate that embedding physics understanding via efficient simulation into VLM reasoning at test time offers a promising path towards generalizable embodied intelligence.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

iCNagkpW3K.title: Steel: Simulation for Generalist Robot Learning
iCNagkpW3K.authors: Dylan Turpin, Jared Mejia, Laki Iinbor, Octi Zhang, Vishal Mandadi, Eric Heiden, Miles Macklin, Deepak Pathak
iCNagkpW3K.abstract: GPU-accelerated simulation at scale has enabled reinforcement learning to produce locomotion and whole-body control policies that transfer to physical robots: thousands of identical environments simulated in parallel under a simple on-policy recipe such as proximal policy optimization (PPO). Manipulation presents a different scaling problem: robots must learn across a large space of tasks and embodiments, interacting with different objects, layouts and mechanisms, so simulation must scale not only the number of environments but their diversity. We present Steel, a GPU rigid-body contact solver for the open-source Newton physics engine whose arrays are laid out per environment: each environment's constraint rows and response vectors occupy a range of fixed capacity, its mass-matrix factor a range sized to its degree-of-freedom group, and the factorization kernels run over groups of articulations of similar degree-of-freedom count, so robots, objects, contact sets and degrees of freedom may differ across the environments simulated in parallel and no robot is padded to the largest one present. Steel reaches 3.8x PhysX's throughput (geometric mean over 20 Isaac Lab tasks, faster on 19 of the 20) and about 1.3x MuJoCo Warp's (geometric mean over the same 20); with 5 to 20 scene types simulated in parallel, each solver at its own peak environment count, its throughput ratio to PhysX rises from 9.2 at 5 types to 13.0 at 20, while MuJoCo Warp, which requires one model for every environment it steps, has no result on mixed scene types.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

ixIEAc2qdi.title: When Does Planning with a World Model Need Search?
ixIEAc2qdi.authors: Ahnaf Adib, Sabbir Ahmed, Ittehadul Karim, Latifur Khan
ixIEAc2qdi.abstract: Latent world models such as DINO-WM, JEPA-WM and LeWM plan by searching, with the cross-entropy method (CEM), for an action sequence whose predicted embedding reaches a goal image. The search takes most of the planning time. We compare CEM with predictive sampling, which scores the candidates of CEM's first iteration once and executes the lowest-cost sequence, on identical episodes across eight environments and three released world models, under one open-loop plan and under replanning. Manipulation and arm reaching need search. CEM leads on Push-T and OGBench-Cube in both settings and on Metaworld under replanning. Point navigation needs search only without feedback. With one open-loop plan CEM leads on Two-Room, Wall and Maze. With replanning and an any-step success test, predictive sampling matches CEM on Two-Room, comes within one episode on Wall, and trails by two or three on Maze. Executing candidates from the start state shows what the search contributes. CEM's last iteration holds better plans than its first in 30 to 32 of 32 episodes per environment. Scoring 9,000 candidates once matches CEM on Wall. On Push-T and Maze, CEM's iterations move the sampling distribution to plans that succeed. On zero-shot RoboCasa with a DROID-trained JEPA-WM, a ninth of the budget changes success by at most two of 143 episodes, and shortening the planning horizon from three steps to one raises success from 18 to 29.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

NDKZldVkVW.title: Wiggle and Go! System Identification for Zero-Shot Dynamic Rope Manipulation
NDKZldVkVW.authors: Arthur Jakobsson, Abhinav Mahajan, Karthik Pullalarevu, Krishna Suresh, Yunchao Yao, Yuemin Mao, Bardienus Pieter Duisterhof, Shahram Najam Syed, Jeffrey Ichnowski
NDKZldVkVW.abstract: Many robotic tasks are unforgiving; a single mistake in a dynamic throw can lead to unacceptable delays or unrecoverable failure. We introduce Wiggle and Go!, a two-stage framework for zero-shot rope manipulation: a brief, safe wiggle action is observed to predict descriptive rope parameters, which instantiate a rope-specific simulator for goal-conditioned trajectory optimization. The identification module is trained entirely in simulation and is task-agnostic, supporting diverse manipulation policies without retraining. We achieve 3.55cm average error on real-world 3D target striking compared with 15.29cm for uninformed baselines, and over 50% success on multi-objective lobbing and draping tasks. Predicted parameters transfer to unseen motions with 0.95 average frequency correlation between simulated and real rope dynamics. A parameter ablation shows that identifying dynamics beyond rope length and lead mass is essential to accurate planning.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

d4ERsNN7PJ.title: World Model MPC for Playing Crane Game
d4ERsNN7PJ.authors: Atsuya Ishizu, Makoto Kawano, KAZUKI OSAMURA, Ryo Moriyama, Junpei Yamaguchi, Hidetsugu Uchida, Narishige Abe
d4ERsNN7PJ.abstract:
Crane games can be viewed as robot manipulation tasks in which a robot indirectly controls a claw through an interface designed for human use and attempts to acquire a prize based on visual observations.
In this study, we formulate this task as a control problem based on predicting future states, and as a preliminary study, we explore robot control using a JEPA-based world model.
We collect visual observations and action sequences from a robot playing a physical crane game and use them to train a world model that predicts one-step-ahead states in a latent space conditioned on the actions.
We then use one-step model predictive control (MPC) to decide whether to continue or terminate the current lever action based on the predicted latent state.
In real-world experiments, the LeKiwi robot operated a crane game machine, achieving an average grasp success rate of 90.0\% and a prize acquisition rate of 73.3\% across two types of prizes requiring different claw stopping positions.
workshops: Bringing Physics Simulation and World Models Together for Robotic Manipulation

y0qBMe2qH3.title: 2AM: Grounding Agent-Side Memory as Guidance for Steerable Action Models in Long-Horizon Manipulation
y0qBMe2qH3.authors: Yutong Hu, FengJiao Chen, Xuezhi Cao, Renaud Detry
y0qBMe2qH3.abstract: Long-horizon robot manipulation requires memory, but not necessarily inside the action policy. To address such tasks, current agentic systems often combine VLAs with planners and geometric tools, sometimes using additional depth or calibrated geometry. These systems confound attribution: gains may come from richer observations or alternative motor tools, while failures may stem from either the policy or an under-specified language interface. We isolate this question through a deliberately constrained design: less tool breadth, but greater interface bandwidth. 2AM makes a multimodal Agent the sole holder of task memory and a single RGB-based, episodically stateless Action Model the sole executor of task-relevant motion. The Agent compiles interaction history into subtask language and optional 2D grasp, place, and move hints that bind its physical intention at different time scales. To teach this steerability to the VLA, we augment demonstrations with structured hint labels and train under condition dropout, spatial noise, and temporal jitter to tolerate imperfect Agent outputs. On LIBERO-Mem, without depth, online geometry, or planner-based object motion, 2AM reaches 76.3\% average completion, a 61.5-point improvement over the strongest reported baseline of 14.8\%, together with 63.0\% relaxed and 11.8\% strict success. These results show that task memory can remain Agent-side. They further show that Action Model capability depends not only on what the policy has learned, but on how precisely the Agent can steer it. Project page: agent-mem-action-model.github.io
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

cRzAMT2Jll.title: [PAPER]: A Few Words Go a Long Way: Language Guided Robot Policy Synthesis
cRzAMT2Jll.authors: Daphne Chen, Archit Ritesh Jain, Eric Goossen, Emma Romig, Michael Murray, Nick Walker, Maya Cakmak
cRzAMT2Jll.abstract: While vision-language-action models have demonstrated impressive zero-shot manipulation capabilities, they remain fundamentally black box policies that are difficult to interpret, adapt, or correct when they inevitably fail. In this work, we propose ARCHITECT, a framework that treats robot policy acquisition as an interactive program synthesis task. ARCHITECT leverages the reasoning capabilities of LLM coding agents to synthesize modular robot programs that utilize a suite of perception and control tools. Unlike end-to-end models where distribution shift leads to unpredictable, cascading failures, our modular architecture allows users to isolate failures and localize feedback at the level of abstraction required. We introduce an iterative process where a human supervisor provides natural language corrections to steer the policy. These corrections are grounded in the policy code by program execution traces and distilled into a persistent skill library, a form of long-term in-context learning which enables the agent to accumulate a repertoire of reusable, interpretable behaviors. In a benchmark evaluation on a Franka Panda robot, ARCHITECT outperforms state-of-the-art VLA models and program synthesis baselines on complex, long-horizon tasks, including articulated object manipulation and cloth folding. Our results demonstrate that the synthesized skill library enables the system to transfer to novel tasks with decreasing human intervention, providing a steerable and data-efficient alternative to black-box robot learning. Website: https://robo-architect.github.io/
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

AVqVpgtKYF.title: Agentic Aerial Cinematography: From Dialogue Cues to Cinematic Trajectories
AVqVpgtKYF.authors: Yifan Lin, Sophie Z. Liu, Ran Qi, George Z. Xue, Xinping Song, Chao QIn, Hugh H.-T. Liu
AVqVpgtKYF.abstract: Agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in digital environments, yet their reasoning abilities alone are insufficient to accomplish tasks in the physical world. We present Agentic Aerial Cinematography: From Dialogue Cues to Cinematic Trajectories (ACDC), an agentic framework that bridges this gap for autonomous aerial cinematography. ACDC provides an execution harness that grounds an agent’s interpretation of cinematic intent and visual judgment in scene geometry and flight constraints. Given a natural-language request and a 3D scene representation, the agent selects relevant viewpoints and guides their refinement through visual feedback, while optimization and motion planning translate these decisions into executable drone trajectories. Experiments across a variety of simulated indoor scenes and hardware-in-the-loop flight tests demonstrate how this framework connects open-ended user intent to prompt-aligned video tours and physical drone execution.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

G9RmahESMC.title: Agentic Real2Sim: Physics-based World Modeling with Vision-Language Agents
G9RmahESMC.authors: Guanxiong Chen, Qianjun Xia, Jiawei Peng, Heng Zhang, Pengyu Jing, Bole Ma, Justin Qian, Yixian Cheng, Ziyi Jiao, Bingyang Zhou, Yiduo Qu, Luoxin Ye, Kaifeng Zhang, Kunyi Wang, Weijia Zeng, Yunuo Chen, Pengzhi Yang, Ziqiu Zeng, Siyuan Luo, Huamin Wang, Chao Liu, Alan Yuille, Fan Shi, Changxi Zheng, Yunzhu Li, Chenfanfu Jiang, Peter Yichen Chen
G9RmahESMC.abstract: Real-to-sim conversion for robotic interaction with objects remains labor-intensive because it requires more than visual reconstruction: a streamlined real2sim process must recover scene geometries and object states, infer physical parameters, and assemble actors, objects, cameras, poses, and trajectories into a runnable physical simulation. Today this process still depends on brittle workflow glue across visual perception tools and simulators: manual tuning of visual foundation models, mesh cleanup, coordinate frame alignments, etc. We introduce Agentic Real2Sim, a framework for generalized physical world modeling with vision-language agents that converts a real-world recording of object-robot interaction into a simulatable episodic twin, and connects the resulting twin to downstream policy fine-tuning and evaluation. We evaluate Agentic Real2Sim on rigid-object manipulation, deformable-object interaction, and humanoid motion scenes, spanning domains that are usually handled by separate Real2Sim pipelines. The framework's agentic decisions can be driven by an open-weight VLM backend at a small fraction of the cost of frontier models, while attaining a comparable conversion success rate. The framework further supports custom scene conversion, fine-tuning of a pretrained policy with data generated from converted episodes, and works effectively as a surrogate for real-world policy evaluation. The project site, including code is available at https://agentic-real2sim.github.io.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

RgpYrdqaFM.title: Agentic World Action Model
RgpYrdqaFM.authors: Zhuoyang Liu, Dantong Niu, Botong Zhang, Boning Shao, Jing Wang, Ruijie Zheng, Yuvan Sharma, Runyu Lu, Jiaming Liu, Renrui Zhang, Roei Herzig, Yutong Bai, Ken Goldberg, Danfei Xu, Yuke Zhu, Guanzhi Wang, Linxi Fan, Trevor Darrell
RgpYrdqaFM.abstract: Recent world action models provide visual foresight and future prediction for robot manipulation, but lack explicit mechanisms for compositional skill reuse. Agentic robotics combines code-based planning and reasoning with reusable skills, but often lacks predictive grounding in physical dynamics. We introduce AW-0, an agentic world action model framework that integrates code-based planning with joint video and action prediction. We jointly model code, future video, and robot actions as three coupled generative streams within a unified mixture-of-transformers architecture. Within this architecture a code expert generates parameterized skill routines and control logic while video and action experts generate future visual states and low-level motor commands. Code serves two complementary roles: it structures multi-step prediction and control within the world model and represents skills as reusable programs for subsequent agentic execution. We further introduce an automated curation pipeline that labels robot and human video trajectories with aligned programs and consolidates recurring routines into reusable skill libraries. Evaluations on RoboTwin 2.0 and physical bimanual manipulation tasks show improved task performance over VLA and WAM baselines, alongside gains in language following, semantic reasoning and robustness, demonstrating that agentic code enables connection between planning, prediction and execution within WAMs.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

LDd7VM2doA.title: ASPIRE: Agentic /Skills Discovery for Robotics
LDd7VM2doA.authors: Runyu Lu, Yubo Wu, Ethan Kou, Haotian Lin, Letian Fu, Wenli Xiao, Ajay Mandlekar, Yinzhen Xu, Guanya Shi, Ken Goldberg, Ang Chen, Mosharaf Chowdhury, Jan Kautz, Yuke Zhu, Linxi Fan, Guanzhi Wang
LDd7VM2doA.abstract: Traditional robot programming is notoriously challenging: it requires orchestrating multimodal perception, managing complex physical contact dynamics, and handling diverse environment configurations and execution failures. We introduce ASPIRE (Agentic Skill Programming through Iterative Robot Exploration), a continual learning system in which a coding agent writes and refines robot control programs and compounds validated fixes into a reusable skill library. ASPIRE combines (1) a closed-loop robot execution engine that exposes per-primitive multimodal traces for failure diagnosis and repair validation, (2) a skill library that distills validated repairs into transferable knowledge, and (3) evolutionary search that explores beyond single-trajectory refinement. ASPIRE surpasses prior methods by up to 77% on LIBERO-Pro, 72% on Robosuite's bimanual handover, and 32% on BEHAVIOR-1K, and its skill library transfers zero-shot to unseen LIBERO-Pro Long tasks (31% versus 4% for prior coding agents). ASPIRE improves as models get stronger: with Claude Opus 5.5 it nearly saturates these benchmarks, reaching 99% average success across all 80 LIBERO-Pro tasks and 100% on representative Robosuite and BEHAVIOR-1K tasks. On real robots, skills discovered in simulation reduce programming effort despite different embodiments and robot APIs, and skills learned online let ASPIRE solve a Rubik's Cube with progressively improving efficiency.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

F1qPCjfU0x.title: Can Astra Solve RoboMME without Breaking the Bank?
F1qPCjfU0x.authors: Bingao Chen, Haoquan Fang, Karen Liu
F1qPCjfU0x.abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires remembering information that is no longer visible, such as an object’s location before occlusion or the order of a demonstrated action sequence. A large vision-language planner can read this history, but calling it before every action chunk is slow and costly. We present a three-tier system for the RoboMME benchmark. GPT-6 Astra (System 2) selects a grounded subtask from stored visual history, a π0.5 vision-language-action policy (System 1) executes it, and a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-4B monitor (System 1.5) checks after each action chunk whether the subtask is finished. The instruction is kept until the monitor reports completion or a task-specific event occurs, while the policy keeps acting on new observations. On RoboMME, the system succeeds in 79.13% of episodes with an average of 3.63 Astra calls and 80.84 seconds per episode. This is 34.62 points above the best published non-oracle baseline and 4.95 points below GroundSG+Oracle, which gives the low-level policy ground-truth subgoals.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

UJHkYOreYB.title: Co-Evolving Robot Orchestrators and Policies through Deployment
UJHkYOreYB.authors: Xilun Zhang, Maggie Wang, Erik Bauer, Hong-Xing Yu, Huang Huang, Jiajun Wu, Marco Pavone
UJHkYOreYB.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies trained on large datasets are capable within their training domains, yet they still fail to generalize to the variety of situations a robot meets in real-world deployment. Agentic robot systems complement the policy with a vision-language model (VLM) orchestrator that learns when to call the policy, how to instruct it, and when to use scripted skills instead. However, because the harness is built around a frozen policy that has limited language steerability, the orchestrator can avoid the policy's failures but never overcome them. The policy becomes the bottleneck of the whole system. Fine-tuning the policy can remove this bottleneck, but updating it alone decouples it from an orchestrator tuned to its old behavior. We propose Robo-COP, in which the orchestrator and policy co-evolve during deployment. Robo-COP curates skill demonstrations from its own executions, fine-tunes the policy when this data can address recurring failures, and adopts each new policy only after it improves the skills it was trained for. Across ten simulated RoboLab tasks, Robo-COP raises mean held-out success from 64.8% to 73.8% over the same harness with a frozen policy, while fine-tuning on a fixed schedule without verification reaches only 65.8%. On three real-world tasks, Robo-COP raises held-out success from 38.3% to 50.0%. Robo-COP turns deployment into a self-improving flywheel in which robots learn by doing, with each improvement in execution producing better data for the next round of learning. Videos and code are available at https://xilunzhangrobo.github.io/robo-cop/.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

l0BBYNeW4A.title: ComDex: A Compositional Framework for Dexterity Learning from Offline Human Manipulation Videos
l0BBYNeW4A.authors: Yunhai Han, Harish Ravichandar, Yashraj Narang, Jie Xu, Wei Yang
l0BBYNeW4A.abstract: Recent advances in vision-based human hand tracking make human manipulation a promising source of rich supervision signals for robot learning. However, the substantial embodiment gap between human hands and robotic manipulators makes direct transfer, such as pose retargeting, insufficient to guarantee successful robot execution. To bridge this gap, recent approaches typically introduce a subsequent optimization stage, often based on reinforcement learning, to refine retargeted robot behaviors using information estimated from the video, such as object-pose trajectories. Despite their effectiveness, these approaches are difficult to apply to precise in-hand manipulation from RGB videos, as commonly used vision-based estimators often fail to accurately recover object poses under severe hand–object occlusions. Additionally, object-tracking-based refinement may fall short when task semantics matter. For example, in assembly, maximizing the object-pose tracking reward alone does not necessarily ensure successful insertion, as pose estimation errors can exceed the tolerance required for precise insertion. To address these two challenges, we first propose an effective in-hand object pose estimation method by leveraging human hand motion and the hand–object interaction. We then introduce an agent-based task-understanding module and a corresponding reward-generation module that autonomously produce simulation-ready task reward functions. Leveraging these components, we develop a “one-button” framework, ComDex, that converts human videos of complex, contact-rich manipulation into robot policies by integrating pose tracking rewards, interaction rewards, task rewards, and CuRobo-enabled collision-aware motion planner. We further validate the framework across diverse manipulation tasks involving in-hand manipulation, contact-rich interactions, and functional manipulation.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

78L8T5nsLM.title: Contact Code: A Typed Program Interface for Measurable and Repairable Contact-Rich Manipulation
78L8T5nsLM.authors: Yanru Wu, Zizhe Zhang, Qi Chen, Haimin Hu, Alan Yuille, Jieneng Chen
78L8T5nsLM.abstract: The ability to adapt to physical feedback is essential for robots performing contact-rich manipulation. Vision-language models (VLMs) provide a promising way to interpret task instructions and configure robot behavior from visual observations. However, adapting these decisions after physical interaction requires connecting execution feedback to the parameters that can be revised. We introduce Contact Code, a typed program interface that supports this connection by organizing controller parameters, measured execution evidence, and permitted updates around individual contact stages. Within predefined task templates, a VLM proposes a task configuration that is validated and instantiated into an executable program. During execution, robot motion and contact measurements provide feedback for controller-level recovery and evidence for subsequent program revision. If execution still fails, the system uses this evidence to select a contact stage and guides the VLM to propose a constrained update before the next attempt. We evaluate Contact Code on eight tasks and 800 held-out instances across ManiSkill, Isaac Lab, and UniVTAC-based simulation, spanning wrist force and fingertip tactile sensing as well as single-arm and bimanual settings. Contact Code increases success from 60.4% on the first rollout to 73.6% after repair and outperforms free-form parameter repair by 8.3% under the same feedback and rollout budget. In a separate study on three representative tasks, we evaluate programs composed by a VLM from shared primitives, with automatically derived evidence bindings and repair interfaces, showing improved success after feedback-guided program repair. We also evaluate Contact Code on a Flexiv arm for peg insertion and nut threading, providing evidence for the effectiveness of feedback-guided program repair and the portability of the interface across robot platforms. This interface provides a foundation for studying how physical feedback can guide program revision, offering a path toward more adaptable language-guided robotic systems.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

CQFstcjx1Z.title: Do Agentic Policies Need to Look at Every Step? Geometric Abstraction for Reasoning and Action
CQFstcjx1Z.authors: Yihang Liu, Yiming Chen, Mingzhe Zheng
CQFstcjx1Z.abstract:
Recent multimodal language models can reason directly about robot scenes, but it is unclear whether they need to repeatedly reinterpret raw visual observations at every step of an interaction. We propose shifting routine spatial reasoning from images to text and symbols through a 3D geometric abstraction that is refreshed locally from observations and read directly by the language models. Specifically, our interface represents scene geometry via typed, evidence-aware symbolic references to object parts, grounds them from calibrated RGB-D, and returns compact textual checkpoints with metric residuals after each action. Symbolic task structure can thus be reused across decisions while metric values are rebound to the current scene, with direct visual reasoning invoked only on demand. Across offline policy synthesis and continuous online execution, reasoning over grounded text and symbols improves multi-step manipulation completion while substantially reducing repeated multimodal queries, positioning explicit geometric state as an effective substrate for agentic
robot policies.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

9HKnVoy6O0.title: Embodied XAI: Tracing Hierarchical Agent Decisions via 4D Spatio-Temporal Saliency
9HKnVoy6O0.abstract: Robots steered by vision-language models are being proposed for spaces people occupy, where an unaccountable choice carries real cost. Yet when these physical AI agents silently pick a target, per-frame 2D saliency cannot say what in the physical world drove them: the planner is re-queried continuously while the robot drives, so each map sits in its own moving camera frame, leaving thousands of disconnected images that cannot be pooled, sliced, or compared. We present \emph{4D spatiotemporal saliency}, a model-agnostic framework that relocates attribution from the camera to the scene: an attribution stage scores the planner's own sampled steering token, each attributed pixel is lifted into world coordinates through depth and pose, and the results accumulate across queries and trials into one heat field growing through time. The explanation thereby becomes an object that can be added up, grouped by outcome, differenced against a reference, replayed, and physically intervened upon. We instantiate it with chosen-action integrated gradients on a quadruped driven by ambiguous instructions, and use the field to certify scene-level attribution patterns as repeatable, separate the signatures of success and failure, watch a decision harden, and run closed-loop occlusion experiments that persistently target the same physical region as the camera moves.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

3c1CfvfHa7.title: EMBODIEDSWE: Coding Agents for Long Horizon Dexterous Robotics
3c1CfvfHa7.authors: Yilang Liu, Zeyu Shen, Haoxiang You, Zhicheng Zheng, Lihan Zha, Kashu Yamazaki, Mingtong Zhang, Suning Huang, Jiankai Sun, Qianzhong Chen, Luxi He, Kaiyuan Liu, Haoran Chang, Katerina Fragkiadaki, Mac Schwager, Dhruv Shah, Peter Henderson, Ian Abraham, Canwen Xu
3c1CfvfHa7.abstract: We study coding agents for long-horizon, dexterous robotics and ask whether their solutions can provide scalable supervision for learning general robot policies. To test this, we develop EMBODIEDSWE-BENCH, a simulation benchmark for coding agents spanning contact-rich manipulation, deformable objects, and long-horizon tasks requiring up to half an hour of continuous interaction. We find that frontier coding agents can solve complex long-horizon tasks and transfer prior solutions across both tasks and embodiments. We also design supporting tools that help agents more effectively solve these tasks. However, the resulting solutions require substantial iterative interaction and are typically specialized to individual task instances. We therefore introduce EMBODIEDSWE-BENCH, which expands a single solution from coding agent into large diverse trajectories for training a VLA. VLA performance improves with more generated demonstrations, and agent-aided diversification improves generalization to held-out task variations. We also show that a VLA finetuned solely on coding-agent-generated simulation demonstrations completes a long-horizon task on real robot. Together, our framework uses coding agents to solve complex robotics tasks and turn verified solutions into scalable supervision for robot policies.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

9CSIakHmiD.title: ENCORE: Few-Shot Agentic Discovery of Manipulation Strategies
9CSIakHmiD.authors: Yifan Kang, Zihan Wang, Zhiwen Fan, Bangya Liu
9CSIakHmiD.abstract:
Coding agents can now write, run, and debug programs with little human help.
Robot tasks, however, are usually specified by a sentence that leaves out how
to grasp, in what order to make contact, and what the result should look
like, and an agent given only the sentence must find these details by trial
and error. We introduce \method{}, which gives the agent a few
demonstrations as evidence to read rather than as training data. A
deterministic builder distills each demonstration into a pack of multi-view
keyframes, gripper events, frame strips, and the full trajectory. A coding
agent studies the pack, writes a policy program against a fixed perception
and action API, checks it with its own sensors over a few development
rollouts, and freezes it before a sealed evaluation that never reveals the
success signal. On LIBERO-PRO, the agent's first program already succeeds in
half of the perturbed tasks with demonstrations and in one task without them, and the
frozen programs outperform the strongest prior agentic system run with the
same language model (96.3\% against 89.3\%). On RoboDojo tasks whose
instructions leave the goal unstated, no program succeeds without
demonstrations. ENCORE also runs on a real bimanual robot, learning cube
handover and cup inversion from five demonstrations each.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

Eq3xq6KZDC.title: FEIJOA: Task-Driven Grounding and Execution for Mobile Manipulation
Eq3xq6KZDC.authors: Aditya Agarwal, William Shen, Sahit Chintalapudi, Lucy Cai, Nishanth Kumar, Aidan Curtis, Travis Manderson, Tomás Lozano-Pérez, Leslie Pack Kaelbling
Eq3xq6KZDC.abstract: A mobile manipulator asked to ``put the toys away in the toy box'' must decide which objects are toys and which container the user means, then find base poses, grasps, and placements it can execute. Because a scene representation is built before the instruction is known, it may lack the attributes, affordances, or concepts needed to resolve the task. We present FEIJOA, a language-model agent that grounds the instruction at test time. It queries a grounding tool over a posed RGB-D scan, inspects the returned candidates, and refines its queries until they resolve the instruction. An embodiment-aware harness checks each skill's preconditions, samples base poses from which the target is reachable, and verifies the skill's effect from observations before and after execution. On 103 open-ended grounding queries, FEIJOA resolves 94.2\% exactly, compared with 68.0\% for the best prebuilt representation. Over 50 real-world trials on Spot, it completes 35 tasks; 17 of these successes follow recovery from a failed tool call or verification check. Of the 15 failed trails, 13 were caused by the robot's physical skills, and only 2 by grounding or the agent's reasoning.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

wKgMn9vqUi.title: Fewer Tokens, Better Action: GPT-6 Astra Robot Agents with 14% Higher Success but 65% Fewer Tokens
wKgMn9vqUi.authors: Ruiyang Si, Jianxin Bi, Shunyu Yang, Rui Ni, Wenbo Huang, Qiang Wang, Shulong Jiang, Duomin Wang, Zhen Dong, Daquan Zhou
wKgMn9vqUi.abstract: Vision language model (VLM) agents can control robots through visual feedback and action primitives, but repeated model invocations and redundant observations incur substantial token overhead. We introduce PyRUA-Lean, an interactive code-execution framework that couples feedback-driven primitive composition with selective observation: the agent composes classical robot primitives and learned vision-language-action (VLA) policies into Python cells that perform conditional checks and local retries, returning only explicitly requested images and state feedback for replanning. Across 700 simulated task instances from LIBERO-PRO, RoboTwin 2.0, and RoboCasa365, we compare PyRUA-Lean with a tool-calling baseline using the same GPT-6 Astra planner and underlying robot primitives. Under equal LLM-call budgets, PyRUA-Lean increases overall success from 63.1\% to 71.7\%. On instances solved by both agents, it uses 49\% fewer LLM calls and 65\% fewer input tokens. The PyRUA-Lean library will be released.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

sU18hA2zbD.title: Generalized Planning Interfaces for Agentic Robotics
sU18hA2zbD.authors: Ben Zandonati, Yifan Kang, Tomás Lozano-Pérez, Leslie Pack Kaelbling
sU18hA2zbD.abstract: Agentic manipulation requires reasoning over semantic task structure and continuous robot motion. Existing robot interfaces determine which decisions an agent can express and which it must resolve explicitly. High-level skill interfaces restrict task coverage, while detailed low-level motion generation imposes substantial inference cost and is more prone to geometric errors. We introduce generalized planning interfaces (GPIs), which let agents specify what a robot should achieve and how it should act, at any level of abstraction. Agents flexibly combine declarative goals and motion constraints with imperative skill sequences and fully specified trajectories. We instantiate a GPI with SPROUT (Sampling and Pooled Refinements of Underspecified Trajectories). SPROUT interleaves spatio-temporal constraint-graph synthesis with sampling and optimization, preserving agent-defined goals and constraints, while supplying the physical variables and constraints needed for execution. Compatible numerical queries are pooled across heterogeneous graphs for GPU execution. Across eight simulated tasks with three scenes each, SPROUT achieves a 29 percentage point increase in success, compared with less flexible agent-robot interfaces.  SPROUT enables agents to solve complex multi-step manipulation tasks, reasoning at the level of abstraction required for the task. Additional information and videos are shown on our website: https://sprout-project-d81650.pages.dev/
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

02FSMHg6ii.title: Guava: Distilling Frontier VLMs into a Compact Agent through a Robotic Manipulation Harness
02FSMHg6ii.authors: Haowen Liu, Xirui Li, Shaoxiong Yao, Peng Shi, Tianyi Zhou, Jia-Bin Huang, Furong Huang, Jiayuan Mao
02FSMHg6ii.abstract: Frontier vision–language models (VLMs) can perform robotic manipulation by interpreting visual observations, invoking robot tools, and adapting to execution feedback, but repeated model calls incur high costs and latency. In this paper, we study the problem of distilling these capabilities into compact VLMs. The key challenges are designing an interaction interface that enables efficient and generalizable distillation, and a data collection protocol that captures diverse scenarios. We present $\texttt{Guava}$, a framework built around a manipulation harness and a simulation-based data generation pipeline. We first study how harness design affects both frontier and compact models, and use the resulting interface for teacher data generation and student deployment. Through this harness, a frontier VLM generates physically executed and validated interaction trajectories in simulation, which we augment with perturbation branches that expose the teacher to execution deviations and recovery trajectories. Using $\texttt{GPT-5.4}$ as the teacher, we collect 2,268 interaction trajectories and fine-tune $\texttt{Qwen3.5-4B}$ to obtain $\texttt{Guava-4B}$. $\texttt{Guava-4B}$ substantially outperforms its base model and approaches $\texttt{GPT-5.4}$ performance across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, while generalizing to unseen objects, instructions, and task compositions. Perturbation trajectories particularly improve unseen-task generalization. With substantially lower inference latency and token usage compared to a frontier model, $\texttt{Guava-4B}$ enables efficient local deployment.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

vTOrVYhBnp.title: Harness VLA: Steering Frozen VLAs into Reliable Manipulation Primitives via Memory-Guided Agents
vTOrVYhBnp.authors: Yixian Zhang, Huanming Zhang, Feng Gao, Xiao Li, Zhihao Liu, Yi Nie, Chunyang Zhu, Jiaxing Qiu, Yuchen Yan, Jiyuan Liu, Wenhao Tang, Jiaji Rao, Zhengru Fang, Changxu Wei, Quanlu Zhang, Yu Wang, Wenbo Ding, Chao Yu
vTOrVYhBnp.abstract: Language-conditioned manipulation requires both precise contact-rich control and robust reasoning over language, scenes, and long horizons. End-to-end Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models provide strong local visuomotor skills, but they are trained on in-distribution task trajectories and often degrade under deployment perturbations such as semantic retargeting, goal re-binding, spatial-layout shifts, and unstable local contacts. LLM coding agents provide complementary semantic and compositional reasoning, but purely analytic primitives struggle with irregular grasping, constrained placement, and articulated-object interaction. We present Harness VLA, a memory-augmented agentic framework that exposes a frozen VLA as a retryable contact-rich primitive and composes it with a small fixed library of analytic primitives for grounding, staging, transport, navigation, and release. Rather than expanding the skill library, the harness learns the operating range of these fixed primitives from task-specific execution traces, global success rules, and failure models. By lifting semantic re-grounding, non-contact execution, and VLA re-staging to the planner while reserving the frozen VLA for local contact-rich phases, Harness VLA extends pretrained VLAs beyond their original trajectory distribution without fine-tuning. Across perturbed tabletop, household kitchen, and clean-to-randomized bimanual manipulation, Harness VLA improves over the strongest relevant baselines by 38.6 and 27.2 percentage points on LIBERO-Pro and RoboCasa365, respectively, and reaches 58.4\% on RoboTwin C2R. Real-world demonstrations on dual-Franka robots further show target redirection, grasp recovery, and new task compositions with the same frozen VLA.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

z5FsJD37Dj.title: How Hard Are Current Robot Memory Benchmarks for Agentic Harnesses?
z5FsJD37Dj.authors: Feiyang Wu, Weirui Ye, Haonan Chen, Haoyu Chen, Jiayu Zhou, Yandong Ji, Yuejiang Liu, Yilun Du
z5FsJD37Dj.abstract: Robot memory research has developed policies with dedicated mechanisms for storing observations and learning representations of history. Recent progress in vision-language agents offers a simpler alternative: a planner can consult explicit records of past observations and actions. We study how challenging current robot memory benchmarks remain under this approach. Our minimalist memory harness supplies a VLM planner with text logs and historical images, without an additional learned memory module. At each decision, it builds a fresh prompt from the task instruction, current image, and permitted history; a fixed controller executes the selected skill. Full text logs fit within the context window, and history channels can be removed while keeping the planner and executor fixed. We freeze the harness, task guidance, and skills before evaluating new instances of familiar tasks. With GPT-6 Astra, the harness achieves 91.9\% success on RoboMME with past execution frames and 95\% on RMBench with an event log. These results suggest that simple external records already enable strong VLM agents to solve most evaluated tasks under fixed task guidance.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

uMkXmX3mAy.title: Impossible Twins: Judge-Free Measurement of Verifier False Positives in Agentic Robot Controller Search
uMkXmX3mAy.abstract: Coding agents that rewrite robot controllers against an automated verifier can converge on the verifier's defects, and separating a false positive from genuine success ordinarily requires a judge. We make these false positives countable without a judge by pairing each task with an impossible twin. No action sequence meets its specification, so every acceptance is a false positive. Across 336 eight-iteration searches on planted defects, gpt-oss-120b on reach ended 8 of 8 runs with a complete exploit once told the defect, under a score or a task objective. An added integrity instruction left that count unchanged. Naming only the checked quantity gave 1 and 5 of 8, and gpt-oss-20b followed a different pattern, so the counts set no general threshold. A route-preservation check shows that a pinned twin largely closes a pushing exploit that a goal-side twin keeps open (4 against 45 of 50 episodes). A behavioral replay shows that 15 of 18 goal-side finals lift the block. On the solvable side, a misaligned proxy holds genuine success at 0.05 against 0.92 with true-checker feedback. A pre-gated repair pilot locates the first limit: over-rejection, which twins cannot show, leaves twin-driven repair at genuine rate 0.46 against 0.53 from one oracle. Impossible twins give a direct measure of false acceptance, and route-preservation, behavioral and solvable-side checks cover what they leave open.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

F7Dp4022mM.title: KPI: A Promptable Kernel for Physical Interaction on Humanoids
F7Dp4022mM.authors: Yikai Wang, Honghao Zhu, Xiao Hu, Hao Zhang, Zelin Wang, Yip Fun Yeung, Ding Zhao, Lingfeng Sun
F7Dp4022mM.abstract: Humanoids now walk, balance and reach with remarkable generality: one whole-body tracking policy follows references from a human, or from an end- to-end policy. That generality travels in the trajectory, and a trajectory alone car- ries limited information about the interaction it should produce: at contact, the ex- ecuting controller determines how the robot behaves. Single-task policies usually reach hard interactions by optimising trajectory and controller together in simula- tion; general stacks usually assume a preset or hand-chosen controller. We present KPI, a promptable kernel for physical interaction between the trajectory source and an unmodified whole-body tracker. Instead of a controller fixed before the task, the trajectory source sends a contract: per direction, track, comply, or hold a force range. From tracking error and a wrench estimate, the kernel adapts the arms’ stiffness, damping, reference and feedforward toward it at contact rate. We demonstrate KPI through an agentic framework: from one instruction, a vision- language agent writes both the reference trajectory and the contract, with no task- specific code. We demonstrate instruction-driven winch operation, door open- ing, and box transport, alongside scripted surface-interaction experiments. In the winch demonstration, the humanoid is able to turn a crank to hoist a second robot fully off the ground. Project website: https://kpi-robot.github.io/.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

ttNVX8zEcB.title: MemBodied: Recurrent Associative Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models
ttNVX8zEcB.authors: Tej Deep Pala, Navonil Majumder, Bryce Goh, Raphael Yee, Jianfei Yang, Liming Chen, Soujanya Poria
ttNVX8zEcB.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models provide a strong foundation for general-purpose robot control, yet a vast majority of policies do not preserve and leverage episode-level information beyond current observation. This limitation is consequential in history-dependent manipulation tasks that depend on information available only in past observations. Retaining past observations in context can aid in recovering this information, but at the significant cost of ever-growing bloated context and inference latency. We thus introduce MemBodied, a fixed-size episodic memory with two complementary components: an associative state that records interactions across policy calls and an episode anchor that preserves a compact representation of the initial scene as a reference. At each policy call, the model conditions action generation on the current input and the memory components, rather than directly using past observations. Across five evaluated RMBench tasks requiring memory, MemBodied achieves $7.81\times$ the mean success rate of a stateless policy and $2.98\times$ of vanilla recurrent memory, while outperforming the strongest memory-augmented baseline by $1.3\times$ with $10\times$ fewer added parameters. On the fully observable LIBERO-Long suite, it reached 90.6\%, a 5.4\% improvement over the stateless $\pi_0$ policy. These findings support MemBodied as a practical alternative to expanding the policy context for history-dependent manipulation.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

JprkI7JQDW.title: PhysCaP: Grounding Code-as-Policy Agent with Physics-Informed Exploration
JprkI7JQDW.authors: Chen-Yu Lin, Jing-Wen Chen, Hsueh-En Chang, Hung-An Chen, Sheng-Hsun Chang, Chi-Pin Huang, Fu-En Yang, Min-Hung Chen, Yi-Ting Chen, Yu-Chiang Frank Wang, Shao-Hua Sun
JprkI7JQDW.abstract: We present PhysCaP, a Physics-Informed Code-as-Policy agent system for active perception in robotic manipulation. While vision-language-action policies excel at imitating demonstrations, they rely on passive observation and fail to infer latent physical properties critical for manipulation. PhysCaP augments code-as-policy frameworks with a physics-informed exploration layer that enables explicit information-seeking through interaction. Our method introduces training-free physical property extraction modules that estimate object mass and stiffness from robot proprioception without additional sensors. To balance exploration costs and the efficiency of information obtained, PhysCaP employs a multi-agent design: a Planner that decides when to explore and when to stop, and a Prioritizer that filters implausible interactions and ranks the remainder using a heuristic priority score, enabling efficient, targeted exploration. We evaluate PhysCaP on three real-world tabletop manipulation tasks and a simulated task in LIBERO. The results show that existing passive and naive interactive baselines either fail when physical properties are hidden or over-explore, whereas PhysCaP achieves comparable performance with fewer interactions and reduced execution time. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of the proposed physical property extraction modules.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

SlmaqmaqW0.title: Physical Agency: Better Robot Performance Through Better Interfaces
SlmaqmaqW0.authors: Liane Galanti, Dhruv Shah, Tri Dao
SlmaqmaqW0.abstract: Frontier models increasingly act as robot-use agents, calling a robot's motor skills as tools much as they interact with a browser or code editor. But exposing skills as tools leaves open how the model should use them: what it emits, what feedback it receives, and when it decides again. We study the interface through controlled comparisons with the robot, cameras, scenes, and motor-policy weights held fixed, and separately measure the benefit of adding a complementary frozen skill. We introduce Pigey (Physical Agency), an agent that (1) issues language-level actions one at a time over a persistent task state, (2) uses verified execution, checking post-action images and robot state and recovering when it detects failure, and (3) draws on an open set of skills exposed as tools it selects for each subgoal. No additional policy training or demonstrations are required. On 30 real-robot tasks designed to probe decisions over existing motor skills, the same frozen π0.5 policy succeeds in 16.7% of trials when called directly and 84.0% through Pigey. Adding a frozen motion planner as a second skill raises success to 97.3%. Removing verification and recovery lowers success by 28 percentage points, the largest ablation drop. Gains also hold in simulation and across Claude, Gemini, and Qwen reasoners. Most of what the policy was missing was an interface, not a skill.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

LkW6BOlHMY.title: Program-Level Adversarial Co-Adaptive Self-Play for Robotic Security
LkW6BOlHMY.authors: Leo Benaharon, Chi Zhang, Wei Zheng, Weifan Zhang, Yifan Wei
LkW6BOlHMY.abstract: Coding agents can adapt robotic software by revising executable programs, but successful responses to an evolving opponent may not remain effective. We present a framework for program-level adversarial co-adaptive self-play in which coding agents generate attacks and defenses from tested opponent code and mission feedback, without model fine-tuning. Environment-specific interfaces support external programs for autonomous driving and SDK-level defenses for humanoid locomotion. Two eight-generation case studies reveal concrete software responses: a driving defender introduces direct-actuation recovery, while a humanoid defender revises incoming-state validation. These responses provide local task recovery but do not establish sustained robustness. The framework makes such adaptation and limitations observable through executable artifacts and task-level evidence.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

xQRzEp0Zhj.title: RAPID: Robot Agentic Programming from Demonstrations
xQRzEp0Zhj.authors: Yuyao Liu, Jiayuan Mao, David Hsu, Leslie Pack Kaelbling, Tomás Lozano-Pérez
xQRzEp0Zhj.abstract: Coding agents have demonstrated enormous success in solving complex programming problems. To leverage their potential for robot systems, this work introduces **Robot Agentic Programming from Demonstrations (RAPID)**, which automatically generates, verifies, and refines robot programs, given a single visual human demonstration. The iterative agentic loop of code refinement requires several key ingredients: (i) a testable task specification, (ii) action primitives for robot execution, and (iii) an interactive environment for program execution and verification. RAPID infers all three from the demonstration automatically. To make the resulting program reusable beyond the demonstration setting, RAPID uses an *object-centric relational program representation* that focuses on the underlying structure of the demonstrated strategy rather than the specific motion *per se*: it expresses the action primitives as trajectory-optimization programs that realize object-level motion effects, while composing them through relational constraints that capture scene-specific geometry at run time. We evaluated RAPID in simulation on eight challenging contact-rich nonprehensile manipulation tasks as well as general prehensile manipulation tasks in the LIBERO-Pro benchmark. We also successfully deployed it on a real Franka arm and evaluated it on all eight nonprehensile tasks. In all experiments, RAPID demonstrated strong performance, with generalization over object pose, shape, material, and environment. Website: https://yuyaoliu.me/projects/rapid.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

RxO0XrZm0h.title: Reconstruct, Practice, Go Real: Guided Self-Improvement for Embodied Agents
RxO0XrZm0h.authors: Yen-Jen Wang, Haozhe Jiang, Shuying Deng, Haoru Xue, Weirui Ye, Rocky Duan, Nika Haghtalab, S. Shankar Sastry, Pieter Abbeel, Haozhi Qi
RxO0XrZm0h.abstract:
Building reliable robot capabilities across diverse tasks requires substantial human effort to develop and maintain skills, design rewards, and integrate perception with control.
We present Reconstruct, Practice, Go Real (RPG), a framework for autonomous improvement of robot execution systems without updating model weights.
RPG identifies manipulation capabilities in an offline dataset, constructs related practice tasks in simulation, and uses execution feedback, privileged simulator state, and available dataset videos to diagnose failures.
From these diagnoses, it develops and refines reusable symbolic skills and revises the system prompt, retaining only changes that pass cross-task evaluation.
On held-out initializations of 22 manipulation tasks, RPG improves task success from 28.6\% after the first practice round to 95.0\% after 15 rounds, outperforming all evaluated baselines, including ASPIRE (75.5\%) and CaP-Agent0 powered by GPT-6 Astra Pro (60.0\%).
After a common calibration and hardware-adaptation procedure, the frozen system succeeds in all 30 physical trials, with ten trials on each of three tasks.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

UPAuYhlq0Y.title: Recovery Credit: Evaluating Robot Decisions Under Physical-State Uncertainty
UPAuYhlq0Y.abstract: Successful task completion sometimes conceals recovery decisions that respect the prescribed procedure in one hidden physical state and violate it in another. We introduce recovery credit as a history-sensitive evaluation framework that couples policy decisions across observationally equivalent latent-state branches and assesses each consequential commitment against a predeclared state-dependent contract. Paired robust completion measures universal terminal success with contract-consistent commitments and endpoint-masked fragility identifies successful branch families containing an earlier contract conflict. The diagnostic suite models interrupted actuation and hidden insertion contact, then extends the evaluation to material transfer under occluded target occupancy. Across all three tasks, scripted normalization-first controls achieve terminal success and paired robust completion of 1.00 with endpoint-masked fragility of 0.00. Blind-retry controls with subsequent endpoint repair attain the same terminal success rate with paired robust completion of 0.00 and endpoint-masked fragility of 1.00. Independent contract checks reproduce the stipulated classifications and exhaustive branch-subset analysis establishes the dependence of admissibility on candidate-state coverage. Fixed-trajectory authorization changes further quantify the sensitivity of robust-completion classifications to declared contracts. These findings establish the admissibility of decisions made under physical uncertainty as a distinct criterion for evaluating robotic recovery, even across trajectories with identical successful endpoints.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

DdoqCu21kt.title: RL$^2$-VLA: Adaptive RL Latent Compositional Steering with Test-Time Scaling for Vision-Language-Action Models
DdoqCu21kt.authors: Derek Ming Siang Tan, Shailesh Shailesh, Srikrishna Iyer, William Teo, Yuanliang Ju, Qiao Gu, Guillaume Adrien Sartoretti
DdoqCu21kt.abstract: Despite the impressive visuomotor capabilities enabled by Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, their performance often degrades on out-of-domain tasks. Recent test-time steering and scaling methods avoid extensive data collection and retraining, but action samples often remain concentrated around similar behaviors and inherit correlated failure modes. We introduce $RL^2$, an adaptive inference-time steering framework that leverages $\underline{\text{R}}$einforcement $\underline{\text{L}}$earning on VLA $\underline{\text{L}}$atents. $RL^2$ composes the flow velocity of a lightweight offline RL policy, conditioned on latents from the VLA action expert, with that of the frozen VLA. This combines the behavioral priors of large-scale imitation learning with the action diversity induced by offline RL beyond dominant demonstration modes. We further discover that inference-time steering follows fundamentally different scaling laws under success and failure states: diversity helps most when the base VLA is likely to fail, but unnecessarily perturbs states when success is already likely. This motivates $RL^2$ to route corrective guidance to the frozen VLA actions only when failure is detected. On SIMPLER and PolaRiS benchmarks, $RL^2$ improves success rates by up to +17.3\% in out-of-domain settings, with ablations highlighting the importance of latent representations and RL training, and real-world experiments  establishing $RL^2$ as a practical and modular steering framework for VLA deployment.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

YxvA7kHDbK.title: RLE-Bench: A Qualifying Exam for Coding Agents as Robot Learning Engineers
YxvA7kHDbK.authors: Haitong Ma, Chenxiao Gao, Rushi Qiang, Bo Dai, Na Li
YxvA7kHDbK.abstract: Coding agents are beginning to move beyond purely digital tasks to tackle physical-world challenges, particularly in robotics. Existing robotics benchmarks, however, primarily focus on the performance of individual artifacts, such as policies or controllers, offering limited coverage of coding agents’ broader engineering capabilities. Real-world robotics extends beyond control: agents must build, integrate, diagnose, and improve heterogeneous artifacts under resource constraints and reason from multimodal feedback.
