To evaluate these broader capabilities, we introduce \rlebench{}, a benchmark of robot-learning tasks spanning four representative robotics development workflows: interactive control, policy learning, perception and estimation, and mechanical design. We use diverse task-specific metrics to evaluate the artifacts submitted by the coding agents, from the success rate the agents achieved to the policy agents trained, the harness agent built, and the mechanical structures the agent designed. We aggregate these metrics into an overall RLE Index and report workflow-specific capability profiles, enabling systematic comparison of coding agents' capabilities across multiple capability dimensions. Beyond performance ranks, we also conduct in-depth case studies examining agent behavior on representative tasks, highlighting both current capabilities and limitations, and pointing to the opportunities robotics tasks have to offer for future agent training.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

C3sG9bZPbs.title: SceneRig: An Agentic System for Simulation-Ready 3D Scene Reconstruction from Single Images
C3sG9bZPbs.authors: Rundong Luo, Yunong Liu, Di Cao, Matthew Tancik, Shyamal Buch, Colton Stearns, Wenqi Xian
C3sG9bZPbs.abstract: Simulation supports robot policy evaluation, but constructing realistic scenes at scale remains difficult. Reconstructing simulation-ready scenes from single images requires accurate object recovery, placement, and physical grounding. Post-hoc settling can yield stable scenes that no longer match the observed workspace. We present SceneRig, an agentic system that reconstructs editable 3D scenes using visual, geometric, and physical tools. Agents recover objects and supports, construct the surrounding scene, and refine placement through simulated edit-and-validate loops. Across diverse tabletop images, SceneRig improves instance recovery, object-centric appearance, and 3D placement while maintaining physical stability. In calibrated RGB-D robotics experiments, its scenes predict real-robot policy outcomes more accurately than the baseline and more reliably replay recorded manipulations without trajectory adaptation. See our project page: https://scenerig.github.io/.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

Hpk5GERa1W.title: SimEX: Simulation-Integrated Robotics AutoResearch
Hpk5GERa1W.authors: Jiaheng Hu, Roberto Martín-Martín, Peter Stone, Rocky Duan, Zhenyu Jiang, Guanya Shi
Hpk5GERa1W.abstract: Coding agents powered by large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable abilities to autonomously reason about and achieve goals in the digital world. However, bringing this success to the physical world remains challenging. On the one hand, direct generation methods (e.g., Code as Policies) often suffer from the LLMs’ insufficient understanding of robots and physical environments. On the other hand, iterative trial-and-error tuning in the physical world (e.g., physical autoresearch) induces significant experimental cost and safety concerns. We introduce SimEX: Simulation-Integrated Robotics AutoResearch, an autoresearch framework that tightly integrates simulated experimentation, enabling coding agents to efficiently acquire physical capabilities for controlling real robots. SimEX operates in two stages. First, the agent conducts open-ended probe-and-optimize iterations in simulation, developing a robot toolbox with robust and generalizable capabilities. Second, the agent adapts the toolbox and the simulator together through only a few physical trials: each trial corrects the simulator, and the corrected simulator is used to diagnose failures and screen candidate repairs. We evaluate SimEX extensively in sim-to-sim settings and on physical robots. On challenging real-world manipulation tasks including towel folding, barcode scanning, and plate manipulation, SimEX enables coding agents to efficiently acquire robot skills without any demonstration and with only 10 minutes of real-robot interaction. These results suggest that simulation can be a critical component in achieving physical intelligence, not only as a source of training data for policies, but also as a laboratory where a coding agent iteratively develops capabilities through experimentation before acting on the robot.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

52exBmCzDf.title: Skill2Real: Agentic Skill Learning for Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Robot Manipulation
52exBmCzDf.authors: Xincheng He, Siyu Ma, Chang Yu, Yunuo Chen, Yanjia Huang, Ying Nian Wu, Yin Yang, Chenfanfu Jiang
52exBmCzDf.abstract: Sim-to-real learning commonly adapts policies or representations to domain variation, often directing the learning budget toward task-agnostic low-level representations at the expense of task-level knowledge. Skill2Real builds on cross-domain grounding from foundation vision-language models (VLMs) to acquire validated, reusable skills in simulation through a shared code-based policy interface. In its asymmetric Proposer--Verifier--Governor (PVG) loop, the Proposer acts from public observations and API returns, the Verifier diagnoses outcomes with privileged simulation evidence, and the Governor admits updates supported by validation rollouts. A Cerebellum learns reusable local manipulation skills; a Brain then composes the frozen library into long-horizon programs with planning and recovery. At deployment, this hierarchy is grounded in real observations through the same interface. On unseen LIBERO-Pro Long, frozen LIBERO-90 skills raise success from 2.0% to 56.3% with Astra and from 0.5% to 49.0% with Opus 5. Robosuite success reaches 85.1--89.4% across seven tasks. On a real UR5e, the same agent's mean completion rises from 27.50% to 78.75% across four tasks with Skill2Real, a controlled gain that, with cross-model improvements, shows Skill2Real adds a capability orthogonal to the foundation model by learning transferable task knowledge in simulation.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

ys5jtBPagk.title: STeP: Signal Temporal Logic for Precise Specifications for Action Generation with Vision Language Models
ys5jtBPagk.authors: Kasra Torshizi, Anukriti Singh, Sidharth Mathur, Khuzema Habib, Leo Du, Pratap Tokekar
ys5jtBPagk.abstract: Natural-language robot instructions often specify more than a coarse task goal: they may impose spatial, temporal, and logical requirements that must remain satisfied throughout execution. We present STeP, a specification-based agentic framework that uses Signal Temporal Logic (STL) as an explicit interface between high-level language reasoning and low-level robot execution. Rather than encoding such requirements implicitly in a learned policy, STeP formalizes them as task specifications that can be decomposed across multi-stage manipulation, enforced during execution, monitored online, and used as structured feedback for replanning. We evaluate STeP on standard LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO, and introduce LIBERO-Constrained, a new benchmark for manipulation tasks with spatial, temporal, and logical requirements, together with real-world tabletop experiments. On LIBERO-PRO, STeP retains 54%-89% success across five of six evaluated perturbation settings, substantially outperforming VLA and code-as-policy baselines under distribution shift. On LIBERO-Constrained, STeP achieves 80% safe success across 49 task-constraint instances; on real-world tasks, it improves safe success over a specification-free model-based baseline across all four task categories, with gains of up to 45 percentage points. These results support explicit formal specifications as a practical interface between foundation-model reasoning and reliable robot execution.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

BCdDYO0jo9.title: SUTO: Failure-Localized Reasoning for Robot Task Planning and Execution
BCdDYO0jo9.authors: Sohan Rudra, Yuezhe Zhang, Kumar Manas, Vignesh Prasad, Georgia Chalvatzaki
BCdDYO0jo9.abstract: A task plan is a structured sequence of actions, instantiated through primitives or skill sequences, to achieve a predefined goal. During long-horizon execution, such plans must remain consistent with the task specification, the relevant entities, and the evolving world state. When execution fails, however, not all prior reasoning becomes invalid. The key challenge is to determine which commitments must be reconsidered and which can be retained. We address this through SUTO, a long-horizon planning framework centered on retry validity. SUTO identifies the highest-level commitment that remains valid after a failure and selectively revises only the dependent artifacts. The framework generates self-verifying local policies using scene-graph grounding and couples their execution with evidence-conditioned failure attribution. This enables localized recovery without restarting the reasoning process. On LIBERO-PRO, SUTO achieves an $11\%$ zero-shot success rate while remaining substantially cheaper than competing approaches, and reaches $50\%$ success in real-world evaluations at approximately $17\times$ lower cost than naive retry based approaches.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

RkzWx9Sfcz.title: Topology-Informed Visual Prompting for Hierarchical Vision-Language-Action Control
RkzWx9Sfcz.authors: Haoyang Wu, Abhinav Kumar, Dmitry Berenson
RkzWx9Sfcz.abstract:
Agentic robot systems often separate high-level reasoning from low-level visuomotor control, motivating the use of intermediate representations that communicate task-relevant constraints between layers. We study this interface in manipulation tasks where partial observations of obstacle geometry can obscure topological relationships that require qualitatively different actions.
While motion planners with full knowledge of environment geometries and object states can reason about these signatures in planning, this information is often not known at deployment.
To address this issue, we present a topology-guided visual-prompting framework that uses simulation-based planning to augment a nominal demonstration dataset and provides vision-based guidance at deployment.
Our method uses a Gauss-Linking-Integral topological signature representation to capture important topological properties of the environment. Using privileged geometry information from a simulation approximation of our environment, we augment a VLA fine-tuning dataset with trajectories that move the system to a demonstrated signature and, from the new configuration, resume task execution.
At deployment, a vision-language model (VLM) estimates the current signature and predicts image-space end-effector waypoints from camera observations. Recomputing both after each VLA action chunk yields a closed-loop hierarchical policy in which the VLM performs topological state estimation and waypoint prediction, while the VLA executes continuous control.
Across three simulated bimanual tasks and a real-world box pickup task, our method outperforms a VLA fine-tuned only on nominal demonstrations and a VLM-prompting baseline that can remove topology-relevant information from observations.
On hardware, it exceeds the strongest baseline by 40\% in task success. Project website: \texttt{https://topology-vla.github.io}.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

cPUMmLHDG6.title: Uncertainty Is the Wrong Trigger: An Exact Account of When an Agent Should Ask Before It Cannot Undo
cPUMmLHDG6.abstract: An agentic robot that can ask a person for help has to decide when to ask, and the field's answer is to ask when it is uncertain - a conformal set that is too large, an entropy above a threshold, a confidence below one. We show that no such rule can be right, and we show it exactly rather than empirically. On a task where the Bayes-optimal asking policy is a closed-form backward recursion, the value of a query is not a function of how uncertain the agent is: it is a function of whether the answer would change what the agent does. Those differ, and they differ in a way that is fatal for a threshold. Across 98 configurations in which the optimum asks at some failure rates and not others, no threshold on entropy reproduces the optimal policy in 3 of them and no threshold on the failure probability itself reproduces it in any (0 of 98); the best entropy threshold agrees with the optimum on as few as 30 of 49 decisions. The mechanism is an asymmetry: uncertainty is symmetric under q -> 1-q and the value of asking is not, so 31% of equal-uncertainty pairs get opposite optimal answers. At q=0.06 and q=0.94, which carry identical uncertainty of 0.33 bits, asking is worth 0.0316 and -0.1292 respectively. The value of asking peaks at a median failure rate of 0.12, never above 0.52 - almost never at maximum uncertainty. A decision-theoretic trigger fixes it: thresholding the value gap between the agent's two best actions recovers a median 97% of the value of asking against 77% for the best-tuned entropy threshold, and is exactly optimal on 473 of 600 tasks against 374. We also report a null we did not expect: irreversibility, the thing the whole practice is meant to guard against, moves the optimal asking rate by a median of 0 percentage points, while query cost moves it from 96% to 4%.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

rNHO9vQF9h.title: World Action Planner: Generalizable Robot Decision-Making with Action-Conditioned World Models
rNHO9vQF9h.authors: XiangCheng Zhang, Runhan Huang, Yilun Du
rNHO9vQF9h.abstract: Building generalizable robot agents for diverse applications remains a fundamental challenge. While imitation learning-based policies can perform well in familiar training environments, they often struggle to generalize to novel scenes, layouts, and task compositions. To this end, we present **World Action Planner**, an agentic robot planning system that proposes and refines executable action plans through imagination with an action-conditioned world model. We perform a principled coarse-to-fine search over robot actions in two stages: (i) global action optimization, where the agent reasons over imagined world-model rollouts to identify potential failures and refine the proposed action plan, and (ii) local action search, where the agent compares the imagined future outcomes of neighboring action candidates and selects the best action for execution. Across compositional long-horizon tasks, novel object layouts, and zero-shot real-robot planning without expert demonstrations, World Action Planner consistently outperforms state-of-the-art end-to-end policy models, including VLAs and WAMs, demonstrating the effectiveness of world-model-based action search for generalizable robot decision making.
workshops: Workshop on Agentic Robotics

kSnt4vdJL6.title: $Z$-sight: Unifying Vision-Language-Action and Latent World Modeling
kSnt4vdJL6.authors: Junjie Ye, Yiqi Zhao, Muchen Xu, Celina Shiyu Wang, Hao Dong, Ruohai Ge, Rong Xue, Benjamin J Kolligs, Aditya Dutt, Sasanka Nagavalli, Nassim A. Samad, Gaurav S. Sukhatme, Jyotirmoy V. Deshmukh, Yue Wang, Yuliang Guo
kSnt4vdJL6.abstract:
We introduce $Z$-sight, a unified robot foundation model that brings
vision-language-action modeling and world modeling together through
feature-space future prediction. Whereas video-based world action models (WAMs)
adapt pretrained video generators at substantial computational cost, $Z$-sight
predicts the future in the native visual representation space of a pretrained
vision-language model (VLM), so the policy perceives the present and predicts
the future within a shared visual foundation. A foresight expert and a
continuous action expert are coupled to the VLM through a
mixture-of-transformers: the foresight expert denoises future spatial visual
tokens, while the action expert attends to this prediction stream to generate
actions, enabling joint learning from robot trajectories and human egocentric
video without pixel reconstruction. On a real humanoid robot, $Z$-sight
achieves a 62% average success rate across five manipulation tasks,
outperforming VLA and WAM baselines by a large margin, while running at
110,ms per action chunk.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

PqygDMdaMX.title: 3D Motion Priors for Data-Efficient and View-Robust Latent Action Learning
PqygDMdaMX.authors: Dongyun Kim, Hanjung Kim, Jinho Jeong, Jaehyun Kang, Youngwoon Lee, Seon Joo Kim
PqygDMdaMX.abstract: Learning generalizable visuomotor policies from limited action-labeled demonstrations remains a key challenge in robot learning. While latent action models leverage action-free videos to learn task-relevant dynamics, their pixel-space latent action representations often entangle physical motion with viewpoint-dependent appearance, limiting robustness to unseen camera views. We propose a geometrically grounded 3D latent action framework that learns compact motion priors from canonical 3D scene motion. These priors supervise policy pre-training, and co-finetuning on limited labeled demonstrations adapts the resulting motion-aware representation to executable control. Combined with a 3D-aware visual encoder, our framework supports robust observation-to-latent-action prediction. Experiments on LIBERO and RoboCasa show that our framework improves novel-view generalization under limited demonstrations, yielding relative gains of 119% on RoboCasa and 33.5% on LIBERO over a 3D encoder-only baseline in the extreme 2-shot setting.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

CR5wVdj5Nc.title: AFFORD2ACT: How Far Can Sparse Keypoints Go for Robot Manipulation?
CR5wVdj5Nc.authors: Anukriti Singh, Kasra Torshizi, Khuzema Habib, Kelin Yu, Ruohan Gao, Pratap Tokekar
CR5wVdj5Nc.abstract: Vision-based manipulation policies are commonly learned from rich visual observations, yet it remains unclear how much of this visual information is required for effective policy learning. Sparse 2D keypoints provide a deliberately compact alternative, giving the policy spatial information while removing direct access to appearance, texture, and background. We use Afford2Act: Affordance-Guided Keypoints to Act to study how much manipulation capability can be retained under this representation constraint. An off-the-shelf language-conditioned affordance model identifies the task-relevant region, from which up to 15 object keypoints are selected; together with 4 end-effector keypoints, each observation is reduced to 19 2D keypoints (38 coordinates). Correspondence preserves keypoint identity across object instances, after which the points are tracked over time and passed to a lightweight gated policy. Across six real-robot manipulation tasks, this compact state outperforms the evaluated RGB, RGB-D, and dense-affordance behavior cloning baselines, degrades less as the number of demonstrations is reduced, and achieves 82% average success in held-out settings. Replacing learned gating with uniform weights reduces success from 92% to 52%. At the same time, the representation depends on reliable affordance localization and keypoint tracking, and remains vulnerable to incorrect masks, occlusion, tracking drift, and distractors.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

3zm6gB0Hh8.title: BFN Policy: Visuomotor Policy Learning for Hybrid Action Spaces via Bayesian Flow Networks
3zm6gB0Hh8.authors: Zhaoyang Li, Aleyna Kara, Abha Jha, Bo-Ruei Huang, Majid Khadiv, Erdem Biyik
3zm6gB0Hh8.abstract: Diffusion Policy is state of the art for continuous control, but robots often act through abstractions pairing a discrete mode with continuous parameters, formalized as Parameterized Action Markov Decision Processes (PAMDPs). Gaussian noise cannot corrupt a discrete choice; relaxing and rounding the mode instead pushes samples off the probability simplex and breaks discrete-continuous coupling. Faster samplers such as DDIM and Consistency Policy inherit the same continuous-only Gaussian process. We introduce BFN Policy, the first Bayesian Flow Network imitation policy, designed for hybrid actions. BFN Policy casts hybrid action generation as structured posterior inference in belief space rather than denoising in data space: conjugate updates flow the categorical belief on the simplex and monotonically sharpen the Gaussian belief. Every intermediate state is a valid posterior, preserving discrete-continuous dependencies without relaxation or rounding, with a test-time step budget needing no distillation. On eight PAMDP benchmarks and Push-T with continuous and hybrid actions, BFN Policy outperforms all diffusion and consistency baselines on hybrid tasks by a margin growing with discrete branching, matches Diffusion Policy on continuous control, and runs at DDIM-level cost, over an order of magnitude faster than DDPM. Sampler diagnostics trace the gain to a discrete representation Gaussian formulations cannot maintain. Code and videos are available at https://anonymousproj-dot.github.io/BFN-Policy.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

PM7I8LhQHE.title: BURGER: Benchmarking and Understanding Robotic Generalization via Embodied dRawing
PM7I8LhQHE.authors: Xiangyu Xu, Bangshuai Peng, Ziyi Liu, Mengjie Zhao, Chenhao Lu, Zhengyang Fan, Huazhe Xu, Kaizhe Hu
PM7I8LhQHE.abstract: How effectively can vision-language-action (VLA) models learn diverse language-conditioned behaviors as training data scales? Investigating this question requires large and varied robot datasets, whose collection on physical robots remains costly. We introduce BURGER, a language-conditioned robotic drawing benchmark with a scalable, prompt-driven pipeline for generating continuous drawing trajectories, both in simulation and the real world. In BURGER, an agent starts from the same blank canvas and controls a robot arm to draw the object or spatial composition specified by language, while each instruction allows an openended variety of valid drawings and stroke orders. Using 28,200 simulated demonstrations spanning 282 drawing tasks, we evaluate five representative VLA models across data scales, language grounding, and multimodal behavior. BURGER supports fine-grained analysis of language grounding, spatial composition, and action generation, revealing distinct failure patterns across VLA models. Our experiments suggest that some VLA models can benefit from greater task diversity and demonstration scale, capture multimodal drawing behaviors, and generalize to unseen object compositions of familiar objects. Finally, we deploy a trained policy on a Franka Panda arm, demonstrating the ability to draw reactively under human intervention. We refer the reader to https://burger-bench.github.io for more visualization.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

jdLfwzLgyG.title: Can the Critic Select Checkpoints in Vision-Language-Action Reinforcement Learning?
jdLfwzLgyG.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training can improve a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policy, but choosing which saved checkpoint to deploy usually requires evaluation episodes on the robot. A signal that requires no evaluation episodes is the critic the RL algorithm already trains, and a guideline from offline RL takes the checkpoint at which its average value peaks. We study this choice in simulation for $\pi_0$ steered through DSRL on task 8, the LIBERO-Long task on which $\pi_0$ succeeds least often in our setup. We find that the critic's value at demonstration states peaks early in training, before success rises, so the checkpoint with the highest value is under-trained on every task-8 run on which we computed the critic's value. Restricting the critic's choice to late training, with a cutoff we chose after seeing most runs' critic values, still performs worse than keeping the final checkpoint, and no other selector we tested that requires no evaluation episodes reliably improves on keeping the final checkpoint. On task 8, keeping the final checkpoint usually gives up little success relative to the best checkpoint whose success we confirmed on a second pool of episodes, but on four of our sixteen task-8 runs the final checkpoint falls more than 10 points below an earlier checkpoint, sometimes because training ends in a collapse. Practice success, the success rate of the episodes the learner collects while training, ranks checkpoints only weakly once we control for training step, so in this setting the chosen checkpoint should still be confirmed on evaluation episodes. Code is available at: https://github.com/Nikash-B/vla-checkpoint-selection.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

PqbgsEMl8U.title: Cross-Embodiment Robot Foundation World Models with Latent Actions
PqbgsEMl8U.authors: Huang Huang, Sriram Yenamandra, Arjun Majumdar, Elie Aljalbout, Tushar Nagarajan, Tsung-Yen Yang, Akshara Rai, Michael Rabbat, Li Fei-Fei, Jiajun Wu, Tingfan Wu, Franziska Meier
PqbgsEMl8U.abstract:
The diversity of robot embodiments and action spaces makes it challenging to build robot world models that generalize across different embodiments. We introduce the Latent Action-Conditioned Robot World Model (LAC-WM), which operates within a learned unified latent action space shared across diverse embodiments. This unified action space improves the world model’s performance when adapted to previously unseen robot embodiments. We compare LAC-WM with an Explicit Action-Conditioned World Model (EAC-WM), which conditions on explicit motion labels. Our results show that explicit action conditioning leads to disjoint action representations across embodiments, limiting downstream performance when adapting to new robots. We evaluate both models on dexterous manipulation
tasks and a modified LIBERO benchmark. LAC-WM improves downstream performance over EAC-WM by up to 46.7% on dexterous manipulation and 11.7% on LIBERO. Crucially, the unified latent action space allows LAC-WM’s downstream performance to scale positively with the number of embodiments used during pretraining. In contrast, the disjoint action space in EAC-WM leads to decreased
performance as the number of pretraining embodiments increases. These results highlight the importance of a unified action space for efficient cross-embodiment learning, addressing a key challenge in robotics.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

SYQVkgOdev.title: CrossBFM: Distilling a Shared Latent Behavior Space Across Humanoid Embodiments
SYQVkgOdev.authors: Tan-Dzung Do, Phuong Tuan Dat, Nico Bohlinger, Cuc T.Trinh, Siwei Ju, Vien Anh Ngo, Jan Peters, Xinchao Wang, An Thai Le
SYQVkgOdev.abstract: Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) give humanoids a promptable policy over a latent behavior space, enabling one single vector to represent a motion to imitate, a pose to reach, or a reward to maximize. Forward-Backward representations successfully produce such spaces, but at the cost of hundreds of GPU-hours for a single robot. Moreover, when the training process is repeated for a second robot, it produces a second space unrelated to the first, resulting in embodiment-specific latents that do not unify or transfer. We address these problems with CrossBFM, treating the latent space as the transferable asset for various embodiments. As retargeting provides frame-level cross-embodiment correspondence, we propose a unified encoder architecture with no robot-specific parameters for distilling the behavior space to address all training embodiments simultaneously in less than a GPU-hour. Following this encoder, latent-conditioned trackers turn the distilled latent into whole-body control in a conventional PPO training manner in just 10 more GPU-hours. On three distilled humanoids, all three prompting modes transfer: motion tracking with latent-conditioned policy losing only 0.025 rad to its joint-conditioned counterpart, smooth goal reaching between poses with no falls, and reward optimization for all 41 reward prompts. Our experiments further reveal that 1) regressing the encoder on a quarter of the motion corpus costs only 5\% of tracking performance and 2) training the encoder on a subset of robots and evaluating on an unseen one recovers up to 89\% of the tracking performance of seen robots, demonstrating cross-embodiment generalization to morphologically similar robots. We also verify the pipeline on real robots across all three prompting modes and with flow-based generated latents. Project website: https://dotandung.github.io/crossbfm/
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

IQPS2BYcbD.title: Does Synthesized Audio Help Action Recognition Beyond Its Predicted Label?
IQPS2BYcbD.abstract: Pretrained generative models are increasingly used to support robot learning, but a downstream gain does not by itself identify which component of a generation pipeline provides the benefit. We study this attribution problem in a controlled human-action recognition setting. We synthesize audio for every clip of NTU RGB+D 60 with a quality-gated pipeline (Qwen3-VL prompting followed by MMAudio); an RGB+audio recognizer trained on it improves over a reproduced RGB-only baseline on X-Sub and loses accuracy significantly when its audio is removed (McNemar $p<10^{-7}$). However, a waveform-free control that directly provides the action label predicted by the vision-language model during synthesis achieves slightly higher accuracy (95.89% vs. 95.78% on X-Sub; 98.23% vs. 98.18% on X-View) with no statistically significant difference on either protocol ($p=0.43$ and $0.66$), and label smoothing without any audio performs comparably. We release the dataset and propose adaptations of this comparison for evaluating generative priors in robot learning, leaving their policy-level validation to future work.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

DxxmuQiUAw.title: DoomShift: How Much Adaptation Do World Models Need Under Domain Shift?
DxxmuQiUAw.authors: Rohan Nagabhirava, Keerthana Chirumamilla, Changliu Liu
DxxmuQiUAw.abstract: World models have become capable simulators, but they are evaluated almost exclusively on held-out rollouts from the domain they were trained on. A small domain shift, such as a new map of the same game, lighting, textures or enemies, can make their outputs drift even when the underlying physics and game engine are unchanged. With DoomShift, a controlled version of this shift in Doom, we measure what breaks and how much adaptation is needed to repair it. We train three diffusion backbones, initialized from pretrained diffusion image models, on four Doom maps and evaluate them on 13 unseen maps. All three preserve their response to controls but fail to reproduce the new scene: scene PSNR drops by 2.8–3.3 dB and LPIPS rises by 0.126–0.145 across the three backbones. This consistent gap shows that action-conditioned behavior transfers more reliably than scene appearance, independent of architecture or model scale. Yet the lost appearance is relatively cheap to recover: rank-16 adapters trained on only eight episodes with 2% of the original training updates recover 72–76% of the LPIPS rise and about half of the lost PSNR. Together, these results suggest that adapting a world model to a new environment may require restoring the scene's appearance rather than relearning the underlying game.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

9SWNois8do.title: Dream What I Can: Sparse Visual Planning for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
9SWNois8do.authors: Chongkai Gao, Wenlong Huang, Haonan Chen, Lin Shao, Yilun Du, Jiajun Wu, Ruohan Zhang, Li Fei-Fei
9SWNois8do.abstract:
Video models provide rich priors for generalizable robotic manipula-
tion, but plausible visual futures are not always executable. We introduce Dream-
Can, a hierarchical policy that grounds video models through sparse visual plan-
ning: a high-level planner adapted from a pre-trained video model and a low-level
visuomotor policy. Rather than predicting dense trajectories, the planner generates
sparse visual subgoals that balance reachability and task utility. We estimate both
quantities from ofﬂine, action-free robot videos and use dynamic programming
to select subgoal sequences without manual annotations. The resulting subgoals
are more reliably attained than uniformly spaced ones, and the full system out-
performs language, dense-video, and uniform-subgoal planners, reaching 91.2%
success on LIBERO-Long with a 0.1B-parameter low-level policy. The system
also scales with suboptimal videos and test-time compute, and performs challeng-
ing real-world bimanual tasks, including box folding and packing with unseen
object combinations.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

0Y6nde4ZbP.title: DreamRehearse: Video World Models Turn Any Source of Action into Robot Demonstrations
0Y6nde4ZbP.authors: Hongyi Chen, Liquan Wang, Shuo Cheng, Qiyang Yan, Jeffrey Ichnowski, Zackory Erickson, Homanga Bharadhwaj, Nur Muhammad Mahi Shafiullah
0Y6nde4ZbP.abstract: Dexterous manipulation is bottlenecked by demonstrations: every new scene, object set or embodiment means teleoperating the robot again. Action-conditioned video world models could supply that data, but the ways they are used remain narrow: a policy is improved by resampling its own rollouts, which requires it to already succeed often enough for anything to be kept; the rollouts stay in the scene the model was fit to; and the platform is almost always a parallel-jaw gripper. We present DreamRehearse, which treats such a model as a demonstration generator and lifts all three restrictions. Conditioning on rendered robot skeletons rather than raw actions makes the model embodiment-invariant, so a single model covers parallel-jaw grippers and multi-finger hands and predicts future video more accurately than action-conditioned baselines. Any source of motion can rehearse inside it, a coding agent, a learned specialist, a generalist VLA or a trajectory validated in simulation, and a success classifier keeps only the rollouts that work. Because filtering a teacher's rollouts by outcome is one step of reward-weighted regression, the student improves on the teachers that produced its data; we make this precise and bound how much of the improvement survives the model's prediction error. On RoboTwin, dreams pooled from five teachers lift $\pi_{0.5}$ from 1.9% to 70.6%, above the teacher (63.1%) and within 97% of training on simulator rollouts. On a bimanual dexterous hand, dreams in rooms the model never saw raise out-of-distribution success from 10.4% to 61.1%. On real hardware, simulated trajectories dreamed into real observations reach 85% success with five real demonstrations on two dexterous manipulation tasks.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

7K2bVb0jp2.title: DreamVLA: From Generated Human Motions to Humanoid Vision-Language-Action Policies
7K2bVb0jp2.authors: Kevin Park, Izat Rasyad, Dvij Rajesh Kalaria, S. Shankar Sastry
7K2bVb0jp2.abstract: Training vision-language-action (VLA) policies typically depends on substantial robot demonstration data, making human teleoperation a costly and cumbersome bottleneck, particularly for whole-body humanoid interaction. Reinforcement learning in simulation offers an alternative for scaling this data, but designing task-specific rewards remains challenging. To address this, we propose DreamVLA, which uses generated motion trajectories to guide reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation, converting them into reliable task execution trajectories. These trajectories train VLA models in simulation without new task-specific teleoperation data. Our central contribution is a reference-conditioned DAgger distillation procedure: after a failed learner rollout, we restart the RL expert from a sampled learner state with the same reference suffix and aggregate successful corrective trajectories, addressing the distribution shift left by offline imitation. We evaluate picking from a platform, opening a drawer, and pressing a button, with ablations of DAgger iterations, residual RL, and generated dataset scale
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

9PZhZHGqL3.title: EqC: Equilibrium Energy Control for Introspective Lifelong Robot Learning
9PZhZHGqL3.authors: Haodong Yang, Runhan Huang, Bowen Zhang, Iofai Lei, Zunzhe Zhang, XiangCheng Zhang, Shaoting Zhu, Linzhan Mou, Yicheng Liu, Hang Zhao
9PZhZHGqL3.abstract: Long-term robot autonomy depends on more than effective action generation: a policy must recognize when its behavior is no longer sufficiently supported and use assistance to improve. We introduce **Equilibrium Energy Control (EqC)**, a framework for introspective lifelong robot learning built around an explicit conditional energy landscape. EqC casts generative action refinement as equilibrium-seeking optimization, while the geometry of the refinement process reveals whether the generated behavior remains consistent with the learned landscape. This competence signal enables Energy-Gated DAgger, where persistent energy-consistency violations trigger expert takeover and the resulting recovery trajectories are aggregated for subsequent policy updates. EqC integrates naturally into both Diffusion Transformer policies and flow-matching-based vision-language-action (VLA) policies. Across simulation and real-world bimanual manipulation, EqC improves task performance and robustness while enabling timely intervention near the policy's competence boundary. A real-world study further shows how these interventions progressively expand the range of situations handled autonomously, providing a practical path from static generative controllers toward self-improving robot systems.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

u2VRZwRMGZ.title: FLEX-π: A Multi-Stream World-Action Model with Compute Flexibility
u2VRZwRMGZ.authors: Ge Yan, Jinghao Liu, Yuzhi Fan, Lei Cai, Minwen Liao, Jesse Zhang, Dieter Fox
u2VRZwRMGZ.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) predict the future to act better, but nearly all of them predict only RGB latents—trained purely for pixel reconstruction, with no explicit signal for the 3D geometry or object semantics manipulation needs. We find a surprising free lunch: the same frozen video-generation VAE that encodes RGB also encodes 3D pointmaps almost losslessly, with no pointmap-specific training at all. This lets us supervise FLEX-π, a 6B-parameter WAM, on 3D geometry and object-centric DINO semantics alongside RGB—at no cost in new sensors, new pre-training, or inference latency. Every visual signal is projected into this shared latent space and denoised jointly with actions inside a Mixture-of-Transformers backbone; per-stream dropout with cross-modality forcing then lets a single trained checkpoint run on any subset of these streams, from a fast action-only mode to full joint generation. The result is a policy that is exceptionally demonstration-efficient and generalizes well, beating the strongest baselines by 2-6× on dexterous, precise, real-world bimanual tasks both in and out of distribution—all while running faster than π0.5. Videos in https://anony-flex-pi.github.io/.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

WPHcKrbaso.title: FOCUS: Action-Conditioned Partial Rollout for World Action Models
WPHcKrbaso.authors: Feiyang You, Shuaijun Liu, Chenglong Zhang, Shuyang Hao, Chengyu Wu, Ningxin Su
WPHcKrbaso.abstract:
Future-conditioned World Action Models generate robot actions from predicted visual states, but dense rollout updates the entire latent scene even when manipulation centers on a localized interaction. The challenge is to select action-relevant changes while preserving the
context needed for control and decoding. We introduce \focus{}, an action-conditioned partial-rollout method that updates selected latent regions and preserves the remaining state through an identity path. Teacher-derived latent change and forward/inverse action relevance supervise support selection, while a residual head calibrates the accepted updates. The complete lattice remains available to downstream action modules and video decoders. Selective updates operate at early denoising steps, followed by dense refinement of the resulting state. We instantiate the same rule in two Fast-WAM interfaces: coupled video--action rollout (Joint) and video rollout followed by inverse dynamics (IDM). Across 40 LIBERO tasks, \focus{}-Joint and \focus{}-IDM attain average success rates of 96.3\% and 96.8\% at 0.49s and 0.58s per policy call, respectively, reducing latency by 13.0\% and 9.7\% relative to their dense baselines. Support-recovery and allocation studies examine the selection rule and the trade-off between control success and policy-call latency.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

JALnEhDNA0.title: FOCUS: Flow-Matching with Offline Critical-Interaction Update Supervision for Robot World Models
JALnEhDNA0.abstract:
Robotic visual world models learn physical dynamics and interaction strategies through dense video prediction. However, existing methods generally employ spatiotemporally uniform supervision mechanisms; consequently, large static background areas dominate the learning signals, severely diluting supervision for the sparse yet critical regions of interaction.
We introduce a fine-grained loss reweighting method
that converts offline region and motion annotations into spatial weights,
concentrating supervision on interaction-relevant changes while retaining
coverage of the full scene. It requires no modification to the architecture or
inference pipeline and applies to any spatial prediction loss. On Fast-WAM
policy evaluation with LIBERO-Plus and DreamDojo video prediction,
preliminary checkpoints match or exceed the policy success and
motion-magnitude alignment of their respective 20k-step baselines with 40\%
and 75\% fewer post-training steps. These results indicate that offline priors
can reduce redundant supervision and improve post-training step efficiency.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

5kCxiubF0f.title: From Reasoning to Action: Consequence-Grounded Alignment for Vision-Language-Action Models
5kCxiubF0f.authors: Yixue Zhang, Wenke Xia, Kun Wu, Wenbo Yu, Pei Ren, Junnan Nie, Di Hu, Zhengping Che, Chang Liu
5kCxiubF0f.abstract:
Reasoning informs decision-making by connecting intended actions with their expected consequences. Building on this principle, recent vision-language-action models incorporate embodied chains of thought (ECoTs) as an intermediate stage in action generation. However, such guidance remains implicit, as actions are conditioned on the generated ECoTs rather than explicitly optimized to align with them.
To bridge this gap, we introduce the Consequence-grounded Reasoning-to-Action alignment method called CoRAct, an offline training framework that explicitly aligns reasoning and action through reward-guided optimization in action noise space.
Specifically, CoRAct formulates two physically grounded ECoT components as verifiable signals: movement specifies the intended motion, whereas waypoints encode the expected spatial consequence of execution. By jointly modeling ECoT reasoning, action generation, and action-conditioned future prediction, a unified Mixture-of-Transformers explicitly couples each action with its articulated intent and predicted consequence. For action candidates generated from sampled noise, CoRAct computes alignment rewards based on motion consistency with the described movement and agreement between predicted outcomes and the specified waypoints. These rewards drive group-relative optimization of the initial noise distribution, steering action generation toward consistency with the articulated intent and expected consequence.
Extensive experiments across RoboCasa, VLABench, and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate consistent gains in task success and generalization over strong ECoT-based VLA baselines. Further analyses reveal improved reasoning–execution alignment and show that our method can ground externally provided ECoTs in executable behavior, supporting zero-shot adaptation to novel scenarios by leveraging knowledge from powerful VLMs.
keywords: Vision-Language-Action Models; Embodied Chain-of-Thought; Reasoning–Action Alignment; Action-Conditioned Future Prediction; Policy Post-Training
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

aLjh7TyU1s.title: FurnitureVLA: Learning Long-Horizon Bimanual Furniture Assembly with Vision-Language-Action Model
aLjh7TyU1s.authors: Chenyang Ma, Yue Yang, Radu Corcodel, Siddarth Jain, Andrew Wu, Chiori Hori, Diego Romeres
aLjh7TyU1s.abstract: Current work on robot furniture assembly mostly focuses on toy-scale settings or single-arm manipulation. We introduce FurnitureVLA, the first systematic study of real-scale bimanual furniture assembly using Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs). We formalize the task, develop a scalable simulation pipeline for expert data generation and evaluation, and build a VR teleoperation system for single-operator bimanual control to collect high-quality real-world demonstrations. To address extreme long-horizon assembly with up to 7 subtasks and 1550 control steps, we propose a progress-enhanced VLA that jointly predicts actions and a continuous progress signal, enabling automatic subtask transitions and reducing compounding errors. FurnitureVLA improves average simulation success from 48% to 80% over baselines across three furniture types, with a further 21% gain from our study of perception and control design factors, and transfers to a real Kinova Gen3 platform with only 16% drop on the hardest task. Project page: https://dannymcy.github.io/furniturevla/
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

FOed6cqAoM.title: GOTT: Object-centric Dexterous Manipulation with a Reusable Cross-Embodiment Primitive
FOed6cqAoM.authors: Yulin Liu, Lai Wei, Yen-Jen Wang, Akash Sharma, Pieter Abbeel, Henrik I Christensen, Haozhi Qi
FOed6cqAoM.abstract: Foundation models and large-scale human data provide rich sources of manipulation intent, but translating this intent into multi-fingered robot behavior remains difficult. Dexterous hands still lack a reusable low-level primitive that reliably establishes contact across tasks and embodiments. We propose GOTT, a reach-acquire-move framework built around a single cross-embodiment contact-acquisition primitive. Given a robot-agnostic object trajectory and a reach specification, GOTT first brings the hand near a task-relevant contact region. The shared closed-loop primitive then establishes stable contact from this approximate initialization, and a pose-conditioned controller tracks the desired object motion. Reach specifications may come from future-aware planning, external models, or human demonstrations, while the primitive and tracking backend remain unchanged. Simulation and real-world experiments show that GOTT is able to establish robust contact across diverse objects, arm-hand platforms, and seen and unseen hand morphologies. It also consistently improves end-to-end task success over open-loop grasp execution.
keywords: Dexterous Manipulation; Cross-Embodiment Learning; Object Trajectory Tracking
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

2APlGcTrI2.title: GRAIL: Generating Humanoid Loco-Manipulation from 3D Assets and Video Priors
2APlGcTrI2.authors: Tianyi Xie, Haotian Zhang, Zi Wang, Jinhyung Park, Bowen Wen, Jiefeng Li, Xueting Li, Qingwei Ben, Haoyang Weng, Yufei Ye, David Minor, Tingwu Wang, Chenfanfu Jiang, Sanja Fidler, Jan Kautz, Linxi Fan, Yuke Zhu, Zhengyi Luo, Umar Iqbal, Ye Yuan
2APlGcTrI2.abstract: Scaling humanoid loco-manipulation requires robot-compatible demonstrations across diverse objects, whole-body motions, and scene geometries, but teleoperation and motion capture are difficult to scale because each collection depends on physical setups, instrumented actors, and robot operation. We present GRAIL, a digital generation pipeline that remains fully virtual until deployment: it composes 3D assets, simulator-ready scenes, and video foundation model (VFM) priors to synthesize interactions without physical scene rebuilds or robot teleoperation. GRAIL starts from fully specified 3D configurations with known object geometry, camera parameters, metric scale, environment depth, and a robot-proportioned character. This privileged setup conditions interaction-aware reconstruction of metric 4D human-object interaction (HOI) trajectories with reduced depth ambiguity and morphology mismatch. We retarget the recovered motions to a humanoid and train complementary task-general trackers: an object-aware latent adaptor for manipulation and a scene-aware tracker for terrain traversal. GRAIL produces over 20,000 sequences spanning pick-up, whole-body manipulation, sitting, and terrain traversal. Egocentric visual policies trained on this generated task data achieve 84% real-world object pick-up success and 90% stair-climbing success on a Unitree G1.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

D2FKtmx0bl.title: Grounded Action Model: 3D Grounding as a Foundation for Robotics
D2FKtmx0bl.authors: Gehao Zhang, Weikai Huang, Shailesh Shailesh, Yiyan Peng, Jiafei Duan, Ranjay Krishna
D2FKtmx0bl.abstract: Manipulation policies must know which objects matter and where they are, yet the pretrained backbones that current robot foundation models build on, from language in vision-language-action models (VLAs) to video generation in world-action models (WAMs), do not directly require this metric grounding, leaving it to be learned implicitly from robot demonstrations. We propose Grounded Action Models (GAMs), a new paradigm of robot foundation models built with 3D grounding. GAM can be conditioned using language, points, or box prompts, which are first transformed into a shared object-centric representation of the selected objects. This representation captures target-focused visual features and metric object geometry, which is mixed with robot state history through a multi-stream transformer to predict action chunks. Although GAMs can be run autonomously, they can also serve as a low-level controller that a high-level planner controls using its various input modalities, allowing for long-horizon and memory-dependent manipulation. On RoboTwin 2.0, GAM achieves an average success rate of 55.3% across 50 tasks (vs. 52.0% for Spatial Forcing), including 47.6% under scene randomization (vs. 30.4% for Abot-M0), with its action policy trained only on clean-scene demonstrations. On LIBERO-PRO, it achieves a state-of-the-art average success rate of 61% (vs. 53% for π0.5) across 16 perturbation settings, with the largest gains when targets are relocated or newly designated. On two real robots, GAM retains 17/20 successes under visual shift on a bimanual YAM versus 4/20 for π0.5, while its composition with a Molmo2 planner on a Franka achieves 64.7% ID and 49.8% OOD step completion on long-horizon and memory-dependent tasks.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

1sc4tQWDgY.title: Guava: Distilling Frontier VLMs into a Compact Agent through a Robotic Manipulation Harness
1sc4tQWDgY.authors: Haowen Liu, Xirui Li, Shaoxiong Yao, Peng Shi, Tianyi Zhou, Jia-Bin Huang, Furong Huang, Jiayuan Mao
1sc4tQWDgY.abstract: Frontier vision–language models (VLMs) can perform robotic manipulation by interpreting visual observations, invoking robot tools, and adapting to execution feedback, but repeated model calls incur high costs and latency. In this paper, we study the problem of distilling these capabilities into compact VLMs. The key challenges are designing an interaction interface that enables efficient and generalizable distillation, and a data collection protocol that captures diverse scenarios. We present $\texttt{Guava}$, a framework built around a manipulation harness and a simulation-based data generation pipeline. We first study how harness design affects both frontier and compact models, and use the resulting interface for teacher data generation and student deployment. Through this harness, a frontier VLM generates physically executed and validated interaction trajectories in simulation, which we augment with perturbation branches that expose the teacher to execution deviations and recovery trajectories. Using $\texttt{GPT-5.4}$ as the teacher, we collect 2,268 interaction trajectories and fine-tune $\texttt{Qwen3.5-4B}$ to obtain $\texttt{Guava-4B}$. $\texttt{Guava-4B}$ substantially outperforms its base model and approaches $\texttt{GPT-5.4}$ performance across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, while generalizing to unseen objects, instructions, and task compositions. Perturbation trajectories particularly improve unseen-task generalization. With substantially lower inference latency and token usage compared to a frontier model, $\texttt{Guava-4B}$ enables efficient local deployment.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

ble6LMrmKz.title: HIGenNTO: Scalable Humanoid Interaction Generation via Noise-Space Trajectory Optimization
ble6LMrmKz.authors: Lalit Jayanti, Kashu Yamazaki, Yuto Shibata, Kotaro Amaya, Katerina Fragkiadaki
ble6LMrmKz.abstract: Humanoid robots can acquire complex skills by imitating kinematic humanoid motion references, yet reliable references for contact-rich interactions remain difficult to obtain: motion capture deteriorates under occlusion and close physical contact, while retargeting introduces additional contact and geometric inconsistencies. We present HIGenNTO, a framework that synthesizes humanoid–scene interaction motion references by optimizing the initial noise of a pretrained text-conditioned motion model under sparse spatiotemporal and scene constraints. The same formulation satisfies desired contacts, avoids collisions, and maintains stable support while retaining the prior's realism and temporal coherence, generating interaction motions from scratch and composing long-horizon behaviors stage-wise. Across robot–environment and robot–object tasks, HIGenNTO produces motions that can be executed by tracking policies in simulation and used to train depth-conditioned visuomotor policies operating solely from onboard sensing. We deploy these policies on a Unitree G1 across four contact-rich tasks. Finally, the task specifications themselves can be written by a coding agent, which proposes interaction tasks and compiles them into prompt, constraint, and scene programs, authoring three of our eight evaluated tasks and four further behaviors. Together, these results establish a scalable path from high-level task descriptions to physically executable humanoid interactions.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

OoI6kXUw6b.title: How Much of Your VLA Is kNN
OoI6kXUw6b.authors: Denis Grachev, Damien LaRocque, Omar Moured
OoI6kXUw6b.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models now exceed 95 % success on the LIBERO simulation benchmark, yet it remains unclear how much of this performance requires generalization beyond the training demonstrations. In this work, we show that retrieving nearby demonstrations and reusing their action chunks achieves a success rate of 91.7 % on LIBERO without policy training. Under LIBERO-Plus perturbations, retrieval shows the smallest drop of all evaluated policies. Across nine publicly available VLAs, fine-tuning mostly makes the vision-language backbone a better retrieval key, and the actions of the VLAs remain close to the demonstrations. In addition, we introduce Local Action Consistency (LAC), an offline metric that measures whether nearby observations in representation space are also associated with similar future actions. We show that LAC tracks the success rate of retrieval and can guide the training of a retrieval key. Our evaluation and source code are available at https://github.com/sereact/lerobot_knn.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

D901c0AIXX.title: IMPLY: Physically Anchored Consistency for World-Model Rollouts
D901c0AIXX.abstract: A world model asked what happens if an object is pushed at several speeds produces several futures. If the model has the object in mind, those futures agree about it: each implies the same mass and friction. The consistency checks now used to vet world-action models ask whether a model's futures agree with each other, and none of them knows any physics. We show that this is not enough, and what to do instead. IMPLY reads the physics each rollout implies by inverting a simulator and scores a set of rollouts by how well one object explains all of them, anchored to two calibration pushes the model has observed. In a controlled setting, a model that ignores the object and always predicts a typical push is as self-consistent as the truth (AUROC 0.70 against the oracle); anchoring exposes it (1.00). On a real model, V-JEPA 2-AC adapted to the scene, the same thing happens. Given its own calibration pushes the model tracks the object (per-object correlation with the truth 0.91); given another object's, it does not (0.05). Self-consistency cannot tell these apart, preferring the right evidence on 52% of objects, chance level, while anchored disagreement prefers it on 73% and correlates 0.92-0.99 with the rollouts' error. Used to choose among candidate rollout sets, it comes within 0.003 of an oracle that sees the truth. A model that has internalised the wrong object is exactly as self-consistent as one that has internalised the right one; consistency has to be anchored to evidence.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

4DMJ6qRQ1X.title: Indistinguishable from a Resize Filter: What LIBERO Can Resolve About the Action Gap
4DMJ6qRQ1X.authors: Adnan Khan, Sam Jeffrey M, SriCharan Ganta
4DMJ6qRQ1X.abstract: Under a symmetric null calibrated to the discordance we measure, a configuration change that does nothing, evaluated at LIBERO's standard 500 rollouts per suite, returns an apparent improvement of at least 0.8 percentage points about 15% of the time, and across three such changes at least one does so with probability about 0.38 under an independence about approximation. We know because we were fooled by exactly that pattern. Sweeping seven settings of OpenVLA-OFT's evaluation harness, three image-pipeline knobs appeared to improve success at n=500 by +0.8, +0.8 and +0.4 points, with consistent signs and a plausible mechanism: each deviates from a pipeline the released code deliberately matches to training. At n=2500 with paired per-episode analysis on matched initial states, all three are equivalent to baseline within ±1 point (+0.04, -0.12, -0.28; paired 95% CIs within [-0.88,+0.59]; exact McNemar p = 1.00, 0.79, 0.44), and the result directionally repeats on a second, less saturated suite, though with an interval too wide to claim equivalence there. The instrument is validated in both directions: three configurations reproduce byte-identical outcome vectors, while removing the wrist camera costs 88.8 points. Beneath the flat aggregates, 2-5% of individual episodes silently change outcome. For the perturbations and the single policy we study, the standard protocol cannot separate these harness changes from a one-point effect, and we give the rollout budgets that can. Progress toward the action gap is settled by deltas of exactly this size. This is a negative result and a reporting proposal, submitted to Track 2.

ePZHQLddx0.title: Inference Latency and Chunk Transitions in Whole-Body Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
ePZHQLddx0.authors: Chuan Qin, Shaoting Zhu, Sadeep Thilakarathna, Priyan Mendis, Kasun Shanaka Kristombu Baduge
ePZHQLddx0.abstract: Inference latency delays the renewal of coordinated whole-body references while a humanoid continues balancing and interacting with objects. We study this effect using WB-WAM and a fixed motion tracker on four HumanoidArena contact tasks. Across 6,400 simulated episodes, we compare synchronous execution, time-aligned asynchronous execution, and training-time real-time chunking (Training-RTC) under controlled delays of 0–200 ms. At 200 ms, Async maintains a four-task mean success rate of 68.63%, close to the zero-delay baseline of 68.75%, while Sync achieves 64.25%. Training-RTC improves the joining of successive plans: mean boundary reference increments decrease by 10.4–21.8% and post-switch measured velocity increments by 3.4–10.6% across all eight task–delay comparisons, with aggregate success broadly comparable to Async. Applying a common physical deadline increases the mean Async–Sync success gap from 4.38 to 7.88 percentage points. Asynchronous execution continues the outgoing motion plan during inference, while Training-RTC improves transitions between successive action chunks. Their respective roles support task completion and whole-body motion continuity under delay.

HOTY4KNjwD.title: InfiNoVA: ∞ Novel View Augmentation for Viewpoint Invariant Robot Policies
HOTY4KNjwD.authors: Sai Puneeth Reddy Gottam, Elmar Rueckert, Vedant Dave
HOTY4KNjwD.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies often rely strongly on the camera viewpoints seen during training, causing substantial performance degradation when deployed from unseen perspectives. Collecting demonstrations from sufficiently diverse physical viewpoints is expensive and still provides only sparse coverage of the viewpoint space. We introduce InfiNoVA, a data-augmentation framework that converts synchronized multi-camera demonstrations into a dense distribution of geometrically consistent training views. InfiNoVA reconstructs each manipulation trajectory as a time-varying 3D Gaussian representation and renders novel observations from sampled camera poses while preserving the original state--action correspondence. This explicit scene representation improves frame-level fidelity and temporal consistency while reducing task-critical hallucinations observed in generative novel-view synthesis. Across four real-world manipulation tasks, policies trained with InfiNoVA achieve $5.4\times$ higher average success under unseen randomized viewpoints than both VISTA-based augmentation and the unaugmented policy. InfiNoVA further achieves $1.7\times$ higher success than training directly on all five physical camera views. These results show that dense, geometrically grounded viewpoint augmentation provides a practical route toward camera-robust robot policies without modifying the underlying policy architecture.

gHB1d45TXJ.title: Iterative Reasoning About Clues that Matter for Navigation
gHB1d45TXJ.authors: Arthur Zhang, Carl Qi, Donne Su, Xiangyun Meng, Amy Zhang, Joydeep Biswas
gHB1d45TXJ.abstract: Scalable mapless navigation from sparse language instructions requires resolving underspecified goals and routes from open-set environmental cues like ramps, signs, or detours. Prior work assumes either a closed set of factor categories or ignore test time motion planning errors. In this work, we argue that pretrained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can overcome these limitations by discovering novel instruction-relevant cues to iteratively refine prior motion plans, but require adaptation to focus on which cues matter and their influence on motion planning. We propose Foresight, the first online self-refinement framework for continuous motion planning. Foresight finetunes a single VLM to alternate between proposing image-space motion plans and critiquing them using the language goal and visual context. We introduce a simple, effective recipe using supervised (SFT) pre-training and reinforcement learning (RL) post-training to enhance cue-goal discovery for motion refinement. We validate these contributions on 56 real-world sparse language goals with unseen sign, structural, and detour cues, and find that Foresight's plan-critique architecture reduces the interventions per mission by 52% relative to state-of-the-art test-time reasoning and foundation-model baselines while running onboard a Jetson AGX Orin. In extensive offline evaluations, our proposed contributions improve expert behavior alignment by 37% on average compared to state-of-the-art test-time reasoning and foundation model baselines. We will release code, data, and training details to support future work on test-time reasoning for robot motion refinement. Additional anonymized robot deployment videos at: https://foresightplanner.github.io/foresight

ytYkhQwgsQ.title: JAMB: Joint Action–Motion Diffusion for Bimanual Manipulation
ytYkhQwgsQ.authors: Chuyang Xiao, Peilin Meng, David Held
ytYkhQwgsQ.abstract: Coordinated bimanual manipulation is challenging because the motion of either arm can alter the shared 3D scene and thereby affect the other arm. Yet most diffusion policies generate actions without explicitly modeling these future geometric consequences, while predictive variants typically use future state only as auxiliary supervision or fixed conditioning. We address this limitation by proposing JAMB, a diffusion policy that jointly denoises bimanual actions and future 3D point tracks. By allowing action and track hypotheses to evolve together within a shared Transformer, each can inform and refine the other throughout denoising. We further ground multimodal representations in a shared spatiotemporal coordinate system to facilitate geometry-aware interaction during joint denoising. We evaluate JAMB on diverse bimanual manipulation tasks in RoboTwin 2.0 and on a real-world robot, comparing it with action-only policies and alternative future-prediction approaches spanning different state representations and learning objectives. Across 16 simulation tasks, JAMB achieves an average success rate of 83.4%, outperforming the strongest baseline by 23.9 percentage points. On three real-world tasks, it outperforms the action-only and auxiliary geometry prediction methods by 50.0 and 21.2 percentage points, respectively. Beyond these performance gains, JAMB shows stronger generalization to cluttered scenes and out-of-distribution backgrounds than the evaluated baselines. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of our joint action-motion modeling framework for coordinated bimanual manipulation. Our project website is available at https://ja-mb.github.io/.

1HkY73V8Pl.title: JEVA: Joint Encoders for Variational Action World Models
1HkY73V8Pl.authors: Aditya Pratap Singh, Sanyam Mehta, Yixin Wang, Nima Fazeli, Bernadette Bucher
1HkY73V8Pl.abstract:
Learning world models for robotic control typically requires large
amounts of action-labeled data, which is expensive to collect, whereas action-
free demonstrations such as video are abundant. Latent action models address this
imbalance by inferring the actions that explain observed transitions, but training
the inverse dynamics model (IDM) jointly with the forward model is unstable.
Existing methods therefore fix the latent action space before training the world
model, or add a separate inverse-dynamics warm-up stage. We introduce JEVA, a
latent-action world model that co-trains an IDM and a forward world model end-
to-end from scratch in a single stage, on a pool of trajectories in which only a
small fraction of transitions carry action labels. JEVA treats the action between
two visual states as a continuous Gaussian latent that can be planned over and
decoded into continuous controls. Variance-reduced routing (VRR) makes single-
stage training work. On labeled transitions, VRR conditions the forward predictor
on the posterior mean instead of a sample. With a warm-up stage and no VRR,
every latent-action dimension collapses. With 5% of episodes labeled, a policy in
JEVA’s latent action space matches or exceeds every baseline trained with 20% of
labels on OGBench Cube-Double and Cube-Triple. Under CEM planning, JEVA
leads the best world-model baseline by 11–22 points on every Cube task.

l7EUpXm16e.title: Latent Memory Palace: Reasoning for Control as Autoregressive Variational Inference
l7EUpXm16e.authors: Chuning Zhu, Eva Xu, Jose Barreiros, Krishnan Srinivasan, Paarth Shah, Abhishek Gupta
l7EUpXm16e.abstract: Human decision-making is highly flexible -- some actions are taken immediately; others require longer deliberation. Language models have exhibited a similar capacity for adaptive "reasoning." However, transferring this capability to continuous control policies has been challenging, as directly reasoning in language space may lack the granularity for spatial understanding and precise motions. In this work, we show that reasoning for control policies can emerge by organizing information in an autoregressive latent space reminiscent of a memory palace, where retrieval is iterative and adaptive. Our method, Latent Memory Palace (LMP), formulates reasoning as variational inference with an autoregressive latent distribution. We derive a latent-space reinforcement learning technique to tractably optimize its variational lower bound. The resulting policy, LMP-$\pi$, achieves strong empirical performance in simulation and real-world domains while exhibiting interpretable, adaptive allocation of test-time compute. We further show that the same framework yields a variable-length action tokenizer, LMP-$\texttt{tok}$, which significantly improves the performance of downstream autoregressive policies. Together, these results present a new perspective on latent reasoning for control through the lens of variational inference.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

i2T2S39Zcm.title: LeWAM: A JEPA World Action Model with Diffusion-Steering-Based MPC
i2T2S39Zcm.authors: Shashank Hegde, Alexander Popov, Elie Aljalbout, Nikolai Smolyanskiy
i2T2S39Zcm.abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict actions and future observations, typically from a reconstruction-based representation that carries noisy, redundant information which can complicate downstream predictions. We introduce LeWAM, a bidirectional transformer for forward, backward, inverse dynamics and policy prediction, on a decoder-free JEPA latent trained end-to-end through all four modes. We see the following benefits. 1) Alignment: linear probing better reads robot and object state over a regular Le World Model (a forward-only JEPA world model), while successfully ignoring distractors, which a regular WAM considerably reconstructs. 2) Acting: Closed-loop evaluations of LeWAM match or exceeds a regular policy (without a world model) on the same encoder and at matched size. 3) Planning: While sampling raw actions in planning with WAMs allows MPC to exploit dynamic model inaccuracies, we show that planning in the noise space of these WAMs improves their closed-loop performance.

b7wZqqQzON.title: Meaning Reaches Object Choice but Not Completion: Where Is a VLA Vulnerable to Landmark Synonyms?
b7wZqqQzON.abstract: VLA policies are fragile to rewording. Success rates alone cannot say whether a policy fails to choose the object or to complete the task, nor where in the policy to intervene. We study the released GR00T N1.7 on two LIBERO-Spatial tasks differing only in the landmark word telling which of two bowls to take. Synonyms absent from the training instructions send the policy to the bowl they name, unlike made-up words, yet complete 67.6% of one task's closed-loop episodes, against the original word's 100%. Before the connector between the vision-language model and the action generator, replacing only the landmark tokens' vectors with the other landmark's (pasting) sends nearly every episode to the other bowl. After the connector, pasting at the landmark, the remaining instruction, or the image tokens alone rarely moves the choice, but any two do. Hiding the landmark tokens from the action generator after the connector still lowers completion for the synonyms that fall short. Finetuning on diversified landmark words repairs that one task's completion for synonyms absent from finetuning; finetuning on the original instructions does not. Training only the connector on the diversified words suffices, as does copying the connector of a policy fully finetuned on them into one finetuned on the original instructions. An open-loop score on starting frames misses that weights outside the connector also carry part of the repair. For now, on this evidence, robustness to rewording should be judged in closed loop, with actions executed, intervening on both sides of the connector, scoring choice and completion separately.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

6Mvoxqkmtx.title: MimicShape: From One Real Object to Many via Real-to-Sim-to-Real Trajectory Replay for Manipulation Policy Learning
6Mvoxqkmtx.authors: Yalcin Tur, Wensi Ai, Chen Geng, Arthur Ilyasov, Cem Gokmen, Jiajun Wu, Yunzhu Li, Li Fei-Fei, Ruohan Zhang
6Mvoxqkmtx.abstract: Generalizing imitation-learned manipulation policies to unseen objects requires demonstrations across many object instances, making real-world data collection costly. Demonstration augmentation can reduce this collection burden, but demonstrated motions are tied to the source object’s geometry, making object diversity difficult to expand while reusing recorded trajectories. We present MimicShape, a real-to-sim-to-real system that expands object diversity in demonstration data by keeping real-world trajectories unchanged and generating compatible objects in simulation. A synchronized digital twin extracts contact and clearance constraints from the recorded trajectories, and an agentic system generates diverse, textured objects that satisfy these constraints. Simulation replay verifies that the original actions succeed on each candidate, yielding new visual observations paired with unchanged real-world actions. Across eight tasks on rigid, articulated, and deformable objects, four real and four simulated, MimicShape improves success rates on unseen objects over the strongest applicable baseline on every task by 15.5 percentage points on average. On real-world mug hanging, augmenting 50 demonstrations on one mug raises success on unseen mugs from 19% to 51%, against 63% for 250 demonstrations collected on five real mugs.
