1kmPjIZRNs.title: MolmoAct2: Action Reasoning Models for Real-World Deployment
1kmPjIZRNs.authors: Haoquan Fang, Jiafei Duan, Donovan Clay, Sam Wang, Shuo Liu, Weikai Huang, Xiang Fan, Wei-Chuan Tsai, Shirui Chen, Yi Ru Wang, Shanli Xing, Jaemin Cho, Jae Sung Park, Ainaz Eftekhar, Peter Sushko, Karen Farley, Angad Wadhwa, Cole Harrison, Winson Han, Ying-Chun Lee, Eli VanderBilt, Rose Hendrix, Suveen Ellawela, Lucas Ngoo, Joyce Chai, Jason Ren, Ali Farhadi, Dieter Fox, Ranjay Krishna
1kmPjIZRNs.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models aim to provide a single generalist controller for robots, but today's systems fall short on the criteria that matter for real-world deployment. Frontier models are closed, open-weight alternatives are tied to expensive hardware, reasoning-augmented policies pay prohibitive latency for their grounding, and fine-tuned success rates remain below the threshold for dependable use. We present MolmoAct2, a fully open action reasoning model built for practical deployment, advancing its predecessor, MolmoAct along five axes. We introduce Molmo2-ER, a VLM backbone specialized for spatial and embodied reasoning, trained on a 3.3M-sample corpus with a specialize-then-rehearse recipe. We release three new datasets spanning low-to-medium cost platforms: MolmoAct2-BimanualYAM Dataset, 720 hours of teleoperated bimanual trajectories that constitute the largest open bimanual dataset to date; MolmoAct2-DROID Dataset, a quality-filtered Franka subset of DROID; and MolmoAct2-SO100/101 Dataset, a quality-filtered SO-100/101 subset. We provide OpenFAST Tokenizer, an open-weight, open-data action tokenizer trained on millions of trajectories across five embodiments. We redesign the architecture to graft a flow-matching continuous-action expert onto a discrete-token VLM via per-layer KV-cache conditioning. Finally, we propose MolmoAct2-Think, an adaptive-depth reasoning variant that re-predicts depth tokens only for scene regions that change between timesteps, retaining geometric grounding at a fraction of prior latency. In the most extensive empirical study of any open VLA to date, spanning 7 simulation and real-world benchmarks, MolmoAct2 outperforms strong baselines including π0.5, while Molmo2-ER surpasses GPT-5 and Gemini Robotics ER-1.5 across 13 embodied-reasoning benchmarks. We release model weights, training code, and complete training data.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

m9avyXDP2i.title: MOMASPLAT: Dynamic Novel-View Demonstration Augmentation for Mobile Manipulation
m9avyXDP2i.authors: Sateesh Kumar, Arnav Balaji, Arpit Bahety, Skand Peri, Georgios Pavlakos, Roberto Martín-Martín
m9avyXDP2i.abstract: Visuomotor policies trained through imitation learning are highly sensitive to changes in camera viewpoint. This is particularly problematic for mobile manipulation (MoMa), where robots rarely execute manipulation from the exact same base pose used during demonstration collection due to navigation uncertainty, localization drift, and environmental constraints. Recent approaches use novel-view synthesis (NVS) to augment demonstrations with unseen viewpoints, but they assume static scenes and therefore fail to re-render the manipu8 lated object during contact-rich interactions, leaving the most critical parts of the demonstration unaugmented. We present MOMASPLAT, a novel-view demonstration augmentation framework for mobile manipulation that synthesizes full manipulation trajectories from unseen robot base poses, including dynamic object interactions. Our key insight is that standard MoMa data collection naturally provides the multi-view observations needed to reconstruct both the static scene and the manipulated object in 3D. MOMASPLAT combines 3D Gaussian Splatting, feed-forward 3D foundation models, and kinematics-based action retargeting to separately reconstruct the scene and manipulated object, render them from novel viewpoints, and generate geometrically consistent synthetic demonstrations paired with transformed actions. We evaluate MOMASPLAT on five real-world mobile manipulation tasks involving both rigid and articulated objects across three scenes. MOMASPLAT substantially improves robustness to unseen base poses, achieving non-trivial success beyond 25 cm where all baselines fail, while reducing the need for large-scale real-world data collection.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

k671debnN4.title: NF-VLA: A Normalizing-Flow Baseline for Vision-Language-Action Learning
k671debnN4.authors: Ruichen Deng, Qinyu Zhao, Yong-Hyun Park, Mutian Tong, Liang Zheng, Jiatao Gu
k671debnN4.abstract: Autoregressive normalizing flows (NFs) provide a tractable density for learning and sampling continuous robot actions. We show that a single maximum-likelihood objective can train vision--language--action (VLA) policies competitive with leading methods on manipulation benchmarks. We present NF-VLA, which combines conditional autoregressive normalizing flows with score-based action refinement. Its deep--shallow architecture concentrates visual, language, and proprioceptive prefix conditioning in a high-capacity deep block, while unconditioned shallow blocks provide a shared invertible action transformation. The vision--language backbone and flow are jointly trained by exact maximum likelihood on Gaussian-smoothed action chunks. The same learned density supplies a single score-based correction at inference, refining generated actions to account for training-time smoothing without a separately trained denoiser. Trained on LIBERO from a pretrained vision--language backbone without robot pretraining, NF-VLA achieves 98.35\% success across the four standard suites and 72.6\% on LIBERO-Plus using the same checkpoint without further fine-tuning. Ablations show that deep-only prefix conditioning and score-based refinement both improve closed-loop success. Together, these results establish carefully structured autoregressive flows as a competitive approach to VLA control, with one learned density supporting policy training, action generation, and refinement.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

TLBjMBWUmO.title: One from Infinity: Actualizing Futures from Pretrained World Models into Robot Actions
TLBjMBWUmO.authors: Bang Du, Yichen Xie, Shuqi Zhao, Yuxin Chen, Menglin Wu, Masayoshi Tomizuka
TLBjMBWUmO.abstract: A pretrained video world model admits many plausible futures for a scene, but a robot must realize the exact task-conditioned one. To turn world models into executable robot policies, existing methods fine-tune the heavy world model backbone using large-scale robot data and computational resources. Challenging this status quo, we argue that the expensive part has already been paid in the world model pretraining since the representation space of a video world model lays out the diverse potential futures. In this case, what remains is to select the future that accomplishes the task and to read out the actions that realize it. We formalize this task as actualization, which learns a task-conditioned selection and realization on top of a prior supplied by a frozen world model. This can be solved by a tiny actualizer model. We implement RoboActualizer with as few as 60M parameters on top of a frozen world model encoder. The actualizer is composed of two lightweight DiT experts that jointly predict future latents and actions by flow matching. The model can be trained entirely on a single GPU with 32 GB peak memory. With up to 100x fewer trainable parameters than existing WAMs and VLAs, RoboActualizer reaches great performance on simulation benchmarks including LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0 and five tasks on two real-world platforms, with a low latency of 39 ms that allows real-time control.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

GpQjVyrHdQ.title: One Trajectory, Two Requirements: Accuracy and  Local Stability in Euler Sampling for Flow Matching Policies
GpQjVyrHdQ.abstract: Flow matching robot policies commonly use a fixed Euler step count selected from offline accuracy sweeps. At inference time, however, each policy input (visual observation, robot state, and language instruction) together with a source-noise draw defines a different ODE trajectory and sequence of local Jacobians. We ask whether a step count that accurately follows the nominal noise-to-action trajectory can still be too coarse for strongly contracting directions around it. An exact two-coordinate system and a controlled augmentation of six trained flow models show that trajectory accuracy and local Euler stability can impose different step requirements even when the original learned transport is unchanged. We then study a frozen $\pi_{0.5}$-LIBERO checkpoint without modifying its weights or action dynamics. Across 30 policy inputs from 10 LIBERO-10 tasks, the Jacobian exhibits strong contracting directions near the action endpoint, yet no sampled mode violates the Euler non-expansion condition. On five of those inputs, accuracy sweeps require 4-9 Euler steps at 5\% terminal error and 87-112 at 1\%. These five paired cases are therefore consistent with accuracy-limited rather than stability-limited sampling under this local criterion, while the controlled experiments show why endpoint accuracy alone cannot rule out a separate stability requirement.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

Q2ZkhLAFo5.title: OpenWAM: An Open, Modular Exploration Towards Systematic World–Action Model Pretraining
Q2ZkhLAFo5.authors: Yuran Wang, Siqiao Huang, Mingleyang Li, Chenhao Zhang, Jiaqi Liang, Weiyang Jin, Yue Chen, Xuemin Chi, Donghao Zhou, Qize Yu, Yu-Kai Wang, Yuhan Rui, Shenzhe Yao, Zhen Yuan, Zhenhao Shen, Kefei Zhu, Zijie Zhu, Ning Gao, Xiaowei Chi, Guanqi He, Shanghang Zhang, Hao Dong, Lin Shao, Hang Zhao
Q2ZkhLAFo5.abstract: World–Action Models inherit world knowledge from video-generative priors, and channel it into executable control signals through embodied experience. Existing systems, however, are monolithic: the generative backbone, visual representation, architecture, information flow, inference procedure, and training data are tightly coupled, obscuring which design choices matter and why. We introduce OpenWAM, an open research stack that turns world–action pretraining into a controlled experimental program. OpenWAM-Infra factorizes the WAM design space into composable modules with unified training, inference, deployment, and evaluation. On this substrate, OpenWAM-Study examines three questions through controlled experiments: what to inherit, how world and action learning interact, and how their synergy scales; and distills three principles: upstream knowledge transfers through a sufficiently capable generative backbone and a compact, information-rich latent space; world–action synergy requires dedicated action capacity, explicit world-to-action information flow, and synchronized joint denoising; and embodied pretraining principally improves out-of-domain generalization, with one-stage co-training over egocentric and robot data integrating world coverage and action grounding. Composing these principles, we build OpenWAM-α, an open WAM pretrained on roughly 6,400 hours of egocentric human and robot data and evaluated across simulation and real-world benchmarks. Across the eight simulation benchmarks and the real-robot experiments, which together span embodiments from single-arm and bimanual manipulation to dexterous hands, OpenWAM-α delivers consistently excellent performance, sustaining its top-tier standing from simulation to the physical world. We release the full stack, including infrastructure, evaluation protocols, pretrained models, and data recipes, to facilitate future research.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

VcS0dE1Aoz.title: Parvulus: A 10M-Scale World Action Model for Robot Manipulation
VcS0dE1Aoz.authors: Abdullah Ali Sivas, Peter Cho-Ho Lam, Zirui Zhou, Yong Zhang
VcS0dE1Aoz.abstract: Vision-based robot manipulation increasingly relies on multi-billion parameter models. However, standard imitation learning uses capacity inefﬁciently. In this work, we show that latent physical grounding improves policy representations. Auxiliary generative decoders ground representations in spatial geometry and dynamics during training. These decoders detach entirely at inference. Trained from scratch on the LIBERO corpus, our 9.9M parameter policy, Parvulus, achieves a 90-92% success rate. It operates at > 100 Hz with < 10 ms latency. By matching models over 100× larger, Parvulus advances the Pareto frontier of parameter efﬁciency among language-conditioned policies.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

aJaH4nEfmC.title: PhysicsMind: Sim and Real Mechanics Benchmarking for Physical Reasoning and Prediction in Foundational VLMs and World Models
aJaH4nEfmC.authors: Chak-Wing Mak, Guanyu Zhu, Boyi Zhang, Hongji Li, Kevin Zhang, Xiaowei Chi, Yichen Wu, Yangfan He, Chun-Kai Fan, Wentao Lu, Kuangzhi Ge, Xinyu Fang, Hongyang He, Kuan Lu, Li Zhang, Yongxin Ni, Zhanhua Zhang, Youhua Li, Shanghang Zhang
aJaH4nEfmC.abstract: Foundation vision--language and video-generative models can produce plausible answers and videos without consistently respecting physical laws, making their suitability for world-to-action grounding difficult to assess. We introduce \textbf{PhysicsMind}, a controlled mechanics benchmark with 480 videos balanced between real and simulated Center of Mass, Lever Equilibrium, and Newton's First Law scenarios. The VQA track evaluates multiple-choice inference from initial frames; the video-generation track evaluates rollouts conditioned on an initial frame and a description of the setup. Scenario-specific metrics measure mask geometry, lever terminal states, and reference-trajectory agreement rather than combining distinct physical signals into a single score. Evaluating 21 VLMs and seven video-generative models reveals uneven performance across mechanics subtasks and no uniformly strong model. In a targeted five-model VQA diagnostic, spatial/geometric grounding and physical reasoning account for 68.4\% of categorized incorrect responses. An eight-model Lever comparison supplies exact masses and lever-arm positions as text, yielding accuracy gains of 0.0--44.2 percentage points while leaving residual errors in several models. Video generators reach 4.76--47.62\% Lever final-state accuracy and show differing strengths across geometric and motion metrics. PhysicsMind provides interpretable diagnostics of mechanics prerequisites relevant to robotics; predictive validity for downstream policies and closed-loop control remains to be established.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

tDsKr7Z5TP.title: Pre-trained Image Generators for Adaptive Robot Simulation
tDsKr7Z5TP.authors: Jiong Lin, Yihong Liu, Judah Goldfeder, Hod Lipson
tDsKr7Z5TP.abstract: Action-conditioned generative models of robots usually use egocentric views from the robot's cameras, which limit the view to the gripper and its workspace and leave the rest of the body unseen. We study the third-person view: given one image of a robot with its end-effector and camera poses, render the whole robot at a new end-effector pose, from a new camera pose, or both. At test time, the model needs no URDF, joint angles or simulator. We fine-tune the image generator FLUX.2 with LoRA on image pairs streamed from MuJoCo, and give it the end-effector and camera poses as condition tokens together with a per-pixel end-effector ray heatmap. On a 5-DoF WidowX 200 in two render styles and a 7-DoF Franka FR3, the predicted arm reaches a body IoU, the mean IoU of the arm links below the wrist, of 0.27–0.53, against at most 0.08 for nearest-neighbor retrieval and 0.19 for large language models that write rendering code. When the robot's upper arm is bent, continuing to train the model on 30–300 trajectories of the modified robot adapts it toward the new body.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

MwnWdUaeBJ.title: Predicting What Matters: interaction-Centric 4D World-Action Models
MwnWdUaeBJ.authors: Luoxin Ye, Baichuan Huang, Kai Gao, Ruolin Ye, Dylan Randle, Jeroen Vanbaar, Alan Yuille, Manikantan Nambi, Jose Barreiros
MwnWdUaeBJ.abstract: Robotic manipulation requires anticipating the evolution of task-relevant entities and translating these predictions into actions. We introduce a compact world-action model that grounds control in functional semantic entities and their 3D motion, without dense RGB reconstruction. A capable System-2 model reasons about task-relevant entities and subtask structure, guiding the construction of dense semantic masks, 3D point tracks, and subtask goals. This structured supervision trains a compact System-1 model to jointly predict goal semantics, interaction-centric scene evolution, and robot actions. By concentrating future prediction on entities and motion that matter for interaction, the model supports reactive control with approximately 0.3B trainable parameters (1.3B total). It achieves a 98.6% success rate on LIBERO and averages 86.0% across seven LIBERO-Plus categories. On real-world dexterous tool use and sequential object removal, it achieves an average success rate of 87.5%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 27.5 percentage points. Controlled ablations examine the choice of future supervision targets and the importance of a capable System-2 model. These results support task-centric semantic and geometric prediction as an effective basis for compact world-action modeling.

QQEU5dmT7w.title: ReasonDPO: Failure-Aware Preference Optimization for Vision-Language-Action Models
QQEU5dmT7w.authors: Udita Ghosh, Jingzong Zhou, Konstantinos Karydis, Mike Grosskopf, Amit Roy-Chowdhury
QQEU5dmT7w.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models map multimodal observations and language instructions directly to control actions, bringing foundation-model capabilities to robotics. However, these models being trained with behavioral cloning from successful trajectories limits generalization capabilities by ignoring diverse failure modes. Preference-based fine-tuning like Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) addresses this by contrasting successful and failed trajectories, but whole-trajectory comparisons are often noisy, as failures can occur at different times and for different reasons. We propose ReasonDPO, a failure-aware preference learning framework that leverages both the timing and cause of failures to localize where execution diverges from success. Instead of applying DPO over entire trajectories, ReasonDPO restricts supervision to segments where meaningful behavioral differences arise, masking earlier portions that are largely indistinguishable and increasing the weight of more severe failures. This avoids penalizing correct actions and focuses learning on informative decision points that determine task success. Experiments on the LIBERO benchmark show that our approach gives significant improvements in both success rates and failure severity on all the tasks suits over standard baselines, highlighting the importance of localized failure reasoning for improving performance in VLA models.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

hDF65o5uoJ.title: Reliability-Aware Future Conditioning for Grounding Generated Videos in Robot Actions
hDF65o5uoJ.authors: Mike Degany, Mohammad Khoshnazar, Deyuan Qu, Qing Yang
hDF65o5uoJ.abstract:
Generative video models can show how a manipulation task should unfold, providing visual guidance for robot policies.
However, a generated video may show the correct task while progressing faster or slower than the robot, making its guidance unreliable.
On CALVIN, shifting a generated future by five frames reduces success from 69.8\% to 34.2\%, below the 54.0\% achieved without future guidance.
We introduce \emph{Reliability-Aware Future Conditioning} (RAFC), which learns how strongly to rely on a generated future and which nearby temporal version to use at each control step.
RAFC combines a static fallback with temporally shifted versions of the future through a learned gate, while a bounded residual policy adjusts the resulting action.
The gate and residual policy learn jointly from task reward, without timing labels, alignment supervision, or online video regeneration.
Across off-grid temporal shifts, RAFC increases average success from 51.8\% to 73.7\%, exceeding uniform averaging of the same candidates by 7.0 percentage points.
Additional tests use independently generated video windows, changes in video playback rate, and sudden timing shifts during execution.
On three physical Franka tasks, aggregate success improves from 26.7\% to 56.7\%.
These results show that adapting how a policy uses generated futures helps translate visual predictions into reliable robot actions.

icPZndFvQI.title: Retriever: Composing the Perception-Reasoning-Action Loop for Long-Horizon Manipulation
icPZndFvQI.authors: Linfeng Zhao, Haojie Huang, Jiayuan Mao, Weiyu Liu, Lawson L.S. Wong, Mykel Kochenderfer
icPZndFvQI.abstract: Building long-horizon robot agents requires composing closed-loop pipelines for perception, belief update, planning, and control whose components run at different clocks and with variable latency. Today, these systems are often assembled with ad-hoc concurrency and pub/sub conventions that make timing and input-consumption semantics implicit, yielding schedule-dependent behavior that is hard to reproduce, debug, and reuse. Current solutions typically solve parts of this problem at either the algorithmic or the systems layer, but not both. In this work, we propose Retriever, which spans the entire stack: an asynchronous decision model, a programming model, a runtime, and an example closed-loop agent pipeline. Retriever represents an agent as a graph of stateful causal stream functions executed on explicit run clocks. We formalize this view via an asynchronous environment-agent loop over continuous-time streams and show that finite-memory causal policies can be represented by compositions of these operators. Retriever compiles these graphs to multiple backends and provides a deterministic replay contract when consumed inputs, clock/commit traces, and stochastic outputs are logged. We evaluate Retriever through a real-robot case study.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

EtgHh96v9D.title: RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Synthetic Data for Robot Learning
EtgHh96v9D.authors: Seungku Kim, Suhyeok Jang, Byungjun Yoon, Dongyoung Kim, John Won, Jinwoo Shin
EtgHh96v9D.abstract: Synthetic data generated by video generative models has shown promise for robot learning as a scalable pipeline, but it often suffers from noisy action labels due to imperfect video generation or inaccurate action prediction. Recently, vision-language models (VLMs) have been leveraged to validate video quality, but they cannot directly evaluate the generated actions themselves. To tackle this issue, we introduce RoboCurate,  a novel framework for action-verified synthetic robot data that addresses inconsistencies between generated videos and annotated actions. Specifically, RoboCurate executes the actions predicted by an inverse dynamics model (IDM) in a simulator and verifies action consistency by measuring the motion agreement between the simulator rollout and the generated video. To better leverage such a framework, we further expand the scene diversity of synthetic data beyond the available dataset through off-the-shelf generative models with structured editing axes. We then use a VLM to pre-filter physically implausible generated videos before verifying their action labels. Across diverse manipulation scenarios, RoboCurate yields substantial relative improvements in success rates compared to using only real data, achieving +90.3\% on GR-1 Tabletop (300 demos), +29.1\% on DexMimicGen in the pre-training setup on simulation benchmarks, and  +179.9\% and +42.9\% in the co-finetuning setup on challenging real-world ALLEX and OpenArm humanoid benchmarks, respectively.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

iHQ7qhCOUl.title: RoboJudge: Multimodal Language Models as Judges for Embodied Video Generation
iHQ7qhCOUl.authors: Siyuan Ma, Yu Qi, Cheng Ye, Ruotian Peng, Xinyi Xu, Zitiantao Lin, Zedong Cai, Yijian Huang, Weiyang Liu, Siyuan Wang, Yandong Wen
iHQ7qhCOUl.abstract: Video generation models are promising foundations for embodied world models, but only if their generated rollouts are physically valid and faithful to task instructions. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to judge these properties, yet their agreement with human judgments on embodied videos has not been systematically evaluated. To address this gap, we introduce ROBOJUDGE-BENCH, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs as judges of embodied video generation. The benchmark measures two fundamental dimensions, Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment, across 800 human-annotated videos from 8 source corpora and 10 video generators, spanning grippers, human hands, and dexterous hands. Experiments reveal uneven alignment between existing judges and human ratings: general-purpose MLLMs show lower agreement on physical adherence, while specialized video judges designed for general-domain physical reasoning do not consistently transfer to embodied scenarios. Motivated by these findings, we construct ROBOJUDGE-TRAIN, comprising 12K videos annotated with 25K human-verified scores and model-assisted rationales for Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment. We fine-tune a 9B MLLM on this dataset with supervised learning followed by reinforcement learning, yielding ROBOJUDGE-9B. Among the model judges evaluated on ROBOJUDGE-BENCH, ROBOJUDGE-9B achieves the highest overall agreement, reaching a Pearson correlation of 0.719 with a statistically significant 0.089 gain over Gemini-3.7-Flash, the best-performing proprietary baseline in our evaluation. Training on ROBOJUDGE-TRAIN also yields gains on external benchmarks, including VideoPhy2 and Physion-Eval. We further use ROBOJUDGE-9B as a downstream evaluator to benchmark video generation models according to Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

izlS0omws9.title: RoboRender: Robot-Oriented Video Generation for Visual Sim-to-Real Transfer
izlS0omws9.authors: Huang Huang, Wensi Ai, Ziyu Chen, Youhui Wang, Zijian Du, Yang Liu, Jiaolong Yang, Li Fei-Fei, Jiajun Wu
izlS0omws9.abstract: Simulation enables large-scale, low-cost robot data generation, but policies trained in simulation often fail to transfer to the real world due to the sim-to-real visual discrepancies. Existing approaches often rely on intermediate representations, which can discard rich semantic information or require additional perception modules at deployment. We address this visual sim-to-real gap with RoboRender, a framework that converts simulated trajectories into photorealistic RGB videos for policy learning. RoboRender trains a robot-oriented video generation model conditioned on simulated depth videos, language instructions, and robot RGB mask videos, preserving simulator geometry, robot motion, and action labels while synthesizing realistic textures, backgrounds, and distractors. The generated RGB videos are paired with simulator-provided states and actions to train policies for zero-shot real-world deployment. On robot video test sets, our video model outperforms depth-conditioned video generation baselines in generation quality. In real-world experiments across pick-and-place, articulated-object manipulation, and mobile manipulation tasks, policies trained on RoboRender-generated data achieve a 71% average success rate, outperforming raw simulation renderings and conventional visual domain randomization by approximately 7.1×and 3.6×, respectively. We further show that policy performance improves with more generated videos per simulation trajectory, increasing opening-task success by 65 percentage points. These results demonstrate that generative video rendering mitigates the visual sim-to-real gap for zero-shot policy transfer.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

XHGXh4cerN.title: Robotic VLA Benefits from Joint Learning with Motion Image Diffusion
XHGXh4cerN.authors: Yu Fang, Kanchana Ranasinghe, Le Xue, Honglu Zhou, Juntao Tan, Ran Xu, Shelby Heinecke, Caiming Xiong, silvio savarese, Daniel Szafir, Mingyu Ding, Michael S Ryoo, Juan Carlos Niebles
XHGXh4cerN.abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved remarkable progress in robotic manipulation by mapping multimodal observations and instructions directly to actions. However, standard VLA training primarily optimizes action prediction and does not explicitly exploit the rich future visual motion available in robot demonstrations. To address this limitation, we propose joint
action-motion learning with motion image diffusion, where action generation and future visual motion generation are optimized together through a shared VLM backbone. Our method extends a pretrained VLA with two parallel generative pathways: the original action head predicts future action in control space, while a motion head, implemented as a Diffusion Transformer (DiT), predicts optical-flow-based future motion images in pixel space. Joint optimization couples action prediction with dense visual-motion supervision, encouraging the shared VLM representation to capture temporally structured and motion-aware information useful for control. Importantly, the resulting policy preserves the original VLA action-generation pathway at deployment and introduces no additional inference-time latency. Experiments in both simulation and real-world manipulation demonstrate the benefits of joint action-motion learning: our method achieves an average success rate of 97.5% on LIBERO, including a substantial improvement on LIBERO-Long, reaches 58.0% on RoboTwin, and improves average real-world success from 50.0% to 66.7% under limited demonstration data. More details can be found at: https://anonymous.4open.science/w/anonymous-6F813R/
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

2Z84lmClzu.title: SCAR: Self-Supervised Continuous Action Representation Learning
2Z84lmClzu.authors: Hongjia Liu, Fan Feng, Minghao Fu, Xinyue Wang, Haofei Lu, Biwei Huang
2Z84lmClzu.abstract: Despite the central role of action in embodied intelligence, learning transferable action representations from visual transitions remains a fundamental challenge, particularly when world models must generalize across embodiments under limited data. We argue that action is not merely an auxiliary conditioning signal, but a distinct representational factor that decouples the controllable change from embodiment-specific actuation. In this work, we propose SCAR, a joint inverse–forward dynamics framework for learning unified action representations across embodiments from visual transitions. Built on a pretrained generative backbone, SCAR uses an inverse dynamics model (IDM) to infer latent actions from latent observation pairs and a forward dynamics model (FDM) to predict future dynamics conditioned on them. To make the latent space transferable rather than a generic visual bottleneck, we regularize the latent action posterior toward a standard Gaussian prior to limit arbitrary visual encoding, and introduce adversarial invariance to suppress embodiment- and environment-specific nuisance factors. Experiments on the Procgen and Robotwin dataset show that the learned unified latent action representation serves as a stronger conditioning interface for world modeling than embodiment-specific raw actions, yielding improved cross-embodiment low-data adaptation and cross-task transfer. Taken together, these results suggest that action can be learned as a shared representation of controllable change across embodiments, providing an interface for more transferable and generalizable world models.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

0jBljtvW7F.title: Seeing Through the Illusion: Test-Time Scaling for World Action Models
0jBljtvW7F.authors: Cheikh Ahmed, Mahdi Mostajabdaveh, Milad Yazdani, Zirui Zhou
0jBljtvW7F.abstract: World action models (WAMs) jointly generate robot actions and imagined future observations, creating an opportunity to improve control at test time by sampling and selecting among multiple candidate rollouts. The key challenge is determining which rollout constitutes the most reliable control proposal before execution. We introduce WISE (World Action Inference Scaling through Evaluation), a process-level selector that evaluates each candidate using three signals: (i) an embodiment-aware prior over action validity and temporal regularity, (ii) an inverse-dynamics consistency score that measures agreement between the co-generated action and imagined transition, and (iii) an instruction-conditioned estimate of task progress or value. These signals are fused to rank native WAM rollouts within a receding-horizon control loop, while keeping the underlying model frozen. We evaluate WISE across two WAM-embodiment settings: Cosmos3 Edge on RoboLab and DreamZero on LIBERO. WISE improves closed-loop success from 6.0% to 24.0% on RoboLab, achieving the highest observed performance among the evaluated selectors. On LIBERO, it improves the frozen DreamZero base on all four suites and raises mean success from 75.1% to 78.3%, yielding the best aggregate result. These results show that pre-execution selection among native world action rollouts can improve closed-loop control without updating the underlying WAM
keywords: World-Action Models; Test-Time Scaling; World Model Evaluation; Action Gap; Physical AI
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

HgkYEexgxA.title: SmolWAM: A Latent World-Action Model for Robotic Manipulation on Edge Devices
HgkYEexgxA.authors: Timi Owolabi, Hikmah Olawore, Frances Adelakun, Ayotomiwa Oyewumi
HgkYEexgxA.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) jointly predict robot actions and future observations, but their video diffusion backbones are costly for edge deployment. We introduce SmolWAM, a compact latent WAM derived from the 2B-parameter Cosmos Policy using single-frame encoding, cached text features with preserved attention sinks, depth pruning, and token compaction. With 12 of 28 transformer blocks and 1,008 tokens, SmolWAM predicts actions and future latents in one rectified-flow step. After 3.6 A100 GPU-hours of training, it achieves 95.5% success over 400 LIBERO episodes at 57ms, 2.3TFLOP, and 2.4GiB per 16-action chunk on an A100: 11$\times$ lower latency and 3.2$\times$ lower memory than the five-step teacher. Its world head predicts scene motion; joint training improves success by 6.2 percentage points over an action-only ablation.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

agrOsamO7R.title: SUAVE: Unified Video-Action Models via Masked Diffusion
agrOsamO7R.authors: Rhythm Syed, Jean Mercat, Sedrick Keh, Kushal Arora, Paarth Shah, Aykut Onol, Mengchao Zhang, Tony Dear
agrOsamO7R.abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) inherit strong semantic grounding from pretrained vision-language backbones but are typically optimized for predicting actions rather than future observations. They can see and act, but they do not imagine the future before acting. World action models (WAMs) built on video diffusion backbones can imagine but treat language as frozen conditioning on a continuous latent space. Unified models bring these modalities into one architecture, but they either decode autoregressively, one token at a time, or keep video continuous with an auxiliary action head. In this work, we present SUAVE, a Single vocabulary Unified Action-Video modEl in which a masked diffusion transformer generates video and actions conditioned on language, with all three modalities represented as discrete tokens in a shared sequence. Choosing which tokens to mask at inference turns the same network into a world model, a robot policy, or a video-action model. For action-free co-training, the action positions of unlabeled video are filled with mask tokens and excluded from the loss. Simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate two findings. First, a single SUAVE model predicts long-horizon video and acts as a policy, competitive with dedicated world models and specialized action policies on static and dynamic manipulation tasks. On a real robot, our model generates subgoal images and an action chunk spanning one second of motion in 1,030 ms on an RTX 5090 GPU, sustaining closed-loop control at 2.5 actions per second. Second, pretraining on robot video and co-training on human video substantially improves policy performance and zero-shot robustness to distribution shift. Together, these results show that masked diffusion is a practical and versatile foundation for unified video-action modeling.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

m2T48NFQL0.title: Task-Relevant Fidelity in Robotic World Models
m2T48NFQL0.authors: Haibo Zhao, Jesse Zhang, Dieter Fox
m2T48NFQL0.abstract: World models increasingly support robotic planning and policy learning, yet reconstruction quality cannot directly compare their effectiveness across video-generative and latent models. We propose an evaluation pipeline using pose estimators and probing networks trained with privileged simulator labels to measure pose and success/failure prediction on paired successful and failed trajectories. Across long-horizon trajectories and local interactions, we find that accurate robot tracking does not ensure accurate object interaction, observed information can be lost during latent rollouts, stronger video generation backbones better preserve interaction outcomes, and predictions can disagree across viewpoints. Agentic simulation generation with GPT-6 Astra provides a strong baseline but remains sensitive to initialization and task type. Motivated by these gaps, a multimodal, view-consistency training scheme improves all four reported metrics on held-out states in both latent and video-generative world models.
keywords: action conditioned world model; video generative model; latent world model; agentic world model
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

yf9SpLTeP2.title: The Bitter Lesson Comes to Robotics
yf9SpLTeP2.abstract: General purpose multimodal language models (LMs) are increasingly capable of directly controlling robotic arms (e.g., by commanding end effector poses) to manipulate their environment. Tracking the development of these capabilities is important for understanding their potential benefits, such as improving industrial automation, and risks, such as enabling malicious users to produce dangerous chemical or biological agents. To this end, we investigate the ability of frontier multimodal LMs to directly control physical robotic arms. We evaluate seven models at multiple reasoning-effort settings on six manipulation tasks taken from the RoboDojo benchmark. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic evaluation of LM manipulation capabilities across multiple models and tasks conducted on physical hardware. We find that current frontier models can directly control real robotic arms to perform a variety of manipulation tasks but are not yet precise or efficient enough to complete them within a practical action budget. However, these capabilities are improving rapidly: performance increases our benchmark between July and September 2026 (inclusive) correspond to a performance doubling time of 44.5 days, while the best recorded execution rate increased by 4.4x and the lowest recorded execution cost fell by a factor of 6.2. These trends raise the possibility that the Bitter Lesson is coming to robotics; the capabilities of embodied general purpose LMs may one day be comparable to those of more specialized models.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

xYaFSMUYyJ.title: The Gaussian Is Enough: Flow-Matching Priors Do Not Help When Fine-Tuning Large Behavior Models
xYaFSMUYyJ.authors: Chen Xu, Rishi Shah, Hadas Kress-Gazit, Haruki Nishimura, Masha Itkina
xYaFSMUYyJ.abstract: Modern robot imitation learning increasingly relies on generative policies based on diffusion or flow-matching models, which generate actions by transforming samples from a prior distribution. Replacing the standard Gaussian with a closer-to-target, non-Gaussian prior has been shown to substantially improve performance when $\textit{training from scratch}$. A natural next step is to ask whether these gains transfer to $\textit{fine-tuning}$ pretrained Large Behavior Models (LBMs) such as LBM 1.0, $\pi_{0.5}$, and GR00T~N1.5, where one might expect even larger gains. Surprisingly, we find that this is not the case, except possibly at very low fine-tuning data fractions. Across over 100K simulation rollouts spanning all three aforementioned LBMs on 40+ tasks in two simulation platforms, and 1250 hardware rollouts on five bimanual manipulation tasks, non-Gaussian priors that are demonstrably closer to the target yield statistically indistinguishable or worse fine-tuning performance than a standard Gaussian prior. Diagnostic analyses suggest why: fine-tuned imitation learning policies converge to similar action predictions across priors, despite their fine-tuned $\textit{encoder embeddings}$ diverging substantially from the pretrained embeddings and each other. A learning-rate ablation further shows that undertraining the observation encoder degrades performance more than any choice of prior we observed.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

7oLmQS6Na5.title: The Human--VLA Communication Gap: What Humans Leave Implicit and What Policies Cannot Recover
7oLmQS6Na5.abstract: A robot may know how to perform a task yet fail when a human asks for it naturally. We study this human--VLA communication gap by separating an \emph{information gap}, where task semantics, grounding, or event structure remain unresolved, from a residual \emph{execution gap}, where even a fully specified task depends on how it is organized and invoked. To do this, we characterize how people naturally express demonstrated objectives and evaluate controlled variants of the same physical tasks, with detailed analysis on $\pi_{0.5}$ and consistent trends on $\pi_0$-FAST and Cosmos3-Edge. Our study reveals that humans increasingly compress instructions as tasks grow, relying more on contextual grounding and implicit execution structure. Current policies are misaligned with this behavior: they tolerate grounding dependence relatively well, but struggle when task semantics or event structure must be reconstructed. Even after the information gap is resolved, execution remains sensitive to command granularity and invocation state. These findings identify concrete targets for human-centered policy learning and interfaces that better bridge natural human objectives to robot behavior.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

QjuCLD4l8q.title: The Layer Mystery of VLA: An Information-Theoretical Analysis of VLA Latent Interface
QjuCLD4l8q.authors: Yuxiang Liu, Lizhi Yang, Fengze Xie, Aaron Ames, Yisong Yue
QjuCLD4l8q.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies connect a pretrained vision-language backbone to an action head through a latent interface, but which backbone layers this interface should expose remains unclear. We study single-layer selection and multi-layer fusion for frozen backbones across three pretrained models and two manipulation benchmarks, LIBERO and CALVIN, with three policy-training seeds per configuration. Across three fusion mechanisms and three layer-subset strategies, 47 of 54 configurations underperform the best observed single-layer policy. Our stastical analysis further confirms that fusion's advantage is very limited. However, the best layer varies substantially across backbones and benchmarks, making layer selection consequential and exhaustive policy sweeps expensive. We further derive a reweighting equivalence between the proposed information-bottleneck objectives for action-conditioned InfoNCE and action prediction, motivating InfoNCE as a proxy for layer quality. Empirically, InfoNCE provides the most consistent positive association with policy success among four evaluated proxies. Selecting the layer with the highest InfoNCE score requires 9–33 times less GPU compute than exhaustive policy sweeps and reduces mean selection regret from 17.89 percentage points for deepest-layer selection to 3.71 points across six settings. Its mean regret is close to the 3.28–3.50 points achieved by fixed-layer heuristics optimized retrospectively using all six oracle sweeps, without requiring closed-loop evaluations during selection.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

RsOz1FOVWH.title: Track, Articulate, Act: Generating Articulation from Casual Human Videos
RsOz1FOVWH.abstract: Human videos contain rich causal evidence for robot manipulation: they reveal how hand motion induces object motion and produces task-relevant changes in object state. In this work, we study articulated objects such as doors, drawers, cabinets, laptops, ovens, and hinged containers that are ubiquitous in daily life and present unique challenges for embodied interaction. These objects cannot be represented by a single pose; their motion depends on the underlying parts and joints. We introduce a real-to-sim framework that reconstructs a simulation-ready articulated object and hand--object interaction from a casual monocular RGB video, without RGB-D or multi-view input, prior scans, manually specified joints, or robot demonstrations. Our key insight is that dense 3D point tracks provide an embodiment-agnostic articulation cue: points on the fixed link remain approximately stationary, while points on the moving link follow coherent revolute or prismatic motion. Our method segments the links, estimates the joint and its state trajectory, reconstructs an articulated asset, and aligns the recovered 3D hand motion with the object. Central to our approach is a modular recipe that repurposes powerful pretrained models for single-image 3D reconstruction, mesh segmentation, and 3D scene flow, connecting their predictions through explicit geometric reasoning to infer articulation. We use the reconstructed articulated object and the human hand trajectory to replay interactions through contact in MuJoCo. The framework shows how pretrained vision models and explicit motion reasoning can turn casual human videos into articulated object models suitable for downstream embodied interactions. We host the code on an anonymous repo https://anonymous.4open.science/r/track-articulate-act-10BB.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

VVWcT5VcYi.title: TrAct: Bridging Robot Control and Visual Prediction with Visual Tracks
VVWcT5VcYi.authors: Zhi Cao, Howard Ji, Kevin Zhang, Kuangzhi Ge, Li Fei-Fei, Jiajun Wu, Huang Huang
VVWcT5VcYi.abstract: Robot actions are inherently embodiment-specific and only weakly aligned with image-space visual changes, limiting their effectiveness as conditioning signals for robot world models. In contrast, visual tracks provide an embodiment-agnostic representation of how task-relevant points move through a scene, offering dense image-space guidance for accurate and spatially precise future video prediction. Building on this observation, we propose TrAct, a world-model-based robot decision-making framework that uses visual tracks as an intermediate interface between control and prediction. TrAct consists of three components: a Vision-Language-Action-and-Track model (VLAT) that jointly predicts candidate actions and corresponding visual tracks from the current observation and language instruction; a track-conditioned world model (TWM) that predicts future visual outcomes conditioned on the proposed tracks; and a vision-language reward model (VLAC) that scores the predicted outcomes. At inference time, VLAT generates candidate action–track pairs, TWM rolls out their visual consequences conditioned on the tracks, and VLAC selects the track whose predicted outcome best satisfies the instruction; the action paired with the selected track is then executed by the robot. Experiments on the proposed LIBERO-INTEGRAL benchmark and real-world Franka manipulation show that TrAct improves success from 27% to 55% in simulation and 49% to 76% on real-world tasks compared to the strong VLA baseline $\pi_{0.5}$. Furthermore, TWM consistently improves video prediction quality over an action-conditioned world model (AWM). These results suggest that visual tracks provide an effective shared interface between robot control and visual prediction, enabling more accurate world modeling and stronger robot generalization.
keywords: Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems
video models and latent world models for robot learning
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

eKaoHK2E1q.title: Transductive Generative Modeling: Learning Robot Policies that can Extend to Unseen Conditions
eKaoHK2E1q.authors: Yating Lin, Necmiye Ozay, Yixin Wang
eKaoHK2E1q.abstract: Conditional generative modeling enables learning multimodal robotic behaviors from demonstrations, while robust generalization to unseen conditions outside the training distribution remains a challenge. In this work, we propose Transductive Generative Modeling (TGM), an algorithm that leverages a transductive reparameterization of conditional generative models for Out-of-Support (OOS) generalization. This reparameterization allows some OOS conditions, which we call delta-representable, to be represented by an in-support anchor and an in-support displacement. TGM combines the anchor and displacement through bilinear transduction, which can be interpreted as a learnable Taylor expansion around the anchor. This interpretation motivates extending transductive prediction to conditional generative models and reveals the structural assumptions. We instantiate TGM across multiple robotics tasks, including navigation and manipulation, and evaluate its performance on different unseen conditions. Across all tasks, TGM outperforms existing methods and demonstrates more robust generalization under unseen conditions.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

CPNmfa0qJf.title: UniWALM: Unified World Action Language Model for Embodied Robot Control
CPNmfa0qJf.authors: Rahul Sajnani, Diego Romeres, Mingyuan Zhang, Kai Gao, Carl Qi, Baichuan Huang, Srinath Sridhar, Dylan Randle, Lillian J. Ratliff, Jose Barreiros, Manikantan Nambi, Jeroen Vanbaar
CPNmfa0qJf.abstract: Motivated by the human ability to integrate experience across language, perception, and action, we introduce UniWALM, a unified world-action-language model that learns video, action, and language in a single shared representation, where each modality serves as both a conditioning signal and a supervision target. Prior world-action models (FastWAM, DreamZero) have already shown that co-denoising video with action in one backbone improves manipulation; language, however, is still consumed only as fixed conditioning, and other systems that do use language either stack a pretrained VLM on top of a video model or run reasoning as a separate autoregressive stage. UniWALM is instead a unified any-to-any model that generates video, action, and language synchronously via per-modality diffusion heads; the generated string (subtask || textual memory) is re-consumed as the next-step prompt, closing a language-as-memory loop with no external planner, VLM, or retrieval buffer. We study two questions: (i) does jointly generating language — on top of video-action co-denoising — improve manipulation further? (ii) does this additional language modality let a world-action model plan, remember, and act, enabling memory-dependent control tasks such as RMBench M(n)? On MolmoSpaces, UniWALM beats same-backbone FastWAM by +13.4% on compositional Pick&Place, isolating the gain from adding language on top of video-action co-denoising. On RMBench's memory-dependent M(n) subset — tasks that same-backbone FastWAM solves at only 13.3% — UniWALM reaches 34.5% without any pretrained language or reasoning model, +21.2 points over FastWAM and above Mem-0's keyframe-equipped setup (28.5%) using only a single anchor frame instead of per-task privileged keyframes. On a real-world Find-the-Item task, textual memory lifts success from 11.1% (FastWAM, no language) to 61.1%, while VLA and WAM baselines stay at or below chance (≤33.3%).
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

AjLDgn6taB.title: Usable but Unused: Diagnosing History-Dependent Prediction in a Latent World Model
AjLDgn6taB.abstract: When a world model fails to predict an outcome that depends on the past, it can appear to have forgotten. We show that a distinction made in the model's own earlier predictions can remain usable even when the model fails to carry it forward. We diagnose this gap by holding the complete latent window and corresponding actions fixed and replacing only the predictor. Using LeWorldModel with frozen perception in a visual TwoRoom variant, we compare histories with identical current images but different outcomes under the same action plan. A predictor deliberately supervised through step 2 but not step 3 distinguishes the outcomes at step 2, yet performs near chance at step 3. On this unchanged input, a reference predictor trained with autoregressive supervision through step 3 raises future-discrimination accuracy from 49.2\% to 93.5\%. Even after step 3 receives supervision from encoded ground-truth windows, predictor replacement further strengthens the target-aligned distinction and reduces prediction error on the unchanged input in every seed. These comparisons reveal a gap between the historical distinctions carried by generated inputs and those expressed in the next prediction.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

smsDWzIc0Q.title: WB-WAM: Heterogeneous Body–Hand Pre-training for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
smsDWzIc0Q.authors: Chuan Qin, Shaoting Zhu, SiYuan Luo, Siqiao Huang, Hongyu Zhao, Kasun Shanaka Kristombu Baduge, Hang Zhao
smsDWzIc0Q.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation demands coordinated body and hand behavior, while conventional robot pre-training data provide limited coverage of such whole-body motion. We present WB-WAM, a World Action Model that incorporates explicit whole-body action supervision into generative video pre-training. A shared physical action space integrates body, root, and dexterous hand annotations from heterogeneous sources, enabling joint video and action learning from 1880.2 hours of partially annotated video and motion data. The resulting priors are refined through PICO mid-training and adapted to robot tasks with auxiliary forward kinematics supervision. We construct WB-Datasets to support these stages with retargeted egocentric human demonstrations and robot trajectories, allowing task-aligned human motion to supplement limited robot data. Evaluations in simulation demonstrate strong whole-body task performance with 81.9\% in HumanoidArena, while real-world experiments further validate WB-WAM with 84.0\% mean success across five tasks. Moreover, task-aligned PICO mid-training improves downstream task performance while reducing the need for real-robot demonstrations. These results support heterogeneous whole-body pre-training and human motion transfer as a practical route to data-efficient humanoid loco-manipulation.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

sDIO0QYNtV.title: Wearable-Free Human Real-to-Sim Supplies Action Supervision for Interactive Robots
sDIO0QYNtV.authors: Sookwan Han, Haeun Ji, Junsu Kim, Sihun Lim
sDIO0QYNtV.abstract: Generative models learn rich knowledge from video, images and 3D data, but such data rarely records the actions behind it, and robot data that does record actions is conventionally collected by teleoperating robots or by recording people with head-worn cameras and handheld grippers, all of which ask the person demonstrating to wear or operate a device. These devices bias how people move, interrupt long-horizon capture for charging and offloading, and add operational cost with every person and session, since each must be fitted and synchronized and records only its user. We present a wearable-free approach where cameras record people moving naturally for long sessions with nothing worn and turn each recording into a comprehensive human real-to-sim of the people, including the objects they handle and their interactions in a digital twin of the room. Rendering each person's view from a consistent 3D avatar in this twin creates egocentric demonstrations for everyone present, each paired with the body motion that produced it, which supplies actions such as where a person picked up and put down an object. At an equal amount of data, policies trained on these demonstrations come close to those trained on a real head-worn camera in selected tasks and improve as the data scales, also for robot cameras that no one wore. Because one recording captures everyone present, the same data teaches a robot to respond to people, and scaling it unlocks interactive abilities such as helping someone who dropped something.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

AGpT1GNvlk.title: WholeBodyWAM: Learning Whole-Body World Action Models with Scalable Motion Priors
AGpT1GNvlk.authors: Bowei Zhang, Qiyao Zhang, Shuanghao Bai, Xinhua Wang, Meng Li, Yilei Wang, Leiwang Zhang, Jian Tang, Lu Zhou, Lei Sun, Zhengping Che
AGpT1GNvlk.abstract: Humanoid whole-body manipulation requires coordinated whole-body dynamics, yet large-scale trajectories from a target robot are expensive to collect and difficult to scale. In contrast, whole-body motion from human and humanoid sources is abundantly available, although such data cannot be directly used as embodiment-specific robot actions. This work asks whether these scalable motion resources can instead provide a transferable predictive prior for humanoid world-action modeling. We introduce WholeBodyWAM, a humanoid world-action model that learns whole-body dynamics from large-scale heterogeneous motion before target-robot training. We curate UniMotion-4K, a motion corpus spanning more than 4K hours from human videos, native 3D motion datasets, and heterogeneous humanoid platforms, and canonicalize these diverse sources into a unified motion space. A language-conditioned Motion Expert is then pretrained to predict future whole-body motion without target-robot action supervision. During robot post-training, the pretrained Motion Expert is integrated with Video and Action Experts through asymmetric Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) attention, enabling predictive scene dynamics and whole-body motion to jointly inform embodiment-specific action generation. Experiments show that WholeBodyWAM consistently benefits from increased motion-pretraining scale, improves future-motion prediction and downstream task performance, and transfers effectively to real-world humanoid manipulation. Moreover, the pretrained motion prior substantially improves data efficiency under limited target-robot demonstrations.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

EXZDc0OHYF.title: World Action Planner: Generalizable Robot Decision-Making with Action-Conditioned World Models
EXZDc0OHYF.authors: XiangCheng Zhang, Runhan Huang, Yilun Du
EXZDc0OHYF.abstract: Building generalizable robot agents for diverse applications remains a fundamental challenge. While imitation learning-based policies can perform well in familiar training environments, they often struggle to generalize to novel scenes, layouts, and task compositions. To this end, we present **World Action Planner**, an agentic robot planning system that proposes and refines executable action plans through imagination with an action-conditioned world model. We perform a principled coarse-to-fine search over robot actions in two stages: (i) global action optimization, where the agent reasons over imagined world-model rollouts to identify potential failures and refine the proposed action plan, and (ii) local action search, where the agent compares the imagined future outcomes of neighboring action candidates and selects the best action for execution. Across compositional long-horizon tasks, novel object layouts, and zero-shot real-robot planning without expert demonstrations, World Action Planner consistently outperforms state-of-the-art end-to-end policy models, including VLAs and WAMs, demonstrating the effectiveness of world-model-based action search for generalizable robot decision making.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

AclXLFoFLt.title: WorldString: Actionable Object Representation
AclXLFoFLt.authors: Kunqi Xu, Shaoqiu Zhang, Jitao Li, Jianglong Ye, Tianshu Tang, Isabella Liu, Sifei Liu, Xueyan Zou
AclXLFoFLt.abstract: Objects are the basic units of interaction in the physical world and serve as essential building blocks for world modeling. Real-world objects exhibit diverse deformation behaviors, ranging from articulated objects and skinning objects to soft deformable objects. While current methods approach object states through category-specific models such as FK, LBS, and FEM, or through scene reconstruction, they do not provide a common state interface across these object types. We propose WorldString, a unified neural architecture for learning object- specific, differentiable representations of actionable object geometry. For each object, structural keypoints provide a compact state representation that is decoded into a continuous occupancy field for arbitrary spatial queries. Across diverse object categories, WorldString outperforms traditional optimization-based methods, neural occupancy-based methods, and Gaussian Splatting approaches, achieving a 26.1% average relative improvement in IoU over the strongest baselines. It also has the potential to serve as a foundational component for physical world models, enabling future integration with learned dynamics and policy learning.
workshops: The action gap: large generative models (video, image, 3D) learn rich knowledge

0jDEzDxNXr.title: Blind Precise Assembly: Proprioceptive Sim-to-Real Peg-in-Hole for Diverse Parts
0jDEzDxNXr.authors: Antonia Bronars, Younghyo Park, Kushal Kedia, Pulkit Agrawal
0jDEzDxNXr.abstract: Every robot already carries high-resolution contact sensors: its own joints. Are they enough for precise assembly, where a robot must find a millimeter-scale opening through light contact? We train a blind insertion policy that observes only a short history of joint positions, velocities, and its own actions, with no visual, force, torque, or tactile sensing and no knowledge of the hole's or the peg's pose. Trained with reinforcement learning entirely in simulation, it transfers zero-shot to a real robot and inserts pegs of different shapes and sizes in \realtbd{74\%} of trials. We also study the tradeoffs of blind versus visual policies. Against a matched visual policy, our blind policy takes longer to succeed, but is more robust to geometric variation like size or cross-section changes. To train on thousands of tight-clearance assemblies, we release an open-source MuJoCo generator of exact convex collision geometry.
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

OJEVRPVueL.title: Contact Morphology Design: Shaping Contact Sensitivity and Repeatability
OJEVRPVueL.abstract:
Dexterous manipulation requires repeated contact establishment,
yet variability in contact responses complicates downstream
learning and control.
We introduce Contact Morphology Design (CMD), a perspective
that treats contact-response variability as a design target.
Using compliant fingertips with rigid internal carriers,
we optimize contact behavior and lateral optical observability
without explicitly optimizing re-contact repeatability.
Across two silicone materials and two indenter sizes,
optimized morphologies reduce same-location optical response
variation by 11.2--41.9\% while improving the balance between
re-contact consistency and neighboring-location distinguishability.
These results suggest that contact morphology can shape
response consistency before downstream learning and control.
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

ldojMpV9eK.title: DCPPT: Domain-Conditioned Policies from Procedural Trajectories for Sim-to-Real Dexterous Tool Use
ldojMpV9eK.abstract: Sim-to-real RL has achieved impressive results in dexterous manipulation but remains limited to tasks with accurate rigid-body simulation. However, these methods cannot be applied to skills that involve deformables and particles, with which the simulation speed will become too slow for large-scale RL learning. We present DCPPT, a sim-to-real framework for end-to-end dexterous tool-use manipulation skills, e.g., sand scooping, play-dough rod-rolling, without simulating non-rigid materials. Our method learns a domain-conditioned RL policy by tracking procedural trajectories parameterized by domain parameters, and distills it into an end-to-end domain-conditioned sensorimotor policy. Furthermore, explicit domain representation enables fast selection of domain parameters that can maximize downstream task performance. We evaluate DCPPT end-to-end on six dexterous manipulation tasks, including sand scooping, play-dough rod-rolling, sand scraping, mouse-wheel scrolling, dispenser pressing, and spray triggering. Our method achieves 1.5-3.8$\times$ in task metrics through the best domain parameter and transfers zero-shot to the real world.
keywords: Dexterous Manipulation; Robot Tool Use; Sim-to-Real
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

A3IyeNEN7Q.title: DexAgent: An Agentic Human2Sim2Robot Framework for Dexterous Manipulation with Self-Evolving Tool Library
A3IyeNEN7Q.authors: Youhui Wang, Yunzhu Li, Li Fei-Fei, Jiajun Wu, Huang Huang
A3IyeNEN7Q.abstract: Human videos are a scalable source of demonstrations for dexterous manipulation, but existing human-to-simulation-to-robot (Human2Sim2Robot) pipelines rely on predefined procedures that struggle with diverse object properties, particularly articulated and deformable objects. We introduce DexAgent, an agentic Human2Sim2Robot framework that converts a single egocentric human video and a task prompt into physically grounded robot trajectories for policy training, through four stages: semantic understanding, property-based simulation reconstruction, trajectory optimization, and robot data generation. At each stage DexAgent selects skills from its tool library or develops new ones, while property-specific verifiers assess outcomes and provide feedback, limiting error propagation. Retained tools make the library self-evolving. Across eleven real-world tasks, policies trained with DexAgent-generated data achieve a 3.5× higher success rate than competing baselines. Project website: https://dexagent1.github.io/
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

ehKIfzvXke.title: Do as I Do: Dexterous Manipulation Data from Everyday Human Videos
ehKIfzvXke.authors: Bhawna Paliwal, Haritheja Etukuru, William Liang, Pieter Abbeel, Nur Muhammad Mahi Shafiullah, Jitendra Malik
ehKIfzvXke.abstract: How can we scalably generate data for robotic manipulation, especially on human-like platforms such as dexterous multi-fingered hands? Learning from human videos has recently emerged as a likely answer to this question. However, difficulties in estimating hand-object interaction and crossing the human-to-robot embodiment gap have hindered the adoption of abundant monocular RGB-only human videos as the primary source of robot manipulation data. In this work, we present DO AS I DO, an algorithm to reconstruct and retarget monocular RGB human videos to multi-fingered dexterous robotic hands. DO AS I DO reconstructs hand-object interactions from various egocentric and exocentric in-the-wild video sources. The algorithm then retargets these hand-object interaction estimates into a sequence of actions executable in the real world, yielding robot-complete manipulation data from disparate human videos. Overall, DO AS I DO outperforms previous state of the art in estimating hand-object interactions and extracting dexterous manipulation trajectories from RGB videos, as we show in experiments on datasets with ground truths and on a dataset of video clips collected online. Our experiments enable us to propose an efficacy playbook for practitioners collecting human data for manipulation.
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

1XxguLFgl2.title: EigenDEXplore: Structured Exploration for Dexterous Manipulation with Human Priors
1XxguLFgl2.authors: Harsh Gupta, Tyler Ga Wei Lum, Changhao Wang, Chuer Pan, Karen Liu, Jeannette Bohg, Shuran Song
1XxguLFgl2.abstract: Dexterous manipulation poses a challenging high-dimensional optimization problem, as useful behaviors require coordinated motion across many hand joints. In reinforcement learning (RL) and sampling-based trajectory optimization, exploration commonly relies on independent robot joint perturbations, making coordinated behaviors difficult to discover. Prior work reduces this search space for grasp learning using low-dimensional spaces of coordinated joint motions learned from human hand data, but this restricts the expressivity required for general manipulation. Some combine learned and joint-space actions to restore expressivity, but this increases dimensionality and introduces redundancy. We study these effects across diverse manipulation settings, varying action dimensionality, exploration strategy, and the source of human data. Our experiments suggest that human-motion priors are most effective when used to structure exploration rather than change the action representation. Motivated by this finding, we propose EigenDEXplore, which induces correlated exploration by adding perturbations along human-derived eigenvectors to independent joint-space noise, leaving the action space unchanged. Across multiple dexterous hands, EigenDEXplore consistently outperforms joint-space and learned action-space baselines in grasping, in-hand reorientation, and contact-rich manipulation. These gains span unstructured and reference-guided RL, trajectory optimization, and sim-to-real deployment, and are largest in settings with less reward shaping and curriculum design.
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

VjYJceQS1M.title: Finetuning VLAs for Dexterous Manipulation: The Right Checkpoint Is All You Need
VjYJceQS1M.authors: Artur Kuramshin, Charlotte Cloutier, Michael Przystupa, Kirsty Ellis, Mohammad Shahanshah Akhter, Glen Berseth
VjYJceQS1M.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models have demonstrated strong manipulation capabilities. A limitation of VLA models is that most manipulation datasets focus on parallel-jaw gripper systems, making transfer to multi-finger hands challenging, particularly as teleoperation datasets are harder to collect with multi-fingered robots. In this work, we study how to best adapt VLAs to dexterous hands by pairing supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with diffusion-steering reinforcement learning (DSRL). Using $\pi_{0.5}$ and a LEAP hand, we evaluate five fine-tuning recipes across two simulation tasks using only a handful of demonstrations. Our empirical analysis yields three key insights: (1) SFT success is poorly correlated with post-DSRL success, meaning the best SFT checkpoint is rarely the most effective to steer; (2) freezing the vision-language model (VLM) and tuning only the action expert produces the most steerable policy for both training and out-of-distribution placements; and (3) low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the least steerable approach. Consequently, we recommend an adaptation recipe that freezes the VLM, fully trains the action expert, and eschews SFT rollout success as a checkpoint selection metric.
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

kUpXd0Tcsq.title: FINGR: Learning Dexterous Hand Control for Real-World Rubik’s Cube Solving
kUpXd0Tcsq.authors: Yutong Liang, Quanquan Peng, Matthew Kim, Xiaolong Wang
kUpXd0Tcsq.abstract: Manipulating a Rubik's Cube with one single dexterous hand is a challenging test of sustained, contact-rich control: the hand must execute successive layer turns while keeping the cube secure. Each turn requires some fingers to support the cube while others push a moving layer, release contact, and reset for the next move. To learn this coordination, we introduce $\textbf{FINGR}$ (Future-supervised Interaction Network with Geometric Representations), a policy that combines finger-relative geometry with future interaction prediction. A shared point encoder expresses the cube relative to each fingertip and aggregates its points without depending on cubie indexing. Learned future tokens share the observation encoder and receive supervision for contact-force changes, layer-turn progress, and finger joint displacement at multiple time scales. The resulting representation conditions a flow policy that directly generates finger actions. On a real dexterous hand, our policy achieves around $99.0\%$ success over 300 turn attempts, compared with $79.7\%$ for the base flow policy. Integrated with grasping and table-assisted regrasping, the policy solves all ten scrambled $2\times2\times2$ cubes in a mean complete-system time of approximately $137$ seconds.
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

iNan5MZzhQ.title: FlashDexRetarget: Accelerating Dexterous Manipulation Data Generation through Multi-Motion Retargeting
iNan5MZzhQ.authors: Kyungmin Lee, Sibeen Kim, Dongyoon Hwang, Yoonsang Oh, Donghu Kim, Youngdo Lee, I Made Aswin Nahrendra, Jaegul Choo, Hojoon Lee
iNan5MZzhQ.abstract:
Human hand-object demonstrations offer a rich source of dexterous robot data, but converting them into physically grounded robot trajectories remains computationally expensive.
We present FlashDexRetarget, a reinforcement learning framework that jointly retargets multiple reference motions with a shared, reference-conditioned controller.
The framework combines geometric and future-motion observations, object-centric rewards, per-hand actor-critic networks, and efficient off-policy learning.
On 50 motions with XHand, it achieves 90\% success under the SPIDER criterion in 29 GPU-hours, compared with 46\% in 2,847 GPU-hours for CHORD's released PPO implementation.
Experiments on two hand embodiments, component ablations, scaling to 1,000 reference motions, and real-world replay show its potential for efficient dexterous robot data generation.
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

HHmIIJbtIj.title: Force-Modulated Dexterity: Unified Compliance for Contact-Rich Manipulation
HHmIIJbtIj.authors: Ying Yuan, David Held, Jitendra Malik, Haozhi Qi
HHmIIJbtIj.abstract:
Teleoperation is widely used to collect high-quality demonstrations for robot
learning. However, teleoperating dexterous manipulation is challenging because
it requires coordinated control of motion and contact forces.
Operators specify motion naturally, but the subtle force adjustments used in
human manipulation are often unconscious and cannot be reproduced reliably
without directly feeling the robot's contacts. We introduce
force-modulated dexterity, a unified formulation that treats the
operator command as a nominal action and modifies its contact-relevant
components using force feedback. The formulation expresses actions in
coordinates defined by task geometry and contact structure, allowing different
feedback laws to share the same underlying principle. 
Across four contact-rich dexterous tasks, our method reduces excessive contact while largely preserving task progress. Policies trained on force-modulated actions also achieve more reliable autonomous execution than those trained on raw teleoperation commands.
These
results suggest that force modulation provides a practical interface between
motion commands and the contact responses required for contact-rich dexterous
manipulation. Videos are shown on our website https://yingyuan0414.github.io/fomo-dex/ .
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

Se8dGtohgn.title: Forward and Reverse Teleoperation for Dexterous Manipulation and Human Intervention
Se8dGtohgn.authors: Zhanpeng He, Joaquin Palacios, Zhangyu Wang, Chenhao Li, Katelyn Lee, Matei Ciocarlie, Karen Liu, Jiajun Wu
Se8dGtohgn.abstract: Teleoperated demonstrations are a primary source of data for robot manipulation, and teleoperated interventions are a primary mechanism for correcting policies at deployment. Yet most teleoperation systems close the loop through vision alone and are built around parallel-jaw grippers, limiting both what the robot can execute and what the operator can express through it. This is most damaging in shared autonomy, where the operator sees the scene only through occluded cameras and must take over a dexterous hand mid-task, often with an object already grasped. We present DITTO-X, a hand-agnostic dexterous teleoperation interface that renders joint-level force and fingertip contact events from sensing already on the robot hand, and drives three commercial dexterous hands (Sharpa, Wuji, and Inspire) without per-hand redesign. Because the exoskeleton is actuated, DITTO-X also supports reverse teleoperation, in which the robot back-drives the operator's fingers into its own configuration before control is transferred, so the human enters the loop already matched to the state they inherit. Our results show that DITTO-X improves demonstration quality and throughput over a commercial hand-tracking glove, both in regular data collection and in human intervention during policy deployment for contact-rich manipulation tasks.
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design
