Boad839qIT.title: FOVI-Dex: Foveation enables efficient perceptive learning of dexterous manipulation in simulation
Boad839qIT.authors: Nicholas Blauch, Nicolas Moënne-Loccoz, Jayjun Lee, Patrick Yin, Mohak Bhardwaj, Muhammad Asif Rana, Jessica Yin, Sam Mady, Karl Van Wyk, Nathan D. Ratliff, Jae-Hyun Jung, Ruth Rosenholtz, Ankur Handa, Gavriel State
Boad839qIT.abstract:
Advanced physics simulators and rendering engines promise to support the next-generation of robotic reinforcement learning (RL), yet training perceptive policies remains challenging due to the high-costs of rendering and perception.
We propose foveation as a solution to this challenge, coupling a novel foveated rendering solution with foveated perception, alongside a careful approach for ensuring transfer to foveated sampling of real uniform cameras. 
We train a language-conditioned visuotactile policy controlling a dexterous arm-hand to find and
grasp a target object in clutter (FOVI-Dex), via online RL without demonstrations. In comparison to a high-resolution fixed-camera control, FOVI-Dex uses 8.9$\times$ less vision tokens, supporting 6$\times$ more
parallel environments and 4.4$\times$ higher training throughput. At matched training budgets, this efficiency enables FOVI-Dex to outperform both the high-resolution baseline and a matched uniform active camera baseline, in both sim and real, with an outsized advantage in the real world.
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

flelaoK766.title: FROM HAND TO HAND: A Shared Wearable Interface and Functional Benchmark for Dexterous Manipulation
flelaoK766.authors: Qiandao Liu, Shengmiao Samuel Jin, Laura Ren, Tapomayukh Bhattacharjee
flelaoK766.abstract: Collecting dexterous manipulation demonstrations across robot hands often requires embodiment-specific sensing hardware or human-motion retargeting. We present \wudi, a Wearable, Unified Interface for Dexterous manipulation that separates a shared sensorized exoskeleton from interchangeable passive hands and linkages. Its 16 sensors remain on the exoskeleton, while a mechanism model reconstructs target-hand joint positions. Wrist images and poses enable robot-free demonstration collection. We also introduce OTHER, an eight-task benchmark inspired by occupational therapy for evaluating functional manipulation. We fabricate WUJI and LEAP configurations, assess usability with 12 participants using WUJI, and validate joint reconstruction on the LEAP thumb and index finger against motion capture. Separate policies trained from 70 demonstrations per task–hand pair achieve 15\%–80\% success across three tasks, with 20 rollouts per pair. For one expert operator using LEAP, WUDI provides higher collection throughput than vision-based teleoperation. These results support shared sensing across embodiments while exposing limitations in reachable motion, contact-force regulation, and passive-hand mechanics. Project Website: https://emprise.cs.cornell.edu/wudi/
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

h1CmpbO5Jp.title: From Teleoperation to Long-Horizon Dexterity: Evaluating Visuomotor Skills and Offline Proxies for Dexterous Manipulation
h1CmpbO5Jp.authors: Ammar Abbas, Aayush Jain, PRASHANTH RAMANATHPUR VISWANATH, Nivesh Gadipudi, Giulia Vilone, Jim Gibbons
h1CmpbO5Jp.abstract: Imitation learning policies are intended to make robotic manipulation robust to variations in object pose, appearance, and environment that challenge pre-programmed motion. However, real-world performance remains difficult to predict, as conventional optimization signals such as validation loss show no consistent relationship with robot success. To identify the design choices that govern real-world performance, 281 imitation-learning policies spanning seven policy families were evaluated in approximately 1,700 real-robot trials of RJ45 connector grasping and insertion using a five-fingered robotic hand. Controlled ablations showed that observation and action representations dominated conventional optimizer and sampling choices. For point-cloud policies, region-of-interest cropping, representation in the robot-base frame, and normalization within the point encoder each improved success by 70–100 percentage points. For the vision-languageaction policy, absolute rather than relative action prediction improved insertion success by up to 70 percentage points. Skill decomposition, multi-view perception, and recovery demonstrations were associated with the strongest-performing systems, although their effects were not independently isolated. Of 67 offline metrics evaluated, only five measures of predicted-motion smoothness and directness reliably correlated with insertion success (r = −0.70 to −0.80), and only within a single policy family. These results identify representation choices as key determinants of real-world imitation-learning performance and show that offline metrics can shortlist policies, but cannot replace real-robot evaluation.
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

KSkuMYhSkC.title: Getting Out and Getting Back: World and Behavior Grounding in Real2Sim2Real Co-Training
KSkuMYhSkC.authors: Samuel Liu, Youngsun Kim, Martin Matak, Gilwoo Lee
KSkuMYhSkC.abstract: Simulation can expand scarce real demonstrations, but how world fidelity and similarity to human behavior affect co-training remains unclear. We independently vary world grounding, which aligns simulation with the real system, and behavior grounding, which aligns simulated trajectories with human motion. On dynamic dexterous pick-and-sort, fully grounded co-training raises the success rate from 52% to 86% using 100 real demonstrations and 1500 simulated trajectories. Rollout observations suggest that policies follow real-derived behavior in demonstrated states and simulation-derived behavior elsewhere. We investigate these transitions through latent-space analysis and examine how both grounding axes affect task performance. We further show that both grounding axes remain consequential when co-training foundation models.
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

zqOJnIDacd.title: GOTT: Object-centric Dexterous Manipulation with a Reusable Cross-Embodiment Primitive
zqOJnIDacd.authors: Yulin Liu, Lai Wei, Yen-Jen Wang, Akash Sharma, Pieter Abbeel, Henrik I Christensen, Haozhi Qi
zqOJnIDacd.abstract: Foundation models and human data provide rich manipulation intent, but dexterous hands lack a reusable contact-acquisition primitive to execute it across tasks and embodiments. We propose GOTT, a reach-acquire-move framework built around a shared cross-embodiment primitive. Given an object trajectory and a reach specification, the robot approaches a task-relevant region, establishes stable contact through closed-loop control, and tracks the desired object motion. This decomposition supports motion specifications from diverse sources through a shared contact-acquisition and tracking backend. Simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate robust contact across diverse objects, arm-hand platforms, and seen and unseen hand morphologies, with higher end-to-end task success than open-loop grasp execution.
keywords: Dexterous Manipulation; Cross-Embodiment Learning; Object Trajectory Tracking
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

i8SFBOmrpb.title: IFG: Internet-Scale Guidance for Functional Grasping Generation
i8SFBOmrpb.authors: Muxin Liu, Mingxuan Li, Kenneth Shaw, Deepak Pathak
i8SFBOmrpb.abstract: Large Vision Models trained on internet-scale data have demonstrated strong capabilities in segmenting and semantically understanding object parts, even in cluttered scenes. However, while these models can direct a robot toward the general region of an object, they lack the geometric understanding required to precisely control dexterous robotic hands for 3D grasping. To overcome this, our key insight is to leverage simulation with a force-closure grasping generation pipeline that understands local geometries of the hand and object in the scene. Because this pipeline is slow and requires ground-truth observations, the generated dataset is distilled into a diffusion model that can operate on camera point clouds. By combining the global semantic understanding of internet-scale models with the geometric precision of a simulation-based locally-aware force-closure, IFG achieves high-performance semantic grasping without any manually collected training data. For visualizations, please visit our website at https://ifgrasping.github.io/
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

cVc4nwjbbs.title: Imperfect Human Data for Dexterous Manipulation: A Controlled Study of Co-Training and Mid-Training
cVc4nwjbbs.authors: Yiming Bao, Qianqian Wang, Heng Yang
cVc4nwjbbs.abstract: Egocentric human video offers scalable supervision for dexterous manipulation, but how should it enter policy training when human and robot differ in task, scene and embodiment? Primarily on the public $\pi_{0.5}$ checkpoint, with 25 demonstrations of a simulated dexterous folding task and up to 29× as many retargeted EgoDex frames, we compare co-training and mid-training against compute-matched robot-only controls with pre-specified tests and three to five seeds. Whether co-training hurts depends on batch composition, not on the human share: the default recipe leaves about one robot frame per batch and drops success from 25.2% to 11.3%, while sample-count mixing degrades at no share from 0.30 to 0.95 and gains +6.7 points at 0.5. Post-training recovers the diluted policy but adds no established benefit. Separating the stages helps most: human-only mid-training then robot post-training reaches 38.6% vs. 25.7% (five seeds), vanishes when the human actions are shuffled, and transfers +8.7 points to a held-out task. The pattern holds across bases: the drop recurs on Zeva-Ego under our loss-weighted recipe and is absent on GR00T N1.7 under sample-count mixing; a real 22-DoF hand shows the same ordering. The drop is dilution of robot supervision, not negative transfer.
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

lsLD91bzd6.title: INVAR: Randomization-Invariant Visual Representations for Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real
lsLD91bzd6.authors: Sunshine Jiang, Shuo Cheng, Francois Robert Hogan, Matthew Chang, Tingfan Wu, Jitendra Malik, Karen Liu, Nur Muhammad Mahi Shafiullah, Akash Sharma
lsLD91bzd6.abstract: Humans know to act consistently across real and simulated environments because they can abstract away visual appearance to what matters for the task. Can robots achieve similar visual invariance? We present INVAR, a visual representation for zero-shot sim-to-real transfer. While classic sim-to-real methods rely on task-specific domain randomization (DR) to train visual encoders and action policies, INVAR distills diverse simulation randomizations into a unified, invariant visual encoder that is self-supervised and scalable. It leverages self-distillation over an unlabeled corpus of simulated play data and robot rollouts without requiring real-world images during representation learning. A policy trained purely on nominal simulation data with a frozen INVAR encoder transfers zero-shot to the real world. INVAR nearly doubles the success rate of identical policies built on state-of-the-art pretrained encoders trained with standard DR, across both dexterous manipulation (0.61 vs. 0.30 mean success) and parallel-gripper manipulation (0.65 vs. 0.32). These results demonstrate that decoupling visual invariance into a task-agnostic encoder unlocks scalable, zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, similar to humans. Our website is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/w/site-5e8c2d7b6a14/.
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

W7WWrEOACa.title: KITE: Decoupling Kinematics and Interaction for Zero-Shot Cross-Embodiment Manipulation
W7WWrEOACa.authors: Qianxu Wang, Shengmiao Samuel Jin, Kuan Fang
W7WWrEOACa.abstract: Generalizing manipulation policies across robot embodiments remains difficult because standard policies tie the interactions needed for a task to the actions of a particular robot. We introduce Kinematic Interaction Transfer across Embodiments (KITE), which decouples manipulation into embodiment-agnostic interaction prediction and embodiment-specific kinematic decoding through a learned contact-based representation of interaction intent. The interaction policy learns from source demonstrations, while the kinematic decoder learns to realize these intents from synthetic data generated using each embodiment's kinematic model. This allows the same interaction policy to control structurally different robots without target-task demonstrations. Across four tasks and six robot embodiments in simulation, KITE achieves an average score of $86.4\%$ over $12$ task--target settings. Real-world deployment further demonstrates transfer from robot and human demonstrations to a Wuji hand.
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

MEBxU0ee6h.title: Learning Dexterous Action Representations from Human Videos
MEBxU0ee6h.authors: Hongyi Zhou, Maximilian Arnold, Mohamed Omran, Pietro Mazzaglia, Rudolf Lioutikov, Daniel Dijkman
MEBxU0ee6h.abstract:
We introduce DexVAE, a latent action representation pretrained on human motion that transfers dexterous motion priors from egocentric human videos to robot policies. 
Although dexterous robot hands promise human-like manipulation, learning to control them requires large and costly robot datasets. Human videos provide dexterous experience at scale, but differences in morphology and action spaces prevent their direct use for robot control. DexVAE bridges this gap by compressing temporally extended hand trajectories, expressed in a shared canonical representation, into compact latent action tokens. We transfer knowledge through a staged pipeline consisting of human-motion pretraining followed by human–robot co-training. We adapt a pretrained VLA model to generate actions in this latent space using flow matching. 
We evaluate our approach on six real-world manipulation tasks using a Unitree H1-2 humanoid with dexterous hands. With only 25 robot demonstrations per task, our method improves average task progression from $38.5\%$ to $49.1\%$, with the largest gain on high-dexterity tasks—from $35.7\%$ to $58.6\%$. Overall, DexVAE matches the raw-action baseline using $1/2$ the robot data and, on high-dexterity tasks, outperforms it using only $1/4$ the data.
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

a367wizddP.title: Learning Tactile-Aware Hierarchical Whole-Body Control Policies for Quadrupedal Loco-Manipulation
a367wizddP.authors: Pokuang Zhou, Le Mao, Xiyue Chen, Zhiyuan Zhang, Joseph Campbell, Yu She
a367wizddP.abstract: Touch provides direct information about contact state, force, slip, and interaction transitions, yet most mobile manipulation policies treat tactile signals only as passive observations rather than explicit control targets. We propose a hierarchical framework consisting of high-level and low-level policies, both conditioned on visual and tactile information. The high-level policy is responsible for planning and generating commands, while the low-level policy executes these commands through whole-body control. The high-level diffusion policy is trained from human demonstrations collected with a handheld visuotactile gripper, whereas the low-level policy is first trained through large-scale reinforcement learning in simulation and then post-trained with reward functions to jointly execute end-effector motion and tactile commands, enabling zero-shot transfer to the real robot. Our system demonstrates the capability to perform challenging long-horizon, complex, and contact-rich loco-manipulation tasks on a Unitree Go2 equipped with a D1 arm and a tactile gripper, including marker reorientation and insertion, valve tightening, delicate object manipulation, wrench-based bolt tightening, and cabinet-door opening. We further evaluate the generalization of the low-level policy across substantially different manipulator configurations, demonstrating the effectiveness and generalizability of our low-level architecture. Despite the nearly twofold difference in manipulator mass, the joint torques remain within approximately $-15$ to $27$ N$\cdot$m during real-world deployment. We also compare our method against an advanced world action approach. Across real-world trials, the full framework improves the average task success rate by 43.7\% over the average performance of all other baselines, demonstrating that tactile information can serve as a planned and controlled action-level representation for robust contact-rich loco-manipulation.
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

iqQJYouXxd.title: No Eyes, No Problem: Zero-Shot Blind Baoding Ball Manipulation with Binary Touch
iqQJYouXxd.authors: Ayush Deshmukh, Nalin Agarwal, Elle Miller, Sethu Vijayakumar
iqQJYouXxd.abstract: Humans manipulate objects within their hands through touch alone with remarkable ease, but for robots, sustained real-world manipulation without vision remains an open challenge. We study this problem through Baoding ball rotation on the Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite, using only proprioception and binary tactile feedback, and achieve zero-shot sim-to-real transfer through a sensor-aligned, coupling-aware embodiment in simulation, tactile calibration, and two novel episodic domain randomisations: slew-rate action limits and STuck-AT Taxels (STAT). On the physical hand, the policy completes 225 consecutive $180^\circ$ rotations (112.5 full rotations) at $\sim0.36$ rot/s in a single continuous trial, the strongest reported hardware result for Baoding ball manipulation in both rotation count and speed irrespective of the sensing modality used. By effectively bridging the sim-to-real gap, our framework sets a new benchmark for sustained tactile-driven dexterous manipulation on physical hardware.
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

xHETNKwCZu.title: OpenTac: An Open Ecosystem for Customizable, Scalable, and Transferable 3D Tactile Sensing
xHETNKwCZu.authors: Ariel Slepyan, Gregory D. Hager, Homanga Bharadhwaj, Anand Bhattad, Krishna Murthy Jatavallabhula, Nitish Thakor
xHETNKwCZu.abstract:
Dexterous manipulation depends on touch, yet tactile skins are usually built for one fixed geometry and often sense only normal pressure. We present OpenTac, a low-cost piezoresistive tactile skin and open design ecosystem that senses distributed normal and shear force and can be generated automatically for new robot surfaces. A structured elastomeric overlay converts tangential load into
differential pressure across neighboring taxels. OpenTac-CAD compiles a 2D outline, a 3D robot surface, or a text request into fabrication-ready flexible PCBs plus a machine-readable manifest shared by simulation, cross-sensor transfer, and adaptive acquisition tools. We fabricated 31 functional sensors; five representative designs compile in 0.7–2.6 s and cover 75–93% of their target regions. Deployments on four robot platforms demonstrate policy learning and contact-rich control: normal-and-shear policies achieve success rates (82% peg-in-hole and 62% plug insertion, versus at most 60% and 36% with normal-only sensing), and shear feedback maintains a bimanual grasp under impulsive loading in 16/20 trials versus 9/20 with a wrist force/torque sensor. Adaptive readout reaches 1286 partial frames/s on a 1024-taxel skin, 19.2× faster than full raster scanning. Anonymous website: https://anonymous.4open.science/w/opentac-workshop-site-4B13/.
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

GwAf1uEbaU.title: orca: A Platform for Open-Source Dexterity Research
GwAf1uEbaU.authors: Francesco Capuano, Maximilian Eberlein, Fabrice Bourquin, Clemens Claudio Christoph
GwAf1uEbaU.abstract:
Dexterous-hand research typically depends on bespoke software coupling robot hands, simulators, tracking devices, and robot learning pipelines. 
Such fragmentation hinders progress and increases the cost of reproducing and extending results in the field.
In this work, we present \orca, a fully open-source software stack making dexterous manipulation reproducible, and accessible across both simulation and real world hardware.
We provide interoperable packages for (1) real-world low-level control, (2) simulation assets and tasks, (3) full-arm integration, as well as (4) teleoperation and (5) retargeting from consumer devices.
\orca~directly interfaces with \lerobot, enabling researchers to collect teleoperated demonstrations, train a policy, and deploy it on simulated or real-world robot hands using a tested, shared platform.
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

rjBEjJS1Iz.title: PanoTac: A Dense Three-Axis Tactile Sensor for Robust Touch-Centric Manipulation
rjBEjJS1Iz.authors: Binglin Andre Wang, Xiaole Alex Jiang, Zicheng Teng, Xinqi Liu, Yunzhu Li, Lerrel Pinto, Zichen Jeff Cui, Binghao Huang
rjBEjJS1Iz.abstract:
Humans use vision and touch to guide everyday manipulation. When scooping grains, contact with the handle reveals the spoon's orientation, while resistance felt through the grasp guides motion. These cues reflect contact geometry and shear forces during interaction. To bring these sensing capabilities to robots, we present PanoTac, a low-cost, compliant tactile fingertip designed for dense three-axis tactile sensing. Each finger provides a $12 \times 32$ taxel grid, with each taxel representing three components: normal ($z$) and shear ($x$, $y$). 
Sensor characterization demonstrates spatially consistent and temporally repeatable responses across all three axes.
Sensor characterization quantifies response repeatability across loading cycles and sensor instances, as well as variation across contact locations.
We integrate PanoTac into a robotic system with a visuo-tactile learning pipeline. Across test tube preparation, grain scooping, and salt pouring, the resulting policies outperform vision-only baselines by an average of 43.3 percentage points. Ablations show that removing either spatial contact information or load feedback reduces overall performance across the task suite. Our project page is available at
https://panotac.github.io.
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

udcKZU9hXr.title: Pitch, Blur and Noise: Cramér-Rao Design Rules for Tactile Taxel Arrays
udcKZU9hXr.abstract: How densely should a dexterous hand be covered in taxels, and how soft should the skin over them be? We answer the question that is answerable exactly: for a point contact of unknown location and force read through a taxel array with an elastomer point-spread function and additive noise, what is the best achievable localisation precision? Computing the Fisher information exactly for Gaussian and compact response kernels over pitch, blur width, signal-to-noise ratio and array size, we find that the localisation bound obeys a single formula, sigma_x = 0.798 d/SNR per axis, whenever the pitch d is at most about 1.5 blur widths, independent of the blur itself; that this makes the achievable super-resolution factor 1.25 x SNR regardless of taxel density; that precision collapses (1.22x worse at two blur widths, 152.14x at four) once responses stop overlapping; and that compact response kernels produce blind spots centred on the taxels themselves, covering 21% of the surface when the contact radius equals the pitch. For a fixed number of taxels on a fixed patch, blur should be 0.8-1.0 pitches for Gaussian skins and at least 2.0 pitches for compact ones. A maximum-likelihood estimator attains the bound within 0.93-1.09x in 24 Monte Carlo cases. The rules are closed-form, hardware-agnostic, and say that beyond the overlap threshold, taxel count buys precision only linearly.
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

cjL7reYAhE.title: Pre-training Visual Dexterity in Simulation
cjL7reYAhE.authors: Sarthak Kamat, Adam Rashid, Satvik Sharma, Aseem Doriwala, Chelsea Finn, Phillip Isola, Karen Liu
cjL7reYAhE.abstract: Large-scale pre-training has made robot policy fine-tuning increasingly data-efficient, but this progress has largely been driven by datasets and embodiments built around simple parallel-jaw grippers. Dexterous, multi-fingered hands remain comparatively data-starved because real teleoperation is costly to scale, while human hand video is off-embodiment and requires lossy pose estimation and retargeting. We introduce Simulation Pre-training for Dexterity (SPD), a pre-training framework for dexterous manipulation that uses data entirely collected in simulation. In SPD, humans manipulate virtual objects inside a VR headset, enabling on-embodiment trajectories and robot-free collection. With the help of five operators, we collect 75 hours of multi-task dexterous manipulation over one week, and use it to pre-train a causal transformer on a sequence modeling objective. We study the benefits of simulation pre-training on real-world tasks by fine-tuning on 1-2 hours of physical demonstrations on a 56-DoF bimanual dexterous setup. We find that our approach outperforms training behavior cloning policies from scratch, showing that simulation teleoperation is a viable pre-training source for real-world dexterous manipulation. We perform ablation studies, measuring the benefits of history conditioning and short action chunks for reactive control.
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

RT9PjZI98I.title: ReForce: Learning Force-aware Retargeting for Dexterous Manipulation
RT9PjZI98I.authors: Yuhang Wu, Lingqi Zeng, Changwei Jing, Geng Chen, Jianglong Ye, Xiaolong Wang
RT9PjZI98I.abstract: Human demonstrations offer a scalable data source for dexterous manipulation, but transferring them to robot actions remains challenging due to the embodiment gap. Today's retargeting is mostly kinematic, yet manipulation is decided by force, which governs how the hand interacts with the object and how the object moves. In this paper, we present ReForce, a Force-aware Retargeting method that turns human motion and forces into robot actions that reproduce the intended contact. ReForce predicts a residual on the kinematically retargeted action to reach the desired force, using a general force tracker trained on large-scale simulation interactions. It supports both online force-aware teleoperation and offline data translation. In simulation and on real hardware, ReForce achieves lower force-tracking error and stronger multi-finger contact engagement on contact-rich tasks such as paper-cup grasping and tongs manipulation.
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

aPbT1KmiK7.title: Rotation-Aware Point-Cloud Embeddings for Vision-Based In-Hand Reorientation
aPbT1KmiK7.abstract: Point-cloud goals provide a direct way to specify a reorientation task: instead of defining an object-specific pose frame or estimating 6D pose at test time, the policy is given the desired 3D geometry of the object. However, extracting the change in object pose between two raw point clouds is not straightforward. Since the points are unordered and independently sampled, directly relating the observations typically requires solving for correspondences or registration. Generic pretrained point-cloud feature extractors do not resolve this issue either, as their embeddings are not organized to directly expose the underlying rotation between observations. This lets a model-free PPO policy learn in-hand reorientation from current and goal point-cloud embeddings without explicit pose, correspondences, dense flow, or teacher-action supervision, while matching privileged-state and distillation-based baselines.
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

8aXwkwmlaB.title: Scan-to-Hand: Automated Design of Personalized 20-DoF Tendon-Driven Hands
8aXwkwmlaB.authors: Ruochen Hou, Feng Xu, Dennis Hong
8aXwkwmlaB.abstract: Transferring human demonstrations to dexterous robots requires accommodating differences in finger proportions, joint geometry, and contact surfaces. We introduce Scan-to-Hand, an automated design pipeline that personalizes robotic hand morphology from an individual’s 3D hand scan, bringing hardware adaptation into the demonstration-transfer problem. The pipeline combines parametric hand-model fitting and engineering adjustments to joint frames with reusable tendon-driven mechanisms and scan-shaped links. The generated tendon-driven hand has 20 degrees of freedom, with four per finger, including independent actuation of the distal joints. Feature-preserving geometry construction maintains tendon passages, knot access, and assembly interfaces while adding motion clearance. Constrained optimization generates smooth palm routes subject to wall-thickness, channel-separation, and bend-radius requirements. We have fabricated and assembled a first personalized prototype and demonstrate its motion, alongside geometric checks of the generated routing. Ongoing imitation-learning experiments use a crossed demonstrator-by-robot comparison to distinguish the effects of robot morphology itself from the advantage of matching a robot hand to its demonstrator. Scan-to-Hand automates the design of personalized robotic hands and supports their fabrication to study how human–robot morphology matching affects learning from human demonstrations.
keywords: Dexterous robotic hands; Automated robot design; Morphology personalization; Tendon-driven actuation; Human demonstration transfer
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

1wu17WAH9f.title: Support-Constrained RL Enables Real-World Policy Improvement without Additional Real-World Experience
1wu17WAH9f.authors: Raymond Yu, William Huey, Mustafa Mukadam, Anusha Nagabandi, Abhishek Gupta
1wu17WAH9f.abstract: Robots trained on real world data tend to be imprecise, slow, and brittle to perturbations. Improving these policies with reinforcement learning (RL) is an appealing alternative, but this process often requires expensive training in the real world. Performing policy improvement in simulation instead provides a far cheaper alternative, but unconstrained RL in simulation can exploit contact and dynamics mismatches, resulting in unsafe behaviors that do not transfer to hardware. Common forms of regularization can furthermore limit improvement by overconstraining to an imperfect behavior prior.  In this work, we propose Support-Constrained Off-Domain REinforcement (\texttt{SCORE}), a real-to-sim-to-real framework that constrains RL in simulation to stay near the \textit{support} of a generative policy pretrained on real data. We instantiate this constraint through \textit{flow steering}, restricting \texttt{SCORE} to explore through modes of the base policy, which ensures transferable behaviors while maximizing policy improvement. Improving a policy with \texttt{SCORE} requires minimal effort: it learns from sparse rewards, avoids distillation, and leaves the base policy untouched. Across eight real-world dexterous multi-fingered robotic manipulation tasks, \texttt{SCORE} improves average success rate from $38.6\%$ to $89.3\%$, compared to $59.8\%$ for the best baseline, and completes tasks $36.7\%$ faster than the base policy. Ultimately, through extensive experiments and ablations, we show that simulation can substantially improve real-world manipulation policies when policy optimization is appropriately constrained, introducing a new paradigm for real-to-sim-to-real policy improvement. Videos are available at https://score-anon.github.io.
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

RiwnwU3act.title: TacSushi: Tactile-Grounded World–Action Modeling for Dexterous Food Manipulation
RiwnwU3act.authors: Haodi Hu, Kaen Kogashi, Toshiaki Koike-Akino
RiwnwU3act.abstract:
Dexterous food manipulation requires control under deformation, occlusion,
and uncertain contact. We present TacSushi, a Cosmos3-based policy that gives current
fingertip touch a feature-wise gated path to the deployed action head while
using logged future visual, tactile, progress, and contact outcomes only as
training supervision. Failed demonstrations retain consequence targets, but
their actions are masked from imitation. Across 600 real-robot rollouts, the
full model reaches 68.3\% average success on three in-distribution tasks
and 37.5\% on two held-out ingredients under a per-rollout human--VLM
visual-quality rule. Matched ablations support complementary
benefits from gated tactile fusion and training-only consequence prediction,
while also revealing limited ingredient-level transfer and open questions
about which predicted outcome matters most.
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

tiLxS2RC4L.title: TACTIC: Diagnosing Tactile Encoder and Fusion Choices for Contact-Rich Robot Manipulation
tiLxS2RC4L.authors: Seongjin Bien, Débora Oliveira Makowski, Carlo Kneissl, Pankhuri Vanjani, Reihaneh Mirjalili, Rudolf Lioutikov, Gitta Kutyniok, Florian Walter, Wolfram Burgard
tiLxS2RC4L.abstract: Tactile sensing can reveal contact information that cameras alone miss, yet it remains unclear how tactile encoder and multimodal fusion choices affect real robot policies across tasks. We present TACTIC, a controlled real-world comparison of five tactile encoders and five fusion strategies with an Action Chunking Transformer across four contact-rich manipulation tasks. The study comprises 2,180 rollouts and tracks progress through task stages, exposing failures hidden by aggregate success rates. No encoder--fusion pair performs best across all tasks: simple concatenation is competitive, while contrastive fusion can help on some tasks and hurt on others. The results suggest that tactile representations and conditioning should be evaluated against task-specific contact demands, with stage-level outcomes used to diagnose where policies fail.
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

9FDrtuUXoN.title: Tactile Sensors Are an Effective Substitute for Wrist Cameras in Contact-Rich or Occluded Manipulation
9FDrtuUXoN.authors: Aijia Yang, Arsh Tangri, Sergey Zakharov, Krishna Murthy Jatavallabhula
9FDrtuUXoN.abstract: Learned manipulation policies often rely on wrist-mounted cameras for close-range visual feedback that complements external views of the workspace. However, contact-rich manipulation requires establishing and maintaining contacts that can remain hidden even from wrist cameras. Tactile sensors mounted on fingers can reliably and directly measure contact, without needing visual access. In this work, we show that this feedback enables policies to recover the performance advantage of wrist cameras using scene and egocentric vision together with touch. Our approach incorporates two low-cost tactile arrays into a visuotactile ACT policy, without wrist images during training or deployment. We evaluate six real-world task families spanning placement, insertion, occluded retrieval, and sustained-contact tool use. On three contact-rich tasks, we independently vary wrist-camera and tactile availability while keeping the demonstrations, policy architecture, and optimization settings fixed. Adding wrist cameras improves success by 18.3-28.3 percentage points over vision without wrist images. Adding tactile sensing instead improves success by 31.7-60.0 percentage points and yields higher observed success than vision-only policies with wrist cameras on all three tasks, with significant advantages on two under Holm-corrected tests. These results support finger-mounted tactile sensing as an effective alternative to wrist cameras in the evaluated contact-rich settings.
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

fmz1B7p1oE.title: Touch Presence Is Not Touch Grounding: Testing Tactile Correspondence in VLM Grasp Understanding
fmz1B7p1oE.abstract: Adding touch can change a vision–language model's (VLM's) answer without showing that the model uses the tactile observation that belongs to the scene. We test four frozen VLMs on OpenTouch-derived grasp questions, using a 28-clip diagnostic set and a separately frozen 40-clip extension from the same four recordings. Holding RGB and the question fixed, we supply either matched touch or touch from eight other interactions (donors). Adding touch changes 9.8–18.1% of answers, but duplicating the RGB image changes 9.3–14.2%. Replacing matched touch with a donor changes answers about as often as swapping one donor for another (paired differences of −1.8 to +0.5 percentage points; all 95% intervals include zero), and answer changes show no clear association with global differences between the pressure maps. Accuracy against coarse taxonomy labels, whose reliability is limited, is consistent with these results. The tested models do not consistently treat the correct touch differently from touch drawn from other interactions. We recommend correspondence, duplicate-input, and repeatability controls whenever tactile grounding is claimed.
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

243ZLWJrpS.title: Video2Sim2Real: Full-Stack Self-Sufficient Dexterous Skill Acquisition from a Single Human Video
243ZLWJrpS.authors: Yunhai Han, Jianuo Qiu, Linhao Bai, Ziyu Xiao, Zihang Zeng, Yangcen Liu, Zhaodong Yang, Shalin Jain, Wenrui Ma, Jiaqi Fu, Yuqian Zheng, Manisha Natarajan, Muhammad Zubair Irshad, Kenneth Shaw, Matthew Craig Gombolay, Zsolt Kira, Harish Ravichandar
243ZLWJrpS.abstract: Learning dexterous manipulation from a single human video requires bridging noisy motion estimates and embodiment differences. We introduce Video2Sim2Real, a self-sufficient framework that converts an RGB-D demonstration into a deployable robot skill without robot demonstrations or manual trajectory authoring. Our object-centric refinement identifies task-defining events from object motion, optimizes robot configurations in a reconstructed digital twin, and uses them to anchor the retargeted trajectory. Our factorized sim-to-real adaptation separates global perception errors from local contact-dynamics errors: a distilled geometry policy recalibrates keyframe poses before execution, while residual reinforcement learning adapts finger actions online. Across seven rigid-object tabletop tasks, refinement achieves 91.4% average simulated success, and the complete system succeeds in 67/70 real-world trials under local object-pose perturbations. Ablations support the complementary roles of geometry and contact adaptation, particularly for grasping. Rollout videos and additional materials are available on our anonymous project website: https://video2sim2real.github.io.
workshops: 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design

AzKGwPLsOl.title: VTAP Gripper: Synergizing Fingertip Sensing and a Visuo-Tactile Active Palm for Dexterous In-Hand Manipulation
AzKGwPLsOl.abstract: This paper presents a tactile-reactive gripper that integrates a Visuo-Tactile Active Palm (VTAP) and compliant, reconfigurable fingers equipped with tactile array sensors. The design exploits structured finger-palm synergy and multi-modal perception to achieve both robust grasping and fine manipulation. The actuated bi-modal palm seamlessly combines long-range visual localization with contact-rich tactile feedback, substantially extending the system's manipulation capability. To bridge the embodiment gap between human hand motion and the heterogeneous three-finger structure, we further propose a staged, gesture-conditioned retargeting framework for dexterous teleoperation. Extensive experiments validate the system across a range of challenging tasks: reactive grasping of YCB and fragile objects, in-hand syringe reorientation and plunger actuation, singulation of clustered objects down to 3 mm in diameter, and vision-tactile peg-in-hole insertion. Results demonstrate that high manipulation performance can be achieved through coordinated finger-palm interaction and multi-modal sensing, without resorting to high degrees of freedom anthropomorphic designs. The VTAP gripper and its retargeting framework offer a practical reference architecture for dexterous gripper design, manipulation, and contact-rich data collection in support of learning-based approaches. A full version of this work was accepted for publication at the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026).

0PFEpskiVZ.title: Whole-Body Dexterity
0PFEpskiVZ.authors: Conor Mc Gartoll, Pranay Thangeda, Carolina Higuera, An Thanh Dang, Nima Fazeli, Manikantan Nambi, Arjun Gupta, Mustafa Mukadam
0PFEpskiVZ.abstract: Current humanoid dexterous manipulation remains largely confined to end-effectors and simple grasps, falling short of humans’ ability to engage the entire body by bracing and sliding bulky objects against the arms and torso. We introduce Whole-Body Dexterity (WBD), a general framework that uses the robot's body and appendages as contact surfaces to grasp and manipulate objects. Our sim-to-real pipeline generates a dataset of feasible whole-body grasps, trains reinforcement-learning experts on an any-to-any repositioning objective, and distills them into a single policy that uses proprioception and object geometry. The distilled controller transfers zero-shot to a real Unitree G1, completing 90% of trials across basketball and box repositioning and a long-horizon shelf task, compared with 18% for direct retargeting and 4% for a generalist whole-body controller. Website: https://wholebodydex.com.
